knowledge_statements.statement_title: Function-Evaluation Economy of Simultaneous Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison with coordinate-wise centered finite differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a simultaneous perturbation vector $h\in\mathbb{R}^N$, evaluate the objective at the two points $x+h$ and $x-h$. These two values are reused to construct estimates for all $N$ gradient components. Coordinate-wise centered finite differences instead evaluate $x+h_i e_i$ and $x-h_i e_i$ for every $i$ and therefore require $2N$ evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous perturbation changes all coordinates together and uses the same two objective evaluations to estimate every gradient component. The evaluation count is two regardless of dimension, compared with two evaluations per coordinate for ordinary centered differences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \#\operatorname{eval}_{\mathrm{simultaneous}}=2,\qquad \#\operatorname{eval}_{\mathrm{coordinate\ centered}}=2N.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simulation Optimization Through Noisy Output Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the simulation-based objective-access model; decision variables may be discrete, continuous, or mixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simulation-optimization problem has the form \(\min_{x\in\Theta} f(x)\), where \(\Theta\) is the feasible region and \(x\) may be discrete, continuous, or mixed. The value \(f(x)\) is not computed exactly; instead, simulation-replication outputs are observed and may be represented by a random variable \(Y(x,\xi)\), where \(\xi\) denotes simulation randomness, and these observations are used to estimate objective performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation optimization minimizes an objective over a feasible region when objective values are not directly available. Performance is instead estimated from random simulation outputs, with discrete, continuous, or mixed decisions allowed.
assumptions_latex: Y(x,\xi)\text{ is observed through stochastic or Monte Carlo simulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in\Theta}f(x)\text{ is accessed through random simulation outputs }Y(x,\xi).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Optimization via Simulation Problem and Estimation Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite feasible-set models defining discrete optimization via simulation, together with assumptions imposed by the described solution methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A discrete optimization-via-simulation problem minimizes an expected simulation response over \(\Theta\), where either \(\Theta=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) indexes possibly unordered categorical alternatives, or \(\Theta=\Phi\cap\mathbb{Z}^d\) for a compact convex set \(\Phi\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), possibly defined by deterministic constraints. In either case, \(\Theta\) is finite. The described solution methods assume \(\operatorname{Var}[Y(\mathbf{x})]<\infty\) for every \(\mathbf{x}\in\Theta\) and an estimator \(\widehat g(\mathbf{x})\) that converges almost surely to \(g(\mathbf{x})\) as the simulation effort allocated to \(\mathbf{x}\) increases. A sample-mean estimator is denoted \(\bar Y(\mathbf{x})\). I.i.d. replications are often available but are not assumed universally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete optimization via simulation uses either finitely many possibly unordered alternatives or the integer points of a compact convex region, hence has finitely many feasible solutions. The methods described in the source assume finite response variance and a strongly consistent objective estimator at every feasible decision. Sample means are denoted by bar Y, while i.i.d. replications are common but not universal.
assumptions_latex: \Phi\subset\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is compact and convex in the integer-vector case}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\Theta|<\infty,\quad\text{and the problem is a discrete optimization-via-simulation problem.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discounted multiarmed bandit and interval-estimation policy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-arm cumulative-reward learning with Gaussian beliefs and an uncertainty-weighted index example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{1,\ldots,M\}\) be arms with unknown reward distributions, let \(S^n=((\mu_x^n,\sigma_x^{2,n}))_{x\in\mathcal X}\) be the Gaussian belief state after \(n\) trials, and let \(X^\pi(S^n)\) select the next arm. An infinite-horizon discounted bandit solves \(\max_\pi\mathbb E\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\gamma^n W_{X^\pi(S^n)}^{n+1}\) for \(\gamma<1\); finite-horizon and undiscounted variants are also possible. The interval-estimation policy selects \(X^{IE,n}(S^n\mid\theta^{IE})\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\{\mu_x^n+\theta^{IE}\bar\sigma_x^{2,n}\}\), where \(\bar\sigma_x^{2,n}=\sigma_x^{2,n}/N_x^n\). At \(\theta^{IE}=0\) it is purely exploitative, while increasing \(\theta^{IE}\) assigns more weight to uncertainty and hence exploration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiarmed bandit repeatedly chooses among finitely many arms with unknown reward distributions and seeks a policy maximizing cumulative reward. Under Gaussian beliefs, an interval-estimation index adds an uncertainty bonus to the estimated mean; zero bonus gives pure exploitation, while a larger bonus encourages exploration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_\pi\mathbb E\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\gamma^n W_{X^\pi(S^n)}^{n+1},\qquad X^{IE,n}\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}(\mu_x^n+\theta^{IE}\bar\sigma_x^{2,n})

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimization via Simulation Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-value optimization when the objective response distribution is unknown but realizations are observable through stochastic simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization-via-simulation problem has the form \(\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta} g(\mathbf{x})\), where \(g(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)]\), \(\xi\) represents simulation randomness, the distribution of \(Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)\) as a function of \(\mathbf{x}\) is unknown, and realizations of \(Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)\) can be observed through simulation. A maximization problem can be converted to an equivalent minimization problem by negating the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimization-via-simulation problem minimizes an expected simulation response over a feasible set. Its response distribution is unknown as a function of the decision, but response realizations can be observed through simulation. Maximization can be converted to minimization by negating the objective.
assumptions_latex: \text{The distribution of }Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)\text{ is unknown as a function of }\mathbf{x}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta}g(\mathbf{x}),\quad\text{with maximization reducible to minimization by objective negation.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous noisy black-box problem is an optimization problem \[\inf_{x\in X} f(x),\qquad f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)],\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) contains continuously variable decisions and the analytic form or derivatives of \(f\) are unavailable. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong law for a uniformly random multidimensional knapsack optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This strengthens the corresponding normalized limit to almost-sure convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the \(n+mn\) coefficients of the random knapsack problem are mutually independent and uniformly distributed on \((0,1)\). For fixed \(m\), let \(\alpha_{mn}=(m+1)\left(n/(m+2)!\right)^{1/(m+1)}\). Then \(\mathbb{P}\!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\mu_{mn}/\alpha_{mn}=1\right)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under independent uniform (0,1) coefficients and fixed m, the normalized random-knapsack optimum mu_mn/alpha_mn converges to 1 almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \text{The }n+mn\text{ problem coefficients are mutually independent and }\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb{P}\!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\mu_{mn}}{\alpha_{mn}}=1\right)=1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distribution-dependent limit for a one-dimensional random knapsack optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two primed quantities are retained as identically defined indicators because that is what the extraction states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\gamma_j,\xi_j)\), \(j=1,\ldots,n\), be i.i.d., with \(0<\gamma_j<1\), \(\xi_j>0\), and with the conditional distribution of \(\gamma_j\) given \(\xi_j\) continuous. For \(t>0\), define \(\xi'_j=\mathbf{1}\{\gamma_j>t\xi_j\}\), \(\gamma'_j=\mathbf{1}\{\gamma_j>t\xi_j\}\), \(F(t)=\mathbb{E}[\xi'_j]\), and \(G(t)=\mathbb{E}[\gamma'_j]\). Then the optimum \(\mu_{1n}\) satisfies \(\mu_{1n}/\bigl(nG(F^{-1}(K/n))\bigr)\Rightarrow1\) as \(n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For iid positive knapsack data with gamma between zero and one and a continuous conditional law of gamma given xi, define F and G from the extracted threshold indicators. The optimum mu_1n, normalized by n times G evaluated at F inverse of K/n, converges to 1 in the mode denoted by the extract's double arrow.
assumptions_latex: (\gamma_j,\xi_j),\ j=1,\ldots,n,\text{ are independent and identically distributed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\mu_{1n}}{nG\!\left(F^{-1}(K/n)\right)}\Rightarrow1\quad\text{as }n\to\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible threshold selection bounds the random knapsack optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A threshold-defined selection satisfying every resource constraint has objective value at least the optimum \(\mu_{mn}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t_1,\ldots,t_m>0\) and, for \(j=1,\ldots,n\), set \(\eta_j=1\) if \(\gamma_j\geq\sum_{i=1}^m t_i\xi_{ij}\), and \(\eta_j=0\) otherwise. If \(\sum_{j=1}^n\xi_{ij}\eta_j\geq1\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\), then \(\sum_{j=1}^n\gamma_j\eta_j\geq\mu_{mn}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose items whose gamma coefficient is at least the positive weighted sum of their xi coefficients. If that selection satisfies all m covering constraints, its total gamma value is at least the knapsack optimum mu_mn.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{j=1}^n\gamma_j\eta_j\geq\mu_{mn}

children.title: Combinatorial Noisy Black-Box Problems
children.top_down_role: Noisy optimization over structured configurations, subsets, sequences, or graph-based decisions.

assumptions_latex: The feasible objects form a family \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq 2^E\) or an equivalent finite combinatorial class.
Each \(C\in\mathcal{C}\) has an integrable simulated response \(Y(C,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is \(\inf_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{E}[Y(C,\xi)]\), with feasibility and neighborhood structure determined by combinatorial constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noisy optimization whose feasible decisions are structured combinatorial objects.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A combinatorial noisy black-box problem is \[\inf_{C\in\mathcal{C}} f(C),\qquad f(C)=\mathbb{E}[Y(C,\xi)],\] where \(\mathcal{C}\) is a family of subsets, permutations, graphs, schedules, paths, or other finitely encoded objects subject to combinatorial feasibility constraints. Simulation at \(C\in\mathcal{C}\) returns a noisy response, while the objective is analytically unavailable. The encoding-induced adjacency or exchange operations provide structure beyond mere enumeration of isolated alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize noisy expected performance over structured objects such as subsets, paths, permutations, schedules, or graphs subject to combinatorial feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Noisy Black-Box Problems

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general discrete-optimization section does not establish the proposed defining distinction based on encoding-induced adjacency or exchange operations. A source specifically supporting this combinatorial noisy-black-box formulation is required.

children.title: Discrete-to-Combinatorial Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions determining whether decisions are treated as isolated points or composed objects.

assumptions_latex: A feasible family \(D\) has a finite encoding \(e:D\to\{0,1\}^m\) or \(e:D\to\mathbb{Z}^m\).
A neighborhood relation \(N(x)\subseteq D\) is available to the optimization method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is combinatorial relative to \((e,N)\) when feasibility and admissible moves exploit relations among encoded components; otherwise it is only pointwise discrete.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary depends on whether an algorithm uses relational structure in the decision encoding.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be discrete. Relative to an encoding \(e\) and neighborhood map \(N\), the problem crosses from pointwise discrete to combinatorial when feasible decisions are composed of finitely encoded components and feasibility or admissible moves are expressed through relations among those components. Formally, membership in \(D\) or membership of \(y\) in \(N(x)\) must depend on joint restrictions on coordinates of \(e(x)\), rather than solely on the identity of \(x\). This boundary is representation-relative: the same finite set can be treated as unstructured alternatives or as structured objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete problem is combinatorial when its encoding exposes component relations that determine feasibility or admissible moves; the distinction depends on representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-to-Combinatorial Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed necessary boundary—joint coordinate restrictions in a selected encoding—is representation-dependent and is not a generally established criterion separating discrete from combinatorial optimization. The cited locator is insufficient to validate this exact condition.

assumptions_latex: For each feasible decision, the simulator returns an integrable response \(Y(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is \(\inf_{x\in X}\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)]\) over coupled variable types.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-variable noisy black-box problem is \[\inf_{x\in X} f(x),\qquad f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)],\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_c}\times\mathbb{Z}^{d_i}\times\mathcal{K}\) couples continuous coordinates, integer coordinates, and categorical or conditional choices from \(\mathcal{K}\). children.title: Structured Simulator Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization using simulator-exposed paths, events, states, likelihoods, derivatives, or random-input transformations.

children.title: Sample-Path-Exposing Simulators
children.top_down_role: Simulators exposing realized trajectories for reuse, differentiation, or pathwise optimization.

assumptions_latex: Randomness is represented by \(\xi\) on a probability space, and \(x\in X\) is the simulator input.
The exposed trajectory \(Z_{0:T}(x,\xi)\) determines the performance \(Y(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A query returns \((Z_{0:T}(x,\xi),Y(x,\xi))\), not merely the scalar response.

notation.meaning: exposed simulated trajectory through horizon T

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simulator interface exposing the realized state path underlying each performance observation.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.5 The black-box and the white-box approach p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sample-path-exposing simulator is a mapping \[S(x,\xi)=\bigl(Z_{0:T}(x,\xi),Y(x,\xi)\bigr),\qquad Y(x,\xi)=H\bigl(x,Z_{0:T}(x,\xi)\bigr),\] that returns the realized trajectory \(Z_{0:T}\) together with, or instead of, its aggregate performance. Consequently, evaluations sharing the same \(\xi\) can reuse a realized path when well-defined, and pathwise derivatives may be computed whenever \(x\mapsto H(x,Z_{0:T}(x,\xi))\) is differentiable almost surely and interchange with expectation is justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulator reveals the realized trajectory generating each response, enabling path reuse or pathwise differentiation when the required regularity holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Path-Exposing Simulators

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.5 The black-box and the white-box approach p. 18

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The black-box/white-box locator does not clearly support the asserted trajectory-returning interface or the consequences concerning path reuse and pathwise differentiation. Reusing a realized path across decisions also requires additional coupling assumptions because the trajectory depends on the decision.

children.title: Likelihood-Exposing Simulators
children.top_down_role: Simulators whose path or transition laws support likelihood-based estimation.

assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in X\), the simulator law \(P_x\) is dominated by a common measure \(\mu\).
The density \(p_x=dP_x/d\mu\) is differentiable and its score is integrable where used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The simulator exposes \(p_x(Z)\) or \(\nabla_x\log p_x(Z)\), permitting likelihood-ratio identities under valid differentiation-expectation interchange.

notation.meaning: law of the simulated path or output under x
density of P_x with respect to mu

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominated simulator laws with evaluable likelihoods or scores for realized outputs or paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A likelihood-exposing simulator generates \(Z\sim P_x\) and additionally makes evaluable the density \(p_x(Z)\), a likelihood ratio \(p_{x'}(Z)/p_x(Z)\), or the score \(s_x(Z)=\nabla_x\log p_x(Z)\). If \(h(Z)\) is integrable and differentiation under the integral is valid, then the exposed score supports \[\nabla_x\mathbb{E}_{P_x}[h(Z)]=\mathbb{E}_{P_x}\bigl[h(Z)s_x(Z)\bigr].\] Exposure of sampled outputs alone does not satisfy this definition; the relevant likelihood quantity must also be computable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulator reveals an evaluable likelihood, likelihood ratio, or score for each realized path, supporting likelihood-ratio estimation under regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood-Exposing Simulators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied for the exact likelihood-exposing interface or its score identity. The mathematical version therefore cannot be promoted at candidate-review level without an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Event-Exposing Simulators

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Exposing Simulators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-event simulator interface revealing clocks, event identities, ordering, innovations, and state updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decision \(x\in X\), an event-exposing simulator represents a path by an ordered marked-event sequence \[\bigl(T_n,K_n,Z_{n-1},Z_n\bigr)_{n\geq 1},\qquad Z_n=\Phi(Z_{n-1},K_n,U_n;x),\] where \(T_n\) is the time of event \(n\), \(K_n\) is its event type, \(U_n\) is the random innovation used at that event, and \(\Phi\) is the state-transition map. The interface reveals event times, event order, event types, and pre- and post-event states, so performance may be reconstructed from the event sequence rather than supplied only as an aggregate output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a chosen decision, the simulator exposes the ordered event times, event types, random event inputs, and associated state transitions from which performance can be reconstructed.
assumptions_latex: The decision belongs to a specified set \(x\in X\).
The simulation state changes at ordered event times \(0=T_0<T_1<T_2<\cdots\).
Each event has a type \(K_n\), a random innovation \(U_n\), and a state update determined by \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exposed event record contains \(\bigl(T_n,K_n,Z_{n-1},Z_n\bigr)\) for each simulated event \(n\geq1\).

children.title: Terminating-Simulation Performance
children.top_down_role: Performance derived from naturally terminating replications.

assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in X\), a replication has an almost surely finite stopping time \(\tau(x)\).
The terminal replication performance \(Y(x)\) is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Performance is \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x)]\) and independent replications yield an unbiased sample-mean estimator.

notation.meaning: natural termination time of a replication

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected performance from complete, naturally terminating, independent simulation replications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Terminating-simulation performance is defined from a replication ending at an almost surely finite, model-determined stopping time \(\tau(x)\). For a measurable integrable functional \(H\), let \[Y(x)=H\bigl(x,Z_{0:\tau(x)}\bigr),\qquad f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x)].\] Given independent complete replications \(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_n(x)\), the standard estimator is \(\widehat f_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(x)\), which satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat f_n(x)]=f(x)\). No steady-state limit is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Performance is the expected output of a complete replication that ends naturally in finite time; independent replication averages estimate it unbiasedly.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminating-Simulation Performance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is mathematically plausible, but no source is supplied for the model-determined stopping-time definition or its placement in the terminating-simulation regime.

children.title: Steady-State Simulation Performance
children.top_down_role: Long-run performance in persistent stochastic systems.

assumptions_latex: For fixed \(x\), the persistent process \((Z_t^x)_{t\geq0}\) is positive recurrent and ergodic with invariant law \(\pi_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The long-run average converges almost surely to \(f(x)=\int g(x,z)\,\pi_x(dz)\).

notation.meaning: persistent simulated state process under x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ergodic long-run average performance for a nonterminating stochastic system.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Infinite Horizon Problems p. 66

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Steady-state simulation performance for decision \(x\) is the invariant-law expectation \[f(x)=\int g(x,z)\,\pi_x(dz).\] If \((Z_t^x)_{t\geq0}\) is positive recurrent and ergodic with invariant distribution \(\pi_x\), and \(g(x,\cdot)\) is \(\pi_x\)-integrable, then \[\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T g(x,Z_t^x)\,dt\longrightarrow f(x)\] almost surely as \(T\to\infty\). The discrete-time analogue replaces the integral by \(T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}g(x,Z_t^x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Steady-state performance is the invariant-distribution mean, estimated by a long-run time average when the persistent simulated process is ergodic.
knowledge_statements.title: Steady-State Simulation Performance

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity-Free Evaluation Windows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon simulation performance defined without steady-state or stationarity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathcal X\) be a decision and let \(Y_{1:H}(x,\xi)=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_H)\) denote one simulated trajectory over a fixed finite horizon \(H\in\mathbb N\). Given a measurable path-loss functional \(L_H\), define the window performance by \[J_H(x)=\mathbb E[L_H(Y_{1:H}(x,\xi))].\] This is a stationarity-free evaluation window when the definition requires neither an invariant distribution nor convergence of \(Y_t\) as \(t\to\infty\). The optimization problem is \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}J_H(x)\), with all initialization and transient effects included in the trajectory law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-window objective averages a measurable loss over finite simulated trajectories, retaining initialization and transient effects without assuming steady state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_H(x)=\mathbb E[L_H(Y_{1:H}(x,\xi))]\) is defined without a stationarity assumption.

notation.meaning: simulated trajectory under decision x and randomness xi

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parametric Bootstrap Test for Estimated KKT Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four-step bootstrap diagnostic based on jointly estimated objective and binding-constraint gradients; fitted-gradient notation is clarified because the extracted residual formula repeats the same symbol on both sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each of \(B=1000\) replications: (i) draw \[\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0;-0}^{*},\widehat{\mathbf B}_{J;-0}^{*})\sim\mathcal N\!\left(\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0;-0},\widehat{\mathbf B}_{J;-0}),\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}\!\left(\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0;-0},\widehat{\mathbf B}_{J;-0})\right)\right);\] (ii) regress the bootstrapped objective gradient by least squares on the bootstrapped binding-constraint gradients, obtaining a fitted gradient \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0;-0}^{*}\) and multipliers \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\lambda}^{*}\); (iii) record \(\widehat{\mathbf e}^{*}=\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0;-0}^{*}-\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0;-0}^{*}\) and whether any component of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\lambda}^{*}\) is negative. Use the resulting empirical residual distributions to reject a zero-residual hypothesis when a coordinate's two-sided \((1-\alpha/(2k))\) interval excludes zero. For the negative-multiplier count \(c^{*}\), reject the associated hypothesis when \(c^{*}/1000\) is significantly greater than \(0.5\), using the stated normal approximation with mean \(0.5\) and variance \(0.00025\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw joint bootstrap gradient estimates, refit the active-gradient KKT relation by least squares, and record fitted-gradient residuals and occurrences of negative multipliers. Test zero residuals with Bonferroni-adjusted intervals and assess the negative-multiplier frequency against one half using the stated normal approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{vec}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0;-0},\widehat{\mathbf B}_{J;-0})\) is sampled from the stated fitted multivariate normal distribution with estimated covariance.
The \(J\) binding-constraint gradients are used as explanatory variables in the least-squares fit.
The procedure uses \(B=1000\) bootstrap replications and examines \(k\) residual coordinates.
The negative-multiplier count is assessed by the stated normal approximation to \(\operatorname{Binomial}(1000,0.5)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Reject a zero-residual hypothesis if a Bonferroni-adjusted bootstrap interval excludes }0;\quad\text{reject the associated multiplier hypothesis if }c^{*}/1000\text{ is significantly greater than }0.5.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence, Convergence, and Weak Differentiability of the Stationary Distribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary-distribution perturbation theory under uniform contraction, weak kernel differentiability, and derivative-growth conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the parameterized Markov kernels satisfy the stated contraction, weak-differentiability, and growth conditions. For every \(x\in U\): (i) there is a unique distribution \(\pi_x\) with \(\pi_x\mathbf P_x=\pi_x\); (ii) for every Lipschitz \(H\) and starting distribution \(\gamma\),
\[
|\gamma\mathbf P_x^nH-\pi_xH|\le L(H)\rho^n r(\gamma,\pi_x);
\]
(iii) as \(s\to0\),
\[
|\pi_{x+s}H-\pi_xH|\le s(1+o(1))K L(H)(1-\rho)^{-1};
\]
and (iv)
\[
\mathbf S_x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(\mathbf P_x^k-\mathbb 1\pi_x)
\]
is well defined, and with \(\pi_x'=\pi_x\mathbf P_x'\mathbf S_x\),
\[
|\pi_{x+s}H-\pi_xH-s\pi_x'H|=L(H)o(s)
\]
for every Lipschitz \(H\). Thus \(x\mapsto\pi_x\) is weakly differentiable with derivative \(\pi_x'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the uniform contraction and weak-differentiability conditions, each kernel has a unique stationary distribution, convergence to stationarity is geometric, the stationary distribution is locally stable in the parameter, and it is weakly differentiable with derivative π_x P'_x S_x.
assumptions_latex: x\mapsto\mathbf P_x\text{ is weakly differentiable with the stated uniform boundedness and growth conditions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi_x\mathbf P_x=\pi_x\text{ uniquely},\quad |\gamma\mathbf P_x^nH-\pi_xH|\le L(H)\rho^n r(\gamma,\pi_x),\quad \pi_x'=\pi_x\mathbf P_x'\mathbf S_x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Statistical Feasibility of a Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility probability, its threshold-augmented event, sampling estimation, and the direction of optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbf z\) have density \(p\) on \(\mathcal Z\), and let \(\mathcal F\) denote feasibility in the joint design-uncertainty space. The statistical feasibility of \(\mathbf x\) is
\[
P((\mathbf x,\mathbf z)\in\mathcal F)=\int_{\mathcal Z}\mathbf 1_{\{(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)\in\mathcal F\}}p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z.
\]
If an objective threshold is required, the event may additionally impose \(f(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)\le y_{\max}\). This probability can be estimated by sampling and is maximized when used as an optimization metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Statistical feasibility is the probability that a design is feasible under the uncertainty distribution. The event may also require the random objective not to exceed a prescribed threshold. The probability can be estimated by sampling and is maximized as a design criterion.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is represented by the measurable event \(\{(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)\in\mathcal F\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P((\mathbf x,\mathbf z)\in\mathcal F)=\int_{\mathcal Z}\mathbf 1_{\{(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)\in\mathcal F\}}p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z\), optionally intersected with \(\{f(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)\le y_{\max}\}\), and this criterion is maximized.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-sure consistency of sampled optimal values and solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of pointwise almost-sure objective convergence to uniform convergence and optimization consistency on a compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Theta\) be compact. Suppose \(f_N(x)\to f(x)\) almost surely for every \(x\in\Theta\), and suppose \(Y(\cdot,\xi)\) satisfies the stated Lipschitz hypothesis. If \(v_N\) and \(x_N\) are an optimal value and an optimal solution of the sampled problem, and \(v^*\) and \(S^*\) are the true optimal value and solution set, then, almost surely,
\[
\sup_{x\in\Theta}|f_N(x)-f(x)|\to0,\qquad v_N\to v^*,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x_N,S^*)\to0.
\]
Under the additional piecewise-linear/finite-set assumption—namely, the stated finite-support piecewise-linear regime or a finite feasible set—one may strengthen the last conclusion to \(x_N\in S^*\) almost surely for all sufficiently large \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact feasible set, pointwise almost-sure convergence together with the stated Lipschitz hypothesis yields uniform almost-sure convergence. Sampled optimal values converge to the true value, and sampled optimizers approach the true solution set. Under the additional piecewise-linear/finite-set regime, sampled optimizers are eventually true optimizers almost surely.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equal-Redistribution Extension to More Than Two Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability normalization rule following an update of one fixed action in a state with more than two actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let state \(i\) have \(m>2\) actions. After updating a fixed action \(x\) by the two-action reward-inaction rule, define
\[
\Delta=p^{k+1}(i,x)-p^k(i,x).
\]
For every \(a\ne x\), set
\[
p^{k+1}(i,a)=p^k(i,a)-\frac{\Delta}{m-1}.
\]
The total probability is thereby preserved, but all actions other than \(x\) are rewarded or penalized equally, irrespective of their individual performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For more than two actions, first update one fixed action x and compute its probability change. Subtract an equal share of that change from every other action probability. This preserves the probability sum but indiscriminately treats all other actions alike, which is a deficiency of the extension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discounted score-trace estimator for stationary Markov-chain gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state ergodic Markov chains with differentiable parameterized transition probabilities and stationary average one-step costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $P(\theta)=[p(x,y\mid\theta)]$ be a continuously differentiable finite-state transition matrix for scalar $\theta\in[a,b]$, with unique invariant distribution $\mu(\theta)$, and let $k(x,y,\theta)$ be continuously differentiable. Define
\[
e(\theta)=\sum_{x,y}\mu(x,\theta)p(x,y\mid\theta)k(x,y,\theta)
\]
and the bounded score
\[
L(x,y,\theta)=\frac{p_\theta(x,y\mid\theta)}{p(x,y\mid\theta)}.
\]
Writing $q(x,\theta)=E_x^\theta[k(x,X_1,\theta)]$, $Q(\theta)=(q(x,\theta))_x$, and $\lambda_q(\theta)=\mu(\theta)^\top Q(\theta)$, the invariant-distribution contribution to $e'(\theta)$ has the centered representation
\[
T_3(\theta)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\mu(\theta)^\top P_\theta(\theta)P(\theta)^m[Q(\theta)-\lambda_q(\theta)\mathbf e].
\]
For $0<\rho<1$, define
\[
C_{n+1}=\rho C_n+L(X_n,X_{n+1},\theta_n),
\]
\[
\lambda_{n+1}=\lambda_n+q_0\epsilon_n[k(X_n,X_{n+1},\theta_n)-\lambda_n],
\]
\[
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n-\epsilon_n\left[k_\theta(X_n,X_{n+1},\theta_n)+L_nk_n+(k_n-\lambda_n)C_n\right],
\]
where $q_0>0$. With $\theta$ held fixed and $\lambda_n$ at its stationary mean, the last term has stationary expectation equal to the $\rho$-discounted version of the series for $T_3(\theta)$. Hence its bias vanishes as $\rho\uparrow1$ when the sensitivity series is summable. Centering by $\lambda_n$ leaves the stationary mean unchanged and reduces estimator variance. Under the applicable constrained state-dependent-noise and stability conditions, the recursion converges to a point close to a stable optimum for $\rho$ sufficiently near one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative of a stationary Markov-chain cost contains direct cost, transition-score, and invariant-distribution sensitivity terms. Samples of the cost derivative and likelihood-ratio score estimate the first two. A discounted score trace estimates the third, with bias that disappears as its discount approaches one. Centering preserves the mean and reduces variance; convergence near a stable optimum additionally requires the cited constrained stochastic-approximation conditions.
assumptions_latex: p(x,y\mid\theta)\text{ and }k(x,y,\theta)\text{ are continuously differentiable in }\theta
P(\theta)\text{ is ergodic with unique invariant distribution }\mu(\theta)
L(x,y,\theta)=p_\theta(x,y\mid\theta)/p(x,y\mid\theta)\text{ is defined and bounded on sampled transitions}
\text{The constrained recursion satisfies the applicable state-dependent-noise and stability hypotheses}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product rule for a parameter-dependent integrand and moving set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leibniz-type rule separating integrand sensitivity from the weak derivative of the integration domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x\mapsto H(x,\cdot) be L^{1+\delta}-differentiable with derivative h(x,\cdot), and suppose H(x,u) is continuous in u. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary intervals, nets, and sequences in base b
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions underlying quasi-Monte Carlo integration, together with the stated integration-error order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\ge2\) and \(s\ge1\). An elementary interval in base \(b\) is \(E=\prod_{j=1}^s[a_j/b^{d_j},(a_j+1)/b^{d_j})\), where \(a_j,d_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(a_j<b^{d_j}\); its volume is \(b^{-\sum_jd_j}\). For \(0\le t\le m\), a sequence of \(b^m\) points is a \((t,m,s)\)-net in base \(b\) if every such interval of volume \(b^{t-m}\) contains exactly \(b^t\) points. An infinite sequence \((u^n)\) is a \((t,s)\)-sequence in base \(b\) if, for every \(k\ge0\) and \(m>t\), its block with \(kb^m\le n<(k+1)b^m\) is a \((t,m,s)\)-net. These nets yield integration approximations with error of order \(O((\log N)^s/N)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elementary base-b interval is a product of aligned base-b subintervals and has volume b to the negative sum of their resolution exponents. A (t,m,s)-net has b^m points and places exactly b^t points in every elementary interval of volume b^(t-m). A (t,s)-sequence has this net property in every aligned block of b^m consecutive points for every m>t. Such nets yield integration error of order (log N)^s/N.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{vol}(E)=b^{-\sum_jd_j},\quad \#(E\cap P)=b^t\ \text{when }\operatorname{vol}(E)=b^{t-m},\quad \text{integration error}=O((\log N)^s/N).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nested evaluation of an adaptive stochastic-search policy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon adaptive policies whose observations can depend on prior decisions or the full training history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a policy \(\pi\) executed for \(N\) iterations, the trajectory is \((x^0,W^1,x^1,\ldots,W^N,x^{\pi,N})\). If observations may depend on prior decisions or history, the training sample path lies in a policy-dependent space \(\omega^\pi\in\Omega^\pi\), and \(x^{\pi,N}\) is random. With a separate testing outcome \(\widehat W\), policy performance is \[F^\pi=\mathbb E\!\left[F(x^{\pi,N},\widehat W)\mid S_0\right]\] and may be decomposed as \[F^\pi=\mathbb E_{S_0}\,\mathbb E_{W^1,\ldots,W^N\mid S_0}\,\mathbb E_{x^{\pi,N}\mid W^1,\ldots,W^N}\,\mathbb E_{\widehat W\mid x^{\pi,N}}F(x^{\pi,N},\widehat W).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive policy produces a random terminal decision because its training observations can depend on earlier decisions or the entire history. Evaluating one realized terminal decision on test samples is distinct from evaluating the policy; policy performance averages over initial-model uncertainty, the policy-dependent training path, any randomness in the terminal recommendation, and a separate testing outcome.

W^n\text{ may depend on }x^{n-1}\text{ or on the full preceding history}
\widehat W\text{ is used for testing rather than for producing }x^{\pi,N}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Action Reward-Inaction Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability update performed whenever a simulated trajectory visits a state having two admissible actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix one of the two actions, denoted by \(x\). When state \(i\) is visited at iteration \(k\), let \(L(i)\) be the action taken on the preceding visit and let \(\phi(i)\) be the computed feedback. The reward-inaction update is
\[
p^{k+1}(i,x)=p^k(i,x)+\alpha\phi(i)I\{L(i)=x\}-\alpha\phi(i)p^k(i,x),
\]
and the probability of the other action is set to \(1-p^{k+1}(i,x)\). Thus the change is \(\alpha\phi(i)[1-p^k(i,x)]\) if \(L(i)=x\), and \(-\alpha\phi(i)p^k(i,x)\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a state with two actions, fix one action x. On each return to the state, update its probability using the feedback, learning rate, and indicator that x was selected on the preceding visit; set the other action's probability to the complement. Strong feedback substantially rewards the selected action and reduces the unselected action, whereas weak feedback produces little change.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathcal A(i)\text{ is fixed throughout the algorithm}
\alpha\text{ is the learning rate and }\phi(i)\text{ is the feedback computed at the visit to }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^{k+1}(i,x)=p^k(i,x)+\alpha\phi(i)I\{L(i)=x\}-\alpha\phi(i)p^k(i,x),\qquad p^{k+1}(i,a_{\mathrm{other}})=1-p^{k+1}(i,x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Convergence in Probability and With Probability One
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete optimization via simulation under the source-stated equivalence between objective-value convergence and optimal-set membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathbf{x}_m^*\in\Theta be the solution reported after iteration m, let g_m^*=g(\mathbf{x}_m^*), let g^* be the global optimal value, and let \Theta^* be the global optimizer set. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-run simulation algorithm for an average-reward SMDP with two actions per state; an MDP is obtained by taking every transition time to be one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(k=0\), \(p(i,a)=1/|\mathcal A(i)|\), \(C_r(i)=C_t(i)=0\) for every state and action, and \(TR=TT=0\). Fix an action label \(x\), initialize \(s_{\min},s_{\max}\), choose a learning rate \(\alpha\), and simulate from a starting state \(i\). On every nonfirst visit to \(i\), compute
\[
R=TR-C_r(i),\quad T=TT-C_t(i),\quad s=R/T,\quad \phi=(s-s_{\min})/(s_{\max}-s_{\min}),
\]
then update
\[
p(i,x)\leftarrow p(i,x)+\alpha\phi I\{L(i)=x\}-\alpha\phi p(i,x)
\]
and set the other action probability so the two probabilities sum to one. Sample \(a\in\mathcal A(i)\) according to \(p(i,\cdot)\), set \(L(i)=a\), \(C_r(i)=TR\), and \(C_t(i)=TT\), simulate the transition to \(j\) with reward \(r(i,a,j)\) and time \(t(i,a,j)\), update \(TR\leftarrow TR+r(i,a,j)\), \(TT\leftarrow TT+t(i,a,j)\), set \(i\leftarrow j\), increment \(k\), and repeat until \(k=\mathrm{MAX\_STEPS}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize uniform action probabilities and state-specific reward/time checkpoints. On each return to a state, use reward per elapsed time since the preceding visit to form normalized feedback and apply the reward-inaction update. Sample and simulate the next action, accumulate reward and transition time, move to the resulting state, and continue until the prescribed iteration limit. For an ordinary MDP, every transition time is one.
assumptions_latex: \text{The model is an average-reward SMDP with }|\mathcal A(i)|=2\text{ for every }i\in\mathcal S.
p(i,a)=1/|\mathcal A(i)|\quad\forall i\in\mathcal S,\ a\in\mathcal A(i)
x\text{ is a fixed admissible action label and }\alpha\text{ is a chosen small learning rate.}
\mathrm{MAX\_STEPS}\text{ is the prescribed number of simulated transitions.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure generates a simulated SMDP trajectory and adaptively updates }p(i,\cdot)\text{ by reward-inaction feedback until }k=\mathrm{MAX\_STEPS};\quad t(i,a,j)\equiv1\text{ gives the MDP specialization.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-horizon and infinite-horizon expected average cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the expected time-average objective. Existence of the infinite-horizon limit and independence from the initial state are separate requirements, not consequences of boundedness alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x(\cdot,\theta)\) be the state process when the parameter is held constant at \(\theta\), and let \(c(\theta,x)\) be a bounded cost rate. For \(T>0\), define
\[
L_T(\theta,x(0))=\frac{1}{T}\,\mathbb E\!\left[\int_0^T c\bigl(\theta,x(t,\theta)\bigr)\,dt\right].
\]
If the limit exists, define
\[
L(\theta,x(0))=\lim_{T\to\infty}L_T(\theta,x(0)).
\]
If this limit is additionally independent of \(x(0)\), it may be denoted by \(L(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-horizon expected average cost is expected accumulated cost divided by the horizon. Its limit, when it exists, is the infinite-horizon average cost per unit time. Writing it solely as a function of the parameter additionally requires independence from the initial state.
assumptions_latex: \(x(\cdot,\theta)\) is the state process with \(\theta\) held constant.
The limit \(\lim_{T\to\infty}L_T(\theta,x(0))\) exists when \(L(\theta,x(0))\) is defined.
Independence from \(x(0)\) is required only for the notation \(L(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_T(\theta,x(0))=\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\!\left[\int_0^T c\bigl(\theta,x(t,\theta)\bigr)\,dt\right],\qquad L(\theta,x(0))=\lim_{T\to\infty}L_T(\theta,x(0)),\text{ when the limit exists.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asynchronous tabular Q-learning and Bellman fixed-point convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite discounted Markov decision processes with componentwise updates indexed by visits to state–action pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite controlled Markov chain with finite action sets, discount factor $0<\beta<1$, stationary conditional mean costs $\bar c_{id}$, and uniformly bounded conditional cost variances, define
\[
(TQ)_{id}=\bar c_{id}+\beta\sum_jp(i,j\mid d)\min_{v\in U(j)}Q_{jv}.
\]
When $(i,d)$ is sampled at time $n$ and the next state is $\psi_{n+1}$, asynchronous Q-learning updates
\[
Q_{n+1,id}=Q_{n,id}+\widetilde\epsilon_{n,id}\left[c_{n,id}+\beta\min_{v\in U(\psi_{n+1})}Q_{n,\psi_{n+1}v}-Q_{n,id}\right],
\]
leaving all other components unchanged, where $\widetilde\epsilon_{n,id}=w_{id}\epsilon_{k(i,d,n)}$. The operator $T$ satisfies
\[
\|TQ-TQ'\|_\infty\le\beta\|Q-Q'\|_\infty,
\]
so it has a unique fixed point $\bar Q$ and $V(i)=\min_{d\in U(i)}\bar Q_{id}$. If every state–action pair is visited infinitely often almost surely and the additional stochastic-approximation hypotheses invoked by the convergence theorem hold, then $Q_n\to\bar Q$ almost surely. Positivity of the steps and $\sum_k\epsilon_k=\infty$ alone are not a complete convergence hypothesis. For the projected algorithm on $[-B,B]$, mutually comparable asymptotic visit counts produce the stated reflected mean ODE; if $B$ is sufficiently large to contain $\bar Q$, its limiting equilibrium is $\bar Q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asynchronous tabular Q-learning updates only the sampled state–action component using its observed cost and the smallest estimated value at the next state. Its Bellman operator is a contraction with a unique fixed point that determines the optimal value function. Almost-sure convergence additionally requires the stochastic-approximation conditions used in the later convergence analysis; infinite exploration and a divergent step-size sum are not by themselves sufficient.
assumptions_latex: \text{The additional noise and step-size hypotheses required by the cited stochastic-approximation convergence result hold.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|TQ-TQ'\|_\infty\le\beta\|Q-Q'\|_\infty,\qquad T\bar Q=\bar Q,\qquad V(i)=\min_{d\in U(i)}\bar Q_{id},\qquad Q_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\bar Q\ \text{under the full convergence hypotheses}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: TD(1) mean drift for linear discounted-value approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prediction under a fixed policy using linear features of a stationary Markov process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\{X_n\}$ be a Markov chain on a compact space with a time-invariant transition kernel and unique invariant measure $\mu$. For $0<\beta<1$, bounded continuous $k$ and $\phi$, define
\[
W(x)=E_x\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\beta^m k(X_m,X_{m+1}),\qquad \widetilde W(x,w)=w^\top\phi(x),
\]
\[
e(w)=\tfrac12E_\mu[(W(X_0)-w^\top\phi(X_0))^2].
\]
TD$(\lambda)$ uses
\[
C_{n+1}=\beta\lambda C_n+\phi(X_{n+1}),
\]
\[
d_n=k(X_n,X_{n+1})+\beta w_n^\top\phi(X_{n+1})-w_n^\top\phi(X_n),
\]
\[
w_{n+1}=w_n+\epsilon_nd_nC_n.
\]
For $\lambda=1$, bounded iterates and the applicable stationary averaging conditions give
\[
\bar g(w)=-\nabla e(w),\qquad \dot w=-\nabla e(w).
\]
This exact gradient identity is not asserted for $\lambda<1$. Projection produces the corresponding projected mean ODE, but convergence of the stochastic recursion still requires the cited stochastic-approximation hypotheses. Under partial observation, replacing $\phi(X_n)$ by observable features $\phi(\widehat X_n)$ fits the stationary least-squares predictor based on those features, provided suitable stationarity and mixing conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: TD(λ) combines a temporal-difference error with an eligibility trace to fit a linear discounted-value approximation from a trajectory. For TD(1), the stationary mean update is exactly the negative gradient of the mean-square value-approximation error when the iterates are bounded and the averaging assumptions hold. The exact gradient interpretation does not extend unchanged to λ below one.
assumptions_latex: \{X_n\}\text{ has a time-invariant transition kernel and unique invariant measure }\mu
k\text{ and every component of }\phi\text{ are bounded and continuous}
\{w_n\}\text{ is bounded for the unprojected mean-ODE identification}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar g(w)=-\nabla e(w),\qquad \dot w=-\nabla e(w)\qquad\text{for }\lambda=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Differences with Simulated Function Evaluations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical derivative approximation when the objective has no available analytical form and its values are estimated by simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If $f$ is differentiable at $x$, then $f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$. For small nonzero $h$, the corresponding centered and forward quotients approximate $f'(x)$. When function values are estimated by simulation, sampling error is added to finite-difference error; the extract recommends common random numbers for the paired evaluations at $x+h$ and $x-h$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centered and forward finite differences approximate a derivative using nearby function values. In simulation optimization, sampling error is added to the finite-difference error. The extract recommends using the same random-number streams for the positive and negative centered evaluations and reports empirical evidence favoring centered differences over forward differences.
assumptions_latex: \widehat f(x-h),\widehat f(x),\widehat f(x+h)\text{ are simulation estimates in the simulation setting}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x)\approx\frac{\widehat f(x+h)-\widehat f(x-h)}{2h}\quad\text{or}\quad f'(x)\approx\frac{\widehat f(x+h)-\widehat f(x)}{h},\qquad h\to0\text{ recovers the deterministic derivative when exact function values are used}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-loss EVI allocation objective and approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-alternative Bayesian selection with linear opportunity loss and stagewise multi-alternative sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given current information \(\mathcal E\), current sample counts \(n_i\), and an additional budget \(\tau\), the LL procedure selects \(\tau_i\ge0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^k\tau_i=\tau\), to approximately minimize a predictive-EOC upper bound \(\operatorname{EOC}_{\mathrm{bnd}}(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_k)\). The bound decomposes into pairwise comparisons between the current posterior-best alternative \((k)\) and every \((i)\ne(k)\), subtracting the expected information supplied by the additional samples from the current pairwise opportunity cost. The continuous allocation derived for asymptotically large \(\tau\) approximates the integer problem; when sampling variances are unknown, Welch approximations for pairwise differences and their degrees of freedom are used. With no additional samples the bound reduces to \(\operatorname{EOC}_{\mathrm{Bonf}}\), an upper bound on posterior EOC, while perfect information makes each pairwise residual opportunity cost vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LL allocates a stage's samples across several alternatives by approximately minimizing a pairwise Bonferroni-type upper bound on predictive expected opportunity cost. Its closed-form allocation is an asymptotic continuous approximation, and unknown variances require Welch approximations. With no new samples the bound is the posterior EOC upper bound; with perfect information its residual terms vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_k)\in\arg\min\operatorname{EOC}_{\mathrm{bnd}}(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_k)\quad\text{approximately}.

children.title: Explicit Constraints with Simulated Objectives
children.top_down_role: Known feasible regions paired with simulation-estimated objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Constraints with Simulated Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Known deterministic feasibility conditions with an objective accessible through stochastic simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and let explicitly evaluable functions \(g_j:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), define \(F=\{x\in\mathcal X:g_j(x)\le 0\text{ for all }j\}\). If a simulator returns an integrable random response \(Y(x,\xi)\) whose mean \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\) is not directly available, then simulation optimization with explicit constraints is \[\min_{x\in F} f(x)=\min_{x\in F}\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)].\] Feasibility can be checked without simulation; simulation is required only to estimate or compare objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible region is known and directly testable, while each objective value is an expectation estimated from stochastic simulator outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in F}\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\) has explicit feasibility and a simulated objective.

children.title: Noisy Response Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraint performance observed through stochastic simulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Response Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-response constraints whose values must be inferred from stochastic simulator observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_0(x,\xi)\) be an objective response and let \(Y_j(x,\xi)\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), be integrable constraint responses. Define \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y_0(x,\xi)]\) and \(c_j(x)=\mathbb E[Y_j(x,\xi)]\). A simulation problem with noisy response constraints is \[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad c_j(x)\le b_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.\] The simulator supplies noisy realizations rather than exact values of \(c_j(x)\), so feasibility itself must be statistically estimated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both objective performance and constraint feasibility depend on unknown mean responses estimated from noisy simulation output.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_j(x,\xi)\) is integrable for every \(x\in\mathcal X\) and \(j=0,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible exactly when \(\mathbb E[Y_j(x,\xi)]\le b_j\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Simulator Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility defined by an unobserved simulator-validity region rather than explicit analytic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a declared input domain and let \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\subseteq\mathcal X\) be an unknown set on which the simulator produces a valid performance response. Hidden simulator feasibility means that no evaluable analytic description of \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\) is supplied. A query at \(x\) returns either a valid response \(Y(x,\xi)\) or feasibility information generated by the simulator. Thus the optimization domain is \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\), but membership must be learned from queries rather than checked before simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulator is valid only on an unknown subset of inputs, and membership in that subset must be learned through simulator queries.
assumptions_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\subseteq\mathcal X\) is fixed during the optimization run.
A valid objective response exists only for \(x\in F_{\mathrm{sim}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\) is the feasible set, but no explicit membership predicate is initially available.

children.title: Binary Simulator Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasibility evidence returned solely as a categorical success or failure outcome.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Simulator Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simulator feasibility observed through a binary random response and an acceptance threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in\mathcal X\), let the simulator return \(B(x,\xi)\in\{0,1\}\), where \(B=1\) denotes a feasible or valid run. Define the feasibility probability \(p(x)=\mathbb P(B(x,\xi)=1)\). Given a tolerance \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), binary simulator feasibility declares \(x\) feasible when \[p(x)\ge 1-\alpha.\] For deterministic simulator validity, this specializes to \(\alpha=0\) and an almost-sure binary membership response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary simulator output records success or feasibility; a decision is accepted when its success probability meets a prescribed threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(B(x,\xi)\) is measurable and binary for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\alpha=\{x\in\mathcal X:\mathbb P(B(x,\xi)=1)\ge1-\alpha\}\) is the binary-response feasible set.

notation.meaning: probability of a feasible simulator response

review_flags: A source is needed to confirm the intended probabilistic threshold convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The probabilistic binary-response formulation is coherent, but the terminal title does not itself determine the chance-threshold convention or the claimed deterministic specialization.

children.title: Simulator Failure as Feasibility Evidence
children.top_down_role: Use of crashes, noncompletion, or invalid outputs as indirect feasibility signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulator Failure as Feasibility Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which run failure may legitimately be interpreted as evidence of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x,\xi)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate successful simulator completion. A failed run \(R=0\) is evidence about feasibility only if the failure mechanism is coupled to feasibility, for example when \(\mathbb P(R=0\mid x\in F)=0\). Under that condition, observing \(R(x,\xi)=0\) certifies \(x\notin F\). If feasible inputs can fail because of numerical errors, timeouts, or unrelated randomness, then a single failure does not certify infeasibility; it identifies only a failed evaluation unless the failure probabilities are separately modeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulator failure certifies infeasibility only when feasible inputs cannot fail; otherwise failures may reflect numerical or operational errors.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathcal X\) is the intended feasible set.
\(R=0\) records failure to produce a valid simulator response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x,\xi)=0\Rightarrow x\notin F\) is valid only under a no-false-failure condition such as \(\mathbb P(R=0\mid x\in F)=0\).
review_flags: The calibration condition is mathematically necessary but lacks a supplied supporting source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container, but the displayed condition conditions on the proposition `x in F` while x is presented as fixed. Certification requires a sourced pointwise no-false-failure condition for every feasible input, together with a clear probability model.

children.title: Offline Terminal Recommendation
children.top_down_role: Simulation effort evaluated by the quality of a final recommended decision.

knowledge_statements.title: Offline Terminal Recommendation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-budget search assessed solely by the final decision recommended after simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an adaptive policy use \(N\) simulator calls and then return a terminal recommendation \(\widehat x_N\in\mathcal X\). For a minimization objective \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\) with optimum \(f^*=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), offline terminal performance is measured by the simple regret \[r_N=\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_N)-f^*].\] Simulator inputs used during search incur no performance charge in this criterion; only the quality of \(\widehat x_N\) after the budget is exhausted is evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An offline policy spends a simulation budget, returns one final decision, and is judged by that recommendation’s expected optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N\) is a fixed simulation budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_N=\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_N)-f^*]\) evaluates terminal recommendation quality.

children.title: Online Cumulative Performance
children.top_down_role: Performance accumulated while information is acquired.

knowledge_statements.title: Online Cumulative Performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential simulation decisions assessed by losses accumulated during information acquisition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At rounds \(t=1,\ldots,T\), an online policy selects \(X_t\in\mathcal X\), observes a stochastic response with mean \(f(X_t)\), and then updates its information. For stationary minimization with \(f^*=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), its expected cumulative regret is \[R_T=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\bigl(f(X_t)-f^*\bigr)\right].\] Unlike an offline terminal criterion, every exploratory decision contributes to performance, so information acquisition and immediate objective quality are jointly assessed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An online policy is judged by the objective gaps accumulated at every decision while it learns, not merely by a final recommendation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T=\mathbb E[\sum_{t=1}^T(f(X_t)-f^*)]\) measures cumulative online performance.
review_flags: The supplied sources do not specifically locate the online cumulative-regret formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stationary cumulative-regret definition fits online cumulative performance and is internally coherent, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-horizon online-learning cumulative reward objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance is accumulated while measurements are selected and information is acquired, rather than evaluated only through a terminal recommendation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a measurement policy \(\pi\), horizon \(N\), stage weights \(\gamma^n\), and decisions \(x^n\) generated by \(\pi\), the online-learning objective is
\[
\operatorname*{maximize}_{\pi}\;\mathbb E^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{N}\gamma^n\mu_{x^n}\right].
\]
The expectation is over the uncertain alternative values and the observations made during learning. Such online-learning problems are called bandit problems; with a finite discrete alternative set, they are multi-armed bandit problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online learning values rewards earned while information is being acquired. A measurement policy maximizes expected weighted cumulative reward over the finite horizon. The finite-discrete specialization is the multi-armed bandit problem.
assumptions_latex: N\in\mathbb N\text{ is the measurement horizon}
x^n\text{ is the stage-}n\text{ decision generated by policy }\pi
\gamma^n\text{ is the stated stage-}n\text{ reward weight}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{maximize}_{\pi}\;\mathbb E^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{N}\gamma^n\mu_{x^n}\right].

children.title: Nonstationary Simulation Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization when simulator responses change over calendar time or decision epochs.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary Simulation Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simulation optimization with objective or response laws that vary over decision time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rounds \(t=1,\ldots,T\), let \(f_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be a time-indexed objective and let the simulator return \(Y_t(x,\xi_t)\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[Y_t(x,\xi_t)]=f_t(x)\). A nonstationary simulation-optimization policy selects \(X_t\) using information available before round \(t\). Relative to instantaneous minimizers \(x_t^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f_t(x)\), a standard tracking criterion is dynamic regret \[R_T^{\mathrm{dyn}}=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\bigl(f_t(X_t)-f_t(x_t^*)\bigr)\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulated response law changes over time, so decisions are compared with the optimum applicable at each round.
assumptions_latex: \(f_t\) attains a minimum on \(\mathcal X\) for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T^{\mathrm{dyn}}\) measures performance against the time-varying sequence of instantaneous optima.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports nonstationary dynamic-regret simulation optimization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The time-indexed simulation model and dynamic-regret criterion fit nonstationary simulation optimization, but no source supports the selected formulation and benchmark.

children.title: Optimum Tracking
children.top_down_role: Maintenance of recommendations near a moving optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimum Tracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance comparison between sequential decisions and instantaneous time-varying minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attain its minimum at some \(x_t^*\) for each \(t=1,\ldots,T\). For a decision sequence \((X_t)_{t=1}^T\), define the pointwise tracking gap \(e_t=f_t(X_t)-f_t(x_t^*)\ge0\). Its cumulative tracking error is \[E_T=\sum_{t=1}^T e_t.\] Consequently, \(E_T=0\) if and only if \(X_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f_t(x)\) for every \(t\); small \(E_T\) quantifies approximate optimum tracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tracking error sums each decision’s gap from the current optimum and vanishes exactly when every decision is currently optimal.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_t\) attains a finite minimum on \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_T=0\iff X_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f_t(x)\) for all \(t=1,ldots,T\).
review_flags: A source for this optimum-tracking criterion is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tracking-gap property is mathematically valid and fits the container, but no source is supplied and the conclusion contains `ldots` instead of `\ldots`.

children.title: Abrupt-Regime Response
children.top_down_role: Adaptation following sudden changes in the simulated system.

knowledge_statements.title: Abrupt-Regime Response
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tracking under piecewise-stationary objectives separated by discrete change points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K<\tau_{K+1}=T+1\) be change points and let \(f^{(0)},\ldots,f^{(K)}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\). An abrupt-regime model has \[f_t=f^{(k)}\quad\text{whenever}\quad \tau_k\le t<\tau_{k+1}.\] If \(x_k^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f^{(k)}(x)\), response after change \(\tau_k\) may be quantified by the first delay \(d_k\ge0\) for which the selected decision satisfies \(f^{(k)}(X_{\tau_k+d_k})-f^{(k)}(x_k^*)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective changes at discrete times and remains fixed between changes; response delay records how quickly decisions become near-optimal afterward.
assumptions_latex: Every regime objective \(f^{(k)}\) attains a minimum on \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_k=\inf\{d\ge0:f^{(k)}(X_{\tau_k+d})-f^{(k)}(x_k^*)\le\varepsilon\}\) measures post-change response.
review_flags: The precise abrupt-change and response-delay convention requires a supporting source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The piecewise-stationary model fits abrupt-regime response, but the response-delay convention lacks a source and does not specify integer delays, the finite admissible time range, or the value when the tolerance is never reached.

children.title: Gradual-Drift Response
children.top_down_role: Adaptation under progressive movement of responses or optimal decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradual-Drift Response
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded-variation condition for objectives that evolve incrementally over time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), \(t=1,\ldots,T\), be time-indexed objectives. Their cumulative uniform drift is \[V_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f_{t+1}(x)-f_t(x)|.\] The sequence satisfies a gradual-drift condition with per-round bound \(\delta\ge0\) when \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f_{t+1}(x)-f_t(x)|\le\delta\) for every \(t<T\). This implies \(V_T\le(T-1)\delta\), providing a quantitative environment-change scale for evaluating tracking response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive objective functions differ uniformly by at most a prescribed amount, bounding total environmental variation over the horizon.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_t\) is real-valued on the common domain \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f_{t+1}(x)-f_t(x)|\le\delta\) for all \(t<T\) implies \(V_T\le(T-1)\delta\).
review_flags: A source for the selected uniform-drift convention is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded uniform-drift condition and its variation bound are correct and the condition kind fits the container, but the selected drift convention has no cited source.

children.title: Simulator Access Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Access patterns governing how optimization procedures submit decisions, receive outputs, or control replications.

assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in X\), the simulator can generate an output from a distribution \(P_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The access interface determines which simulator operations an optimization method may invoke.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-level taxonomy for stochastic simulators used by optimization procedures.

source_refs.locator: 3. Simulation-Based Optimization: An Overview p. 29
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simulator access interface is an oracle \(\mathcal O\) whose permitted queries are specified from the following operations: sampling, \(\mathcal O(x)\sim P_x\); coupled sampling, \((\mathcal O(x_1,u),\ldots,\mathcal O(x_k,u))\) under a shared random input \(u\); and, when exposed, structural queries returning pathwise derivatives, likelihood ratios, constraints, or state trajectories. An optimization method is compatible with the interface only if every observation it uses is obtainable through the declared operations. A sampling-only interface reveals neither an analytic expression for \(P_x\) nor exact values of expectations under \(P_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An access interface specifies whether an optimizer may request independent samples, coupled samples, trajectories, constraints, or derivative information from the simulator.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulator Access Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Simulation-Based Optimization: An Overview p. 29
source_witnesses.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the proposed oracle taxonomy and the claims about coupled, derivative, constraint, and trajectory queries are more specific than the cited overview locator can presently support. The plain statement also calls samples independent although the LaTeX statement does not impose independence. A source directly defining simulator-access models is required.

children.title: Simulator Evaluation Contracts
children.top_down_role: Evaluation protocols governing returned responses, execution status, metadata, or resource limits.

assumptions_latex: Each evaluation uses a declared decision \(x\in X\), fidelity or horizon \(h\), and randomization identifier \(s\).
All returned quantities are measurable functions of the simulator inputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The contract fixes the conditional law and metadata required to interpret, reproduce, and compare simulator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal contract for interpreting individual evaluations and their dependence structure.

source_refs.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simulator evaluation contract is satisfied when every call with inputs \((x,h,s)\) returns a tuple \((Y,C,M)\), where \(Y\) is the objective observation, \(C\) contains declared constraint observations, and \(M\) records cost, horizon, fidelity, termination status, and randomization metadata. The contract must specify the conditional law \(\mathcal L((Y,C)\mid x,h,s)\), whether distinct calls are independent, and whether equal identifiers induce common random numbers. It must also declare integrability requirements, failure handling, and which component estimates the target performance \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluation contract specifies returned outputs, their conditional distribution, dependence across calls, computational metadata, failure handling, and the target performance being estimated.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulator Evaluation Contracts

source_witnesses.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role is plausible, but this detailed evaluation contract, including seeds, fidelity, metadata, failure handling, and common-random-number semantics, is a synthesized interface specification not reliably supported by the cited general simulation section. A direct source or explicit standard-field rationale is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variance-Minimizing Importance-Sampling Density
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal proposal density for a single-sample importance-sampling estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\sim\psi\) and \(Y=H(V)\varphi(V)/\psi(V)\). Among admissible proposal densities \(\psi\), the variance of \(Y\) is minimized by choosing \(\psi(w)\) proportional to \(|H(w)\varphi(w)|\); when \(0<C:=\int |H(w)\varphi(w)|\,dw<\infty\), one normalized minimizer is \(\psi^*(w)=|H(w)\varphi(w)|/C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the importance-sampling estimator Y = H(V) φ(V)/ψ(V) with V drawn from ψ, variance is minimized when the proposal density is proportional to the absolute value of H times φ. If the normalizing integral C is positive and finite, the normalized optimizer is ψ*(w)=|H(w)φ(w)|/C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi^*(w)=\frac{|H(w)\varphi(w)|}{\int |H(u)\varphi(u)|\,du}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\psi}\operatorname{Var}_{\psi}\!\left(H(V)\frac{\varphi(V)}{\psi(V)}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comonotone coupling minimizes the variance of a difference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded fixed-marginal coupling theorem, with finite second moments required for the variance comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) have fixed distribution functions \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) and finite second moments. Among all joint distributions with these marginals, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_1-Y_2)\) is minimized by the comonotone joint distribution \[\mathbb P(Y_1\leq s,Y_2\leq t)=\min\{G_1(s),G_2(t)\}.\] Equivalently, a minimizing coupling is \[Y_1=G_1^{-1}(U),\qquad Y_2=G_2^{-1}(U),\qquad U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1],\] where the inverses are generalized quantile functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed square-integrable marginals, using the same uniform random variable in both quantile representations produces the comonotone coupling and minimizes the variance of their difference.
assumptions_latex: Y_1\text{ and }Y_2\text{ have fixed distribution functions }G_1,G_2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Var}(G_1^{-1}(U)-G_2^{-1}(U))=\min_{\text{couplings of }G_1,G_2}\operatorname{Var}(Y_1-Y_2),\qquad U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variance reduction by mixture-component sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equality characterization requires positive mixture weights; components with zero weight are irrelevant. Variance claims require finite second moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\mu_i\), where \(c_i>0\), \(\sum_i c_i=1\), and each \(\mu_i\) is a probability measure. Let \(V\sim\mu\), and let the possibly dependent variables \(V_i\sim\mu_i\). For every integrable \(H\), \[\mathbb E[H(V)]=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^k c_iH(V_i)\right]=\mu H.\] Whenever the variances are finite, \[\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^k c_iH(V_i)\right)\leq\operatorname{Var}(H(V)),\] with equality if and only if \(H(V_i)=H(V_j)\) almost surely for every \(i\ne j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separately sampling every positively weighted component of a probability mixture and combining the function values with the mixture weights gives an unbiased estimator whose variance does not exceed direct mixture sampling. Equality occurs exactly when all component function values agree almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \mu_i\text{ is a probability measure and }\mu=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\mu_i
V\sim\mu,\quad V_i\sim\mu_i\text{ under an arbitrary joint coupling}
H\text{ is integrable; finite second moments are assumed for the variance claim}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[H(V)]=\mathbb E\left[\sum_{i=1}^k c_iH(V_i)\right]=\mu H,\quad \operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^k c_iH(V_i)\right)\leq\operatorname{Var}(H(V)),\text{ with equality iff }H(V_i)=H(V_j)\text{ a.s. for all }i\ne j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expectation and Quantile Objectives from Simulation Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives expectation and quantile functionals as possible scalar objectives derived from simulation output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a simulation-output random variable \(Y(x,\xi)\), the objective is often \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)]\), but it may instead be an \(\alpha\)-quantile \(f(x)=q_\alpha(x)\), where \(0<\alpha<1\) and \[q_\alpha(x)=\sup\{y:\mathbb{P}(Y(x,\xi)\le y)\le\alpha\}.\] If \(Y(x,\xi)\) has a continuous distribution, then \(\mathbb{P}(Y(x,\xi)\le q_\alpha(x))=\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simulation objective is often the expected response, but it can instead be an alpha-quantile of the response. For a continuous response distribution, the cumulative probability at the stated quantile equals alpha.
assumptions_latex: Y(x,\xi)\text{ is a simulation-output random variable}
Y(x,\xi)\text{ has a continuous distribution for the equality characterization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)\text{ may equal }\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)]\text{ or }q_\alpha(x),\quad \mathbb{P}(Y(x,\xi)\le q_\alpha(x))=\alpha\text{ under continuity}.
