children.title: Independent-Replication Estimation
children.top_down_role: Replication-based estimation for terminating simulations.

assumptions_latex: For a fixed decision \(x\), the terminating-run outputs \(Y_1(x),Y_2(x),\ldots\) are independent and identically distributed.
The mean \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y_1(x)]\) exists and the variance satisfies \(0<\sigma^2(x)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1(x))<\infty\).
The finite-sample estimators are formed with an integer \(n\ge 2\), and the confidence level uses \(0<\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sample mean is unbiased with variance \(\sigma^2(x)/n\), and its Studentized error is asymptotically standard normal.

notation.meaning: standard-normal quantile of cumulative probability p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminating simulations with independent, identically distributed replications.

source_refs.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\bar Y_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(x)\) and \(S_n^2(x)=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i(x)-\bar Y_n(x))^2\). Then \(\mathbb E[\bar Y_n(x)]=f(x)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n(x))=\sigma^2(x)/n\). As \(n\to\infty\), \(\sqrt n(\bar Y_n(x)-f(x))/S_n(x)\Rightarrow N(0,1)\). Consequently, \(\bar Y_n(x)\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}S_n(x)/\sqrt n\) is an asymptotic two-sided confidence interval with coverage \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent and identically distributed terminating runs with positive finite variance, the sample mean is unbiased, its variance decreases inversely with the replication count, and Studentization gives an asymptotic normal confidence interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Replication Estimation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bias and quadratic-deviation bounds for a Markov-chain estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded statement under the preceding, unextracted estimator and contraction hypotheses defining all notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the preceding hypotheses for \(\widehat H_n\), \(L(H)\), \(r\), \(\gamma\), and \(\rho\), \[\left|\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat H_n)\right|=\left|\mathbb E(\widehat H_n)-\pi H\right|\leq \frac{L(H)r(\gamma,\pi)}{n(1-\rho)},\] and \[\operatorname{QDev}(\widehat H_n)\leq \frac{[L(H)]^2\pi(R_\pi^2)}{n(1-\rho)}+O(n^{-2}),\qquad R_\pi(u)=r(\delta_u,\pi).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the lemma's preceding Markov-chain assumptions, the estimator has bias of order at most 1/n and quadratic deviation bounded by a leading term of order 1/n plus an order-1/n² remainder.
assumptions_latex: \text{The preceding hypotheses defining }\widehat H_n,L(H),r,\gamma,\rho\text{ and QDev hold.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|\mathbb E(\widehat H_n)-\pi H\right|\leq \frac{L(H)r(\gamma,\pi)}{n(1-\rho)},\qquad \operatorname{QDev}(\widehat H_n)\leq \frac{[L(H)]^2\pi(R_\pi^2)}{n(1-\rho)}+O(n^{-2}).

children.title: Batch-Means Estimation
children.top_down_role: Aggregation-based output analysis for serially dependent simulation observations.

assumptions_latex: The stationary output sequence \((Y_t)_{t\ge1}\) has mean \(\mu\) and satisfies a central limit theorem with long-run variance \(\tau^2\).
The run length is \(n=ab\), with batch size \(b\to\infty\) and number of batches \(a\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Batch averages estimate the sampling variance of the overall mean while retaining within-batch dependence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonoverlapping batch means for a stationary dependent simulation output sequence.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) into \(a\) consecutive nonoverlapping batches of length \(b\). Compute \(\bar Y_j^{(b)}=b^{-1}\sum_{t=(j-1)b+1}^{jb}Y_t\), \(\bar Y_n=a^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^a\bar Y_j^{(b)}\), and \(\widehat{\tau}^2=b(a-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^a(\bar Y_j^{(b)}-\bar Y_n)^2\). Report \(\bar Y_n\) with estimated variance \(\widehat{\tau}^2/n\), stopping when a prespecified run budget or confidence-interval half-width criterion is met. Under the stated limits and standard mixing conditions, \(\widehat{\tau}^2\) is consistent for \(\tau^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide one dependent run into long consecutive batches, treat batch averages as asymptotically independent, and use their sample variance to estimate the mean's long-run variance.
knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Means Estimation

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf and its formulas use the conventional long-run-variance scaling. However, a central limit theorem alone does not imply consistency of the batch-means variance estimator, and the phrase 'standard mixing conditions' does not state sufficient hypotheses. The cited Markov-chain locator is indirect and cannot establish the required batch-means consistency theorem.

children.title: Time-Series Output Estimation
children.top_down_role: Dependence-aware estimation based on temporal models or spectral structure.

assumptions_latex: The process \((Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}\) is covariance-stationary with mean \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The variance of the sample mean is governed by the spectral density at frequency zero, not merely by the marginal variance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary time-series representation of uncertainty in a dependent simulation average.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\), 
\[n\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)\gamma_k\longrightarrow \tau^2:=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\gamma_k=2\pi g(0).\]
Thus consistent uncertainty quantification for \(\mu\) requires an estimator of \(\tau^2\), such as a consistent spectral-variance or batch-means estimator. If a central limit theorem also holds, then \(\sqrt n(\bar Y_n-\mu)\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For dependent stationary output, the sample mean's uncertainty is determined by all autocovariances, equivalently the spectrum at zero frequency.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Series Output Estimation

children.title: Serial-Dependence Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Assessment of dependence patterns that affect output-estimation choices.

assumptions_latex: After removal of any prescribed transient, \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are observations from a covariance-stationary process.
The sample autocovariances are computed using a common declared normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Autocorrelation and effective-sample-size diagnostics quantify observed serial dependence but do not by themselves establish stationarity or independence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample diagnostics for dependence in a single simulation-output series.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For chosen lag limit \(K<n\), compute \(\widehat\rho_k=\widehat\gamma_k/\widehat\gamma_0\) for \(1\le k\le K\), inspect the autocorrelation sequence, and estimate \(\widehat n_{\mathrm{eff}}=n/(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k\widehat\rho_k)\) using declared nonnegative truncation weights \(w_k\). Large persistent values of \(\lvert\widehat\rho_k\rvert\), or \(\widehat n_{\mathrm{eff}}\ll n\), diagnose material serial dependence. A portmanteau statistic may test selected zero-autocorrelation restrictions, but failure to reject them is not a certificate of independence or adequate warm-up.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample autocorrelations, effective sample size, and portmanteau tests can flag serial dependence, but cannot certify stationarity or independence.
knowledge_statements.title: Serial-Dependence Diagnostics

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a diagnostic procedure rather than a mathematical condition, so algorithm is the better terminal kind. Moreover, the finite-lag effective-sample-size denominator can be nonpositive or unstable, and its interpretation depends on a specified truncation or initial-sequence rule. The indirect Markov-chain locator does not support these diagnostic conventions or the portmanteau claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Atom and regenerative return cycles for an ergodic Markov chain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition together with the regenerative-block consequence stated in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf P\) be an ergodic Markov transition kernel with unique stationary probability measure \(\pi\). A Borel set \(A\) is an atom for \(\mathbf P\) if, for every measurable \(B\), \(\mathbf P(w,B)\) is independent of \(w\in A\), and \(\pi(A)>0\). If \(M(0)\in A\), define \[T_1^{(A)}=\min\{n:M(n)\in A\},\qquad T_{i+1}^{(A)}=\min\{n>T_i^{(A)}:M(n)\in A\}.\] Then \(M(1),M(T_1^{(A)}+1),M(T_2^{(A)}+1),\ldots\) have the same distribution, and the path segments delimited by successive return times are independent regenerative pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom is a positive-stationary-probability Borel set on which the transition law is constant. When the chain starts in the atom, successive returns delimit independent regenerative path pieces.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf P\text{ is an ergodic Markov transition kernel with unique stationary law }\pi
M(0)\in A\text{ for the regenerative-cycle conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall B,\ \mathbf P(w,B)\text{ is constant for }w\in A\bigr]\land \pi(A)>0,\quad\text{and successive returns to }A\text{ delimit independent regenerative pieces.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regenerative cycle formula for stationary expectations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded cycle-reward representation using the regeneration time defined in the surrounding text.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf P\) be an ergodic Markov process with atom \(A\) and stationary distribution \(\pi\). For every measurable \(H\) integrable with respect to \(\pi\), \[\int H(w)\,d\pi(w)=\frac{\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{T^{(A)}}H(M(n))\right]}{\mathbb E[T^{(A)}]}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an ergodic Markov process with an atom, a stationary expectation equals the expected reward accumulated during one regenerative cycle divided by the expected cycle length.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf P\text{ is an ergodic Markov process with atom }A
\pi\text{ is the stationary distribution of }\mathbf P
H\text{ is measurable and integrable with respect to }\pi
T^{(A)}\text{ is the regenerative cycle time defined in the surrounding text}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int H\,d\pi=\frac{\mathbb E\left[\sum_{n=1}^{T^{(A)}}H(M(n))\right]}{\mathbb E[T^{(A)}]}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interval-estimation policy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Action selection using an optimistic percentile or confidence-bound score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given value estimates \(\bar\mu_x^n\), estimated standard deviations \(\bar\sigma_x^n\), and a tunable multiplier \(\theta^{IE}\), the interval-estimation policy is \[X^{IE}(S^n\mid\theta^{IE})\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x}\{\bar\mu_x^n+\theta^{IE}\bar\sigma_x^n\}.\] Under a percentile interpretation, the added uncertainty term values an action optimistically. As the number of observations of action \(x\) tends to infinity, \(\bar\sigma_x^n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an action maximizing its estimated value plus a tunable multiple of its estimated standard error. The uncertainty bonus vanishes as that action is observed indefinitely.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar\mu_x^n\) estimates the value of each admissible action \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X^{IE}(S^n\mid\theta^{IE})\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x}\left(\bar\mu_x^n+\theta^{IE}\bar\sigma_x^n\right),\qquad \bar\sigma_x^n\to0\text{ as the observation count for }x\to\infty.

children.title: Natural Regeneration
children.top_down_role: Regeneration arising directly from simulated system dynamics.

assumptions_latex: The simulated process \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) has stopping times \(0=T_0<T_1<T_2<\cdots\) at which its physical state naturally resets.
Post-regeneration evolution is independent of the past and has the same law after every \(T_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The complete cycles between successive regeneration times are independent and identically distributed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regeneration induced by an actual recurrent reset state or event of the simulated system.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Natural regeneration occurs when stopping times \((T_k)_{k\ge0}\) are generated by events in the original simulated dynamics and, for every \(k\), the shifted future \((X_{T_k+t})_{t\ge0}\) is independent of the history through \(T_k\) and has a common law. For a reward \(r\), define \(L_k=T_k-T_{k-1}\) and \(R_k=\sum_{t=T_{k-1}}^{T_k-1}r(X_t)\). Then the complete cycle pairs \((R_k,L_k)\) are independent and identically distributed, permitting estimation of the steady-state mean by ratios of accumulated cycle rewards and lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A natural reset event makes successive simulation cycles independent and identically distributed, so steady-state performance can be estimated from cycle rewards and lengths.
knowledge_statements.title: Natural Regeneration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regenerative system and regeneration cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines probabilistic regeneration and states the cycle structure available under additional regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A system is regenerative at deterministic or random times \(\tau_0<\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots\) when, at each \(\tau_i\), it probabilistically restarts: its future behavior has the applicable restart law and is independent of its past behavior. Under suitable additional conditions, successive regenerative cycles are independent and identically distributed stochastic processes. If the regeneration points are random, their successive cycle lengths \(\tau_{i+1}-\tau_i\) are i.i.d. random variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regenerative system probabilistically starts anew at each regeneration time, making its future independent of its past. Under suitable additional conditions, successive cycles are i.i.d.; when regeneration times are random, the cycle lengths are also i.i.d.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_0<\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots\) are deterministic or random regeneration times.
At every \(\tau_i\), the system has the applicable restart law and its future behavior is independent of its past behavior.
Suitable additional conditions hold for the asserted i.i.d. cycle conclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successive regenerative cycles are i.i.d.; if the regeneration points are random, then \(\{\tau_{i+1}-\tau_i\}_{i\ge 0}\) are i.i.d. random lengths.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: State-dependent minorization condition for artificial regeneration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded kernel domination condition used to construct regenerative structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist a measurable function \(\lambda\) satisfying \(0\leq\lambda(z)<1\) and a probability measure \(\nu\) such that, for every applicable state \(z\) and measurable set \(B\), \[\mathbf P(z,B)\geq \lambda(z)\nu(B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transition kernel dominates a fixed probability measure at each state, with a measurable state-dependent coefficient between zero and one.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf P\text{ is a Markov transition kernel}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf P(z,B)\geq\lambda(z)\nu(B)\quad\text{for every applicable }z\text{ and measurable }B.

children.title: Constructed Regeneration
children.top_down_role: Artificial regenerative structure introduced through model-specific state or event design.

assumptions_latex: A Markov kernel \(P\) admits an exactly implementable decomposition on a measurable set \(C\).
The auxiliary randomization used to declare regenerations is independent conditional on the simulated transition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented simulation has regeneration times while preserving the original \(X\)-marginal transition kernel.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Artificial cycle construction that preserves the simulator's marginal dynamics.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a valid mixture \(P(x,\cdot)=\varepsilon\nu(\cdot)+(1-\varepsilon)R(x,\cdot)\) for \(x\in C\), augment the simulation with \(\Delta_n\in\{0,1\}\). Whenever \(X_n\in C\), draw \(\Delta_n\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\varepsilon)\); if \(\Delta_n=1\), draw \(X_{n+1}\sim\nu\), and otherwise draw \(X_{n+1}\sim R(X_n,\cdot)\). Outside \(C\), draw from \(P(X_n,\cdot)\). Declare \(n+1\) a regeneration time when \(\Delta_n=1\). Output complete augmented cycles, discarding any initial incomplete cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construct regeneration by expressing selected transitions as an exact mixture, sampling a latent mixture indicator, and declaring regeneration whenever its state-independent component is selected.
knowledge_statements.title: Constructed Regeneration

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed mixture construction is recognizable, and algorithm is the correct role, but the assumption that auxiliary randomization is independent conditional on the simulated transition is ambiguous and does not directly describe the generative split used in the statement. The cited general Markov-chain section does not provide inspectable support for this exact construction.

children.title: Split-Chain Regeneration
children.top_down_role: Regenerative structure obtained through an augmented chain representation.

assumptions_latex: For a Markov kernel \(P\), a measurable set \(C\), constant \(\varepsilon>0\), and probability measure \(\nu\), \(P(x,A)\ge\varepsilon\nu(A)\) for every \(x\in C\) and measurable \(A\).
The chain returns to \(C\) with probability one from the relevant initial laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nummelin splitting yields an augmented chain with an atom whose returns are regeneration times and whose \(X\)-marginal kernel remains \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time Nummelin splitting under a one-step small-set minorization.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in C\), define the residual kernel \(R(x,A)=(P(x,A)-\varepsilon
u(A))/(1-\varepsilon)\) when \(\varepsilon<1\). The split transition selects \(
u\) with probability \(\varepsilon\) and \(R(x,\cdot)\) otherwise; outside \(C\), it uses \(P\). Its marginal transition satisfies \(\varepsilon
u(A)+(1-\varepsilon)R(x,A)=P(x,A)\). In the augmented state space, the selected \(
u\)-component is an atom, and successive returns to that atom define regenerative cycles under the recurrence assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small-set minorization decomposes a Markov transition into state-independent and residual parts; an auxiliary indicator turns the state-independent part into a regenerative atom.
knowledge_statements.title: Split-Chain Regeneration

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minorization and residual-kernel identity are standard, but merely saying that the chain returns to the small set with probability one does not explicitly guarantee the repeated returns needed for successive regenerative cycles. The atom construction also depends on the precise split-chain convention. A direct theorem locator with the recurrence hypotheses is required.

children.title: Artificial-Regeneration Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limitations affecting whether introduced regeneration supports reliable output analysis.

assumptions_latex: Artificial regeneration is proposed for a simulated process with transition kernel \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regenerative inference is invalid unless the augmentation preserves \(P\) and produces genuinely regenerative, integrable cycles.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions whose failure invalidates artificial-regeneration estimators or their uncertainty statements.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Artificial-regeneration inference fails if the alleged minorization is false, if the residual kernel is not nonnegative, or if the auxiliary splitting rule changes the \(X\)-marginal kernel \(P\). Even with a valid split, ordinary regenerative variance estimation is unavailable when regeneration times are not almost surely recurrent, \(\mathbb E[L_1]=\infty\), or the moment conditions required for the cycle central limit theorem fail, such as \(\mathbb E[(R_1-\mu L_1)^2]=\infty\). Approximate resets or merely frequent visits to a set do not create independent and identically distributed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Artificial regeneration is invalid if splitting changes the original chain, lacks a true minorization, fails to recur, or produces cycles without the moments required for inference.
knowledge_statements.title: Artificial-Regeneration Validity Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct content kind, and the listed failure modes are plausible. The exact recurrence and moment requirements for regenerative laws of large numbers, central limit theorems, and variance estimation must nevertheless be tied to a direct regenerative-process source; the cited general Markov-chain section is insufficient.

children.title: Monte Carlo Sampling Error
children.top_down_role: Finite-simulation uncertainty in estimated performance.

assumptions_latex: For a fixed decision \(x\), the simulator outputs \(Y_1(x),Y_2(x),\ldots\) are independent and identically distributed with mean \(f(x)\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2(x)\).
The replication count \(n\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite replication produces zero-mean estimation error with standard deviation \(\sigma(x)/\sqrt n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat f_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(x)\) and \(E_n(x)=\widehat f_n(x)-f(x)\). Then \(\mathbb E[E_n(x)]=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(E_n(x))=\sigma^2(x)/n\), and \(E_n(x)=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\). If the classical central limit theorem applies, then \(\sqrt nE_n(x)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2(x))\). This error is conditional on the chosen simulator model, horizon, initialization, discretization, and decision; it excludes bias and input-model uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monte Carlo sampling error is the random difference between an average of independent and identically distributed simulator outputs and their simulator expectation; its standard deviation decreases at the square-root rate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monte Carlo sample mean and empirical variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment estimation for a possibly design-dependent objective using samples from an uncertainty distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given samples \(\mathbf z^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf z^{(m)}\) from a distribution \(p\) on \(\mathcal Z\), Monte Carlo integration approximates the objective mean and variance by
\[\widehat\mu=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m f(\mathbf z^{(i)}),\qquad \widehat v=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m f(\mathbf z^{(i)})^2-\widehat\mu^2.\]
If \(f=f(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)\), these quantities are recomputed for each new design point \(\mathbf x\), even when \(\mathbf x\) is suppressed from the notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For samples from the uncertainty distribution, the sample mean is the average objective value and the empirical variance is the average squared objective value minus the squared sample mean. When the objective also depends on a design point, both estimates are recomputed at each new design point.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf z^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf z^{(m)}\text{ are sampled from }p\text{ on }\mathcal Z
f(\mathbf z^{(i)})\text{ and }f(\mathbf z^{(i)})^2\text{ are evaluable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_{\mathbf z\sim p}[f(\mathbf z)]\approx\widehat\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_{\mathbf z\sim p}[f(\mathbf z)]\approx\widehat v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-Monte Carlo and randomized-shift integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Low-discrepancy quadrature on the unit cube, including the regularity needed for its standard deterministic error rate and random shifts for uncertainty assessment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\bar f=\int_{[0,1]^D}f(x)\,dx\), QMC uses a low-discrepancy sequence \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) and \(\widehat f_N=N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^N f(x_n)\). If \(f\) has bounded Hardy--Krause variation and the sequence has star discrepancy \(D_N^*=O((\log N)^D/N)\), then
\[|\bar f-\widehat f_N|\leq V_{HK}(f)D_N^*=O((\log N)^D/N),\]
whereas ordinary independent Monte Carlo has root-mean-square error \(O(N^{-1/2})\) when \(f(X)\) has finite variance. A randomized shift sets \(y_{i,r}=(x_i+u_r)\bmod 1\), with independent \(u_r\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^D)\); every \(y_{i,r}\) is marginally uniform, and independent repetitions permit empirical uncertainty estimation while retaining a randomized low-discrepancy design.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi-Monte Carlo replaces independent random points by low-discrepancy points. Under the standard bounded-variation and discrepancy assumptions, its deterministic integration error is of order (log N)^D divided by N, compared with root-mean-square order N to the minus one half for ordinary Monte Carlo. Randomly shifting the point set modulo one gives uniform marginal points and repeated randomized estimates from which uncertainty can be assessed.
assumptions_latex: f:[0,1]^D\to\mathbb R\text{ has bounded Hardy--Krause variation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\bar f-\widehat f_N|=O((\log N)^D/N),\qquad \operatorname{RMSE}_{MC}=O(N^{-1/2}),\qquad y_{i,r}=(x_i+u_r)\bmod 1\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^D).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-form Bayesian Monte Carlo for Gaussian inputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm for the posterior mean and variance of a Gaussian-process integral with a Gaussian kernel and normally distributed input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given GP observations (Z,\mathbf y), Gaussian-kernel widths \mathbf w, and \mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_z,\Sigma_z), set W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1^2,\ldots,w_n^2),\ K=K(Z,Z), and q_i=|W^{-1}\Sigma_z+I|^{-1/2}\exp[-\tfrac12(\mathbf z^{(i)}-\boldsymbol\mu_z)^\top(W+\Sigma_z)^{-1}(\mathbf z^{(i)}-\boldsymbol\mu_z)]. Return \mu_I=\mathbf q^\top K^{-1}\mathbf y and v_I=|2W^{-1}\Sigma_z+I|^{-1/2}-\mathbf q^\top K^{-1}\mathbf q.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Form the diagonal matrix of squared Gaussian-kernel widths and the inverse kernel matrix on the observed inputs. Compute one Gaussian-overlap weight for each observation, then return q-transpose K-inverse y as the estimated integral mean and a determinant term minus q-transpose K-inverse q as its posterior variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_I,v_I)=\left(\mathbf q^\top K^{-1}\mathbf y,\ |2W^{-1}\Sigma_z+I|^{-1/2}-\mathbf q^\top K^{-1}\mathbf q\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Antithetic-pair variance reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired unbiased estimation using negatively correlated samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y_1,Y_2\) have finite second moments and satisfy \(\mathbb E[Y_1]=\mathbb E[Y_2]=\theta\). Then \(\widehat\theta=(Y_1+Y_2)/2\) is unbiased and
\[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)+\operatorname{Var}(Y_2)+2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)}{4}.\]
Thus, for fixed marginal variances, negative covariance reduces variance relative to independent pairing. For \(Y_1\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), choosing \(Y_2=1-Y_1\) preserves the uniform marginal and gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)=-1/12<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The average of two samples having the target mean is unbiased. Its variance includes their covariance, so coupling the samples negatively reduces variance relative to independent samples with the same marginal variances. For a uniform sample, its antithetic partner 1 minus the sample is also uniform and is negatively correlated with it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[\widehat\theta]=\theta,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)+\operatorname{Var}(Y_2)+2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)}{4},\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)<0\Rightarrow\text{variance reduction versus independent pairing}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: IID Monte Carlo Average: Unbiasedness, Variance, and Asymptotics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic finite-sample and asymptotic properties of an IID Monte Carlo average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let s=\mathbb{E}_p[f(X)] and let X_1,\ldots,X_n\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}p. Define \widehat{s}_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i). Then \mathbb{E}[\widehat{s}_n]=s. If \sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}_p(f(X))<\infty, then \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{s}_n)=\sigma^2/n, \widehat{s}_n\to s almost surely, and \sqrt n(\widehat{s}_n-s)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2). Estimating \sigma^2 from the sampled values and dividing by n yields an estimated variance for \widehat{s}_n and supports asymptotic normal confidence intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent samples from the target distribution, the sample average is unbiased. If the integrand has finite variance, the estimator variance is that variance divided by the sample size, the average converges almost surely to the target expectation, and its normalized error is asymptotically normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb{E}[\widehat{s}_n]=s,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{s}_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\quad \widehat{s}_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}s,\quad \sqrt n(\widehat{s}_n-s)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gaussian-process posterior mean and variance of an integral
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayesian Monte Carlo representation, including the analytic Gaussian-kernel and Gaussian-input case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let I(\widehat f)=\int_{\mathcal Z}\widehat f(\mathbf z)p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z, where \widehat f has Gaussian-process posterior mean \widehat\mu and covariance C. Then \mathbb E_{\widehat f}[I(\widehat f)]=\int_{\mathcal Z}\widehat\mu(\mathbf z)p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z and \operatorname{Var}_{\widehat f}[I(\widehat f)]=\int_{\mathcal Z}\!\int_{\mathcal Z}C(\mathbf z,\mathbf z')p(\mathbf z)p(\mathbf z')\,d\mathbf z\,d\mathbf z'. For observations Z and kernel matrix K, C(\mathbf z,\mathbf z')=k(\mathbf z,\mathbf z')-k(\mathbf z,Z)K(Z,Z)^{-1}k(Z,\mathbf z'). If \mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_z,\Sigma_z) and k(\mathbf x,\mathbf x')=\exp[-\tfrac12\sum_j(x_j-x_j')^2/w_j^2], with W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1^2,\ldots,w_n^2), then the posterior integral mean is \mathbf q^\top K^{-1}\mathbf y, where q_i=|W^{-1}\Sigma_z+I|^{-1/2}\exp[-\tfrac12(\boldsymbol\mu_z-\mathbf z^{(i)})^\top(\Sigma_z+W)^{-1}(\boldsymbol\mu_z-\mathbf z^{(i)})], and its variance is |2W^{-1}\Sigma_z+I|^{-1/2}-\mathbf q^\top K^{-1}\mathbf q.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a Gaussian-process posterior, the mean of an integral is the integral of the posterior mean, while its variance is the double integral of the posterior covariance. For a Gaussian input distribution and anisotropic Gaussian kernel, both quantities have closed forms involving the kernel matrix and a vector q determined by the input mean, covariance, kernel widths, and observed inputs.
assumptions_latex: I(\widehat f)=\int_{\mathcal Z}\widehat f(\mathbf z)p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z\text{ exists and the displayed expectations and integrals may be interchanged}
\text{For the closed form: }\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_z,\Sigma_z),\quad k(\mathbf x,\mathbf x')=\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12\sum_j\frac{(x_j-x_j')^2}{w_j^2}\right],\quad w_j>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_{\widehat f}[I(\widehat f)]=\int\widehat\mu(\mathbf z)p(\mathbf z)d\mathbf z,\quad \operatorname{Var}_{\widehat f}[I(\widehat f)]=\iint C(\mathbf z,\mathbf z')p(\mathbf z)p(\mathbf z')d\mathbf z d\mathbf z',\text{ with the stated Gaussian closed forms.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monte Carlo sample-mean estimator and its variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation estimation and finite-sample uncertainty for independent sampling from a probability density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)} be independent draws from a probability density p, with \operatorname{Var}_{X\sim p}(f(X))<\infty. The Monte Carlo sample mean \widehat{\mu}_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(X^{(i)}) estimates \mathbb{E}_{X\sim p}[f(X)]=\int f(x)p(x)\,\mathrm{d}x, and \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\mu}_n)=\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim p}(f(X))/n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent draws from the density p, the sample mean estimates the expectation of f(X). When f(X) has finite variance, the variance of this estimator equals the variance of f(X) divided by the sample size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{\mu}_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(X^{(i)})\ \text{estimates}\ \mathbb{E}_{X\sim p}[f(X)]=\int f(x)p(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\mu}_n)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim p}(f(X))}{n}.

children.title: Warm-Up Deletion Regimes
children.top_down_role: Output-analysis regimes distinguished by how early observations are excluded.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Up Deletion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion schedules for estimating a steady-state mean from one finite simulation run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given outputs \(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_n(x)\), choose an integer deletion schedule \(w_n\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and return
\[\widehat\mu_n(x)=\frac{1}{n-w_n}\sum_{t=w_n+1}^{n}Y_t(x).\]
Three deletion regimes are fixed deletion \(w_n=w\), fractional deletion \(w_n=\lfloor\rho n\rfloor\) with \(0<\rho<1\), and increasing sublinear deletion with \(w_n\to\infty\) and \(w_n/n\to0\). Stop at a prescribed horizon \(n\), and report both \(w_n\) and the retained sample size \(n-w_n\) with the estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete a fixed, fractional, or increasing sublinear prefix, then average retained observations and report the deletion and retained sample sizes.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_n(x)\) are sequential outputs from one simulation run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\mu_n(x)=(n-w_n)^{-1}\sum_{t=w_n+1}^{n}Y_t(x)\).

notation.meaning: fraction deleted in the fractional regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bias Rates of Markov Sensitivity Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic initialization- and finite-horizon bias rates for three Markov sensitivity estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be bounded and Lipschitz, and let the process start with distribution \(\gamma\). As \(n,m\), respectively \(N\), tend to infinity,
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{weak})})=O(r(\gamma,\pi_x))O(\rho^m)+O(\rho^n),
\]
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{single})})=O(r(\gamma,\pi_x))O(N\rho^N)+O(\rho^N),
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{average})})=O(N^{-1}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded Lipschitz H, the weak and single-run estimators have geometrically decreasing bias terms involving initialization and horizon length, while the averaged estimator has bias of order 1/N.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{weak})})=O(r(\gamma,\pi_x))O(\rho^m)+O(\rho^n),\quad\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{single})})=O(r(\gamma,\pi_x))O(N\rho^N)+O(\rho^N),\quad\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{average})})=O(N^{-1}).

children.title: Finite-Horizon Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion caused by evaluating a system over a bounded simulation horizon.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias caused by replacing an infinite-horizon or steady-state objective with finite simulation time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J_\infty(x)\) be the target infinite-horizon performance and let \(J_T(x)\) be the expected performance computed over horizon \(T<\infty\) under the same decision and model. The finite-horizon bias is
\[b_T^{\mathrm{FH}}(x)=J_T(x)-J_\infty(x).\]
For a time-average criterion, \(J_T(x)=T^{-1}\mathbb E[\sum_{t=1}^{T}Y_t(x)]\). Finite-horizon consistency means \(b_T^{\mathrm{FH}}(x)\to0\) as \(T\to\infty\); its sign is not determined without additional monotonicity or transient assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-horizon bias is the expected truncated-horizon performance minus its infinite-horizon target; its sign need not be fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(J_T(x)\) and \(J_\infty(x)\) are finite and use the same decision \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_T^{\mathrm{FH}}(x)=J_T(x)-J_\infty(x)\).

children.title: Numerical-Discretization Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion caused by approximate temporal, spatial, or state discretization.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Discretization Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak bias induced by numerically discretizing a continuous-state or continuous-time simulator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) denote an exact simulated object, \(X^{(h)}\) its numerical approximation at resolution \(h>0\), and \(F\) an integrable performance functional. The numerical-discretization bias is
\[b_h^{\mathrm{disc}}=\mathbb E[F(X^{(h)})]-\mathbb E[F(X)].\]
The approximation has weak order \(p>0\) for \(F\) if constants \(C,h_0>0\) exist such that \(\lvert b_h^{\mathrm{disc}}\rvert\leq Ch^p\) for every \(0<h\leq h_0\). This bias is distinct from Monte Carlo sampling error at fixed \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discretization bias is the difference between expected performance under a numerical simulator and under the exact model; weak order describes its decay.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_h^{\mathrm{disc}}=\mathbb E[F(X^{(h)})]-\mathbb E[F(X)]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak-error definition is standard and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for either the bias formula or weak-order condition.

children.title: Approximation-Scale Bias Interaction
children.top_down_role: Joint bias behavior when horizon length and numerical resolution vary together.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Scale Bias Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition separating horizon, discretization, and nonadditive interaction biases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J_{T,h}(x)\) be expected simulated performance at horizon \(T\) and discretization scale \(h\), with limits \(J_{T,0}(x)\), \(J_{\infty,h}(x)\), and \(J_{\infty,0}(x)\) well defined. Then
\[J_{T,h}-J_{\infty,0}=(J_{T,0}-J_{\infty,0})+(J_{\infty,h}-J_{\infty,0})+\Delta_{T,h},\]
where
\[\Delta_{T,h}=J_{T,h}-J_{T,0}-J_{\infty,h}+J_{\infty,0}.\]
Thus \(\Delta_{T,h}\) is the approximation-scale interaction: it vanishes exactly when the joint horizon-discretization bias is additive at \((T,h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total approximation bias equals pure horizon bias plus pure discretization bias plus a cross-difference measuring their nonadditive interaction.
assumptions_latex: All four quantities use the same decision \(x\) and performance convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{T,h}-J_{\infty,0}=(J_{T,0}-J_{\infty,0})+(J_{\infty,h}-J_{\infty,0})+\Delta_{T,h}\).

notation.meaning: performance at horizon T and scale h

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cross-difference is an exact and appropriate representation of nonadditive interaction, but the record has no cited source supporting this interpretation in the simulation-bias setting.

children.title: Input-Model Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty inherited from estimated input laws and dependence models.

children.title: Parametric Input Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty in fitted input parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Input Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncertainty propagated from finite-data estimation of parameters within a fixed input family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the simulator input law belong to a fixed family \(\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\), let \(D\) be input data generated under \(P_{\theta_0}\), and let \(\widehat\theta(D)\) estimate \(\theta_0\). For decision \(x\), write \(\mu(x;\theta)=\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[Y(x)]\). Parametric input uncertainty is the sampling-induced uncertainty in
\[U_D(x)=\mu(x;\widehat\theta(D))-\mu(x;\theta_0),\]
with randomness taken over repeated input datasets \(D\). It conditions on the chosen parametric family and therefore excludes uncertainty about whether that family is correctly specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parametric input uncertainty is variation in simulated performance caused by estimating a fixed input model's parameters from finite data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_D(x)=\mu(x;\widehat\theta(D))-\mu(x;\theta_0)\).

notation.meaning: mean simulation response under parameter theta

children.title: Distributional-Family Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty about the family or shape of simulator input distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional-Family Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input uncertainty arising from ambiguity over the parametric or nonparametric distribution family itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M\) index candidate input-distribution families \(\mathcal P_m\), and let \(\mathcal A(D)\subseteq\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal M}\mathcal P_m\) contain distributions compatible with input data \(D\). For decision \(x\), define \(\mu(x;P)=\mathbb E_P[Y(x)]\). Distributional-family uncertainty is present when there exist \(m\neq m'\), \(P\in\mathcal A(D)\cap\mathcal P_m\), and \(Q\in\mathcal A(D)\cap\mathcal P_{m'}\) such that
\[\mu(x;P)\neq\mu(x;Q).\]
It concerns variation across families, rather than parameter estimation within one fixed family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributional-family uncertainty occurs when data-compatible input laws from different model families produce different expected simulation responses.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A(D)\) contains input laws judged compatible with the observed data.
\(\mu(x;P)\) is finite for every considered law \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists P,Q\in\mathcal A(D)\) from distinct families with \(\mu(x;P)\neq\mu(x;Q)\).

notation.meaning: candidate distribution family indexed by m

children.title: Tail-Behavior Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty concentrated in extreme input behavior or rare outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Behavior Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input uncertainty caused by poorly identified probabilities or magnitudes of extreme events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A(D)\) be a set of data-compatible input laws and let \(T_\tau(P)\) be a tail functional, such as an exceedance probability or an upper-tail quantile at level \(\tau\). Tail-behavior uncertainty relevant to decision \(x\) is present if there exist \(P,Q\in\mathcal A(D)\) satisfying the imposed central-distribution constraints but
\[T_\tau(P)\neq T_\tau(Q)\quad\text{and}\quad \mu(x;P)\neq\mu(x;Q),\]
where \(\mu(x;P)=\mathbb E_P[Y(x)]\). The definition isolates performance variation attributable to unresolved tail behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail-behavior uncertainty exists when data-compatible laws agree on central features but differ in tails and consequently in simulated performance.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) satisfy the same specified central-distribution constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\tau(P)\neq T_\tau(Q)\) and \(\mu(x;P)\neq\mu(x;Q)\).

children.title: Dependence-Structure Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty about temporal, cross-sectional, or multivariate input dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence-Structure Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input uncertainty induced by unknown joint dependence when marginal distributions are fixed or separately estimated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_d\) be prescribed input marginals and let \(\mathcal C(D)\) be a data-compatible set of copulas. Each \(C\in\mathcal C(D)\) induces a joint law \(P_C\) with those marginals. For decision \(x\), dependence-structure uncertainty is present if there exist \(C,C'\in\mathcal C(D)\) such that
\[\mu(x;P_C)=\mathbb E_{P_C}[Y(x)]\neq\mathbb E_{P_{C'}}[Y(x)]=\mu(x;P_{C'}).\]
Thus the response changes solely through admissible dependence structures, not through marginal input laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependence-structure uncertainty occurs when different data-compatible copulas with identical marginals yield different expected simulation responses.
assumptions_latex: \(P_C\) and \(P_{C'}\) have the same prescribed marginals.
The corresponding simulation responses are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C,C'\in\mathcal C(D)\) with \(\mu(x;P_C)\neq\mu(x;P_{C'})\).

notation.meaning: joint input law induced by copula C and fixed marginals

children.title: Search-Selection Bias Coupling
children.top_down_role: Bias produced when noisy data are reused for search and evaluation.

children.title: Optimization Bias
children.top_down_role: Optimistic distortion arising from optimizing over noisy performance estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Downward bias from minimizing unbiased noisy objective estimates over a finite candidate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be finite, let \(\mu(x)\) be the true objective for minimization, and suppose \(\widehat\mu(x)\) is integrable with \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(x)]=\mu(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\). Define
\[B_{\mathrm{opt}}=\mathbb E\!\left[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\widehat\mu(x)\right]-\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x).\]
Then
\[B_{\mathrm{opt}}\leq0.\]
The inequality requires no independence among the estimators. For maximization, replacing both minima by maxima reverses the inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of unbiased noisy estimates is optimistically biased downward; the maximum is biased upward.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat\mu(x)\) is integrable and pointwise unbiased for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\widehat\mu(x)]\leq\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)\).

children.title: Selection Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion arising from evaluating alternatives after data-dependent selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias in an in-sample estimate caused by selecting the reported candidate using the same estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be finite and nonempty, let \(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}\widehat\mu(x)\) under a fixed measurable tie rule, and let \(\mu(x)\) be true expected performance. The selection bias of the reported in-sample value is
\[B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(\widehat x)-\mu(\widehat x)].\]
Pointwise unbiasedness of \(\widehat\mu(x)\) does not imply \(B_{\mathrm{sel}}=0\), because \(\widehat x\) depends on the estimation errors. If, additionally, \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(x)]=\mu(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\) and all candidates have the same true mean, then
\[B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb E\!\left[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}(\widehat\mu(x)-\mu(x))\right]\leq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selection bias is the expected in-sample estimation error at a candidate chosen using those same estimates. Pointwise unbiasedness does not generally remove it; with equal true means and pointwise-unbiased estimates, it is nonpositive for minimization.
assumptions_latex: The tie-breaking rule defining \(\widehat x\) is measurable and fixed in advance.
For the nonpositivity conclusion, \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(x)]=\mu(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), and \(\mu(x)\) is constant over \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(\widehat x)-\mu(\widehat x)]\); under equal true means and pointwise unbiasedness, \(B_{\mathrm{sel}}\leq0\).

notation.meaning: candidate selected by minimizing noisy estimates

children.title: Search-Generated Evaluation Bias
children.top_down_role: Evaluation distortion caused by reusing exploratory simulation evidence for final assessment.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Generated Evaluation Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of fixed-design unbiasedness when search and evaluation reuse the same random data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be simulation data, let \(g(x,Z)\) satisfy \(\mathbb E[g(x,Z)]=\mu(x)\) for every fixed \(x\), and let search return the data-dependent decision \(\widehat x=s(Z)\). Reusing \(Z\) gives adaptive evaluation bias
\[B_{\mathrm{SG}}=\mathbb E[g(s(Z),Z)-\mu(s(Z))],\]
which need not vanish because fixed-\(x\) unbiasedness does not extend to \(s(Z)\). If \(Z'\) is independent of \(Z\) and \(g(x,Z')\) is unbiased for every fixed \(x\), then
\[\mathbb E[g(\widehat x,Z')-\mu(\widehat x)\mid\widehat x]=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusing search data for evaluation can create bias at the adaptive decision; independent unbiased validation removes this reuse bias conditionally.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x,Z)\) is integrable and unbiased for every fixed decision \(x\).
Validation data \(Z'\), when used, are independent of \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{SG}}\) may be nonzero, whereas \(\mathbb E[g(\widehat x,Z')-\mu(\widehat x)\mid\widehat x]=0\).

children.title: Common Random Numbers
children.top_down_role: Shared random inputs across alternatives or perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Common Random Numbers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired comparison of two simulated alternatives using identical random inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let simulator outputs be \(Y_a=g(a,U)\) and \(Y_b=g(b,U)\), where both alternatives use the same random input \(U\). For independent replications \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\), estimate \(\Delta=\mathbb E[Y_a]-\mathbb E[Y_b]\) by \(\widehat\Delta_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(g(a,U_i)-g(b,U_i)\bigr)\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\Delta_n)=n^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Var}(Y_a)+\operatorname{Var}(Y_b)-2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_a,Y_b)\bigr)\). Thus common random numbers reduce variance relative to independent streams exactly when the induced covariance is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared random inputs yield an unbiased paired difference estimator and reduce its variance when the two simulated outputs are positively correlated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_a,Y_b)>0\) implies lower variance than using independent input streams.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The paired-estimator variance identity, hypotheses, plain statement, and principle content kind fit the Common Random Numbers container. However, the record has no inspectable citation, so the positive-covariance variance-reduction claim requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-stage indifference-zone selection with CRN sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: CRN ranking-and-selection procedure with a common adaptive sample size and probability-of-correct-selection guarantee. Normality and covariance sphericity delimit the stated guarantee; Bonferroni-based variants can remove sphericity at the cost of larger samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(K\) alternatives, \(\delta>0\), \(\alpha\), and \(n_0\), collect \(n_0\) replications per alternative, using the same synchronized random-number seed across alternatives at each replication \(k\) and a new seed for each \(k\). Define \(M_1(i)=n_0^{-1}\sum_k y_k(\boldsymbol\theta_i)\), \(M_2(k)=K^{-1}\sum_i y_k(\boldsymbol\theta_i)\), and \(M_3=(Kn_0)^{-1}\sum_{i,k}y_k(\boldsymbol\theta_i)\), and compute \(s^2=\frac{2\sum_{i=1}^K\sum_{k=1}^{n_0}[y_k(\boldsymbol\theta_i)-M_1(i)-M_2(k)+M_3]^2}{(K-1)(n_0-1)}\). With the prescribed multivariate-\(t\) critical value \(t\), set \(n=\max\{n_0,\lceil t^2s^2/\delta^2\rceil\}\), collect \(n-n_0\) additional replications independently of stage one while retaining CRN coupling across alternatives, and select the alternative with the smallest combined mean \(\bar L_i=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^ny_k(\boldsymbol\theta_i)\). Under normality and covariance sphericity, if \(L(\boldsymbol\theta_j)-L(\boldsymbol\theta^*)\ge\delta\) for every \(j\ne *\), then the probability of correct selection is at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use synchronized common random numbers across all alternatives in each replication, estimate a pooled residual variance after removing alternative and replication means, choose one common total sample size from that variance, collect a second stage with the same coupling, and select the smallest combined mean. Under normality and covariance sphericity, the probability of selecting the unique best alternative is at least 1−alpha whenever all competitors are worse by at least delta.
assumptions_latex: Replications are i.i.d. over \(k\), while outputs for different alternatives at the same \(k\) use synchronized common random numbers; the second stage is independent of the first.
The vector \((y_k(\boldsymbol\theta_1),\ldots,y_k(\boldsymbol\theta_K))^T\) is normally distributed and its covariance matrix satisfies the required sphericity condition.
The critical value \(t=t_{K-1,(K-1)(n_0-1)}^{(\alpha)}\) is chosen for the specified multivariate-\(t\) procedure.
There is a unique best alternative \(\boldsymbol\theta^*\), and \(L(\boldsymbol\theta_j)-L(\boldsymbol\theta^*)\ge\delta\) for every \(j\ne *\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: n=\max\left\{n_0,\left\lceil\frac{t^2s^2}{\delta^2}\right\rceil\right\},\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(\arg\min_i\bar L_i=\boldsymbol\theta^*\right)\ge1-\alpha.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-random-numbers coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired Monte Carlo comparison of two parameter choices or alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To compare \(\mu(\theta)=\mathbb E[f(\theta,Z)]\) and \(\mu(\theta')=\mathbb E[f(\theta',Z)]\), evaluate both alternatives using the same draws \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_S\sim p\): \[\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{CRN}}=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S\bigl(f(\theta,Z_s)-f(\theta',Z_s)\bigr).\] Its variance is \[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{CRN}})=\frac1S\left(\operatorname{Var}(f(\theta,Z))+\operatorname{Var}(f(\theta',Z))-2\operatorname{Cov}(f(\theta,Z),f(\theta',Z))\right).\] Thus common random numbers reduce variance relative to independent evaluations when the induced covariance is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common random numbers evaluate competing parameter values with the same random inputs. This reduces the variance of their paired comparison when the resulting outputs are positively correlated. Holding the samples fixed can also produce a deterministic sampled objective as a function of the parameters.
assumptions_latex: Variance reduction relative to independent sampling requires \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(\theta,Z),f(\theta',Z))>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive covariance induced by shared random inputs reduces the variance of the paired Monte Carlo comparison.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variance-minimizing common random numbers under componentwise monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes full componentwise common-random-number coupling as variance minimizing for each coordinate of the paired gradient estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathbf V_k^{(+)}\) and \(\mathbf V_k^{(-)}\) have the same number of components, the components within each vector are independent, and cross-vector dependence is permitted only between matching components. Suppose they are generated componentwise by inverse transforms of \(\mathbf U_k^{(+)}\) and \(\mathbf U_k^{(-)}\). For almost every \(\boldsymbol\Delta_k\), assume that \(Q(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k+c_k\boldsymbol\Delta_k,\mathbf V_k^{(+)})\) and \(Q(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k-c_k\boldsymbol\Delta_k,\mathbf V_k^{(-)})\) are monotone in the same direction in each matching component over its allowable range, although that direction may vary between components. Then, for every \(i\), \(\operatorname{var}[\widehat g_{ki}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k)\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k]\) is minimized by setting \(\mathbf U_k^{(+)}=\mathbf U_k^{(-)}=\mathbf U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When paired simulation outputs are generated componentwise by inverse transforms and are monotone in the same direction in every matching input component, using identical uniforms for the plus and minus evaluations minimizes each coordinate's conditional gradient-estimator variance.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbf V_k^{(+)}\) and \(\mathbf V_k^{(-)}\) have the same number of components, with independent components within each vector.
Dependence between the two vectors is allowed only for matching components: \(V_{ki}^{(+)}\) and \(V_{ki}^{(-)}\) may be dependent, while \(V_{ki}^{(+)}\perp V_{kj}^{(-)}\) for \(i\ne j\).
Both vectors are generated componentwise by inverse transforms of \(\mathbf U_k^{(+)}\) and \(\mathbf U_k^{(-)}\).
For almost every \(\boldsymbol\Delta_k\), the paired outputs are monotone in the same direction in each matching component throughout its allowable range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf U_k^{(+)}=\mathbf U_k^{(-)}=\mathbf U_k\quad\text{minimizes}\quad \operatorname{var}\!\left[\widehat g_{ki}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k)\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k\right]\quad\text{for every }i.

children.title: Partial Common Random Numbers
children.top_down_role: Partial coupling when complete stream alignment is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Common Random Numbers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling only a selected component of each alternative's random input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the input for alternative \(d\) is decomposed as \((U,V_d)\). A partial-common-random-numbers coupling uses the same realization of \(U\) for all compared alternatives while generating the residual inputs \(V_d\) according to a joint law whose marginal for each \(d\) equals its required simulation law. For alternatives \(a,b\), the paired estimator remains unbiased, and its variance is determined by the covariance induced through the shared component \(U\) and any permitted dependence between \(V_a\) and \(V_b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial common random numbers share only selected input components while preserving every alternative's correct marginal simulation law.
assumptions_latex: Each coupled pair \((U,V_d)\) has the prescribed marginal input law for alternative \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting paired difference estimator is unbiased for the difference of expected performances.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the intended partial-coupling container and correctly emphasizes preservation of each alternative's marginal input law. Because Partial Common Random Numbers is less standardized terminology and no citation is supplied, the precise definition and unbiasedness claim need authoritative support.

children.title: Antithetic Variates
children.top_down_role: Negatively associated random-input constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Antithetic Variates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance reduction by averaging negatively correlated, identically distributed outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^s)\), let \(Y=g(U)\in L^2\), and form the antithetic output \(Y^{\mathrm a}=g(\mathbf 1-U)\). Since \(\mathbf 1-U\) is also uniform, \(\overline Y^{\mathrm a}=(Y+Y^{\mathrm a})/2\) is unbiased for \(\mathbb E[Y]\), with \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y^{\mathrm a})=\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(Y)+\tfrac12\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Y^{\mathrm a})\). It improves upon the mean of two independent outputs exactly when \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Y^{\mathrm a})<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging an output with its reflected-input counterpart is unbiased and beats two independent runs precisely when their covariance is negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Y^{\mathrm a})<0\) gives variance below that of two independent replications.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reflected-uniform construction and variance comparison are mathematically precise, and principle is an appropriate content kind for this variance-reduction mechanism. No source reference or inspectable locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Antithetic-variates estimator and variance-reduction condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired antithetic estimation for independent random-vector components using componentwise complementary uniforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(N\) be even. For \(j=1,\ldots,N/2\), generate independent \(U^j\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^{d_\xi})\) and construct \((\underline\xi^j,\bar\xi^j)\) from \((U^j,1-U^j)\), with each member having the distribution of \(\xi\). Then
\[
f_{N,\mathrm{AV}}(x)=\frac{2}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N/2}\frac{Y(x,\underline\xi^j)+Y(x,\bar\xi^j)}{2}
\]
is unbiased and satisfies
\[
\operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{AV}}(x))=\frac{\sigma^2(x)}{N}+\frac{1}{N}\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(Y(x,\underline\xi^j),Y(x,\bar\xi^j)\right),
\quad \sigma^2(x)=\operatorname{Var}(Y(x,\xi)).
\]
Thus it has strictly smaller variance than crude Monte Carlo when the within-pair output covariance is negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Antithetic variates pair inputs generated from complementary uniform vectors. The paired-average estimator is unbiased, and its variance equals the crude Monte Carlo variance plus one over N times the within-pair output covariance. Negative output covariance therefore gives strict variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[f_{N,\mathrm{AV}}(x)]=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)],\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\underline\xi^j),Y(x,\bar\xi^j))<0\Rightarrow\operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{AV}}(x))<\sigma^2(x)/N

children.title: Control Variates
children.top_down_role: Variance reduction using correlated reference statistics.

knowledge_statements.title: Control Variates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear control-variate estimator with known auxiliary mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\in L^2\) have unknown mean \(\mu\), and let \(C\in L^2\) have known mean \(m_C\) and positive variance. For independent copies \((Y_i,C_i)\), define \(\widehat\mu_\beta=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(Y_i-\beta(C_i-m_C)\bigr)\). This estimator is unbiased for every fixed \(\beta\). Its variance is minimized by \(\beta^*=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)/\operatorname{Var}(C)\), yielding \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\beta^*})=\operatorname{Var}(Y)(1-\rho_{YC}^2)/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting an optimally weighted, centered reference statistic preserves the target mean and reduces variance by the squared correlation fraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta^*=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)/\operatorname{Var}(C)\) minimizes variance over fixed scalar coefficients.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar control-variate estimator, optimal fixed coefficient, and variance formula are correctly scoped. Representation is suitable because the record presents the canonical estimator form, but the claims lack an authoritative citation and locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal scalar control-variate coefficient and plug-in bias boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample unbiasedness and variance minimization for a fixed coefficient, together with the limitation of estimating the coefficient from data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb E[C]=0\), \(0<\operatorname{Var}(C)<\infty\), and \(\sigma^2(x)=\operatorname{Var}(Y(x,\xi))<\infty\). For i.i.d. paired observations \((Y(x,\xi^j),C^j)\) and fixed \(\lambda\), \[f_{N,\mathrm{CV}}(x;\lambda)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(Y(x,\xi^j)+\lambda C^j\bigr)\] is unbiased and has variance \[\frac1N\left(\sigma^2(x)+\lambda^2\operatorname{Var}(C)+2\lambda\operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\xi),C)\right).\] Its variance is minimized at \[\lambda^*=-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\xi),C)}{\operatorname{Var}(C)},\] giving \[\operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{CV}}(x;\lambda^*))=\frac1N\left(\sigma^2(x)-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\xi),C)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(C)}\right).\] This is strictly smaller than crude Monte Carlo variance exactly when \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\xi),C)\ne0\). A coefficient estimated from the data generally need not preserve exact finite-sample unbiasedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed coefficient multiplying a zero-mean control variable preserves unbiasedness. The variance-minimizing coefficient is minus the response-control covariance divided by the control variance, and it gives strict variance reduction exactly when the covariance is nonzero. A coefficient estimated from data generally need not preserve exact finite-sample unbiasedness.
assumptions_latex: \lambda\text{ is fixed for the unbiasedness statement}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda^*=-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)}{\operatorname{Var}(C)},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{CV}}(x;\lambda^*))=\frac1N\left(\sigma^2(x)-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(C)}\right),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{CV}})<\frac{\sigma^2(x)}N\iff\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)\ne0.

children.title: Conditional Monte Carlo
children.top_down_role: Variance reduction through conditional averaging.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Monte Carlo
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rao–Blackwell variance reduction by conditioning simulation output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\in L^2\) be a simulation output and \(\mathcal G\) a sub-sigma-algebra for which \(Z=\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G]\) can be evaluated. Then \(\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E[Y]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)-\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\mathcal G)]\leq\operatorname{Var}(Y)\). Consequently, the sample mean of independent copies of \(Z\) is unbiased and has no greater variance than the sample mean of the same number of independent copies of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing an output by an evaluable conditional expectation preserves its mean and removes the expected conditional variance.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is a sub-sigma-algebra and \(\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G]\) is evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E[Y]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\leq\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-expectation and total-variance identities accurately express the defining variance-reduction property of Conditional Monte Carlo, and property is an appropriate content kind. The record nevertheless has no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rao–Blackwellized Monte Carlo estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional averaging as a Monte Carlo variance-reduction method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=f(X,Y)\) have finite variance and suppose \(g(X)=\mathbb E[U\mid X]\) is tractable. For iid \(X_1,\ldots,X_S\sim p_X\), define \[\widehat f_{\mathrm{RB}}=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S g(X_s).\] Then \(\widehat f_{\mathrm{RB}}\) is unbiased for \(\bar f=\mathbb E[U]\), and \[\operatorname{Var}(g(X))=\operatorname{Var}(U)-\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(U\mid X)]\leq\operatorname{Var}(U).\] Consequently, its variance is no greater than that of the naive iid estimator \(S^{-1}\sum_s f(X_s,Y_s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When one component of a joint Monte Carlo sample can be integrated out conditionally, replace each raw value by its conditional expectation. The Rao–Blackwellized estimator remains unbiased and has variance no greater than the naive joint-sampling estimator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_{\mathrm{RB}}]=\mathbb E[f(X,Y)]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_{\mathrm{RB}})\leq\operatorname{Var}(S^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^S f(X_s,Y_s))\).

children.title: Structured Sampling Methods
children.top_down_role: Variance control through systematic coverage of random inputs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Economics-of-selection allocation and stopping principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential ranking and selection under linear reward and costly simulation, without discounting in the stated specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ESP policy values not only the immediate evidence produced by the current sampling stage but also the option to continue sampling afterward. Under a linear reward or opportunity-loss model, it jointly determines sample allocation and stopping by trading the expected economic benefit of improved selection against sampling costs. In the no-discounting specialization, each simulation sample has a marginal cost but implementation delay carries no additional discount penalty; decreasing the assumed per-sample cost weakly favors taking more samples before selecting an alternative. Discounted-delay and combined delay-plus-marginal-cost variants are separate regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: ESP procedures are nonmyopic selection policies: they account for the future option to gather more information and derive both allocation and stopping decisions from the expected economic benefit of better selection versus simulation cost. In the stated case samples have marginal cost but decision delay is not discounted; assigning a lower sampling cost favors longer sampling.
assumptions_latex: \text{Terminal performance is represented by a linear economic reward or opportunity loss.}
c_i\ge0\text{ is the marginal cost of sampling alternative }i.
\text{For the stated specialization, there is no additional discount penalty for implementation delay.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Choose allocation and stopping jointly to maximize expected selection reward net of sampling cost, including continuation value.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic quasi-Monte Carlo estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic point-set approximation of an expectation over a uniform unit hypercube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(x\), let \(\xi\) have independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) components and let \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\). Given carefully selected deterministic points \(\widehat\xi^1,\ldots,\widehat\xi^N\in[0,1]^{d_\xi}\), define
\[
f_{N,\mathrm{QMC}}(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y(x,\widehat\xi^i).
\]
Under the hypotheses of the Koksma–Hlawka inequality, approximation error is controlled jointly by the point set's star discrepancy and the total variation of \(Y(x,\cdot)\). Low-discrepancy sequences are constructed to keep star discrepancy small as \(N\) varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi-Monte Carlo replaces random uniform samples with carefully selected deterministic points and averages the integrand over them. When the Koksma–Hlawka hypotheses apply, error is controlled by both star discrepancy and integrand variation.
assumptions_latex: \text{The discrepancy–variation claim is conditional on the hypotheses of the Koksma--Hlawka inequality}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{N,\mathrm{QMC}}(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y(x,\widehat\xi^i),\quad\text{and, when applicable, its error is controlled by star discrepancy and total variation}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generic Random Search Algorithm for Simulation Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generic iterative framework allowing iteration-dependent sampling strategies and sample counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a sampling strategy \(\mathcal S_1\) and set \(n=1\). children.title: Stratified Sampling

knowledge_statements.title: Stratified Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased estimation using a finite measurable partition and within-stratum samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_H\) be a measurable partition with \(p_h=\mathbb P(X\in A_h)>0\). Draw \(n_h\geq1\) independent samples from the conditional law of \(X\) given \(X\in A_h\), independently across strata, and set \(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{str}}=\sum_{h=1}^H p_h n_h^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_h}f(X_{hj})\). Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{str}}]=\mathbb E[f(X)]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{str}})=\sum_{h=1}^H p_h^2\operatorname{Var}(f(X)\mid X\in A_h)/n_h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted averages of within-stratum sample means unbiasedly estimate the population mean, with variance determined by conditional variances and allocations.
assumptions_latex: \(A_1,\ldots,A_H\) form a measurable partition with positive probabilities.
Samples are conditionally independent within and across strata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed estimator is unbiased with variance \(\sum_h p_h^2\sigma_h^2/n_h\).

children.title: Latin Hypercube Simulation
children.top_down_role: Marginally stratified multivariate simulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Latin Hypercube Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized design stratifying every uniform input coordinate into equal-probability intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(n\)-point Latin hypercube design in \([0,1]^s\) is generated by independently choosing, for each coordinate \(k\), a uniform random permutation \(\pi_k\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and independent jitters \(V_{ik}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), then setting \(U_{ik}=(\pi_k(i)-V_{ik})/n\). For every coordinate, exactly one point lies in each interval \(((j-1)/n,j/n)\), while each \(U_i\) is marginally uniform on \([0,1]^s\). Hence \(n^{-1}\sum_i f(U_i)\) is unbiased for the uniform integral of integrable \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Latin hypercube places one randomized point in every marginal stratum of every coordinate while retaining uniform point marginals and unbiased integration.
assumptions_latex: The permutations, jitters, and coordinate constructions are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each marginal stratum is occupied once, and \(n^{-1}\sum_i f(U_i)\) is unbiased for \(\int_{[0,1]^s}f(u)\,du\).

children.title: Randomized Quasi-Monte Carlo
children.top_down_role: Randomized low-discrepancy simulation designs.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Quasi-Monte Carlo
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized low-discrepancy integration retaining uniform marginals and replication-based error assessment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\subset[0,1]^s\) be a low-discrepancy point set. A randomized quasi-Monte Carlo design is a random transformation producing \(\widetilde P_n=\{\widetilde U_1,\ldots,\widetilde U_n\}\) such that each \(\widetilde U_i\) is uniform on \([0,1]^s\) and the transformed set retains the designated low-discrepancy structure almost surely. For integrable \(f\), \(\widehat I_n=n^{-1}\sum_i f(\widetilde U_i)\) is unbiased for \(I=\int_{[0,1]^s}f(u)\,du\); independent randomizations provide independent estimator replications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomization makes every low-discrepancy point uniform, preserving unbiased integration while independent randomizations permit statistical error estimation.
assumptions_latex: Each randomized point is marginally uniform on \([0,1]^s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat I_n]=I\), and independent randomizations yield independent copies of \(\widehat I_n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record states a reasonable general definition through uniform marginals and preservation of designated low-discrepancy structure, but the latter condition depends on the randomization class and is not independently verifiable from any cited source. An authoritative RQMC source must establish the stated generality and replication claim.

children.title: Rare-Event Variance Reduction
children.top_down_role: Variance control for low-probability events affecting objectives or constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Importance-sampling variance criterion and zero-variance density
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance formula, necessary and sufficient comparison with crude Monte Carlo, formal zero-variance proposal, and its optimization-context limitation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\), let \(\xi\sim p\), \(\widetilde\xi\sim q\), \(p\ll q\), and \(\mathcal L=p/q\). If the required second moments are finite, then \[\operatorname{Var}[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x)]=\frac1N\left(\mathbb E_p[Y(x,\xi)^2\mathcal L(\xi)]-\mathbb E_p[Y(x,\xi)]^2\right).\] Hence importance sampling has smaller variance than crude Monte Carlo if and only if \(\mathbb E_p[Y^2\mathcal L]<\mathbb E_p[Y^2]\). If \(Y(x,\cdot)\ge0\) and \(\mu(x)=\mathbb E_p[Y(x,\xi)]>0\), the formal zero-variance density is \[q_x^*(\xi)=\frac{p(\xi)Y(x,\xi)}{\mu(x)}.\] It depends on the unknown target mean and generally on \(x\), so it is unattainable directly and a single proposal need not perform well for every \(x\in\Theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The importance-sampling variance equals one over N times its weighted second moment minus the squared target mean. It is lower than crude Monte Carlo variance exactly when the weighted second moment is lower. For a nonnegative response with positive mean, sampling from a density proportional to p times the response gives zero variance formally, but this density requires the unknown mean and usually depends on the decision x; one proposal can therefore help some decisions and harm others.
assumptions_latex: Y(x,\xi)\ge0\ \ p\text{-a.s. and }\mu(x)=\mathbb E_p[Y(x,\xi)]>0\quad\text{for the zero-variance formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Var}[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x)]=\frac1N\left(\mathbb E_p[Y^2\mathcal L]-\mu(x)^2\right),\quad \operatorname{Var}[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}]<\operatorname{Var}[f_N]\iff\mathbb E_p[Y^2\mathcal L]<\mathbb E_p[Y^2],\quad q_x^*=pY/\mu(x).
