knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a target probability measure and \(Q\) a simulation probability measure on the same measurable space, with \(P\ll Q\), and define the likelihood ratio \(L=dP/dQ\). For a measurable integrand \(h\) satisfying \(hL\in L^1(Q)\), \(\mu=\mathbb E_P[h(X)]=\mathbb E_Q[h(X)L(X)]\). Thus independent draws \(X_i\sim Q\) give the unbiased estimator \(\widehat\mu_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n h(X_i)L(X_i)\). If \(hL\in L^2(Q)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}_Q(\widehat\mu_n)=\operatorname{Var}_Q(hL)/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the target measure is dominated by the simulation measure, likelihood-ratio weighting preserves the target expectation; square integrability of the weighted integrand gives finite variance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Importance-sampling estimator, unbiasedness, and variance boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Change-of-measure estimator for a fixed simulation response, including its support requirement and the failure of admissibility alone to guarantee variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\Theta\). Let \(\xi\) have density \(p\) on \(\Xi\), let \(q\) be another density with \(p\ll q\), and define \(\mathcal L=p/q\), taking \(\mathcal L=0\) where both densities vanish. For i.i.d. \(\widetilde\xi^1,\ldots,\widetilde\xi^N\sim q\), \[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N Y(x,\widetilde\xi^j)\mathcal L(\widetilde\xi^j).\] If the weighted response is integrable, then \(\mathbb E_q[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x)]=\mathbb E_p[Y(x,\xi)]\). Thus the estimator is unbiased, but an admissible choice of \(q\) can increase rather than reduce variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Importance sampling draws independently from a proposal density q and weights each response by p/q. Absolute continuity and integrability give an unbiased estimator of the original expectation, but they do not guarantee variance reduction; a poor proposal can increase variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_q[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x)]=\mathbb E_p[Y(x,\xi)],\qquad \operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x))\text{ need not be below the crude Monte Carlo variance.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Importance-sampling change-of-measure identity and estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General change-of-measure representation underlying importance sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\) and \(q\) be probability densities with \(p\ll q\) wherever \(f p\neq 0\), and suppose \(f(X)p(X)/q(X)\) is integrable under \(q\). Then
\[
\mathbb E_{X\sim p}[f(X)]=\mathbb E_{X\sim q}\!\left[f(X)\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right].
\]
For samples \(X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)}\) drawn from \(q\), the corresponding Monte Carlo estimator is
\[
\widehat\mu_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f\!\left(X^{(i)}\right)\frac{p\!\left(X^{(i)}\right)}{q\!\left(X^{(i)}\right)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the target distribution p is dominated by the sampling distribution q on the relevant support, an expectation under p equals an expectation under q weighted by the likelihood ratio p/q. Samples from q therefore yield the sample-average importance-sampling estimator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_{X\sim p}[f(X)]=\mathbb E_{X\sim q}\!\left[f(X)\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right]\approx\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f\!\left(X^{(i)}\right)\frac{p\!\left(X^{(i)}\right)}{q\!\left(X^{(i)}\right)}

children.title: Rare-Event Splitting
children.top_down_role: Population replication or pruning organized around intermediate rare-event levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Rare-Event Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multilevel particle replication for estimating a rare hitting probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose nested sets \(B_0\supset B_1\supset\cdots\supset B_m=B\), an initial particle count \(N\), and offspring counts \(r_1,\ldots,r_{m-1}\). Simulate each particle until it reaches \(B_1\) or fails; every success at level \(k<m\) is replaced by \(r_k\) conditionally independent continuations from its entrance state. Assign each child its parent's weight divided by \(r_k\). Stop particles upon failure or arrival at \(B\), and output the sum of the terminal weights of particles reaching \(B\), divided by \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Particles reaching successive rare-event levels are replicated with divided weights; summed terminal weights estimate the final hitting probability.
assumptions_latex: Continuation simulations have the correct conditional law from each entrance state.
Splitting decisions use only information available at the corresponding entrance time.
Initial particles are independent and correctly distributed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an unbiased estimator of the probability of reaching \(B\) under weight-conserving splitting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind for this terminal container, but the particular fixed-offspring, entrance-state continuation scheme and its unbiasedness conclusion depend on filtration, stopping, and weight-conservation details that require an authoritative source. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Subset Simulation
children.top_down_role: Rare-event estimation through nested conditional-event populations.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rare-event probability factorization estimated through sequential conditional sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose nested events \(F_0\supset F_1\supset\cdots\supset F_m=F\) with \(F_0=\Omega\). Using samples from the law conditional on \(F_{k-1}\), estimate \(p_k=\mathbb P(F_k\mid F_{k-1})\) by the observed fraction in \(F_k\); use selected samples in \(F_k\) as seeds for a Markov transition kernel invariant for the law conditional on \(F_k\). Continue until \(F\) is reached and output \(\widehat p_F=\prod_{k=1}^m\widehat p_k\), corresponding to \(\mathbb P(F)=\prod_{k=1}^m p_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset simulation factors a rare probability into moderate conditional probabilities estimated through sequential conditional sampling over nested events.
assumptions_latex: Each transition kernel has the required conditional distribution as an invariant law.
The stopping level and probability estimator follow the stated nested-event factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target probability satisfies \(\mathbb P(F)=\prod_{k=1}^m\mathbb P(F_k\mid F_{k-1})\), estimated by the displayed product.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the Subset Simulation leaf, and the exact nested-event probability factorization is correct. However, the sequential MCMC sampling procedure and product estimator are method-specific; invariance alone does not resolve initialization, dependence, or finite-sample behavior. An authoritative source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Intermediate-Level Design
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing level placement and population progression.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate-Level Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Design criterion for stable multilevel rare-event probability estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nested events \(F_0\supset F_1\supset\cdots\supset F_m=F\), define \(p_k=\mathbb P(F_k\mid F_{k-1})\). An admissible intermediate-level design requires \(0<p_k<1\) for every level, supports simulation from or continuation under the conditional law given \(F_{k-1}\), and satisfies \(\mathbb P(F)=\prod_{k=1}^m p_k\). A balanced design additionally selects levels so that the \(p_k\) are approximately equal and bounded away from zero, preventing any single conditional stage from remaining a rare event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intermediate levels must preserve the nested probability factorization and make every conditional transition simulable; balanced levels avoid extremely small stage probabilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid design has simulable stages with \(0<p_k<1\) and \(\mathbb P(F)=\prod_{k=1}^m p_k\).

notation.meaning: conditional probability of advancing one level

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is an appropriate content kind for an intermediate-level design criterion. The nested-event factorization is standard, but requiring every conditional probability to be strictly below one and characterizing approximately equal probabilities bounded away from zero as balanced are method-dependent design choices that need a cited authoritative formulation.

children.title: Change-of-Measure Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instability from poorly targeted measures or degenerate simulation weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Change-of-Measure Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure conditions for importance-sampling estimators under an inadequately chosen proposal measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the target be \(\mu=\mathbb E_P[H(X)]\), and suppose samples are drawn from \(Q\). A likelihood-weighted estimator requires \(P\ll Q\) on \(\{x:H(x)\ne0\}\), with weight \(W=dP/dQ\). It is invalid if domination fails, and it has infinite variance whenever \(\mathbb E_Q[H(X)^2W(X)^2]=\infty\). Even with finite variance, concentration of \(W\) on vanishingly few samples causes effective-sample-size degeneration and unstable finite-sample estimates. Thus unbiasedness alone does not ensure a usable change of measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Change of measure fails through missing support, infinite weighted second moments, or extreme weight concentration that leaves effectively few useful simulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\not\ll Q\) on the payoff support invalidates reweighting; \(\mathbb E_Q[H^2W^2]=\infty\) implies infinite estimator variance.

notation.meaning: Likelihood ratio where the Radon–Nikodym derivative exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probability Coupling Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a coupled pair using densities g_1 and g_2 and one shared uniform variate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate \(Y_1\sim g_1\) and \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\). If \(U g_1(Y_1)\le g_2(Y_1)\), return \((Y_1,Y_1)\). Otherwise, repeatedly generate \(Y_2\sim g_2\) until \(U g_2(Y_2)\ge g_1(Y_2)\), and then return \((Y_1,Y_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw Y1 from density g1 and U uniformly from [0,1]. Return the identical pair (Y1,Y1) when U g1(Y1) is at most g2(Y1). Otherwise repeatedly draw Y2 from g2 until U g2(Y2) is at least g1(Y2), then return (Y1,Y2).
assumptions_latex: g_1\text{ and }g_2\text{ are probability densities on a common measurable space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{return}\begin{cases}(Y_1,Y_1),&U g_1(Y_1)\le g_2(Y_1),\\(Y_1,Y_2),&U g_1(Y_1)>g_2(Y_1)\text{ and }U g_2(Y_2)\ge g_1(Y_2).\end{cases}

children.title: Sample-Path Recycling

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Path Recycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-input reuse across several parameter evaluations of a simulator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given design points \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K\), a simulator \(h(\theta,U)\), and replication count \(n\), generate independent base inputs \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) once. For every \(k\), compute \(Y_{ik}=h(\theta_k,U_i)\) and return \(\widehat F_n(\theta_k)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_{ik}\). Stop after all requested designs are evaluated or a prescribed simulation budget is exhausted. Each marginal estimate remains unbiased for \(F(\theta_k)=\mathbb E[h(\theta_k,U)]\); recycling induces covariance across designs, which can reduce the variance of paired comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate each exogenous path once, evaluate every requested design on it, and use the induced coupling to estimate objectives or differences.
assumptions_latex: \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) are independent with a distribution not depending on \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat F_n(\theta_k)]=F(\theta_k)\), while paired differences retain the covariance created by common paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood Reweighting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Off-policy representation of parameterized expectations using samples from a reference distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_\theta\) and \(P_{\theta_0}\) be probability measures on a common measurable space \((\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\), let \(P_\theta\ll P_{\theta_0}\), and let \(H_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be measurable. With \(w_{\theta,\theta_0}=dP_\theta/dP_{\theta_0}\), if \(H_\theta w_{\theta,\theta_0}\) is integrable under \(P_{\theta_0}\), then \[F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[H_\theta(X)]=\mathbb E_{P_{\theta_0}}[H_\theta(X)w_{\theta,\theta_0}(X)].\] Hence independent reference samples \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_{\theta_0}\) give the unbiased estimator \[\widehat F_n(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nH_\theta(X_i)w_{\theta,\theta_0}(X_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the parameterized simulation law is absolutely continuous with respect to a reference law, its expectation can be represented and estimated from reference samples using likelihood-ratio weights.
assumptions_latex: \(P_\theta\) and \(P_{\theta_0}\) are probability measures on \((\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\), with \(P_\theta\ll P_{\theta_0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{P_{\theta_0}}[H_\theta(X)w_{\theta,\theta_0}(X)]\), and \(\mathbb E[\widehat F_n(\theta)]=F(\theta)\).

notation.meaning: Radon–Nikodym likelihood ratio relative to the reference law.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-cumulative construction for the two component distributions represented by \(\dot p_i(x)\) and \(\ddot p_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate \(U,V\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contractive coupled-transition simulator assumption
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step coupling condition for two Markov-process replicas used in sensitivity simulation; replica notation is normalized from internally inconsistent extraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists \(\widetilde\rho<1\) such that, for every pair of admissible starting states \(u,v\), a joint simulator can generate \(\dot M_x(1),\ddot M_x(1)\) satisfying \(\dot M_x(1)\sim\delta_u\mathbf P_x\), \(\ddot M_x(1)\sim\delta_v\mathbf P_x\), and \[\mathbb E\!\left[r\!\left(\dot M_x(1),\ddot M_x(1)\right)\right]\leq \widetilde\rho\,r(u,v).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Random-directions gradient estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided random-direction estimator and its perturbation moment condition, contrasted with simultaneous perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For perturbation vector \Delta and scale c, the random-directions estimator has component \widehat g_i^{\mathrm{RD}}(\theta)=\frac{[Y(\theta+c\Delta,\xi_2)-Y(\theta-c\Delta,\xi_1)]\Delta_i}{2c_i}. Unlike the simultaneous-perturbation estimator, it multiplies rather than divides by \Delta_i. Its convergence-related perturbation condition therefore requires zero mean and a bounded second moment rather than a finite inverse second moment, permitting Gaussian perturbations. Componentwise inversion of the perturbation gives a formal correspondence with the simultaneous-perturbation estimator, although the resulting stochastic-approximation algorithms can perform substantially differently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The random-directions estimator multiplies a shared two-sided output difference by each perturbation component instead of dividing by that component as SPSA does. Its perturbations must have zero mean and bounded second moment, so Gaussian directions are allowed. Taking componentwise reciprocals gives a formal correspondence with SPSA, but the resulting algorithms may behave quite differently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat g_i^{\mathrm{RD}}(\theta)=\frac{\left[Y(\theta+c\Delta,\xi_2)-Y(\theta-c\Delta,\xi_1)\right]\Delta_i}{2c_i},\quad\text{and Gaussian perturbations are admissible under the stated moment condition.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: STAR Gradient Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional hybrid estimator combining a finite-difference secant with averaged direct stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), \(c>0\), simulation output \(Y\), and direct stochastic gradient estimator \(g\), the Secant-Tangents AveRaged estimator is
\[
g^{\mathrm{STAR}}(x,\xi)=\alpha\frac{Y(x+c,\xi)-Y(x-c,\xi)}{2c}+(1-\alpha)\frac{g(x+c,\xi)+g(x-c,\xi)}2.
\]
The same noise realization \(\xi\) is used at both perturbed points, for example through common random numbers. This convexly combines a symmetric finite-difference secant with the average of two direct-gradient tangents, potentially reducing variance at the cost of bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: STAR combines a centered finite difference of paired simulation outputs with the average of direct gradient estimates at the same perturbed points. Common random numbers may couple the evaluations, and alpha controls the variance-bias tradeoff.
assumptions_latex: Y(x+c,\xi)\text{ and }Y(x-c,\xi)\text{ use the same noise realization }\xi
g(x\pm c,\xi)\text{ are direct stochastic gradient estimates}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g^{\mathrm{STAR}}(x,\xi)=\alpha\frac{Y(x+c,\xi)-Y(x-c,\xi)}{2c}+(1-\alpha)\frac{g(x+c,\xi)+g(x-c,\xi)}2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-sided and central finite-difference simulation-gradient estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise finite differences for stochastic simulator output, including evaluation cost, perturbation trade-offs, and common-random-number coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For stochastic simulator output $Y(\theta,\xi)$, coordinate vector $e_i$, and $c_i\ne0$, the forward and central estimators are
\[
\widehat g_i^{\mathrm F}(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+c_i e_i,\xi_{2,i})-Y(\theta,\xi_{1,i})}{c_i},\qquad
\widehat g_i^{\mathrm C}(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+c_i e_i,\xi_{2,i})-Y(\theta-c_i e_i,\xi_{1,i})}{2c_i}.
\]
The central estimator is more accurate but uses $2d$ simulator evaluations for a full gradient, whereas the forward estimator uses $d+1$. Setting $\xi_{1,i}=\xi_{2,i}$ gives common-random-number coupling, which can substantially reduce variance when the paired simulations are properly synchronized. Excessively small perturbations amplify simulation noise, producing a bias--variance trade-off that may require componentwise scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward estimator compares the nominal output with one positive coordinate perturbation, while the central estimator compares positive and negative perturbations. Central differences are more accurate but require 2d evaluations per gradient rather than d+1. Common random numbers can substantially reduce variance when paired simulations remain synchronized. Very small perturbations amplify stochastic noise and create a componentwise bias–variance trade-off.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat g_i^{\mathrm F}(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+c_i e_i,\xi_{2,i})-Y(\theta,\xi_{1,i})}{c_i},\qquad \widehat g_i^{\mathrm C}(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+c_i e_i,\xi_{2,i})-Y(\theta-c_i e_i,\xi_{1,i})}{2c_i}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indirect versus direct simulation gradient estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of stochastic gradient estimators by their use of model knowledge and simulator modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indirect gradient estimator treats the simulator as a black box: it uses neither knowledge of the simulator's underlying mechanics nor any modification of its execution, and it estimates an approximation to the true gradient using output evaluations of the original system. A direct gradient estimator instead targets the true gradient using additional analysis of the model's stochastic structure; it may use model knowledge even when simulator execution is unchanged. In stochastic approximation, these categories generally correspond to Kiefer--Wolfowitz and Robbins--Monro approaches, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indirect estimator uses only output evaluations from an unmodified black-box simulator, without exploiting its internal stochastic mechanics, and generally estimates an approximation to the true gradient. A direct estimator targets the true gradient using additional knowledge or analysis of the model's stochastic structure, even if it does not alter simulator execution. These categories generally correspond to Kiefer–Wolfowitz and Robbins–Monro stochastic approximation, respectively.
assumptions_latex: \text{For an indirect estimator, no simulator-mechanism knowledge is used in its derivation.}
\text{For an indirect estimator, execution of the simulator is not modified.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Finite differences and simultaneous perturbation are indirect estimators; indirect and direct estimators generally induce gradient-free Kiefer--Wolfowitz and Robbins--Monro SA schemes, respectively.}

children.title: Coordinate Finite Differences
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise simulator perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Finite Differences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central coordinatewise gradient estimation from perturbed simulator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) for \(\theta\) in an evaluation domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). Given \(\theta\in D\), \(c>0\), and \(m\in\mathbb N\), for each coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\) generate \(m\) pairs \((U_{ij}^+,U_{ij}^-)\) whose two marginals equal the law of \(U\), independently across \(i\). Compute \[\widehat g_j(\theta)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{Y(\theta+ce_j,U_{ij}^+)-Y(\theta-ce_j,U_{ij}^-)}{2c}.\] Common random numbers use \(U_{ij}^+=U_{ij}^-\); independent sampling may instead be used. Return \(\widehat g=(\widehat g_1,\ldots,\widehat g_d)\) after evaluating the requested coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate each gradient component by averaging central simulator differences along that coordinate, using inputs with the correct marginal law and optionally common random numbers.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \(\theta\in D\), and \(\theta\pm ce_j\in D\) for every evaluated coordinate \(j\).
Each \(U_{ij}^+\) and \(U_{ij}^-\) has the same marginal distribution as \(U\), and pairs are independent across replications.
\(\mathbb E[|Y(\theta\pm ce_j,U)|]<\infty\) for every evaluated coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_j(\theta)]=(F(\theta+ce_j)-F(\theta-ce_j))/(2c)\).

notation.meaning: Simulator output at design theta and random input U.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Finite-Difference Policy-Gradient Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise policy-parameter perturbations evaluated through Monte Carlo trajectory returns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each coordinate \(i=1,\ldots,n\), form \(\theta_i^+=\theta+\delta\mathbf e_i\). Estimate both \(U(\theta_i^+)\) and \(U(\theta)\) using \(m\) rollouts of depth \(d\), with initial states sampled from \(b\) and return \(R(\tau)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\gamma^{k-1}r_k\). If these estimates are denoted by \(\widehat U_{m,i}^+\) and \(\widehat U_{m,i}^0\), return \[\widehat g_i=\frac{\widehat U_{m,i}^+-\widehat U_{m,i}^0}{\delta},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every policy-parameter coordinate, estimate the rollout utility at a positive coordinate perturbation and at the current parameters, then divide their difference by the step size. Each utility estimate averages discounted returns from m trajectories of depth d. The algorithm does not itself specify coupling the random samples across evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{\nabla U}(\theta)=\left(\frac{\widehat U_{m,i}^+-\widehat U_{m,i}^0}{\delta}\right)_{i=1}^{n}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise central finite differences with simulation noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central finite-difference gradient estimation using separate simulator evaluations in every coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x^n\in\mathbb R^K\), coordinate vector \(e_k\), perturbation radius \(h_n>0\), and simulator outputs driven by samples \(W_k^{n+1,+}\) and \(W_k^{n+1,-}\), define \[g_k^n=\frac{F(x^n+h_ne_k,W_k^{n+1,+})-F(x^n-h_ne_k,W_k^{n+1,-})}{2h_n},\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.\] One full gradient estimate requires \(2K\) simulator evaluations. Smaller \(h_n\) reduces finite-difference bias but amplifies simulation noise, whereas larger \(h_n\) increases bias; vanishing asymptotic differencing bias requires \(h_n\to0\), while a constant radius remains a tunable bias-noise compromise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate each gradient coordinate from simulator responses at equal positive and negative coordinate perturbations. A full estimate costs two simulations per coordinate. Shrinking the perturbation reduces differencing bias but magnifies noise, while a fixed perturbation retains a tunable bias-noise tradeoff.
assumptions_latex: F(x,W)\text{ is observable through simulator runs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_k^n=\frac{F(x^n+h_ne_k,W_k^{n+1,+})-F(x^n-h_ne_k,W_k^{n+1,-})}{2h_n},\quad \text{with }2K\text{ evaluations per full estimate}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Forward Finite-Difference Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise forward differences, including their specialization to policy-utility gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{x}\), then for each coordinate \(i\), \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{x})=\lim_{\delta\to0}\frac{f(\mathbf{x}+\delta\mathbf e^{(i)})-f(\mathbf{x})}{\delta}.\] Thus, for a small nonzero step \(\delta\), the quotient gives a forward finite-difference approximation. Applied to policy utility, \(\partial U/\partial\theta_i\) is approximated by \([U(\theta+\delta\mathbf e^{(i)})-U(\theta)]/\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each gradient component is the limit of a coordinatewise forward difference quotient. A small finite step gives an approximation, and the same construction applies to expected policy utility as a function of its policy parameters.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf e^{(i)}\text{ is the }i\text{th standard basis vector}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{f(\mathbf{x}+\delta\mathbf e^{(i)})-f(\mathbf{x})}{\delta}\to\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{x})\quad\text{as }\delta\to0.

children.top_down_role: Randomized directional perturbations replacing coordinate sweeps.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Direction Differences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided gradient estimation using randomized simultaneous perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) for \(\theta\in D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). Given \(c>0\) and \(m\in\mathbb N\), independently draw directions \(\Delta_i\in\{-1,1\}^d\) with independent Rademacher coordinates. For each \(i\), generate inputs \(U_i^+\) and \(U_i^-\) having the law of \(U\), independently of \(\Delta_i\), and compute \[G_i=\frac{Y(\theta+c\Delta_i,U_i^+)-Y(\theta-c\Delta_i,U_i^-)}{2c}\,\Delta_i.\] The two inputs may be coupled by common random numbers. Return \(\widehat g_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mG_i\). If the third derivatives of \(F\) are bounded on a neighborhood containing all perturbed points, then \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_m]=\nabla F(\theta)+O(c^2)\) as \(c\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average two-sided simulator differences along random sign directions; with correctly distributed simulation inputs and bounded third derivatives, the result has quadratic finite-perturbation bias.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) is finite near the evaluated point.
The third partial derivatives of \(F\) are bounded on a neighborhood containing \(\theta\pm c\Delta\).
Each \(U_i^+\) and \(U_i^-\) has the law of \(U\) and is independent of \(\Delta_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_m]=\nabla F(\theta)+O(c^2)\) as \(c\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: Random vector with independent Rademacher coordinates.

children.title: Perturbation Bias-Variance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Estimator behavior across perturbation scale, simulation noise, and coupling regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Bias-Variance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling laws for central finite differences under independent or coupled simulation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) for a scalar parameter \(\theta\), and define \(Y_i^+=Y(\theta+c,U_i^+)\), \(Y_i^-=Y(\theta-c,U_i^-)\), and \[\widehat g_c=\frac{1}{2mc}\sum_{i=1}^m(Y_i^+-Y_i^-).\] If the pairs are identically distributed and independent across \(i\), then \[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat g_c)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_1^+-Y_1^-)}{4mc^2}.\] If \(F\) has bounded third derivative near \(\theta\), then \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_c]-F'(\theta)=O(c^2)\). Independent perturbation noise with nonvanishing difference variance gives \(O((mc^2)^{-1})\) variance, whereas a common-random-number coupling satisfying \(\mathbb E[(Y(\theta+c,U)-Y(\theta-c,U))^2]=O(c^2)\) gives \(O(m^{-1})\) variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Central differences have quadratic truncation bias. Their variance scales inversely with the squared step under uncoupled noise but stays bounded in the step size under a sufficiently smooth common-random-number coupling.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) and \(F\) has bounded third derivative near \(\theta\).
Each \(U_i^+\) and \(U_i^-\) has the law of \(U\), and the pairs are independent across \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat g_c)=O(c^2)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat g_c)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1^+-Y_1^-)/(4mc^2)\).

notation.meaning: Simulator outputs at the positive and negative perturbations in replication i.

knowledge_statements.title: Pathwise Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interchange of differentiation and expectation for regular simulator paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d\) be open, let \(	heta_0\in\Theta\), and define \(F(	heta)=\mathbb E[Y(	heta,U)]\). Suppose \(\mathbb E[|Y(	heta_0,U)|]<\infty\), \(Y(\cdot,U)\) is almost surely differentiable on a neighborhood \(N\) of \(	heta_0\), and there is an integrable random variable \(M\) such that \(\sup_{	heta\in N}\|
abla_	heta Y(	heta,U)\|\le M\) almost surely. Then \[
abla F(	heta_0)=\mathbb E[
abla_	heta Y(	heta_0,U)].\] Consequently, the sample-path derivative is an unbiased estimator of \(
abla F(	heta_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the output is integrable at the base point and simulator paths have locally dominated derivatives, differentiation and expectation can be interchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(Y(\cdot,U)\) is almost surely differentiable on a neighborhood \(N\) of \(\theta_0\).
\(\sup_{\theta\in N}\|\nabla_\theta Y(\theta,U)\|\le M\) almost surely for an integrable \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla F(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta Y(\theta_0,U)]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiation of an expected finite maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiates the expectation of a finite maximum when the active component is almost surely unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let H_1(x,\cdot),\ldots,H_n(x,\cdot) be continuous in w and L^{1+\delta}-differentiable in x, with derivatives h_1,\ldots,h_n. Define
\[
H(x,w)=\max_{1\le k\le n}H_k(x,w)
\]
and assume
\[
\mu\{w:H_k(x,w)=H_\ell(x,w)\}=0\qquad(k\ne\ell).
\]
For C_k(x)=\{w:H_k(x,w)=\max_jH_j(x,w)\},
\[
H(x,w)=\sum_k H_k(x,w)\mathbf 1_{C_k(x)}(w)\quad\text{a.s.}
\]
and
\[
\nabla_x\int H(x,w)\,d\mu(w)=\sum_k\int h_k(x,w)\mathbf 1_{C_k(x)}(w)\,d\mu(w).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If pairwise ties between finitely many differentiable random functions have measure zero, the expected maximum is differentiated by integrating the derivative of the almost surely unique active component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(x,w)=\sum_kH_k(x,w)\mathbf 1_{C_k(x)}(w)\ \text{a.s.},\qquad \nabla_x\int H(x,w)\,d\mu(w)=\sum_k\int h_k(x,w)\mathbf 1_{C_k(x)}(w)\,d\mu(w)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L^1 Differentiability of a Scalar-Parameterized Random Process
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition at a scalar parameter value x.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An integrable stochastic process $H(x,\omega)$ is $L^1$-differentiable at $x$ if there exists an integrable random variable $h(x,\omega)$ such that
\[
\frac{1}{|s|}\int\left|H(x+s,\omega)-H(x,\omega)-s h(x,\omega)\right|\,d\mu(\omega)\to0\quad(s\to0).
\]
The random variable $h(x,\omega)$ is the $L^1$ derivative. Equivalently, $s^{-1}[H(x+s,\cdot)-H(x,\cdot)]\to h(x,\cdot)$ in $L^1(\mu)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable scalar-parameterized stochastic process is L1-differentiable at x when its difference quotient converges in L1 to an integrable random variable h; that limit is its L1 derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{H(x+s,\cdot)-H(x,\cdot)}{s}\xrightarrow[s\to0]{L^1(\mu)}h(x,\cdot)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L^1 Differentiability of a Maximum under Almost-Sure Non-Ties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure rule for the pointwise maximum of two scalar random processes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose $H_1(x,\omega)$ and $H_2(x,\omega)$ are $L^1(\mu)$-differentiable at $x$, with derivatives $h_1(x,\omega)$ and $h_2(x,\omega)$, and
\[
\mu\{\omega:H_1(x,\omega)=H_2(x,\omega)\}=0.
\]
Then $H(x,\omega)=\max\{H_1(x,\omega),H_2(x,\omega)\}$ is $L^1$-differentiable at $x$, with derivative
\[
h(x,\omega)=h_1(x,\omega)\mathbf{1}_{\{H_1(x,\omega)>H_2(x,\omega)\}}+h_2(x,\omega)\mathbf{1}_{\{H_1(x,\omega)<H_2(x,\omega)\}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of two L1-differentiable random processes is L1-differentiable at x if they tie only on a null set. Its derivative selects the derivative of whichever process is strictly larger.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L^p Differentiability of a Scalar-Parameterized Random Process
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition at a scalar parameter value x.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $H(x,\cdot)\in L^p(\mu)$. The process is $L^p$-differentiable at $x$ if there exists $h(x,\cdot)\in L^p(\mu)$ such that
\[
\frac{1}{|s|^p}\int\left|H(x+s,\omega)-H(x,\omega)-s h(x,\omega)\right|^p\,d\mu(\omega)\to0\quad(s\to0).
\]
The random variable $h(x,\omega)$ is the $L^p$ derivative. Equivalently, $s^{-1}[H(x+s,\cdot)-H(x,\cdot)]\to h(x,\cdot)$ in $L^p(\mu)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar-parameterized stochastic process is Lp-differentiable at x when its difference quotient converges in Lp to some h in Lp; h is the Lp derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{H(x+s,\cdot)-H(x,\cdot)}{s}\xrightarrow[s\to0]{L^p(\mu)}h(x,\cdot)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced Process Derivative from a Distribution Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density-based construction of a reduced process derivative pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(G_x\) has density \(g_x\) and \(x\mapsto G_x(u)\) is differentiable. Wherever the quotient is defined, let \[L(x,u)=-\frac{\partial_xG_x(u)}{g_x(u)}.\] If \(Z_x\sim G_x\) and \(Y_x=L(x,Z_x)\), then \((Z_x,Y_x)\) is a reduced process derivative pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a parameterized distribution function is differentiable and has a density, minus its parameter derivative divided by its density gives a reduced process derivative when evaluated at a random variable having that distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (Z_x,Y_x)\text{ is a reduced process derivative pair.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expectation derivative from a process derivative pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the derivative of an expectation using a process 2-derivative of the underlying probability-law family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let H be differentiable with Lipschitz derivative H'. If x\mapsto\mu_x is process 2-differentiable with process derivative pair (Z_x,Y_x), then
\[
\nabla_x\int H(w)\,d\mu_x(w)=\mathbb E\bigl[Y_xH'(Z_x)\bigr].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a process 2-differentiable family of probability laws and a test function with Lipschitz derivative, the derivative of the expectation equals the expectation of the process derivative multiplied by the test-function derivative.
assumptions_latex: x\mapsto\mu_x\text{ is process }2\text{-differentiable with process derivative pair }(Z_x,Y_x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla_x\int H(w)\,d\mu_x(w)=\mathbb E\left[Y_xH'(Z_x)\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector-Parameter Weak Derivative of a Probability-Measure Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet-type weak differentiability with a vector of finite signed derivative measures and its probability-measure difference representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open and \(x\mapsto\mu_x\in\mathcal P\). The family is weakly differentiable at \(x\) if there are finite signed measures \(\mu'_{x,1},\ldots,\mu'_{x,d}\) such that, for every bounded continuous \(H\), \[\frac{1}{\|s\|}\left|\int H\,d\mu_{x+s}-\int H\,d\mu_x-\sum_{i=1}^d s_i\int H\,d\mu'_{x,i}\right|\longrightarrow0\quad(s\to0).\] Each component may be represented as \(\mu'_{x,i}=c_{x,i}(\dot\mu_{x,i}-\ddot\mu_{x,i})\), where \(\dot\mu_{x,i}\) and \(\ddot\mu_{x,i}\) are probability measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability law indexed by a vector parameter is weakly differentiable when every bounded continuous test expectation has a first-order expansion whose coefficients are integrations against a vector of finite signed measures. Each component signed measure may be expressed as a scaled difference of probability measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int H\,d\mu_{x+s}=\int H\,d\mu_x+\sum_{i=1}^d s_i\int H\,d\mu'_{x,i}+o(\|s\|),\qquad \mu'_{x,i}=c_{x,i}(\dot\mu_{x,i}-\ddot\mu_{x,i}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Law-Determination of the Reduced Process Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of the conditional derivative representation up to almost-sure equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((Z_x,Y_x)\) be a process derivative pair for the family \((\mu_x)\), and define a measurable version \(K\) by \(K(Z_x)=\mathbb E[Y_x\mid Z_x]\). Then \(K\) is determined \(\mu_x\)-almost surely by the family \((\mu_x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a process derivative pair, the conditional derivative given the process value is, up to almost-sure equality, determined by the parameterized family of probability laws.
assumptions_latex: (Z_x,Y_x)\text{ is a process derivative pair for }(\mu_x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is determined almost surely by }(\mu_x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simultaneous-run central finite differences for diffusion optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two coupled simulations estimate a parameter derivative and induce a reflected mean ODE.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\delta\theta>0\), simulate \(x^{\epsilon,+}\) at \(\theta_n^\epsilon+\delta\theta\) and \(x^{\epsilon,-}\) at \(\theta_n^\epsilon-\delta\theta\), preferably with the same Wiener process, and replace the derivative integrand by \([c(\theta_n^\epsilon+\delta\theta,x^{\epsilon,+}(s))-c(\theta_n^\epsilon-\delta\theta,x^{\epsilon,-}(s))]/(2\delta\theta)\). If the run families and invariant measures are tight and each fixed-parameter state process has a unique invariant measure, the mean ODE is \(\dot\theta=-[\int c(\theta+\delta\theta,\xi)\mu(d\xi\mid\theta+\delta\theta)-\int c(\theta-\delta\theta,\xi)\mu(d\xi\mid\theta-\delta\theta)]/(2\delta\theta)+z\), where \(z\) keeps \(\theta\) in \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run two diffusion simulations at symmetric parameter perturbations and use their cost difference as a central finite-difference observation. Common random numbers are normally preferred. Under the stated tightness and invariant-measure assumptions, the stochastic approximation has the displayed boundary-regulated mean ODE. Only the marginal fixed-parameter processes need unique invariant measures; uniqueness for their coupled pair is unnecessary because the two expectations enter additively.
assumptions_latex: For each fixed \(\theta\), the state process has a unique invariant measure \(\mu(\cdot\mid\theta)\).
The applicable stochastic-approximation invariant-measure convergence conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dot\theta=-\frac{1}{2\delta\theta}\left[\int c(\theta+\delta\theta,\xi)\mu(d\xi\mid\theta+\delta\theta)-\int c(\theta-\delta\theta,\xi)\mu(d\xi\mid\theta-\delta\theta)\right]+z,\quad \theta(t)\in[a,b].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Weak Derivative of a Probability-Measure Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a probability-measure family indexed by a scalar parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R\) be open and let \(x\mapsto\mu_x\in\mathcal P\). The family is weakly differentiable at \(x\in U\) if there exists a finite signed measure \(\mu_x'\) such that, for every bounded continuous function \(H\), \[\frac{1}{s}\left(\int H(w)\,d\mu_{x+s}(w)-\int H(w)\,d\mu_x(w)\right)\longrightarrow\int H(w)\,d\mu_x'(w)\quad(s\to0).\] Equivalently, \(\frac{d}{dx}\int H\,d\mu_x=\int H\,d\mu_x'\) for every such \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar-parameterized probability-measure family is weakly differentiable at x when its expectations of every bounded continuous test function are differentiable there and their derivatives are integration against one finite signed measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{s\to0}\frac{\int H\,d\mu_{x+s}-\int H\,d\mu_x}{s}=\int H\,d\mu_x'.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L^2-to-L^1 Chain Rule under a Lipschitz Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar composition rule for parameterized random variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $x\mapsto H(x,\cdot)$ be $L^2$-differentiable with derivative $h(x,\cdot)$. If $G:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is everywhere differentiable and $G'$ is Lipschitz continuous, then $x\mapsto G(H(x,\cdot))$ is $L^1$-differentiable and
\[
D[G\circ H](x,\omega)=G'(H(x,\omega))h(x,\omega).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If H is L2-differentiable and G has a globally Lipschitz-continuous derivative, then G composed with H is L1-differentiable with the usual chain-rule derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\mapsto G(H(x,\cdot))\text{ is }L^1\text{-differentiable with derivative }G'(H(x,\omega))h(x,\omega)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Process p-differentiability and process derivative pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines differentiability of a parametric probability-law family through an Lp-differentiable process representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A family (\mu_x)_x is process p-differentiable at x_0 if it admits, in a neighborhood of x_0, a process representation (Z_x)_x and a random variable Y_{x_0} such that
\[
\|s\|^{-1}\bigl\|Z_{x_0+s}-Z_{x_0}-sY_{x_0}\bigr\|_p\longrightarrow0\qquad(s\to0).
\]
The variable Y_{x_0} is a process derivative, and (Z_{x_0},Y_{x_0}) is a process derivative pair. Process derivative pairs are identified by their joint distributions, and need not be unique for a given family (\mu_x)_x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of probability measures is process p-differentiable when it has a common process representation that is differentiable in Lp. Its value and derivative form a generally nonunique process derivative pair, considered up to joint distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_x)_x\text{ is process }p\text{-differentiable at }x_0;\ Y_{x_0}\text{ is a process derivative and }(Z_{x_0},Y_{x_0})\text{ is a process derivative pair}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tightness, uniform-integrability, and averaging conditions for SDE sensitivity SA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence assumptions for a pathwise-sensitivity stochastic-approximation application.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that for every \(\theta\in[a,b]\), \(L_t(\theta,x(0))\) converges as \(t\to\infty\). For every compact \(A\subset\mathbb R^{2k}\), the families \(\{u(t,\theta):t<\infty,u(0,\theta)\in A\}\) and \(\{u^\epsilon(t):t<\infty\}\) are tight; \(\{y(t,\theta):t<\infty,u(0,\theta)\in A\}\) is uniformly integrable uniformly over \(\theta\in[a,b]\); and \(\{y^\epsilon(t):t<\infty\}\) is uniformly integrable. Moreover, there is a continuous \(\bar g\) such that \(n^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}E_0^\epsilon g(\theta,x(iT,\theta),y(iT,\theta))\to\bar g(\theta)\) in mean, uniformly over initial states in each compact set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convergence analysis assumes long-run convergence of the average cost, tightness of both frozen-parameter and slowly varying state-sensitivity processes, uniform integrability of their sensitivity components, and a continuous limiting mean field obtained through mean Cesàro averaging uniformly over compact sets of initial conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(\forall A\subset\mathbb R^{2k}\) compact and \(\forall\theta\in[a,b]\), \(\{u(t,\theta):t<\infty,u(0,\theta)\in A\}\) is tight.
\(\{y(t,\theta):t<\infty,u(0,\theta)\in A\}\) is uniformly integrable uniformly in \(\theta\in[a,b]\), and \(\{y^\epsilon(t):t<\infty\}\) is uniformly integrable.
There exists continuous \(\bar g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) satisfying the stated uniform-on-compacts mean averaging limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}E_0^\epsilon g(\theta,x(iT,\theta),y(iT,\theta))\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{L^1}\bar g(\theta)\quad\text{uniformly over initial conditions in every compact set.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Representation of Quantile Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative formula and distributional representation for parameterized quantiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x\mapsto Z_x\) is \(L^{1+\delta}\)-differentiable with derivative \(Y_x\) for some \(\delta>0\), \(Z_x\) has continuous distribution function \(G_x\) with density \(g_x\), and assumptions (i), (iii), and (iv) of the referenced regularity theorem hold. For every \(p\) such that \(g_x(G_x^{-1}(p))>0\), \[\lim_{s\to0}\frac{G_{x+s}^{-1}(p)-G_x^{-1}(p)}{s}=\mathbb E[Y_x\mid Z_x=G_x^{-1}(p)].\] Consequently, \(x\mapsto G_x^{-1}(p)\) is differentiable and, for \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]\), \[(Z_x,\mathbb E[Y_x\mid Z_x])\overset d=\left(G_x^{-1}(U),\frac{\partial}{\partial x}G_x^{-1}(U)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated integrability, density, and referenced regularity assumptions, the derivative of a quantile at every probability level having positive density equals the conditional mean of the pathwise derivative at that quantile. The random variable and its reduced derivative therefore have the same joint law as the quantile transform of a uniform variable and its parameter derivative.
assumptions_latex: Z_x\text{ has continuous distribution function }G_x\text{ and density }g_x
\text{Assumptions (i), (iii), and (iv) of the referenced regularity theorem hold}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\partial}{\partial x}G_x^{-1}(p)=\mathbb E[Y_x\mid Z_x=G_x^{-1}(p)],\qquad (Z_x,\mathbb E[Y_x\mid Z_x])\overset d=\left(G_x^{-1}(U),\frac{\partial}{\partial x}G_x^{-1}(U)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Differentiability of Order p
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak differentiation tested against continuous functions having at most p-th-order polynomial growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((\mu_x)_{x\in U\subseteq\mathbb R}\) of probability measures on \(\mathbb R^m\) is weakly differentiable of order \(p\) if there exists a finite signed measure \(\mu_x'\) such that, for every continuous \(H\) satisfying \(|H(u)|\le C(1+\|u\|^p)\) for all \(u\) and some constant \(C\), \[\frac{1}{s}\left(\int H(w)\,d\mu_{x+s}(w)-\int H(w)\,d\mu_x(w)\right)\longrightarrow\int H(w)\,d\mu_x'(w)\quad(s\to0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar-parameterized family of probability measures on Euclidean space is weakly differentiable of order p when the derivative identity holds for every continuous test function growing no faster than a constant times one plus the p-th power of the norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{s\to0}\frac{\int H\,d\mu_{x+s}-\int H\,d\mu_x}{s}=\int H\,d\mu_x'.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak-solution and ergodicity conditions for SDE finite differences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity assumptions shared by finite-difference sensitivity procedures for a parameterized diffusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\theta\) and initial state \(x\), assume the state SDE has a unique weak solution. Let \(c\) be bounded, require \((x,\theta)\mapsto E[\int_0^T c(\theta,x(s,\theta))ds\mid x(0)=x]\) to be continuous, and require the transition law \((x,\theta)\mapsto P\{x(t,\theta)\in\cdot\mid x(0)=x,\theta\}\) to be weakly continuous. For each fixed \(\theta\), assume there is a unique invariant measure \(\mu(\cdot\mid\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-difference sensitivity methods require only a unique weak solution for each parameter and initial state, a bounded cost with continuous finite-horizon expected integral, weak continuity of the transition law in state and parameter, and a unique invariant measure for every fixed parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(\forall(\theta,x)\), the parameterized SDE has a unique weak solution from \(x(0)=x\).
The transition kernel is weakly continuous in \((x,\theta)\).
\(\forall\theta\), there is a unique invariant measure \(\mu(\cdot\mid\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These weak-solution, continuity, and invariant-measure properties constitute the common assumptions for the finite-difference procedures.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transfer of Differentiability Between Density Powers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A chain rule transferring L^p differentiability of one density power to L^r differentiability of another when r<p.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that \(x\mapsto g_x^{1/p}\) is \(L^p\)-differentiable with derivative \(\nabla_x g_x\), and let \(r<p\). Then \(x\mapsto g_x^{1/r}\) is \(L^r\)-differentiable and its derivative is \(\frac{p}{r}g_x^{1/r-1/p}\nabla_x g_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the p-th root of a parameterized density is differentiable in Lp and r is smaller than p, then its r-th root is differentiable in Lr, with the stated power-chain-rule derivative.
assumptions_latex: x\mapsto g_x^{1/p}\text{ is }L^p\text{-differentiable with derivative }\nabla_x g_x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_x\bigl(g_x^{1/r}\bigr)=\frac{p}{r}g_x^{1/r-1/p}\nabla_x g_x\quad\text{in }L^r.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hazard Representation of a Reduced Process Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced process derivative expressed through the hazard and cumulative-hazard derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_x\) have distribution function \(G_x\), hazard function \(\lambda_x\), and cumulative hazard \(\Lambda_x\). Wherever \(\lambda_x(Z_x)\ne0\), \[\left(Z_x,-\frac{\partial_x\Lambda_x(Z_x)}{\lambda_x(Z_x)}\right)\] is a reduced process derivative pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a parameterized distribution with hazard function, the negative parameter derivative of the cumulative hazard divided by the hazard, evaluated at the random variable, is its reduced process derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(Z_x,-\frac{\partial_x\Lambda_x(Z_x)}{\lambda_x(Z_x)}\right)\text{ is a reduced process derivative pair.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Properties of Process Derivative Pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convolution and differentiable-pushforward rules for process derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((Z_x^{(1)},Y_x^{(1)})\) and \((Z_x^{(2)},Y_x^{(2)})\) are independent process derivative pairs for \((\mu_x)\) and \((\nu_x)\), respectively, then \((Z_x^{(1)}+Z_x^{(2)},Y_x^{(1)}+Y_x^{(2)})\) is a process derivative pair for \((\mu_x*\nu_x)\). If \(S\) is boundedly differentiable and \((Z_x,Y_x)\) is a process derivative pair for \((\mu_x)\), then \((S(Z_x),Y_xS'(Z_x))\) is a process derivative pair for the pushforward family \((\mu_x^S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent process derivative pairs add to a process derivative pair for the convolution of their probability laws. A boundedly differentiable transformation sends a process derivative pair to the transformed pair obtained by multiplying its derivative component by the transformation derivative.
assumptions_latex: (Z_x^{(1)},Y_x^{(1)})\text{ is a process derivative pair for }(\mu_x)
(Z_x^{(2)},Y_x^{(2)})\text{ is an independent process derivative pair for }(\nu_x)
(Z_x,Y_x)\text{ is a process derivative pair for }(\mu_x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (Z_x^{(1)}+Z_x^{(2)},Y_x^{(1)}+Y_x^{(2)})\text{ differentiates }(\mu_x*\nu_x),\quad (S(Z_x),Y_xS'(Z_x))\text{ differentiates }(\mu_x^S).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L1 Density Differentiability Implies Weak Measure Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for weak differentiability and a Jordan-type probability-measure representation of the derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\mu_x\ll
u\) has density \(g_x\), and \(x\mapsto g_x\) is differentiable in \(L^1(
u)\) with derivative \(g_x'\). Then \(x\mapsto\mu_x\) is weakly differentiable with signed derivative density \(g_x'\). Let \(c_x=	frac12\|g_x'\|_1=	frac12\int|g_x'(u)|\,d
u(u)\). When \(c_x>0\), the derivative has the representation \(\mu_x'=c_x(\dot\mu_x-\ddot\mu_x)\), where \[ rac{d\dot\mu_x}{d
u}= rac{[g_x']^+}{c_x},\qquad  rac{d\ddot\mu_x}{d
u}= rac{[g_x']^-}{c_x},\] with \([a]^+=\max(a,0)\) and \([a]^-=-\min(a,0)\). If \(c_x=0\), then \(g_x'=0\) in \(L^1(
u)\) and the weak derivative is the zero signed measure; the displayed normalized densities require a separate convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: L1 differentiability of the densities of a probability-law family implies weak differentiability of the laws. The signed derivative splits into its positive and negative density parts, each normalized to a probability measure when the derivative is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_x'\ll\nu,\quad \frac{d\mu_x'}{d\nu}=g_x',\quad c_x=\frac12\|g_x'\|_1,\quad \mu_x'=c_x(\dot\mu_x-\ddot\mu_x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pathwise mean-square sensitivity process for a parameterized SDE
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct parameter differentiation of a diffusion trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\in[a,b]\) and let \(x(t,\theta)\in\mathbb R^k\) solve \(dx(t,\theta)=b(x(t,\theta),\theta)\,dt+\sigma(x(t,\theta))\,dw(t)\). Define \(y(t,\theta)\) by \(dy=[b_x(x,\theta)y+b_\theta(x,\theta)]\,dt+D\sigma(x)[y] \,dw\), where its \(i\)-th diffusion component is \(\sum_{j,p}(\partial\sigma_{ij}/\partial x_p)y_p\,dw_j\). Then \(y(t,\theta)\) is the pathwise mean-square derivative of \(x(t,\theta)\) with respect to \(\theta\). Under the bounded-derivative assumptions, the state and sensitivity equations have unique strong and weak solutions for each initial condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smoothly parameterized diffusion with bounded first derivatives, differentiating the drift and diffusion coefficients yields a linearized SDE whose solution is the pathwise mean-square parameter derivative of the state trajectory. Both SDEs have unique strong and weak solutions for each initial condition.
assumptions_latex: \(\theta\in[a,b]\), \(x(t,\theta)\in\mathbb R^k\), and \(w\) is a standard vector-valued Wiener process.
\(b(x,\theta)\) is continuously differentiable with bounded first partial derivatives in \(x\) and \(\theta\).
\(\sigma(x)\) is continuously differentiable with bounded first partial derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y(t,\theta)=\frac{\partial x(t,\theta)}{\partial\theta}\text{ in the pathwise mean-square sense, and both displayed SDEs have unique strong and weak solutions for each initial condition.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Differentiability of a Moving Set with Respect to a Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through the first-order weak expansion of the measure restricted to a parameterized set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\mapsto A(x)\) be a parameterized family of measurable sets and let \(\mu\) be a measure. The mapping is weakly differentiable with respect to \(\mu\) at \(x\) if there exists a finite signed measure \(\mu'_{A(x)}\) such that, for every bounded continuous function \(H\), \[\lim_{s\to0}\frac{1}{|s|}\left[\int H(w)\bigl(\mathbf 1_{A(x+s)}(w)-\mathbf 1_{A(x)}(w)\bigr)\,d\mu(w)-s\int H(w)\,d\mu'_{A(x)}(w)\right]=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moving measurable set is weakly differentiable with respect to a measure when the change in every bounded continuous weighted set integral admits a first-order expansion represented by one finite signed measure, with a remainder that is little-o of the parameter increment's magnitude.
assumptions_latex: x\mapsto A(x)\text{ is a family of measurable sets}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int H(\mathbf1_{A(x+s)}-\mathbf1_{A(x)})\,d\mu=s\int H\,d\mu'_{A(x)}+o(|s|)\quad(s\to0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blockwise pathwise-sensitivity observation for diffusion stochastic approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A frozen-parameter state-sensitivity simulation used to construct stochastic-approximation observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(T>0\). On each block \([nT,nT+T)\), hold the parameter at \(\theta_n^\epsilon\), evolve \(dx^\epsilon=b(x^\epsilon,\theta_n^\epsilon)\,dt+\sigma(x^\epsilon)\,dw\) and \(dy^\epsilon=[b_x(x^\epsilon,\theta_n^\epsilon)y^\epsilon+b_\theta(x^\epsilon,\theta_n^\epsilon)]\,dt+D\sigma(x^\epsilon)[y^\epsilon] \,dw\), and form \(Y_n^\epsilon=-T^{-1}\int_{nT}^{nT+T}[\nabla_xc(\theta_n^\epsilon,x^\epsilon(s))^Ty^\epsilon(s)+c_\theta(\theta_n^\epsilon,x^\epsilon(s))]ds\). Define \(g(\theta,x,y)=E[Y_n^\epsilon\mid\theta_n^\epsilon=\theta,x^\epsilon(nT)=x,y^\epsilon(nT)=y]\); this conditional mean is independent of \(n\) and \(\epsilon\). Because the parameter changes between blocks, \(y^\epsilon\) is not the pathwise derivative of the complete time-varying process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On each sampling block, freeze the parameter, jointly simulate the diffusion and its linearized sensitivity equation, and average the chain-rule derivative of the running cost to obtain the stochastic-approximation observation. The sensitivity is only a frozen-parameter approximation when the parameter varies between blocks, not an exact derivative of the full time-varying process.
assumptions_latex: The coefficients and cost possess the derivatives appearing in the state, sensitivity, and observation equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Y_n^\epsilon=-\frac1T\int_{nT}^{nT+T}\left[\nabla_xc(\theta_n^\epsilon,x^\epsilon(s))^Ty^\epsilon(s)+c_\theta(\theta_n^\epsilon,x^\epsilon(s))\right]ds,\quad g(\theta,x,y)\text{ is independent of }n\text{ and }\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L^p-to-L^1 Chain Rule for Bounded-Variation Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar composition rule for parameterized random variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $x\mapsto H(x,\cdot)$ be $L^p$-differentiable with derivative $h(x,\cdot)$. Let $G:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be everywhere differentiable, with $G'=G_1'-G_2'$ for monotone functions $G_1'$ and $G_2'$. If $1/p+1/q=1$ and each map $x\mapsto G_i'(H(x,\cdot))$ is continuous in $L^q(\mu)$, $i=1,2$, then $x\mapsto G(H(x,\cdot))$ is $L^1$-differentiable and
\[
D[G\circ H](x,\omega)=G'(H(x,\omega))h(x,\omega).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If H is Lp-differentiable, G is differentiable with derivative expressible as the difference of two monotone functions, and the two composed derivative terms vary continuously in the conjugate Lq space, then G composed with H is L1-differentiable with the usual chain-rule derivative.
assumptions_latex: x\mapsto G_i'(H(x,\cdot))\text{ is continuous in }L^q(\mu),\quad i=1,2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\mapsto G(H(x,\cdot))\text{ is }L^1\text{-differentiable with derivative }G'(H(x,\omega))h(x,\omega)

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothed Perturbation Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian smoothing converts an irregular objective into a differentiable surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\), let \(\sigma>0\), and define \(F_\sigma(\theta)=\mathbb E[F(\theta+\sigma Z)]\) for \(Z\sim N(0,I_d)\). Draw independent perturbations \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\sim N(0,I_d)\) and simulator inputs such that \(\mathbb E[Y(\theta+\sigma Z_i,U_i)\mid Z_i]=F(\theta+\sigma Z_i)\). Choose integrable baselines \(b_i\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[b_iZ_i]=0\), and compute \[\widehat g_\sigma=\frac{1}{m\sigma}\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(Y(\theta+\sigma Z_i,U_i)-b_i\bigr)Z_i.\] Under the stated integrability conditions, return \(\widehat g_\sigma\), which is unbiased for \(\nabla F_\sigma(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian smoothing produces a differentiable surrogate whose gradient can be estimated with random perturbations and any integrable baseline orthogonal to the perturbation direction.
assumptions_latex: Each \(b_i\) is integrable and satisfies \(\mathbb E[b_iZ_i]=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_\sigma]=\nabla F_\sigma(\theta)=\sigma^{-1}\mathbb E[F(\theta+\sigma Z)Z]\).

notation.meaning: Integrable baseline orthogonal in expectation to its perturbation direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Sample-Path Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient local regularity conditions for valid pathwise sensitivity estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A jointly measurable simulator \(Y:\Theta\times\mathcal U\to\mathbb R\) is in the regular sample-path regime at \(\theta_0\in\operatorname{int}\Theta\) if \(\mathbb E[|Y(\theta_0,U)|]<\infty\) and there is a neighborhood \(N\) of \(\theta_0\) such that almost every map \(\theta\mapsto Y(\theta,U)\) is differentiable on \(N\), the simulated event identities and path dimension remain locally constant except on a null set, and an integrable random variable \(M\) satisfies \(\sup_{\theta\in N}\|\nabla_\theta Y(\theta,U)\|\le M\) almost surely. These conditions permit differentiation under expectation at \(\theta_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular regime requires an integrable base output, almost-sure local differentiability, stable path structure, and an integrable uniform bound on path derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla_\theta\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]|_{\theta=\theta_0}=\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta Y(\theta_0,U)]\).

notation.meaning: Neighborhood of the parameter under consideration.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Discontinuity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator simulation demonstrating failure of naive pathwise differentiation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y(\theta,U)=\mathbf 1\{U\le\theta\}\) for \(0<\theta<1\). For every fixed \(\theta\), the sample path is locally constant for all \(U\ne\theta\), so \(\partial_\theta Y(\theta,U)=0\) almost surely. Nevertheless, \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]=\theta\), and hence \(F'(\theta)=1\). The expectation changes through paths crossing the moving discontinuity, a contribution invisible to the almost-sure path derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an indicator with a moving threshold, almost every path derivative is zero although the expected output has derivative one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\partial_\theta Y(\theta,U)]=0\ne1=F'(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Reordering Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Competing-event simulation where a parameter perturbation changes which event occurs first.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) be the time of one event, let a competing event occur at time \(\theta\in(0,1)\), and define \(Y(\theta,U)=\mathbf 1\{\theta<U\}\). Away from the crossing \(U=\theta\), the event order and output are locally constant, giving \(\partial_\theta Y(	heta,U)=0\) almost surely. However, \(F(\theta)=\mathbb P(U>\theta)=1-\theta\), so \(F'(\theta)=-1\). Pathwise differentiation therefore omits the first-order mass of trajectories whose event order changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When perturbing a scheduled event changes which competing event occurs first, locally constant paths can conceal a nonzero expectation derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\partial_\theta Y(\theta,U)]=0\ne-1=F'(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Topology Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mechanism by which topology-switching paths contribute missing first-order sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y(\theta,U)\) be pathwise differentiable within each fixed-topology region, and let a topology switch be represented locally by \(s(\theta,U)=0\). For \(h>0\), define \(A_h=\{U:s(\theta,U)s(\theta+h,U)\le0\}\), and let \(J_h(U)\) denote the signed output jump attributable to the topology switch. Suppose \(\mathbb P(A_h)=\lambda h+o(h)\) for some \(\lambda>0\) and \(\mathbb E[J_h\mid A_h]\to j\ne0\). Then \[\mathbb E[J_h\mathbf 1_{A_h}]=\lambda jh+o(h).\] Thus switching paths produce a nonzero one-sided derivative contribution \(\lambda j\) that derivatives computed solely within fixed-topology regions omit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pathwise differentiation crosses its validity boundary when an order-step set of switching paths has a nonvanishing average signed jump, producing a first-order contribution absent from fixed-topology derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(Y(\theta,U)\) is differentiable within each fixed-topology region.
The topology switch is represented locally by a measurable function \(s\).
The signed switch jump satisfies \(\mathbb E[J_h\mid A_h]\to j\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h^{-1}\mathbb E[J_h\mathbf 1_{A_h}]\to\lambda j\ne0\), so fixed-topology path derivatives omit this switching contribution.

notation.meaning: Local switching function for event topology.
Set of paths crossing the switching surface under a positive perturbation h.
Signed output jump attributable to the topology switch.
First-order switching-rate coefficient and limiting conditional signed jump.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrability and Expectation Identity for the Score Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded sufficient condition for likelihood-ratio differentiation of an expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\geq1\) and let \(q\) be its Hölder conjugate. If \(x\mapsto\varphi_x^{1/p}\) is differentiable in \(L^p(\nu)\), then \(l_x\in L^p(\mu_x)\). If additionally \(H\in L^q(\mu_x)\) and \(Z_x\sim\mu_x\), then \[\mathbb E\!\left[H(Z_x)l_x(Z_x)\right]=\nabla_x\int H(w)\,d\mu_x(w).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lp differentiability of the pth root of the density makes the score Lp-integrable; with an Lq performance function, the score-weighted expectation equals the derivative of the expected performance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: l_x\in L^p(\mu_x),\qquad \mathbb E[H(Z_x)l_x(Z_x)]=\nabla_x\int H(w)\,d\mu_x(w)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Score Function and Score-Function Gradient Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition for likelihood-ratio sensitivity estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_x\) have density \(\varphi_x\) with respect to \(\nu\), with \(L^1\)-derivative \(\varphi_x'\). The score function is \(l_x(w):=\varphi_x'(w)/\varphi_x(w)\), where the formal notation \(\partial_x\log\varphi_x(w)\) denotes this ratio. If \(Z_x\sim\mu_x\) and \(F(x)=\mathbb E[H(Z_x)]\), then \(Y_x:=H(Z_x)l_x(Z_x)\) is the score-function estimator of \(\nabla_xF(x)\). Moreover, \(\mathbb E[l_x(Z_x)]=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The score is the density derivative divided by the density. Multiplying it by the simulated performance gives the score-function gradient estimator, and the score has mean zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: l_x(w):=\frac{\varphi_x'(w)}{\varphi_x(w)},\qquad Y_x:=H(Z_x)l_x(Z_x),\qquad \mathbb E[l_x(Z_x)]=0

knowledge_statements.title: Path Likelihood-Ratio Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-path score representation for a differentiable finite-horizon simulation law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_\theta\) have density \(p_\theta\) relative to a fixed measure, and let \(J(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[Y(X)]\), where \(Y\) has no direct dependence on \(\theta\). If differentiation may pass under the integral and \(S_\theta(X)=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta(X)\) is integrable with \(Y\), then \[J'(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[Y(X)S_\theta(X)].\] For a path \(X_{0:T}\) with density \(p_{\theta,0}(x_0)\prod_{t=1}^T p_{\theta,t}(x_t\mid x_{0:t-1})\), \[S_\theta(X_{0:T})=\partial_\theta\log p_{\theta,0}(X_0)+\sum_{t=1}^T\partial_\theta\log p_{\theta,t}(X_t\mid X_{0:t-1}).\] Thus \(Y S_\theta\) is an unbiased path likelihood-ratio estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative of an expected path payoff equals the expected payoff times the sum of the initial and transition log-likelihood scores.
assumptions_latex: \(p_\theta\) has parameter-independent support and is differentiable in \(\theta\).
Differentiation and integration may be interchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J'(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[Y S_\theta]\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reward-to-go localization of transition scores for additive path performance when the initial law is parameter independent.

source_refs.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) be the path filtration, let \(Y=\sum_{u=0}^T R_u\), where each \(R_u\) is \(\mathcal F_u\)-measurable, and let \(s_t=\partial_\theta\log p_{\theta,t}(X_t\mid X_{0:t-1})\). Assume the initial path law is independent of \(\theta\). Since \(\mathbb E_\theta[s_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\), \(\mathbb E_\theta[R_u s_t]=0\) whenever \(u<t\). Consequently, when the likelihood-ratio identity and the required integrability conditions hold, \[J'(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[Y\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\right]=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\sum_{u=t}^T R_u\right].\] The right-hand expression is a transition-local score representation using each transition's reward-to-go.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the initial law is parameter independent, past rewards can be removed from each transition-score product, yielding an unbiased representation based on transition scores and their rewards-to-go.

children.title: Score-Estimator Variance Growth
children.top_down_role: Long-horizon or rare-event deterioration of likelihood-based estimators.

knowledge_statements.title: Score-Estimator Variance Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear long-horizon variance growth caused solely by accumulated transition scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((s_t,\mathcal F_t)_{t=1}^T\) be square-integrable score increments satisfying \(\mathbb E[s_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[s_t^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\ge c>0\). Then the cumulative score \(S_T=\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\) obeys \[\operatorname{Var}(S_T)=\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E[s_t^2]\ge cT.\] In particular, for the constant payoff \(Y\equiv1\), the likelihood-ratio estimator \(G_T=Y S_T=S_T\) is unbiased for the zero derivative of \(\mathbb E_\theta[Y]\), yet \(\operatorname{Var}(G_T)\ge cT\). Thus unbiasedness does not prevent horizon-induced deterioration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a constant payoff, an unbiased cumulative-score estimator can have variance growing at least linearly with the simulation horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(G_T)\ge cT\) for \(G_T=\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\).

notation.meaning: Cumulative path score through horizon T.
Uniform lower bound on conditional score variance.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Derivative Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed-measure representation of a derivative through two probability laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_\theta\) be a differentiable family of probability measures whose weak derivative at \(\theta\) admits the decomposition \[P_\theta'=c_\theta(P_\theta^+-P_\theta^-),\] where \(c_\theta\ge0\) and \(P_\theta^+,P_\theta^-\) are probability measures. For every measurable performance \(h\) integrable under both component laws, \[\frac{d}{d\theta}\int h(x)P_\theta(dx)=c_\theta\left(\mathbb E_{P_\theta^+}[h(X^+)]-\mathbb E_{P_\theta^-}[h(X^-)]\right).\] Hence paired or independent simulations from the two component laws produce the unbiased estimator \(c_\theta(h(X^+)-h(X^-))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak derivative decomposed into two probability laws yields sensitivity as a scaled difference of their expected performances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}P_\theta h=c_\theta(P_\theta^+h-P_\theta^-h)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Process-Derivative Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled simulation of positive and negative derivative-process laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a horizon \(T\), scale \(c_\theta\), component process laws \(P_{\theta,T}^+\) and \(P_{\theta,T}^-\), a performance \(H\), and replication count \(m\). For each replication \(r\), simulate a coupling \((X_{0:T}^{+,r},X_{0:T}^{-,r})\) having the prescribed marginal laws and compute \[G_r=c_\theta\left(H(X_{0:T}^{+,r})-H(X_{0:T}^{-,r})\right).\] Output \(\widehat J_m'=m^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^mG_r\). If the path-law derivative is \(P_{\theta,T}'=c_\theta(P_{\theta,T}^+-P_{\theta,T}^-)\), then \(\mathbb E[\widehat J_m']=J_T'(\theta)\). The coupling may be chosen to reduce variance without changing this expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulate coupled positive and negative derivative processes, difference their path performances, scale, and average to estimate sensitivity without bias.
assumptions_latex: Each simulated pair has marginals \(P_{\theta,T}^+\) and \(P_{\theta,T}^-\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat J_m']=J_T'(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Couple paths \(X^{\theta+h}\) and \(X^\theta\), define \(A_h=\{X^{\theta+h}\ne X^\theta\}\), and set \(\Delta_h=H(X^{\theta+h})-H(X^\theta)\). Suppose, as \(h\downarrow0\), that \(\mathbb P(A_h)=\lambda h+o(h)\) for some \(0<\lambda<\infty\), that \(\Delta_h=0\) off \(A_h\), and that \(\mathbb E[\Delta_h\mid A_h]\to d\). Then \[\lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\mathbb E[H(X^{\theta+h})]-\mathbb E[H(X^\theta)]}{h}=\lambda d.\] Thus the one-sided sensitivity separates into a perturbation-event intensity and its limiting conditional effect. If additionally \(\mathbb E[\Delta_h^2\mid A_h]\to v\) for some \(0<v<\infty\), then \[\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_h/h)\sim\frac{\lambda v}{h}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If coupled paths differ with positive probability proportional to the perturbation size, the one-sided sensitivity equals the event intensity times the limiting conditional payoff change; the raw difference quotient has inverse-perturbation variance under a positive limiting conditional second moment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monte Carlo likelihood-ratio policy-gradient estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon discounted-return estimator using trajectory policy scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), simulate a depth-\(d\) trajectory \(\tau_i\) from \(s_0\sim b\) under \(\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\). Define \(R(\tau_i)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\gamma^{k-1}r_{ik}\) and \(S(\tau_i)=\sum_{(s,a)\in\tau_i}\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\). Return \(\widehat g=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}S(\tau_i)R(\tau_i)\) as the policy-gradient estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulate m finite-depth trajectories, multiply each trajectory's discounted return by the sum of its action log-policy gradients, and average these products to estimate the policy gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regression finite-difference policy-gradient estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-direction finite differences of finite-horizon discounted rollout returns.

With \(D\) having rows \(\Delta\theta_i^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\Delta U_i=U(\theta+\Delta\theta_i)-U(\theta)\), return \(\widehat g=D^{\dagger}\Delta U\) as the policy-gradient estimate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A triple $\bigl(c(\theta),F^{(+)},F^{(-)}\bigr)$ is a weak derivative of the c.d.f. $F(\cdot;\theta)$ if, for every $g\in\mathcal L$ that does not depend on $\theta$, $$\frac{d}{d\theta}\int g(x)\,dF(x;\theta)=c(\theta)\left(\int g(x)\,dF^{(+)}(x;\theta)-\int g(x)\,dF^{(-)}(x;\theta)\right).$$

knowledge_statements.title: Analytic-Simulation Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Analytic differentiation of a tractable term plus simulated residual sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the objective admits the decomposition \[J(\theta)=A(\theta)+\mathbb E[R(\theta,\xi)],\] where \(A\) is analytically differentiable. Let \(G(\theta,\xi)\) be an integrable simulation estimator satisfying \(\mathbb E[G(\theta,\xi)]=\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E[R(\theta,\xi)]\). Then \[J'(\theta)=A'(\theta)+\mathbb E[G(\theta,\xi)],\] and, for independent replications \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\), \[\widehat J_m'(\theta)=A'(\theta)+\frac1m\sum_{r=1}^mG(\theta,\xi_r)\] is unbiased. Only the residual derivative requires simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiate the tractable objective component exactly and add an unbiased simulation estimate of the residual derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(G(\theta,\xi)\) is integrable and unbiased for the residual derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat J_m'(\theta)]=J'(\theta)\).
