knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential OCBA Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential allocation of a finite simulation budget using estimated performance gaps and output variability, including the integer-rounding failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $k$ alternatives, total budget $\beta$, batch size $\tau$, and initial allocation $n_0\ge 5$, where $\beta-kn_0$ is a nonnegative multiple of $\tau$, initially sample each alternative $n_0$ times. At iteration $t$, update the sample means $\bar x_i$ and standard deviations $\widehat\sigma_i$, and designate an empirically best alternative $(k)\in\arg\max_i\bar x_i$. Compute continuous target allocations whose total budget is increased by $\tau$ and which satisfy, for nonbest alternatives $(i),(j)$, $\frac{n_{(i),t+1}}{n_{(j),t+1}}=\left(\frac{\widehat\sigma_{(i)}/d_{(i)(k)}}{\widehat\sigma_{(j)}/d_{(j)(k)}}\right)^2$ and $n_{(k),t+1}=\widehat\sigma_{(k)}\sqrt{\sum_{i:(i)\ne(k)}n_{(i),t+1}^2/\widehat\sigma_{(i)}^2}$. After integer rounding, simulate alternative $i$ an additional $(n_{(i),t+1}-n_{(i),t})^+$ times and repeat while the accumulated sample count is below $\beta$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initially sample every alternative n0 times. Repeatedly estimate means and standard deviations, identify an empirically best alternative, and calculate OCBA targets: nonbest allocations follow squared standard-deviation-to-gap ratios, and the best allocation satisfies the balancing equation. Round the targets and add the resulting positive sample deficits until the budget is reached. If a newly calculated target is below an alternative's current sample count, monotone sample counts, all OCBA allocation equations, and an exact batch increase of tau may be mutually incompatible; a rounding or allocation constraint must then be relaxed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The allocation is updated sequentially according to the OCBA ratio and balancing equations until the sampling budget is reached, subject to integer rounding and possible constraint relaxation when a target falls below a current allocation.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Budget, EOC-bound, and PCS-bound stopping conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-alternative selection using either OCBA or EVI allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Three stopping rules are: (i) the deterministic budget rule \(S\), which continues sampling iff \(\sum_{i=1}^k n_i<\beta\); (ii) the EOC-bound rule, which continues while \(\operatorname{EOC}_{\mathrm{Bonf}}>\varepsilon^*\) and stops once \(\operatorname{EOC}_{\mathrm{Bonf}}\le\varepsilon^*\), where \(\varepsilon^*>0\); and (iii) the Slepian PCS-bound rule, which stops once \[\operatorname{PCS}_{\mathrm{Slep}}=\prod_{(i)\ne(k)}\Phi_{v_{(i)(k)}}(d_{ik}^*)\ge1-\alpha^*,\] where \(\alpha^*>0\) is the acceptable posterior probability-of-incorrect-selection level. These rules may be paired with either OCBA or EVI allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequential selection procedure can stop when a fixed total budget is exhausted, when an upper bound on posterior expected opportunity cost falls below a chosen tolerance, or when a Slepian lower bound on posterior probability of correct selection reaches the required confidence level. The adaptive rules apply to both OCBA and EVI allocation.
assumptions_latex: \text{The relevant posterior EOC or PCS bounds are computable.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Stop if }\sum_i n_i\ge\beta\text{, or }\operatorname{EOC}_{\mathrm{Bonf}}\le\varepsilon^*\text{, or }\operatorname{PCS}_{\mathrm{Slep}}\ge1-\alpha^*\text{, according to the chosen rule.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential optimal computing budget allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-budget sequential OCBA allocation recipe; it does not by itself state an asymptotic efficiency or probability-of-correct-selection theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=|\mathcal X|\), choose \(n_0>1\), and suppose \(B\ge Mn_0\) is divided after initialization into increments \(\Delta\). Initially take \(n_0\) observations from every alternative. At iteration \(n\), compute \(\theta_x^n\), \(\widehat\sigma_x^{2,n}\), and the current best \(b=x^n\in\arg\max_x\theta_x^n\). For nonbest \(x,x'\), choose the next target allocation so that \[\frac{N_x^{n+1}}{N_{x'}^{n+1}}=\frac{\widehat\sigma_x^{2,n}/(\theta_b^n-\theta_x^n)^2}{\widehat\sigma_{x'}^{2,n}/(\theta_b^n-\theta_{x'}^n)^2},\] and choose the best alternative's allocation by \[N_b^{n+1}=\widehat\sigma_b^n\sqrt{\sum_{i\ne b}\left(\frac{N_i^{n+1}}{\widehat\sigma_i^n}\right)^2},\] subject, up to rounding, to \(\sum_xN_x^{n+1}=B^n+\Delta\). Simulate alternative \(x\) an additional \(\max\{N_x^{n+1}-N_x^n,0\}\) times. Repeat until the total budget \(B\) is reached, then return \(\arg\max_x\theta_x^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential OCBA begins with equal pilot samples, repeatedly estimates each alternative's mean and variance, and identifies the current best. Each budget increment is allocated according to estimated variances and squared performance gaps; allocations that decrease cause no new simulations for that alternative. At the total budget, the alternative with the largest sample mean is returned.
assumptions_latex: \theta_b^n-\theta_x^n\ne0\quad\text{for each nonbest alternative used in the ratio rule}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}N_x^n=B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \widehat x\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\theta_x^n

children.title: OCBA Efficiency Results
children.top_down_role: Large-budget allocation and selection-efficiency families.

assumptions_latex: There is a unique best alternative \(b\), and all mean gaps \(\delta_i=\mu_i-\mu_b\) for \(i\ne b\) are nonzero.
Observations are independent normal variables with variances \(0<\sigma_i^2<\infty\).
Allocation fractions converge to strictly positive limits satisfying the classical OCBA equations with true parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected smallest sample mean converges almost surely to \(b\), and the limiting fractions satisfy the OCBA ratio system.

notation.meaning: unique true best alternative for minimization
true mean gap relative to b

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency and classical large-budget allocation ratios under independent normal sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(n_i(N)/N\to\alpha_i>0\), then every alternative is sampled infinitely often, so the sample means converge almost surely to their true means and selection by the smallest sample mean is consistent. The classical OCBA limiting fractions obey \[\frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_j}=\frac{(\sigma_i/\delta_i)^2}{(\sigma_j/\delta_j)^2}\quad(i,j\ne b),\qquad \alpha_b=\sigma_b\sqrt{\sum_{i\ne b}\frac{\alpha_i^2}{\sigma_i^2}},\qquad \sum_i\alpha_i=1.\] These equations express the standard large-budget OCBA efficiency prescription.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive limiting sampling fractions ensure consistent selection; classical OCBA further prescribes asymptotic fractions determined by each alternative's variance and mean gap.
knowledge_statements.title: OCBA Efficiency Results

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consistency implication from strictly positive limiting fractions is plausible, but the OCBA equations are already assumed and therefore are not proved as an efficiency result by this statement. The leaf calls for an efficiency result, which should be recorded as a theorem or complexity/efficiency result with an exact source and noncircular hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LL multi-alternative allocation with nonnegativity correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagewise Bayesian value-of-information allocation under linear opportunity loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an additional budget \(\tau\), current counts \(n_i\), estimated variances \(\widehat\sigma_i^2\), and LL weights \(\gamma_i\), the continuous allocation is
\[
\tau_{(i)}=\frac{\left(\tau+\sum_{j=1}^k n_j\right)(\widehat\sigma_{(i)}^2\gamma_{(i)})^{1/2}}{\sum_{j=1}^k(\widehat\sigma_j^2\gamma_j)^{1/2}}-n_{(i)},
\]
where, for \((i)\ne(k)\),
\[
\gamma_{(i)}=\widehat\lambda_{ik}^{1/2}\frac{v_{(i)(k)}+(d_{ik}^*)^2}{v_{(i)(k)}-1}\phi_{v_{(i)(k)}}(d_{ik}^*),
\qquad
\gamma_{(k)}=\sum_{j:(j)\ne(k)}\gamma_{(j)}.
\]
This rule asymptotically minimizes the LL approximation when \(\tau\) is arbitrarily large and the resulting allocations are nonnegative. For smaller \(\tau\), initialize \(\mathcal S=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), recompute the allocation over \(\mathcal S\), remove alternatives assigned \(\tau_i\le0\), and repeat until all retained allocations are positive; excluded allocations are zero and the retained values are rounded so that \(\sum_i\tau_i=\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LL rule allocates samples according to estimated variance and information weights after accounting for samples already collected. Its continuous formula is asymptotically optimal for the LL approximation at large stage budgets. At smaller budgets, alternatives with nonpositive tentative allocations are removed and the rule is recomputed, then rounded to the integer budget.
assumptions_latex: \widehat\sigma_i^2\text{ and the LL pairwise statistics are available.}
v_{(i)(k)}>1\text{ wherever the displayed weight is used.}
\text{Asymptotic optimality concerns the large-}\tau\text{ continuous allocation.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau_i\ge0\ \forall i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\tau_i=\tau,\qquad \text{and the uncorrected rule asymptotically minimizes the LL approximation as }\tau\to\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: ESP Allocation and Stopping Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A heuristic, asymptotically motivated sequential policy for ranking and selection with more than one alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k>1\) alternatives with estimated posterior means \(\bar x_{i,t}\), sampling costs \(c_i>0\), sampling variances \(\sigma_i^2\), and sample counts \(n_{i,t}\), define \(\widehat\Delta_{i,t}=\left|\bar x_{i,t}-\max_{j\ne i}\bar x_{j,t}\right|\), with any known-mean standard included in the comparison set. The \(ESP_b\) rule continues sampling while there exists an \(i\) such that \[c_i^{1/3}\sigma_i^{2/3}b\!\left(\frac{\sigma_i^{2/3}}{c_i^{2/3}n_{i,t}}\right)>\widehat\Delta_{i,t}.\] While continuing, it allocates one sample to an alternative in \[\arg\max_i\left\{b\!\left(\frac{\sigma_i^{2/3}}{c_i^{2/3}n_{i,t}}\right)-\frac{\widehat\Delta_{i,t}}{c_i^{1/3}\sigma_i^{2/3}}\right\}.\] If \(\sigma_i^2\) is unknown, implementations may substitute the sample variance \(\widehat\sigma_i^2\). The approximation presumes that one sample is allocated at a time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For more than one alternative, continue sampling while at least one alternative lies inside its approximate continuation boundary relative to the best estimated mean among the other alternatives. At each continuing stage, sample an alternative maximizing its standardized depth inside that region. A sample variance may replace an unknown sampling variance, and the heuristic presumes one-at-a-time sampling.
assumptions_latex: \text{The boundary function }b\text{ and its asymptotic approximation are applicable.}
\text{One sample is allocated per decision stage.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Continue while }\exists i:\ c_i^{1/3}\sigma_i^{2/3}b\!\left(\frac{\sigma_i^{2/3}}{c_i^{2/3}n_{i,t}}\right)>\widehat\Delta_{i,t};\quad \text{if continuing, sample an }i\in\arg\max_i\left\{b\!\left(\frac{\sigma_i^{2/3}}{c_i^{2/3}n_{i,t}}\right)-\frac{\widehat\Delta_{i,t}}{c_i^{1/3}\sigma_i^{2/3}}\right\}.

children.title: Knowledge Gradient for Finite Alternatives
children.top_down_role: Value-of-information allocation for independent or correlated alternatives.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many alternatives with an integrable Bayesian posterior for their unknown means.
A single additional observation may be taken from any alternative, with its predictive distribution determined by the current information state.
The terminal recommendation maximizes posterior mean reward.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The knowledge-gradient action is any \(x_n\in\arg\max_x \nu_x^n\).

notation.meaning: posterior mean of alternative i after n observations
posterior mean after hypothetically sampling x once
one-step knowledge-gradient value of sampling x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step Bayesian value of information for finite independent or correlated alternatives.

source_refs.locator: 7.4 The Knowledge Gradient Algorithm for Discrete Alternatives p. 262

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At information state \(\mathcal F_n\), define the one-step value of measuring alternative \(x\) by \[\nu_x^n=\mathbb E\!\left[\max_i m_i^{n+1}(x)\mid\mathcal F_n\right]-\max_i m_i^n.\] Choose \(x_n\in\arg\max_x\nu_x^n\), observe its noisy response, and update the joint posterior; correlated posteriors may update unmeasured alternatives as well. Repeat until the sampling budget is exhausted, then recommend any \(i^\star\in\arg\max_i m_i^N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Knowledge gradient samples the alternative with the largest expected one-step increase in the best posterior mean, updates the posterior, and finally recommends the largest posterior mean.
knowledge_statements.title: Knowledge Gradient for Finite Alternatives

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-alternative small-sample EVI rule (LL1/KG1)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-stage lookahead allocation for finite alternatives under posterior expected opportunity cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At each stage, constrain the entire additional batch \(\tau\) to one alternative. For every alternative \(i\), compute \(\operatorname{EVI}_{LL,(i)}\), the expected reward improvement from sampling \(i\) and then selecting the alternative with the greatest updated sample mean. Choose
\[
i^*\in\arg\max_{1\le i\le k}\operatorname{EVI}_{LL,(i)},
\qquad \tau_{i^*}=\tau,
\qquad \tau_\ell=0\quad(\ell\ne i^*).
\]
For a nonbest alternative, its valuation compares it with the best of the other alternatives; for the current best, the relevant comparison is with the second-best alternative. The choice is recomputed at subsequent stages. Because only one alternative is sampled per stage, this rule avoids the LL asymptotic allocation, Bonferroni, and Welch approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LL1, also called KG or KG1 in this setting, assigns the entire stage budget to the alternative with the largest one-step expected value of information. The choice is recomputed each stage and avoids the approximations used by the multi-alternative LL allocation.
assumptions_latex: \text{Exactly one alternative receives the stage budget.}
\text{Posterior expected opportunity cost, equivalently the stated expected reward improvement, is the criterion.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i^*\in\arg\max_i\operatorname{EVI}_{LL,(i)},\qquad \tau_{i^*}=\tau,\qquad \tau_\ell=0\ \forall\ell\ne i^*.

children.title: Bayesian Ranking Policies
children.top_down_role: Posterior-driven ranking and recommendation policies.

assumptions_latex: A finite set of alternatives has a posterior distribution for its unknown performance vector after each observation.
A measurable terminal loss \(L(a,\mu)\) is specified for recommendation \(a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The posterior ranking is induced by \(r_i^n\), and the Bayes recommendation minimizes posterior expected terminal loss.

notation.meaning: posterior ranking score for alternative i

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Bayesian ranking policy computes measurable posterior scores \(r_i^n=r_i(\mathcal F_n)\) and orders alternatives by these scores; posterior means, posterior probabilities of being best, and posterior expected losses are admissible score choices when defined. Its terminal recommendation is a Bayes action \[a_n\in\arg\min_a\mathbb E[L(a,\mu)\mid\mathcal F_n].\] For simple regret under maximization, this reduces to \(a_n\in\arg\max_i\mathbb E[\mu_i\mid\mathcal F_n]\). Sampling actions may be chosen from the current posterior ranking or by a separate value-of-information rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayesian policy ranks alternatives using posterior-derived scores and makes its final recommendation by minimizing posterior expected loss; under simple regret it chooses the largest posterior mean.

children.title: Search-Generated Candidate Screening
children.top_down_role: Reduction of a candidate set produced by preceding search.

assumptions_latex: A preceding search returns a finite random candidate set \(C\).
Fresh screening observations can be generated conditionally independently of the search history.
A screening statistic and threshold are fixed before the fresh observations are inspected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The retained set \(C'=\{i\in C:T_i\le c_i\}\) is the output passed to final selection.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic fresh-data screening interface after stochastic search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Condition on the search history and its finite output \(C\). Generate a prespecified fresh screening sample for every \(i\in C\), compute statistics \(T_i\), and retain \[C'=\{i\in C:T_i\le c_i\}.\] The direction and thresholds are chosen so that larger \(T_i\) means stronger evidence of inferiority. If \(C'=\varnothing\), apply a prespecified fallback, such as retaining the candidate with smallest \(T_i\). Output only \(C'\) and the fresh screening data required by the subsequent final-selection procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After search generates a finite candidate set, fresh data and prespecified thresholds remove candidates showing sufficient evidence of inferiority, with a predefined fallback if all are removed.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-Generated Candidate Screening

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record specifies a plausible generic screening interface, but no source establishes the statistic orientation, threshold construction, fallback, or data passed to final selection. A specific screening procedure or an authoritative source for this interface is required.

children.title: Independent Final Selection
children.top_down_role: Final selection using simulation evidence separated from candidate generation.

assumptions_latex: A finite candidate set \(C\) is measurable with respect to a search history \(\mathcal H\).
Conditional on \(C\), the final-stage data are independent of \(\mathcal H\) and follow the sampling model assumed by a fixed-set selection procedure.
For every deterministic admissible candidate set, that procedure has conditional erroneous-selection probability at most \(\alpha\), where \(0\le\alpha\le 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\widehat i\text{ is an erroneous selection}\mid C)\le\alpha\) almost surely and hence \(\Pr(\widehat i\text{ is an erroneous selection})\le\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-splitting result for preserving fixed-set final-selection guarantees.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Ranking and Selection p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate final-stage observations independently of \(\mathcal H\) conditional on the realized candidate set \(C\), and apply the prespecified fixed-set selection procedure to those observations only. If its erroneous-selection probability is at most \(\alpha\) for every admissible deterministic candidate set, then \[\Pr(\widehat i\text{ is an erroneous selection}\mid C)\le\alpha\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad \Pr(\widehat i\text{ is an erroneous selection})\le\alpha.\] Thus candidate generation does not invalidate the final guarantee, provided the guarantee is interpreted relative to the realized candidate set and the fresh-data assumptions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If fresh final-stage data are conditionally independent of candidate generation and a fixed-set procedure controls erroneous selection for every admissible set, then it retains the same conditional and unconditional error bound for the random realized candidate set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-stage indifference-zone selection with independent sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-sampling finite-alternative selection procedure with adaptive alternative-specific sample sizes and a probability-of-correct-selection guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\delta>0\), \(0<\alpha<1\), and a first-stage size \(n_0\). For each of \(K\) alternatives, collect \(n_0\) i.i.d. observations, independently across alternatives, and compute its sample variance \(s_i^2\). Using the prescribed critical constant \(h\), set \(n_i=\max\{n_0,\lceil h^2s_i^2/\delta^2\rceil\}\). Collect \(n_i-n_0\) additional observations independently of the first stage and of all other alternatives, form \(\bar L_i=n_i^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n_i}y_k(\boldsymbol\theta_i)\), and select an alternative with the smallest \(\bar L_i\). Under the normal-output assumptions of the indifference-zone procedure, if the best alternative \(\boldsymbol\theta^*\) satisfies \(L(\boldsymbol\theta_j)-L(\boldsymbol\theta^*)\ge\delta\) for every \(\boldsymbol\theta_j\ne\boldsymbol\theta^*\), its probability of selection is at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independently sample each alternative, use its first-stage variance to determine its total sample size, independently collect the remaining observations, and select the smallest combined sample mean. Under the procedure's normal-output assumption, the probability of selecting the best alternative is at least 1−alpha when every competitor is worse by at least delta.
assumptions_latex: Observations for each alternative are i.i.d., with independence across alternatives and between stages.
The simulation outputs satisfy the normality assumption used by the indifference-zone procedure.
The prescribed critical constant \(h\) corresponds to the chosen \(K\), \(n_0\), and \(\alpha\).
A best alternative \(\boldsymbol\theta^*\) satisfies \(L(\boldsymbol\theta_j)-L(\boldsymbol\theta^*)\ge\delta\) for every \(\boldsymbol\theta_j\ne\boldsymbol\theta^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: n_i=\max\left\{n_0,\left\lceil\frac{h^2s_i^2}{\delta^2}\right\rceil\right\},\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(\boldsymbol\theta^*\text{ is selected}\right)\ge 1-\alpha.

children.title: Noisy Random Search
children.top_down_role: Random proposal and acceptance families under simulation noise.

assumptions_latex: The feasible region \(X\) is measurable and each simulation call returns an integrable noisy observation \(Y(x)\) with mean \(f(x)\).
A proposal kernel \(Q_t(\cdot\mid x_t)\), replication rule, and measurable acceptance rule are specified.
The algorithm has a finite simulation budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The incumbent sequence is generated by random proposals and noise-aware acceptance, and the terminal incumbent is returned.

notation.meaning: estimated objective difference between proposal and incumbent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic minimization template for random-proposal search under simulation noise.

source_refs.locator: 1.4.1 Random search techniques p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in X\). At iteration \(t\), draw \(z_t\sim Q_t(\cdot\mid x_t)\), generate the prescribed replications at \(z_t\) and, if required, at \(x_t\), and form an estimate \(\widehat\Delta_t\) of \(f(z_t)-f(x_t)\). With a prespecified measurable acceptance function \(A_t\), set \[x_{t+1}=z_t\quad\text{if }A_t(\widehat\Delta_t,\text{estimated uncertainty})=1,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t\quad\text{otherwise}.\] Stop when the simulation budget is exhausted and return the terminal incumbent or the best independently validated visited point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noisy random search proposes random feasible points, compares them with the incumbent using replicated noisy observations, applies a fixed acceptance rule, and returns a terminal or validated incumbent.

children.title: Noisy Simplex Search
children.top_down_role: Simplex-based local exploration with uncertain comparisons.

assumptions_latex: The domain is a subset of \(\mathbb R^d\), and a simplex has \(d+1\) affinely independent feasible vertices.
Each vertex or trial point can be assigned replicated noisy objective observations.
Comparison and replication rules are fixed and measurable with respect to accumulated data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Noise-aware ordering followed by simplex transformations and replication updates defines the incumbent simplex sequence.

notation.meaning: estimated mean objective at vertex v
trial point produced by a simplex transformation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic replicated noisy extension of simplex direct search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a feasible simplex \(S_0=\{v_{0,0},\ldots,v_{0,d}\}\). At iteration \(t\), allocate replications to obtain \(\widehat f_t(v)\) and uncertainty estimates for vertices requiring comparison. Order the vertices using a prespecified noise-aware comparison rule, generate a feasible trial point \(z_t\) by a fixed simplex transformation such as reflection, expansion, contraction, or shrinkage, and simulate \(z_t\). Accept the transformation only according to the same comparison rule; otherwise increase replication or shrink the simplex. Stop at the budget or declared size-and-precision criterion and return the best validated vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noisy simplex search repeatedly estimates vertex performance, applies reflection or related simplex transformations using uncertainty-aware comparisons, adds replications when needed, and returns the best validated vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Simplex Search

children.title: Noisy Pattern Search
children.top_down_role: Structured local polling over simulation-evaluated pattern directions.

assumptions_latex: The objective is \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\) on \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), and simulation provides sample-mean estimates with finite variance.
Each polling set \(D_k\) is finite and positive spanning, and feasible trial points have the form \(x_k+\Delta_k d\) with \(d\in D_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The incumbent sequence is generated entirely from noisy function comparisons, with successful iterations moving to an accepted poll or pattern point and unsuccessful iterations reducing the mesh size.

notation.meaning: Incumbent and positive mesh size at iteration \(k\).

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in X\), \(\Delta_0>0\), expansion \(\gamma_+\geq1\), contraction \(\gamma_-\in(0,1)\), and replication rules \(m_k\), evaluate feasible poll points \(P_k=\{x_k+\Delta_kd:d\in D_k\}\). Using the prescribed noisy acceptance rule, select an accepted \(y_k\in P_k\), optionally followed by a feasible pattern point continuing the successful displacement. If a point \(z_k\) is accepted, set \(x_{k+1}=z_k\) and \(\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_+\Delta_k\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) and \(\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_-\Delta_k\). Stop when the simulation budget is exhausted or \(\Delta_k\leq\Delta_{\min}\), and return the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Poll a positive-spanning mesh with replicated simulations, accept an estimated improvement, enlarge after success, shrink after failure, and return the final incumbent.

children.title: Noisy Compass Search
children.top_down_role: Coordinate-oriented polling under noisy simulation responses.

assumptions_latex: The objective is \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\) on a feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\).
Simulation estimates at every tested point use a specified finite replication count or sequential sampling rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iteration tests only coordinatewise neighbors; acceptance moves the incumbent, while failure contracts the common coordinate step.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in X\), \(\Delta_0>0\), and constants \(\gamma_+\geq1\), \(\gamma_-\in(0,1)\). At iteration \(k\), simulate the feasible compass neighbors \(C_k=\{x_k+\Delta_kd:d\in\{\pm e_1,\ldots,\pm e_d\}\}\). If the prescribed noisy comparison accepts some \(y_k\in C_k\), choose an accepted point with smallest estimated objective, set \(x_{k+1}=y_k\), and set \(\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_+\Delta_k\). If none is accepted, set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) and \(\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_-\Delta_k\). Stop at a budget limit or when \(\Delta_k\leq\Delta_{\min}\), and output \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulate positive and negative coordinate moves, accept a statistically adequate improvement, expand or retain the step after success, and contract it after failure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: COMPASS most-promising-area stochastic search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A locally oriented random-search procedure for discrete optimization via simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with \(x_0\in\Theta\), \(\mathcal V_0=\{x_0\}\), \(x_0^*=x_0\), simulate \(n_0(x_0)\) i.i.d. observations, and set \(\Theta_0=\Theta\). At iteration \(m\ge1\), sample \(t_m\) points independently and uniformly from \(\Theta_{m-1}\), allowing duplicates; add them to the visited set \(\mathcal V_m\); allocate and simulate \(n_m(x)\) additional i.i.d. replications for every \(x\in\mathcal V_m\) according to the sample-allocation rule; update cumulative counts and sample means; choose \(x_m^*\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal V_m}\bar Y_m(x)\); and set \(\Theta_m=\{x\in\Theta:\|x-x_m^*\|\le \|x-y\|\ \forall y\in\mathcal V_m\setminus\{x_m^*\}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: COMPASS repeatedly samples uniformly from a most-promising region, updates simulation estimates for every visited solution, selects a visited solution with minimum sample mean, and replaces the region by the feasible points at least as close to that incumbent as to any other visited solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\), a local-search radius, an initial replication count \(m_0\), and batch size \(b\). At iteration \(k\), generate a local trial \(y_k\). For stages \(j=0,1,\ldots\), simulate until \(m_{k,j}=m_0+jb\) paired or independent replications are available and construct a valid confidence interval \([L_{k,j},U_{k,j}]\) for \(f(y_k)-f(x_k)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Model-free Q-learning update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-based state-action value updating for a discounted Markov decision process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After observing or simulating a transition $i\xrightarrow{a}j$ with reward $r(i,a,j)$, update $Q^{k+1}(i,a)\leftarrow(1-\alpha^{k+1})Q^k(i,a)+\alpha^{k+1}\left[r(i,a,j)+\lambda\max_{b\in\mathcal A(j)}Q^k(j,b)\right]$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robbins-Monro step-size summability conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard diminishing learning-rate conditions forming part of the hypotheses for stochastic-approximation convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two required step-size conditions are $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha^k=\infty$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(\alpha^k)^2<\infty$. The schedules $\alpha^k=A/(B+k)$ for suitable parameters and $\alpha^k=\log(k)/k$ satisfy these two conditions, whereas a fixed positive step size violates square summability. These two conditions alone do not replace the additional technical hypotheses required for convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard learning-rate sequence has an infinite total sum but a finite sum of squares. Reciprocal-affine and logarithmic-over-linear schedules pass these two tests, while a positive constant rate fails the second. Further technical conditions are also required for an optimal-convergence guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \text{Additional algorithmic and technical convergence conditions hold when optimal convergence is asserted}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha^k=\infty,\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(\alpha^k)^2<\infty;\qquad \alpha^k\equiv c>0\implies\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(\alpha^k)^2=\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recursive sample-mean update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive estimation of a finite mean from independent samples as a basic Robbins-Monro specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ be independent samples of $X$ and let $X^k=k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^kx_i$. Then $X^{k+1}=(1-\alpha^{k+1})X^k+\alpha^{k+1}x_{k+1}$ with $\alpha^{k+1}=1/(k+1)$. This recursion equals direct averaging, and $X^k\to\mathbb E[X]$ almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sample mean can be updated recursively by combining the current estimate with the next independent sample. With learning rate 1/(k+1), the recursion is exactly ordinary averaging and converges almost surely to the true mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X^{k+1}=\left(1-\frac1{k+1}\right)X^k+\frac1{k+1}x_{k+1},\qquad X^k\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mathbb E[X].

assumptions_latex: The observation satisfies \(G_k=\nabla f(x_k)+M_{k+1}+r_k\), where \(M_{k+1}\) is a martingale difference with bounded conditional second moment.
The steps obey \(a_k>0\), \(a_k\to0\), \(\sum_k a_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_k a_k^2<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected stochastic approximation iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines projection-constrained stochastic approximation and records when the projection is single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let G\subset\mathbb{R}^d be compact and let \Gamma project onto G, acting as the identity on \operatorname{int}(G) and mapping each point outside G to a nearest point of G in Euclidean distance, or in another chosen equivalent metric. Projected stochastic approximation uses
\[
x_{n+1}=\Gamma\!\left(x_n+a(n)\bigl[h(x_n)+M_{n+1}\bigr]\right).
\]
Consequently x_{n+1}\in G. The projection may be set-valued for a general compact G, but it is single-valued when G is convex; for a suitably regular nonconvex boundary it can also be single-valued at exterior points sufficiently close to \partial G.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected stochastic approximation applies a projection onto a prescribed compact set after every stochastic update, so every updated iterate lies in that set. Nearest-point projection can be set-valued for a general compact set, is single-valued for a convex set, and may be locally single-valued near a sufficiently regular nonconvex boundary.
assumptions_latex: \Gamma\text{ maps onto }G\text{ and is a nearest-point projection outside }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{n+1}=\Gamma\!\left(x_n+a(n)[h(x_n)+M_{n+1}]\right)\in G;\quad G\text{ convex}\implies\Gamma\text{ is single-valued}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected stochastic-approximation recursion for simulation optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive estimated-gradient optimization of an expected performance measure over a continuous parameter space, including the constrained-projection boundary and classical Robbins–Monro and Kiefer–Wolfowitz estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a continuous parameter space and \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)]\). Stochastic approximation uses the recursion
\[
x_{n+1}=\Pi_\Theta\!\left(x_n-a_n\widehat{\nabla}f(x_n)\right),\qquad a_n>0,
\]
to seek a sequence converging to the unique local optimizer \(x^*=\arg\min_{x\in\Theta}f(x)\), and returns \(x_N\) at stopping time \(N\). Projection is required only in the constrained setting; replacing descent by ascent gives the maximization version. Robbins--Monro uses unbiased direct-gradient estimates, whereas Kiefer--Wolfowitz uses finite-difference gradient estimates. Under their respective additional conditions, their stated asymptotic convergence rates are \(O(n^{-1/2})\) and \(O(n^{-1/3})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an expected performance objective over a continuous parameter space, stochastic approximation recursively subtracts a positive gain times an estimated gradient and projects the result back into the feasible set. The recursion is intended to converge to the unique local optimizer, with the iterate at a stopping time returned as output. Projection is needed only for constrained problems, and the ascent-sign version handles maximization. Robbins–Monro uses unbiased direct-gradient estimates, while Kiefer–Wolfowitz uses finite-difference estimates. Under respective additional conditions not specified in the extract, their stated asymptotic rates are O(n^−1/2) and O(n^−1/3).
assumptions_latex: x^*=\arg\min_{x\in\Theta}f(x)\text{ is the unique local optimizer sought}
\text{The stated Robbins--Monro and Kiefer--Wolfowitz rates require respective additional conditions not specified in the extract.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{n+1}=\Pi_\Theta\!\left(x_n-a_n\widehat{\nabla}f(x_n)\right),\qquad x_N\text{ is returned at stopping time }N;\qquad \mathrm{rate}_{\mathrm{RM}}=O(n^{-1/2}),\quad \mathrm{rate}_{\mathrm{KW}}=O(n^{-1/3})\text{ under the respective additional conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Multiplier stability is ensured by either of two regimes. In the projection regime, replace the orthant projection by projection onto a known compact convex set \(\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}_+^m\) containing a dual solution. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multipliers remain stable when explicitly projected onto a suitable compact set or when a radially unbounded Lyapunov function has negative drift outside a compact region.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[x_{k+1}=x_k+a_k(v_k+M_{k+1}+r_k),\qquad v_k\in H(x_k).\] Define times \(t_0=0\), \(t_{k+1}=t_k+a_k\), and let \(\bar x(t)\) linearly interpolate \(x_k\) on \([t_k,t_{k+1}]\). Under the assumptions, every time-shifted subsequential limit of \(\bar x\) is an absolutely continuous solution of \[\dot x(t)\in H(x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t.\] Thus the differential inclusion, rather than a single ordinary differential equation, represents the limiting dynamics when the mean field is nonsmooth or genuinely set-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded stochastic recursion with compact convex set-valued drift is asymptotically represented by the corresponding differential inclusion; its limit set is internally chain-transitive.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of boundedness without projection or inward Lyapunov drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=1\), let \(H(x)=\{x\}\), choose \(x_0>0\), and take noise and bias identically equal to zero. For any steps satisfying \(a_k>0\), \(a_k\to0\), and \(\sum_k a_k=\infty\), the recursion is \[x_{k+1}=x_k+a_kx_k=(1+a_k)x_k,\qquad x_k=x_0\prod_{j<k}(1+a_j),\] and satisfies \(x_k\to+\infty\). Thus a continuous, singleton-valued, convex-valued drift of linear growth does not ensure bounded stochastic-approximation iterates; an additional stability mechanism such as projection, coercivity, or negative Lyapunov drift outside a compact set is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With zero noise and drift H(x)={x}, every positive initial state diverges under diminishing positive steps whose sum is infinite. Regularity of the set-valued drift alone therefore does not ensure stability.
assumptions_latex: The steps satisfy \(a_k>0\), \(a_k\to0\), \(\sum_k a_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_k a_k^2<\infty\).
No projection, coercive Lyapunov condition, or inward-drift condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Even a continuous singleton-valued drift with linear growth can produce unbounded iterates; regularity of the set-valued map alone does not establish stochastic-approximation stability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Correlated-noise Kiefer–Wolfowitz recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-mean decomposition of a paired finite-difference stochastic-approximation update into drift, finite-difference bias, centered observation noise, and a correction term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y_n=(Y_n^- -Y_n^+)/(2c_n)\), where \(c_n\ne0\). Let \((\mathcal F_n)\) be nondecreasing and measure at least \(\{\xi_i^\pm,Y_{i-1},\theta_i:i\le n\}\). Suppose \(\xi_n=(\xi_n^+,\xi_n^-)\) is random, \(\gamma_n^\pm\) and \(g_n\) are measurable, \(\beta_n\) is random, and
\[
E_nY_n^\pm=\gamma_n^\pm(\theta_n,c_n,\xi_n^\pm),\qquad
\frac{\gamma_n^-(\theta_n,c_n,\xi_n^-)-\gamma_n^+(\theta_n,c_n,\xi_n^+)}{2c_n}=g_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\beta_n.
\]
Define
\[
\delta M_n=(Y_n^- -E_nY_n^-)-(Y_n^+ -E_nY_n^+).
\]
Then the expanded recursion is
\[
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+\epsilon_ng_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\epsilon_n\beta_n+\epsilon_n\frac{\delta M_n}{2c_n}+\epsilon_nZ_n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For paired finite-difference observations, decompose the conditional mean difference into a drift and finite-difference bias and center both observations. The resulting update consists of the drift, bias, centered observation-noise term divided by twice the perturbation scale, and the additional correction term.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal F_n)\text{ is nondecreasing and measures at least }\{\xi_i^\pm,Y_{i-1},\theta_i:i\le n\}
\xi_n=(\xi_n^+,\xi_n^-)\text{ is random, }\gamma_n^\pm\text{ and }g_n\text{ are measurable, and }\beta_n\text{ is random}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+\epsilon_ng_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\epsilon_n\beta_n+\epsilon_n\frac{\delta M_n}{2c_n}+\epsilon_nZ_n

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Kiefer-Wolfowitz Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical coordinatewise central-difference stochastic approximation for unconstrained smooth minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given noisy observations \(Y(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon\), initialize \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\). At iteration \(k\), obtain independent observations \(Y_{k,i}^{\pm}\) at \(x_k\pm c_k e_i\) and form \[\widehat g_k=\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{Y_{k,i}^{+}-Y_{k,i}^{-}}{2c_k}e_i.\] Update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-a_k\widehat g_k\). Stop at a prescribed iteration or when a chosen stochastic stationarity diagnostic is met, and return the final iterate or an iterate average. Each iteration uses \(2d\) function measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate every gradient coordinate by two noisy symmetric function evaluations, then take a stochastic-approximation step; one iteration costs twice the dimension in measurements.
assumptions_latex: Observation errors have conditional mean zero and finite conditional variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-a_k\widehat g_k\), using \(2d\) measurements per iteration.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Kiefer–Wolfowitz central-difference recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise two-sided finite-difference stochastic approximation, its bias-noise decomposition, and its conditional mean-ODE interpretation; the extract does not provide a sufficient convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(\theta)=\mathbb E[F(\theta,\chi)]\) be continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb R^r\), let \(c_n>0\), and set \(Y_{n,i}=-[F(\theta_n+c_ne_i,\chi_{n,i}^+)-F(\theta_n-c_ne_i,\chi_{n,i}^-)]/(2c_n)\). With \(Y_n=(Y_{n,1},\ldots,Y_{n,r})\), the Kiefer–Wolfowitz recursion is \(\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+\epsilon_nY_n\). If \([f(\theta_n+c_ne_i)-f(\theta_n-c_ne_i)]/(2c_n)=f_{\theta^i}(\theta_n)-\beta_{n,i}\), then \(\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n-\epsilon_n\nabla f(\theta_n)+\epsilon_n\psi_n/(2c_n)+\epsilon_n\beta_n\). Vanishing bias and local averaging of the scaled noise are necessary ingredients for convergence to a local minimum; under this asymptotic interpretation the associated mean ODE is \(\dot\theta=-\nabla f(\theta)\). The effective noise has scale \(1/c_n\), while keeping \(c_n\) positive reduces noise at the cost of persistent finite-difference bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coordinate Kiefer–Wolfowitz method estimates every gradient coordinate with two noisy function values and applies a stochastic descent update. Its recursion separates the gradient term, finite-difference bias, and noise amplified by the reciprocal perturbation size. Vanishing bias and locally averaging scaled noise support the gradient-flow mean-ODE interpretation but are not stated as a complete convergence theorem. A fixed perturbation reduces noise while retaining bias.
assumptions_latex: \(\theta_n\in\mathbb R^r\) and \(f(\theta)=\mathbb E[F(\theta,\chi)]\) is continuously differentiable.
Noisy function values are observed at \(\theta_n\pm c_ne_i\) for every coordinate \(i\).
For the stated mean-ODE interpretation, \(\beta_n\to0\) and the scaled noise \(\epsilon_n\psi_n/(2c_n)\) averages locally to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n-\epsilon_n\nabla f(\theta_n)+\epsilon_n\psi_n/(2c_n)+\epsilon_n\beta_n\), with associated mean ODE \(\dot\theta=-\nabla f(\theta)\) under the stated asymptotic bias and noise conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Kiefer–Wolfowitz recursion for a nonsmooth convex objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The finite-difference approximation result is conditional on convergence of the iterates and vanishing perturbation radius. The differential inclusion is the stated mean model, not a standalone iterate-convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and convex, and let \(\gamma_n\) be the coordinatewise centered finite-difference vector at \(\theta_n\) with radius \(c_n\). The Kiefer–Wolfowitz recursion is
\[
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n-\epsilon_n\gamma_n+\epsilon_n\frac{\psi_n}{2c_n}.
\]
Each coordinate difference is a subgradient of the corresponding one-dimensional convex slice at some point in \([-c_n,c_n]\). If \(\theta_n\to\theta\) and \(c_n\to0\), then
\[
\operatorname{dist}(\gamma_n,SG(\theta))\to0.
\]
The associated mean limiting model is
\[
\dot\theta\in-SG(\theta).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous convex objective that may be nonsmooth, coordinatewise finite differences drive the Kiefer–Wolfowitz update. Conditional on the iterates approaching a point and the differencing radius vanishing, the finite-difference vector approaches that point's subdifferential. The negative-subdifferential inclusion is the associated mean model; the extract does not itself prove iterate convergence.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous and convex}
\gamma_n\text{ is the coordinatewise centered finite-difference vector at }\theta_n\text{ with radius }c_n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(\gamma_n,SG(\theta))\to0,\qquad \dot\theta\in-SG(\theta)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential cyclic-coordinate Kiefer–Wolfowitz update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-component-at-a-time realization of coordinate Kiefer–Wolfowitz stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each cycle \(n=0,1,\ldots\) and \(i=0,\ldots,r-1\), define \(\widetilde Y_{nr+i}=[F(\theta_{nr+i}-c_ne_{i+1},\chi_{nr+i}^-)-F(\theta_{nr+i}+c_ne_{i+1},\chi_{nr+i}^+)]/(2c_n)\) and update \(\theta_{nr+i+1}=\theta_{nr+i}+\epsilon_ne_{i+1}\widetilde Y_{nr+i}\). One complete cycle updates every component once. The estimator mean may be periodic in the iteration index, requiring analysis that permits iteration-dependent mean values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sequential Kiefer–Wolfowitz scheme cycles through the coordinates, updating one coordinate from a symmetric noisy finite difference at each subiteration. A full cycle updates all coordinates, and the estimator mean may be periodic rather than stationary.
assumptions_latex: For each cycle \(n\), coordinates are visited in the order \(i=0,\ldots,r-1\).
Noisy function values are available at \(\theta_{nr+i}\pm c_ne_{i+1}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Kiefer–Wolfowitz recursion and averaging assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions A3.1–A3.4 for the projected coordinatewise finite-difference stochastic-approximation recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\mathcal F_n) be nondecreasing, with \mathcal F_n measuring at least \{\theta_0,Y_{i-1}^{\pm}:i\le n\}, and let E_n denote conditional expectation. For observations Y_{n,i}^{\pm} at \theta_n\pm c_ne_i, assume \sup_nE|Y_n^{\pm}|^2<\infty; uniformly-in-n continuous functions g_n and random variables \beta_n satisfy E_n[Y_n^- -Y_n^+]/(2c_n)=g_n(\theta_n)+\beta_n; a continuous \bar g satisfies \lim_{n,m\to\infty}m^{-1}\sum_{i=n}^{n+m-1}(g_i(\theta)-\bar g(\theta))=0 for every \theta\in H, along every joint divergence of n and m; and \epsilon_n/c_n^2\to0. The recursion is \theta_{n+1}=\Pi_H[\theta_n+\epsilon_n(Y_n^- -Y_n^+)/(2c_n)]=\theta_n+\epsilon_ng_n(\theta_n)+\epsilon_n\beta_n+(\epsilon_n/(2c_n))\delta M_n+\epsilon_nZ_n, where \delta M_n=(Y_n^- -Y_n^+)-E_n[Y_n^- -Y_n^+].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For coordinatewise observations at symmetric perturbations of the current iterate, assume uniformly bounded second moments, a uniformly continuous conditional mean decomposition, moving-average convergence of its drift to a continuous limiting field for every point in the constraint set, and a step-to-perturbation condition ε_n/c_n²→0. The projected Kiefer–Wolfowitz update then has the stated drift, bias, martingale-difference, and projection-correction decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta_{n+1}=\Pi_H\!\left[\theta_n+\epsilon_n\frac{Y_n^- -Y_n^+}{2c_n}\right]=\theta_n+\epsilon_ng_n(\theta_n)+\epsilon_n\beta_n+\frac{\epsilon_n}{2c_n}\delta M_n+\epsilon_nZ_n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-point random-direction Kiefer–Wolfowitz recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-direction finite-difference stochastic approximation, including observation cost, bias-noise decomposition, dependence boundary, and mean ODE.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d_n\in\mathbb R^r\) be random directions such that \(d_nd_n^	op\) averages locally to \(I\); mutual independence and the pointwise condition \(\mathbb E[d_nd_n^	op]=I\) are not required. Given observations \(Y_n^\pm=f(	heta_n\pm c_nd_n)+\psi_n^\pm\), the two-point update is \(	heta_{n+1}=	heta_n-\epsilon_nd_n(Y_n^+-Y_n^-)/(2c_n)\). For differentiable \(f\), it can be written as \(	heta_{n+1}=	heta_n-\epsilon_n[
abla f(	heta_n)- eta_n]+\epsilon_nd_n(\psi_n^--\psi_n^+)/(2c_n)+\epsilon_n\psi_n^d\), where \(\psi_n^d=(I-d_nd_n^	op)
abla f(	heta_n)\). Its mean ODE is \(\dot	heta=-
abla f(	heta)\). Each iteration uses two observations. One may take \(c_n	o0\), or keep \(c_n\) positive to reduce noise while accepting finite-difference bias; moreover, \(d_n\) and the observation noise generally need not be independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random-direction Kiefer–Wolfowitz step uses two noisy evaluations along a sampled direction and multiplies their symmetric difference by that direction. Local isotropy of the direction outer products replaces a full coordinate gradient estimate, producing the same gradient-flow mean ODE. The decomposition exposes finite-difference bias, amplified observation noise, and random-direction noise. Fixed perturbations reduce noise at the price of bias, and direction-noise independence generally cannot be assumed.
assumptions_latex: \(d_n\in\mathbb R^r\) and \(d_nd_n^\top\) averages locally to \(I\); successive directions may be correlated.
Either \(c_n>0\) tends to zero, or it is held positive with a corresponding nonvanishing-bias tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n-\epsilon_nd_n(Y_n^+-Y_n^-)/(2c_n)\), with decomposition through \(\beta_n\) and \(\psi_n^d=(I-d_nd_n^\top)\nabla f(\theta_n)\), and associated mean ODE \(\dot\theta=-\nabla f(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Direction Stochastic Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-measurement random-direction analogue of coordinate Kiefer-Wolfowitz search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Independently draw a direction \(u_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[u_ku_k^{\mathsf T}]=I_d\), observe \(Y_k^{\pm}\) at \(x_k\pm c_ku_k\), and set \[\widehat g_k=\frac{Y_k^+-Y_k^-}{2c_k}u_k.\] Update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-a_k\widehat g_k\) and return the final or averaged iterate. For smooth \(f\), conditional expectation over the direction and centered observation noise gives \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+O(c_k^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random direction replaces the coordinate sweep, producing an approximately unbiased gradient estimate from two noisy evaluations regardless of dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(u_k\) is independent of the past, centered, and has sufficiently many finite moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-a_k\widehat g_k\) with two measurements and \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+O(c_k^2)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Random-direction Kiefer–Wolfowitz recursion under correlated noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point random-direction stochastic approximation decomposed into drift, directional finite-difference bias, centered observation noise, directional-isotropy error, and correction terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d_n\) be uniformly bounded and let \((\mathcal F_n^d)\) be nondecreasing and measure at least \(\{\theta_i,d_i,Y_{i-1}:i\le n\}\). Let \(\gamma_n\) and \(g_n\) be measurable and \(\xi_n^\pm\) and \(\beta_n\) be random variables such that, for \(c_n\ne0\),
\[
E_{\mathcal F_n^d}Y_n^\pm=\gamma_n(\theta_n\pm c_nd_n,\xi_n^\pm)
\]
and
\[
\frac{\gamma_n(\theta_n-c_nd_n,\xi_n^-)-\gamma_n(\theta_n+c_nd_n,\xi_n^+)}{2c_n}=d_n^\top g_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\beta_n.
\]
Define
\[
\delta M_n=(Y_n^- -E_{\mathcal F_n^d}Y_n^-)-(Y_n^+ -E_{\mathcal F_n^d}Y_n^+).
\]
Then
\[
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+\epsilon_nd_nd_n^\top g_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\epsilon_nd_n\beta_n+\epsilon_nd_n\frac{\delta M_n}{2c_n}+\epsilon_nZ_n,
\]
equivalently,
\[
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+\epsilon_ng_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\epsilon_nd_n\beta_n+\epsilon_nd_n\frac{\delta M_n}{2c_n}+\epsilon_n(d_nd_n^\top-I)g_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\epsilon_nZ_n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For uniformly bounded random directions and paired observations at opposite directional perturbations, center the observations and decompose their conditional mean finite difference into directional drift and bias. The update may be written using the projected drift or as the full drift plus the directional-isotropy error.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal F_n^d)\text{ is nondecreasing and measures at least }\{\theta_i,d_i,Y_{i-1}:i\le n\}
\gamma_n\text{ and }g_n\text{ are measurable, and }\xi_n^\pm\text{ and }\beta_n\text{ are random variables}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+\epsilon_ng_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\epsilon_nd_n\beta_n+\epsilon_nd_n\frac{\delta M_n}{2c_n}+\epsilon_n(d_nd_n^\top-I)g_n(\theta_n,\xi_n)+\epsilon_nZ_n

knowledge_statements.title: Kiefer-Wolfowitz Convergence Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical strongly convex rate with central differences and independent bounded-variance noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose coordinate Kiefer-Wolfowitz search uses \(a_k=a/(k+1)\) and \(c_k=c(k+1)^{-1/6}\). If \(f\) is strongly convex with Lipschitz gradient, has uniformly bounded third coordinate derivatives, and the independent observation errors have uniformly bounded variance, then suitable positive constants \(a,c\) give \[\mathbb{E}\lVert x_k-x^\star\rVert^2=O(k^{-2/3}),\qquad \mathbb{E}[f(x_k)-f(x^\star)]=O(k^{-2/3}).\] Thus the root-mean-square iterate error is \(O(k^{-1/3})\); constants may depend on dimension and noise variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balancing central-difference bias against amplified independent noise yields mean-square iterate and objective-error rates of order two-thirds in the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is strongly convex, smooth, and has bounded third coordinate derivatives.
Observation errors are independent, centered, and uniformly square-integrable.
The gain constants satisfy the usual stable stochastic-approximation range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\lVert x_k-x^\star\rVert^2=O(k^{-2/3})\) and \(\mathbb{E}[f(x_k)-f(x^\star)]=O(k^{-2/3})\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-sided versus two-sided Kiefer–Wolfowitz scaling rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized-error scaling under the stated smoothness, stability, integrability, and tightness conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(f\in C^2\), \(\epsilon_n=n^{-\gamma}\), \(c_n=cn^{-\alpha}\), \(\beta+\alpha=\gamma/2\), and \(\beta=\alpha\) for the one-sided balance. Let \(A=-f_{\theta\theta}(\bar\theta)\) be negative definite and, when \(\gamma=1\), require \(A+\beta I\) to be negative definite. Assume the stated local uniform integrability, conditions (A2.2) and (A2.7), and tightness of \(U_n=n^\beta(\theta_n-\bar\theta)\). With \(\widehat B_i(\theta)=f_{\theta^i\theta^i}(\theta)/2\), the best normalization exponent is \(\beta=\gamma/4\) for one-sided differences and \(\beta=\gamma/3\) for two-sided differences; hence the two-sided scheme has the faster convergence rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated assumptions, balancing the step-size and perturbation exponents gives β=γ/4 for one-sided finite differences and β=γ/3 for two-sided finite differences. The two-sided Kiefer–Wolfowitz scheme therefore has the faster normalized rate.
assumptions_latex: \{Y_{n,i}I_{\{|\theta_n-\bar\theta|\leq\rho\}}:i=0,\ldots,r,\ n>0\}\text{ is uniformly integrable for small }\rho>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \beta_{\mathrm{one\text{-}sided}}=\frac{\gamma}{4}<\frac{\gamma}{3}=\beta_{\mathrm{two\text{-}sided}},\quad\text{so the two-sided case has the faster rate.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean-square error bound for coordinate Kiefer–Wolfowitz approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample product-sum mean-square bound for coordinatewise central-difference stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define $f_n(x)=\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{F(x+c_ne_i)-F(x-c_ne_i)}{2c_n}e_i$. Suppose $f_n$ and $f$ have unique roots $x_n^*$ and $x^*$, respectively, and $f_n(x)^T(x-x_n^*)\ge k_0\|x-x_n^*\|^2$, $\|f_n(x)\|\le K_1\|x-x^*\|+K_2$, $\|x_n^*-x^*\|\le Kc_n$, $\mathbb E\|Z(x)-F(x)\|^2\le\sigma^2$, $\sum_n a_n=\infty$, $\sum_n a_nc_n<\infty$, and $\sum_n a_n^2/c_n^2<\infty$. With $C_1=KK_1K_1$, $C_2=K_1^2+K_2^2$, and $C_3=K(K_1+K_2)$, the displayed product-sum bound holds for $\mathbb E\|X_n-x^*\|^2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated directional-growth, linear-growth, root-bias, simulation-variance, step-size, and perturbation conditions, coordinate Kiefer–Wolfowitz iterates satisfy the source's finite-sample product-sum mean-square error bound.
assumptions_latex: f_n(x_n^*)=0,\quad f(x^*)=0,\quad x_n^*\text{ and }x^*\text{ are unique}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E\|X_n-x^*\|^2\le \mathbb E\|X_1-x^*\|^2\prod_{j=1}^n(1-a_jk_0+a_jc_jC_1+2a_j^2K_1^2)+\sum_{j=1}^n\left(2a_j^2C_2+\frac{a_j^2\sigma^2}{c_j^2}+a_jc_jC_3\right)\prod_{i=j+1}^n(1-a_ik_0+a_ic_iC_1+2a_i^2K_1^2),\quad C_1=KK_1,\ C_2=K_1^2+K_2^2,\ C_3=K(K_1+K_2).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Functional-noise regularity conditions for Kiefer–Wolfowitz diffusion analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic expansion, Wiener-process convergence, auxiliary conditional sums, and finite-horizon moment bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(B\) is continuous and, for each \(\xi\), \(\widetilde g_n(\theta,\xi)\) is twice continuously differentiable with \[\widetilde g_n(\theta,\xi_n)=\widetilde g_n(\bar\theta,\xi_n)+\widetilde g'_{n,\theta}(\bar\theta,\xi_n)(\theta-\bar\theta)+\widetilde y_n|\theta-\bar\theta|^2,\] where, for sufficiently small \(\rho>0\), \[\sup_nE\![\left.|\widetilde y_n|^2I_{\{|\theta_n-\bar\theta|\leq\rho\}}\right.\u001b]<\infty.\] Suppose \[W^n(t)=\sum_{i=n}^{m(t_n+t)-1}\sqrt{\epsilon_i}\,[\widetilde g_i(\bar\theta,\xi_i)+\delta M_n(\bar\theta)]\Rightarrow W(t),\] where \(W\) is a Wiener process and \(\delta M_n(\theta)\) is the martingale difference at iterate \(n\) when parameter \(\theta\) is used. For \(T>0\), define \[\Gamma_i^n=\sum_{j=i}^{m(t_n+T)-1}E_i g_j(\bar\theta,\xi_j),\qquad \Lambda_i^n=\sum_{j=i}^{m(t_n+T)-1}E_i\widetilde g'_{j,\theta}(\bar\theta,\xi_j),\] and assume, for every \(T>0\), \[\sup_n\sup_{n\leq i\leq m(t_n+T)}E\![|g_i(\bar\theta,\xi_i)|^2+|\widetilde g_{i,\theta}(\bar\theta,\xi_i)|^2+|\delta M_i(\bar\theta)|^2\u001b]<\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diffusion analysis assumes continuity of B, a twice-differentiable local expansion with a uniformly square-integrable quadratic remainder near the target, convergence of the stated accumulated process to a Wiener process, the stated auxiliary conditional sums, and uniform second-moment bounds on every finite time horizon.
assumptions_latex: W^n\Rightarrow W\text{, where }W\text{ is a Wiener process}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated local-expansion, functional-noise, auxiliary-sum, and moment conditions are imposed.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion of Theorem 3.1 under a different explicitly listed assumption package.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the preceding conditions and algorithm form, let \(\epsilon_n,c_n,\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) be as in Theorem 3.1, and set \(U_n=n^\beta(\theta_n-\bar\theta)\). If conditions (A2.2), (A2.9), (A2.11), (A2.13), and (A3.2) hold, then the conclusions of Theorem 3.1 hold for \((U^n,W^n)\). Thus, for \(\gamma<1\), \((U^n,W^n)\) converges weakly to the stationary process satisfying \(dU=AU\,dt-c^2B(\bar\theta)\,dt+dW/(2c)\) together with a Wiener process \(W\) of covariance \(\Sigma_1\); when \(\gamma=1\), \(A+\beta I\) replaces \(A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity conditions for a two-sided Kiefer–Wolfowitz diffusion limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions (A3.1)–(A3.5), including the stability modification when the step size is 1/n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sufficiently small \(\rho>0\), assume \(\{Y_n^{\pm}I_{\{|\theta_n-\bar\theta|\leq\rho\}}\}\) is uniformly integrable and \(\{U_n\}\) is tight. Suppose measurable functions \(g_{n,i}\) satisfy \(E_nY_{n,i}^{\pm}=g_{n,i}(\theta_n\pm e_ic_n)\) and have continuous derivatives through order three. Define \(B_{n,i}(\theta)=g_{n,i,\theta^i\theta^i\theta^i}(\theta)/3!\) and assume \(m^{-1}\sum_{i=n}^{n+m-1}[B_i(\bar\theta)-B(\bar\theta)]\to0\). With \(\gamma_{n,i}=g_{n,i,\theta^i}\), assume \(\epsilon_n^{2/3}\sum_{i=n}^{n+mt-1}\gamma_i(\bar\theta)\to0\) uniformly on a bounded \(t\)-interval, \(\gamma_n(\theta)=\gamma_n(\bar\theta)+\gamma'_{n,\theta}(\bar\theta)(\theta-\bar\theta)+o(\theta-\bar\theta)\) uniformly in \(n\), and \(\{\gamma_i(\bar\theta),\gamma_{i,\theta}(\bar\theta)\}\) is bounded. Finally, for a Hurwitz matrix \(A\), assume \(m^{-1}\sum_{i=n}^{n+m-1}[\gamma'_{i,\theta}(\bar\theta)+A]\to0\). If \(\epsilon_n=1/n\), also require \(A+\beta I\) to be Hurwitz, where \(\beta=2\alpha=\gamma/3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two-sided Kiefer–Wolfowitz diffusion analysis assumes local uniform integrability, tight normalized errors, third-order smooth conditional means, averaged convergence of the bias and linearization terms, a uniform local linearization with bounded coefficients, and a Hurwitz limiting drift. For step size 1/n, the shifted drift A+βI must also be Hurwitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (A3.1)--(A3.5) are imposed for the Kiefer--Wolfowitz diffusion-limit theorem.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume algorithm (3.1), conditions (A2.2), (A2.7), and (A3.1)--(A3.5). If \(\gamma<1\), then \((U^n,W^n)\Rightarrow(U,W)\) in \(D^r[0,\infty)\times D^r(-\infty,\infty)\), where \(W\) is a Wiener process with covariance matrix \(\Sigma_1\) and \(U\) is the stationary process satisfying \[U(t)=\int_{-\infty}^t e^{A(t-s)}\left[\frac{dW(s)}{2c}-c^2B(\bar\theta)\,ds\right],\qquad dU=AU\,dt-c^2B(\bar\theta)\,dt+\frac{dW}{2c}.\] If \(\gamma=1\), the same conclusion holds with \(A+\beta I\) in place of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated algorithmic and regularity assumptions, the normalized two-sided Kiefer–Wolfowitz error process and its noise process converge weakly to a stationary linear diffusion and a Wiener process. The drift includes the finite-difference bias −c²B, and the diffusion coefficient is 1/(2c). At γ=1, A is replaced by A+βI.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (U^n,W^n)\Rightarrow(U,W),\quad dU=AU\,dt-c^2B(\bar\theta)\,dt+\frac{dW}{2c},\quad\operatorname{Cov}(W)=\Sigma_1;\qquad\gamma=1\implies A\mapsto A+\beta I.

knowledge_statements.title: Kiefer-Wolfowitz Finite-Difference Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local truncation bias of the symmetric coordinate finite-difference estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For coordinate \(i\), define \(D_{i,c}f(x)=[f(x+ce_i)-f(x-ce_i)]/(2c)\). If the one-dimensional restriction \(t\mapsto f(x+te_i)\) is five times continuously differentiable near zero, then \[D_{i,c}f(x)=\partial_i f(x)+\frac{c^2}{6}\partial_{iii}f(x)+O(c^4).\] Consequently, centered observation noise does not change the conditional bias, and the coordinate Kiefer-Wolfowitz gradient estimator satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat g(x,c)]-\nabla f(x)=O(c^2)\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric coordinate difference has second-order bias; centered simulation noise changes its variance but not its conditional mean.
assumptions_latex: For every coordinate, \(t\mapsto f(x+te_i)\) is five times continuously differentiable near \(0\).
Noisy function observations have conditional mean \(f\) at each queried point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{i,c}f(x)-\partial_i f(x)=\frac{c^2}{6}\partial_{iii}f(x)+O(c^4)\), hence the estimator bias is \(O(c^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Dependence Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias-variance regimes for averaged central differences under differently coupled simulation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Average \(n\) replicated central differences of radius \(c\), with deterministic bias \(O(c^2)\). If the paired observation-error difference satisfies \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon^+-\varepsilon^-)=O(c^{2q})\) for \(0\le q\le1\), then the gradient mean-square error is \[O(c^4)+O\!\left(n^{-1}c^{2q-2}\right).\] Balancing the terms gives \(c\asymp n^{-1/(6-2q)}\) and mean-square error \(O(n^{-4/(6-2q)})\). Independent noise corresponds to \(q=0\), giving \(O(n^{-2/3})\); sufficiently smooth common-random-number coupling corresponds to \(q=1\), giving \(O(n^{-1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stronger coupling of paired simulation noise reduces finite-difference variance and improves the optimally balanced gradient-estimation rate from two-thirds to the parametric rate.
assumptions_latex: The symmetric finite-difference bias is uniformly \(O(c^2)\).
Replicates are independent across pairs and have uniformly bounded second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The balanced gradient mean-square error is \(O(n^{-4/(6-2q)})\), ranging from \(O(n^{-2/3})\) to \(O(n^{-1})\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-measurement SPSA estimator and perturbation-moment condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard symmetric simultaneous-perturbation estimator, its dimension-independent simulation cost, and the stated perturbation requirement associated with almost-sure convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\Delta=(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_d)$ and $C=\operatorname{diag}(c_1,\ldots,c_d)$. The simultaneous-perturbation estimator is
\[
\widehat g_i(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+C\Delta,\xi_2)-Y(\theta-C\Delta,\xi_1)}{2c_i\Delta_i}.
\]
Because every component shares the same numerator, a full gradient estimate requires two simulator evaluations independently of $d$. The perturbations are generally taken independent across components and identically distributed over iterations. A key perturbation-sequence requirement stated for almost-sure SPSA convergence is $\mathbb E[\Delta_i]=0$ and $\mathbb E[\Delta_i^{-2}]<\infty$. This excludes Gaussian perturbations and admits symmetric Bernoulli perturbations such as $\mathbb P(\Delta_i=1)=\mathbb P(\Delta_i=-1)=1/2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SPSA evaluates the simulator at one positive and one negative simultaneous perturbation. Dividing their shared output difference by each scaled perturbation component produces every gradient component, so only two simulator evaluations are needed regardless of dimension. The stated key perturbation requirement for almost-sure convergence is zero mean and finite inverse second moment; Gaussian perturbations fail it, while symmetric Bernoulli perturbations satisfy it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat g_i(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+C\Delta,\xi_2)-Y(\theta-C\Delta,\xi_1)}{2c_i\Delta_i},\qquad N_{\mathrm{eval}}=2\ \text{independently of }d.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-Sure Convergence of the Referenced Simultaneous-Perturbation Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies only to the algorithm referenced as Eq. (10.16), whose update equation is absent from this extracted item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the algorithm defined by Eq. (10.16). Suppose \(f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}\) is nonnegative and continuously differentiable with globally Lipschitz gradient; \(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\mu^m=\infty\) and \(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(\mu^m)^2<\infty\); and, for some scalars \(A,B\), \(\mathbb{E}[w^m(i)\mid\mathcal{F}^m]=0\) for every coordinate \(i\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|w^m\|^2\mid\mathcal{F}^m]\le A+B\|\nabla f(x^m)\|^2\). Then, with probability one, \(\{f(x^m)\}_{m=1}^{\infty}\) converges and \(\lim_{m\to\infty}\nabla f(x^m)=0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb{P}\!\left(\{f(x^m)\}_{m=1}^{\infty}\text{ converges and }\lim_{m\to\infty}\nabla f(x^m)=0\right)=1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Variable Taylor Expansion and Its Regularity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract claims equality with the infinite Taylor series from infinite differentiability alone. In general, smoothness does not ensure equality with the Taylor series; analyticity or a suitable remainder formulation is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=(x(1),x(2))\) and increment \(h=(h(1),h(2))\), the second-order terms of the Taylor expansion are \[f(x+h)=f(x)+h(1)\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x(1)}+h(2)\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x(2)}+\frac{1}{2}\left(h(1)^2\frac{\partial^2f(x)}{\partial x(1)^2}+2h(1)h(2)\frac{\partial^2f(x)}{\partial x(1)\partial x(2)}+h(2)^2\frac{\partial^2f(x)}{\partial x(2)^2}\right)+\cdots.\] Equality with the full infinite series requires more than \(C^\infty\) smoothness in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displayed bivariate Taylor expansion has the usual linear and quadratic derivative terms, but infinite differentiability alone does not guarantee that the infinite Taylor series equals the function.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ has the displayed partial derivatives near }x
\text{Equality with the infinite series requires analyticity or another sufficient Taylor-remainder condition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x+h)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^Th+\frac12h^T\nabla^2f(x)h+\cdots\quad\text{under a sufficient Taylor-series validity condition}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Two-Measurement SPSA Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic first-order SPSA using paired symmetric loss measurements and a stochastic-approximation update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(k=0\), \(\widehat{\mathbf\theta}_0\), and nonnegative coefficients \(a,c,A,\alpha,\gamma\), with \(a_k=a/(k+1+A)^\alpha\) and \(c_k=c/(k+1)^\gamma\). At iteration \(k\), generate a \(p\)-dimensional perturbation \(\mathbf\Delta_k\) with independently generated, zero-mean components satisfying the stated SPSA conditions; evaluate \(y(\widehat{\mathbf\theta}_k+c_k\mathbf\Delta_k)\) and \(y(\widehat{\mathbf\theta}_k-c_k\mathbf\Delta_k)\); form the simultaneous-perturbation gradient approximation in (7.2), optionally averaging independent approximations; and apply the stochastic-approximation update (7.1). Modify an infeasible update when constraints are present, increment \(k\), and repeat until the stopping rule is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the iterate and gain sequences. At every iteration, generate an admissible random perturbation vector, take two symmetric loss measurements, form the SPSA gradient approximation, optionally average independent approximations, and apply the stochastic-approximation update. Correct constraint violations when relevant and repeat until termination.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbf\Delta_k\in\mathbb R^p\text{ has independently generated, zero-mean components satisfying the stated SPSA perturbation conditions}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat{\mathbf\theta}_{k+1}\text{ is obtained from the paired-measurement SPSA gradient approximation and update (7.1)}\)
