knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmically cooled stochastic-approximation annealing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded continuous- and discrete-time Langevin annealing schedules; the extract does not enumerate all regularity and stability hypotheses used by the cited convergence analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The annealed diffusion is
\[
dX_t=-\nabla f(X_t)\,dt+\eta(t)\,dW_t,
\qquad \eta(t)=\sqrt{\frac{C}{\log t}},\quad C>\Lambda(f),
\]
and merely requiring \(\eta(t)=o(1)\) is insufficient. Its discrete-time counterpart is
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n+a(n)[-\nabla f(x_n)+M_{n+1}]+b(n)W_{n+1},
\]
with
\[
a(n)=\frac{A}{n},\qquad b(n)=\sqrt{\frac{B}{n\log\log n}},\qquad n\ge2.
\]
Under the standing regularity, stability, and noise hypotheses of the referenced analysis, which are not specified in this extract, the threshold condition \(B/A>C\) yields convergence in probability to the global-minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method combines stochastic approximation with deliberately added Gaussian noise that cools logarithmically. Noise tending merely to zero is not enough. With the displayed continuous-time and discrete-time schedules, the stated threshold conditions, and the omitted standing hypotheses of the referenced analysis, the discrete iterates converge in probability to the global-minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: \text{The referenced analysis's additional regularity and stability assumptions hold}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}\!\left(x_n,\operatorname{Argmin}f\right)\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0.

children.title: Annealing Cooling-Convergence Coupling
children.top_down_role: Global-convergence and noise-cooling compatibility families.

children.title: Annealing Global-Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes associated with global rather than merely local annealing behavior.

assumptions_latex: The state space \(S\) is finite and the proposal kernel is irreducible and reversible with positive probabilities on its neighborhood edges.
The objective \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) is observed exactly, and \(D^*\) denotes the maximal energy barrier separating a nonoptimal state from lower-energy states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(S^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x)\), the annealing chain satisfies \(\mathbb P(X_k\in S^*)\to1\).

notation.meaning: critical depth of the objective landscape under the proposal graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-state logarithmic-cooling convergence in probability for exact Metropolis annealing.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.2 Simulated annealing p. 48

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X_k)\) be the inhomogeneous Metropolis chain for minimizing \(f\), with acceptance probability \(\min\{1,\exp(-(f(y)-f(x))/T_k)\}\) for a proposed move from \(x\) to \(y\). If the logarithmic cooling constant exceeds the landscape critical depth, then
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbb P\!\left(X_k\in S^*\right)=1,
\qquad S^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x).
\]
Thus logarithmic cooling above the barrier threshold gives global convergence in probability. The assertion does not imply eventual absorption at a single minimizer, and faster schedules are not covered by this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite connected state space, logarithmic cooling slower than the critical barrier threshold drives exact annealing toward the global minimizers in probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Annealing Global-Convergence Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.2 Simulated annealing p. 48

children.title: Annealing Cooling-Schedule Families
children.top_down_role: Major temperature-decay families used in simulation-based annealing.

assumptions_latex: A cooling schedule is a deterministic sequence \((T_k)_{k\geq0}\) satisfying \(T_k>0\), \(T_{k+1}\leq T_k\), and \(T_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Logarithmic, polynomial, and geometric schedules are distinguished by their asymptotic decay rates and generally support different convergence guarantees.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard deterministic temperature families, classified by asymptotic cooling rate.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.2 Simulated annealing p. 48

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Three common cooling-schedule families are
\[
T_k=\frac{c}{\log(k+2)},\qquad T_k=\frac{T_0}{(k+1)^p},\qquad T_k=T_0r^k,
\]
where \(c>0\), \(T_0>0\), \(p>0\), and \(r\in(0,1)\). They are called logarithmic, polynomial, and geometric cooling, respectively. Their rates satisfy \(T_k^{\mathrm{geom}}=o(T_k^{\mathrm{poly}})\) and \(T_k^{\mathrm{poly}}=o(T_k^{\log})\) for fixed admissible parameters. A piecewise-constant schedule is specified by temperatures \(\tau_j\downarrow0\) and holding times \(h_j\), with \(T_k=\tau_j\) throughout stage \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cooling schedules commonly decrease logarithmically, polynomially, geometrically, or by temperature stages; these families cool at materially different asymptotic rates.
knowledge_statements.title: Annealing Cooling-Schedule Families

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.2 Simulated annealing p. 48

children.title: Annealing Noise-Cooling Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Relationships between simulation-error control and temperature decay.

assumptions_latex: At iteration \(k\), the estimated loss difference is \(\widehat\Delta_k=\Delta_k+E_k\), and \(E_k\) is conditionally sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(2\sigma^2/n_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed summability and scale conditions make simulation comparison errors asymptotically negligible relative to annealing.

notation.meaning: replications used in an iteration-k comparison

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient sub-Gaussian replication condition for noisy Metropolis comparisons.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.2 Simulated annealing p. 48
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sufficient noise-cooling compatibility condition is
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\exp\left(-\frac{n_k\varepsilon_k^2}{4\sigma^2}\right)<\infty
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{\varepsilon_k}{T_k}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The sub-Gaussian tail bound then gives \(\sum_k\mathbb P(|E_k|>\varepsilon_k\mid\mathcal F_k)<\infty\), so comparison errors exceeding \(\varepsilon_k\) occur only finitely often almost surely under the conditional Borel--Cantelli criterion. The second condition makes the remaining error negligible in the Metropolis exponent. Consequently, replication counts must grow as temperature falls; fixed \(n_k\) generally does not satisfy this sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation effort must increase fast enough that large comparison errors are summable and residual errors are small relative to temperature.
knowledge_statements.title: Annealing Noise-Cooling Compatibility

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.2 Simulated annealing p. 48
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tempering for Multimodal Markov-Chain Mixing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-temperature deformation and the tempered-transition and parallel-tempering strategies, including their mixing boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an energy-based target p_1(x)\propto e^{-E(x)}, define p_\beta(x)\propto e^{-\beta E(x)} for \beta>0. On a finite discrete state space, p_\beta approaches the uniform distribution as \beta\downarrow0; as \beta\uparrow\infty, it concentrates on the states minimizing E. Tempering uses distributions with \beta<1 to flatten modes and facilitate movement across low-probability barriers. Tempered transitions temporarily traverse higher-temperature distributions before returning to \beta=1. Parallel tempering evolves states at several temperatures and uses stochastic swaps between temperature levels, with the \beta=1 level supplying target-distributed samples when the joint transition is correctly constructed. Critical temperature regions can still require slow temperature movement and limit mixing improvements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tempering flattens an energy-based distribution by lowering its inverse temperature, making movement between separated modes easier. Tempered transitions temporarily visit hotter distributions, while parallel tempering runs several temperatures and swaps states, retaining the unit-temperature level for target samples. Critical temperature regions can still make mixing slow.
assumptions_latex: \text{the uniform-limit claim assumes a finite discrete state space}
\text{the low-temperature limit assumes that global energy minimizers exist}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_\beta\to\operatorname{Unif}(\mathcal X)\ \text{as }\beta\downarrow0\ \text{on finite discrete }\mathcal X,\qquad p_\beta\ \text{concentrates on }\arg\min E\ \text{as }\beta\uparrow\infty;\quad \beta<1\ \text{is used to facilitate intermodal mixing.}

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Discrete Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood descent driven by sequential simulation comparisons, with distinct certified and budget-limited termination outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in S\). At iteration \(k\), select one or more candidates from \(N(x_k)\), allocate simulation replications to the incumbent and candidates, and apply a specified sequential comparison rule with controlled error probabilities. If a candidate \(y_k\) is declared better than \(x_k\), set \(x_{k+1}=y_k\); otherwise increase sampling, examine another neighbor, or retain \(x_k\) according to the declared policy. Stop either when every neighbor required by the policy has been tested and rejected as nonimproving or when a sampling or total-budget limit is reached. Return the incumbent, the comparison statistics, and a termination status distinguishing certified local termination from unresolved budget termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequentially simulate neighboring decisions and move to a statistically preferred neighbor. Report whether termination certifies that the required neighbors were nonimproving or merely records exhaustion of the sampling budget.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(S\) is finite or countable, and every \(x\in S\) has a finite neighborhood \(N(x)\).
Simulation output has finite mean \(f(x)\) for every feasible decision.
The comparison procedure terminates with a declared winner or an unresolved outcome at its prescribed sampling limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Certified local termination reports no improving neighbor under the adopted comparison rule; budget-limited termination makes no such certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood Local Optimality, Local Convergence, and Testing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete optimization via simulation with a specified neighborhood map and, for finite-time testing, an available statistical comparison procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let N(\mathbf{x})\subseteq\Theta be the neighborhood of each \mathbf{x}\in\Theta. A point \mathbf{x} is locally optimal if g(\mathbf{x})\leq g(\mathbf{y}) for every \mathbf{y}\in N(\mathbf{x}); consequently, the local optimizer set \mathcal{L} depends on the neighborhood map N. For reported solutions \mathbf{x}_m^*, local convergence in probability and with probability one are defined respectively by \lim_{m\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{x}_m^*\in\mathcal{L})=1 and \mathbb{P}(\lim_{m\to\infty}\mathbf{1}\{\mathbf{x}_m^*\in\mathcal{L}\}=1)=1. When the neighborhood can be statistically compared with controlled errors, local optimality at \mathbf{x} may be tested using H_0:g(\mathbf{x})\leq\min_{\mathbf{y}\in N(\mathbf{x})}g(\mathbf{y}) against H_1:g(\mathbf{x})>\min_{\mathbf{y}\in N(\mathbf{x})}g(\mathbf{y}), providing a finite-time stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution is locally optimal when it is no worse than every member of its specified neighborhood, so local optima depend on the neighborhood definition. Local convergence requires the reported solution to enter the local-optimum set with probability tending to one or with probability one. If the neighborhood admits a statistical comparison with controlled errors, the corresponding hypothesis test can support a finite-time stopping rule.
assumptions_latex: \text{for the stopping-rule claim, a statistical test controlling type-I and type-II errors is available}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{m\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{x}_m^*\in\mathcal{L})=1\quad\text{or}\quad\mathbb{P}\!\left(\lim_{m\to\infty}\mathbf{1}\{\mathbf{x}_m^*\in\mathcal{L}\}=1\right)=1

children.top_down_role: Adaptive partitioning of discrete decision spaces.

assumptions_latex: The discrete feasible set \(S\) admits recursive finite partitions.
Every sampled decision has an integrable simulation loss with mean \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm adaptively refines promising regions while retaining the ability to backtrack to their complements.

notation.meaning: children forming a partition of the current region

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic nested-partitions search on a recursively partitionable discrete space.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with \(R_0=S\). At iteration \(k\), partition \(R_k\) into disjoint children \(R_{k,1},\ldots,R_{k,q_k}\), include \(S\setminus R_k\) as a surrounding region when nonempty, and sample feasible decisions from every candidate region. Estimate a prescribed region score, such as the smallest adequately sampled loss observed within that region. Select the region with the best score: descend to that child if it lies inside \(R_k\), or backtrack to the appropriate ancestor when the surrounding region wins. Update incumbent statistics, and stop at the partition-depth or simulation budget limit; return the best resampled decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively partition the current region, simulate candidates in its children and surrounding region, then descend or backtrack according to estimated promise.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse-Sampling Online Planning Recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-depth online action selection for a discrete stochastic decision problem using a fixed number of sampled transitions per action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For state $s$, depth $d$, sample count $m$, terminal value function $U$, and discount factor $\gamma$, return $(\varnothing,U(s))$ when $d\le 0$. Otherwise, for each available action $a$, sample $m$ transitions $(s_i',r_i)$, recursively obtain continuation estimates $u_i'$ at depth $d-1$, compute $\widehat u(a)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m(r_i+\gamma u_i')$, and return an action maximizing $\widehat u(a)$ together with its estimated value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At nonpositive depth, sparse sampling returns the terminal value. Otherwise it samples m successor transitions for every action, recursively estimates their discounted returns, averages them, and returns an action having the largest sampled value estimate.
assumptions_latex: (s_i',r_i)\text{ is sampled from the transition-reward mechanism for }(s,a)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a^*,\widehat u(a^*)),\qquad a^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\mathcal A(s)}\widehat u(a)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monte Carlo Tree Search Simulation and Backup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One finite-depth Monte Carlo tree-search simulation with state expansion and incremental sample-mean backup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given state $s$ and remaining depth $d$, return $U(s)$ if $d\le0$. If $s$ is unexpanded, initialize $N(s,a)=Q(s,a)=0$ for every $a\in A$ and return $U(s)$. Otherwise select $a$ using the exploration policy, sample $(s',r)=TR(s,a)$, set $q=r+\gamma\operatorname{simulate}(s',d-1)$, update $N(s,a)\leftarrow N(s,a)+1$ and $Q(s,a)\leftarrow Q(s,a)+\frac{q-Q(s,a)}{N(s,a)}$, and return $q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulation returns the terminal estimate at the depth limit. At a newly encountered state it initializes all action counts and values and returns that estimate. Otherwise it selects an exploratory action, samples a transition, recursively computes the discounted return, and backs it up using an incremental sample mean.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is a finite nonempty enumerable action set}
\text{The count and value dictionaries obey the algorithm's all-actions initialization invariant}

children.title: Statistical Node Bounds
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty-aware bounds supporting branching and pruning.

assumptions_latex: For each active node \(V\), \(L(V)=\inf_{x\in V}f(x)\) is the node's true minimization bound.
The reported bounds satisfy a simultaneous coverage event with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On the simultaneous coverage event, pruning by comparing a node lower bound with an incumbent upper bound cannot discard a globally optimal node.

notation.meaning: true best objective value attainable in node V
statistical lower confidence bound for node V
upper confidence bound for the incumbent value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous confidence bounds as a probabilistic safe-pruning certificate.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A\) be the active-node set and let \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\) be the incumbent. A statistical pruning certificate at level \(1-\alpha\) is the event
\[
\mathcal E=\left\{\underline L(V)\leq L(V)\ \text{for all }V\in\mathcal A,\quad f(x^{\mathrm{inc}})\leq\overline U\right\},
\qquad \mathbb P(\mathcal E)\geq1-\alpha.
\]
On \(\mathcal E\), any node satisfying \(\underline L(V)\geq\overline U\) has \(L(V)\geq f(x^{\mathrm{inc}})\) and may be pruned without removing a strictly better solution. The certificate is verifiable from the reported bounds and their simultaneous coverage calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneously valid node lower bounds and an incumbent upper bound certify pruning whenever a node cannot beat the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Node Bounds

children.title: Erroneous-Pruning Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of optimal candidates through underresolved simulation bounds.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(S=\{a,b\}\), with true losses \(f(a)=0\) and \(f(b)=\delta>0\).
One simulation observation at each decision is Gaussian with variance \(\sigma^2>0\), independently across decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A one-replication comparison prunes the optimal decision with strictly positive probability \(\Phi(-\delta/(\sqrt2\sigma))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-decision Gaussian example showing positive-probability loss of the optimum.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y_a\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) and \(Y_b\sim N(\delta,\sigma^2)\) be independent one-replication loss estimates. A rule that retains only the decision with the smaller observed loss prunes the true optimizer \(a\) whenever \(Y_a>Y_b\). Since \(Y_a-Y_b\sim N(-\delta,2\sigma^2)\),
\[
\mathbb P(Y_a>Y_b)=\Phi\left(-\frac{\delta}{\sqrt2\sigma}\right)>0.
\]
Thus pruning from underresolved point estimates can permanently delete the unique optimum. The failure disappears only through a valid error-control mechanism, not merely because the comparison is unbiased.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even unbiased Gaussian estimates can rank two decisions incorrectly, so one-shot pruning discards the unique optimum with positive probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Erroneous-Pruning Failure

children.title: Simulation-Based Branching Policies
children.top_down_role: Node expansion and subdivision choices for simulation-driven search trees.

assumptions_latex: Each active node represents a subset of the discrete feasible set and has a prescribed finite collection of children.
Node statistics are updated from simulation observations, with all sampling and tie-breaking rules specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy selects either a node for refinement or a node requiring additional simulation before a reliable branching decision.

notation.meaning: estimated promise score of node V

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-bound branching with explicit resampling for statistically unresolved nodes.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\mathcal A_0\) with the root node and compute simulation-based bounds. At iteration \(k\), remove nodes certified unable to improve the incumbent. For every remaining node, form a measurable priority \(I_k(V)\) from its lower bound, uncertainty, depth, and sampling cost, and select
\[
V_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{V\in\mathcal A_k}I_k(V).
\]
If the uncertainty of \(V_k\) exceeds the declared branching tolerance, allocate additional simulations and recompute its statistics. Otherwise replace \(V_k\) by its children, initialize their bounds, and update the incumbent. Stop when no active node can improve the incumbent at the required confidence level or when the budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prioritize an active node using estimated promise and uncertainty, resample it if unresolved, and otherwise replace it by its children.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulation-Based Branching Policies

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46

children.title: Simulation-Based Bound Construction
children.top_down_role: Construction of node-level bounds from uncertain simulation evidence.

assumptions_latex: A node \(V\) is a finite set of decisions, and decision \(x\in V\) has \(n_x\geq1\) independent simulation observations with mean \(f(x)\).
Each centered observation is sub-Gaussian with known common variance proxy \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed node statistic is a lower confidence bound for \(\min_{x\in V}f(x)\) with coverage at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-node lower bound obtained from simultaneous sub-Gaussian confidence intervals.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For confidence parameter \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define decisionwise lower limits and the node bound by
\[
\ell_\alpha(x)=\overline Y_x-\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\log(|V|/\alpha)}{n_x}},
\qquad
\underline L_\alpha(V)=\min_{x\in V}\ell_\alpha(x).
\]
The sub-Gaussian tail inequality and a union bound give simultaneous inequalities \(\ell_\alpha(x)\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in V\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\). Hence
\[
\mathbb P\left(\underline L_\alpha(V)\leq\min_{x\in V}f(x)\right)\geq1-\alpha.
\]
Separate error allocation is required when bounds are repeatedly recomputed across many nodes or times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take the minimum of simultaneous lower confidence limits for decisions in a finite node to obtain a valid node lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulation-Based Bound Construction

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

children.title: Population-Based Simulation Search
children.top_down_role: Evolutionary and population search under noisy simulated fitness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Core noise-free evolution-strategy iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers both the \((N+\lambda)\)-ES and \((N,\lambda)\)-ES survivor-selection rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(N\) candidates \(\theta\in\Theta\) and evaluate \(L\) exactly. At each iteration generate \(\lambda\) constraint-satisfying offspring. In an \((N+\lambda)\)-ES, retain the \(N\) best candidates from the parents and offspring; in an \((N,\lambda)\)-ES with \(\lambda>N\), retain the \(N\) best offspring only. Stop when a stopping criterion holds or the fitness-evaluation budget is exhausted; otherwise repeat offspring generation and selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize and evaluate a population of N candidates. Repeatedly generate lambda feasible offspring. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fitness Assignment Conditions for Genetic Algorithms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cuckoo Search Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Literal algorithmic specification, including the objective-value assignment in the supplied abandonment step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a minimization objective $f$, nests $\{(x_i,y_i):y_i=f(x_i)\}_{i=1}^m$ with $x_i\in\mathbb{R}^n$, iteration limit $k_{\max}$, abandonment fraction $p_a$, and flight distribution $C$, set $a=\operatorname{round}(mp_a)$. At each iteration, sample $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ uniformly, form $x=x_j+(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)$ with independent $\xi_\ell\sim C$, and replace nest $i$ by $(x,f(x))$ if $f(x)<y_i$. Rank nests by decreasing objective value; for each of the $a$ worst ranks $r$, sample a rank $s\in\{a+1,\ldots,m\}$ and replace its position by $x_{p_s}+(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_n)$, $\zeta_\ell\sim C$, while the supplied pseudocode assigns the replacement value $f(x_{p_r})$ evaluated at the old worst position. After $k_{\max}$ iterations, return the population.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, cuckoo search repeatedly generates a random flight from a sampled nest and replaces another sampled nest when the new objective value is smaller. It then ranks nests from worst to best and abandons a rounded fraction of the worst nests by perturbing better-ranked nests. In the supplied pseudocode, an abandoned nest's stored value is evaluated at its old worst position rather than at its newly assigned position. The population is returned after the prescribed number of iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm returns the population after }k_{\max}\text{ stochastic update iterations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Core Genetic Algorithm for Noise-Free Fitness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generational genetic algorithm with fitness-based selection, probabilistic crossover, mutation, optional elitism, and termination by a stopping rule or evaluation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(N\) chromosomes and evaluate their noise-free fitness. At each generation, set \(N_e=0\) if elitism is unused and choose \(0<N_e<N\) otherwise. Retain the \(N_e\) best chromosomes and select with replacement \(N-N_e\) parents from the full population, favoring chromosomes with higher fitness. For each parent pair, apply crossover with probability \(P_c\); otherwise produce two parental clones. Replace the nonelite chromosomes by the offspring. In bit-based implementations, mutate individual bits with probability \(P_m\); in real-coded implementations, apply an analogous small modification. Whether elites are eligible for mutation is an implementation choice. Evaluate the new population and terminate if the stopping criterion is met or the fitness-evaluation budget is exhausted; otherwise repeat from parent selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize and score a population under noise-free fitness. In each generation, optionally retain a proper subset of elites, select the other parents with replacement in favor of higher fitness, apply probabilistic crossover or cloning, replace nonelites with offspring, and mutate the chosen representation. Reevaluate fitness and stop when the stopping rule or evaluation budget is reached.
assumptions_latex: N_e=0\text{ if elitism is absent, and }0<N_e<N\text{ otherwise}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Selection, crossover or cloning, replacement, mutation, and reevaluation repeat until the stopping criterion or fitness-evaluation budget is reached.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Roulette-Wheel Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fitness-proportional random selection from a finite genetic-algorithm population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given individuals \(x^1,\ldots,x^{\bar p}\) with fitness values \(f^1,\ldots,f^{\bar p}>0\), roulette-wheel selection chooses \(x^i\) with probability \[\Pr(x^i)=\frac{f^i}{\sum_{j=1}^{\bar p}f^j}.\] Consequently, \(\Pr(x^i)>0\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^{\bar p}\Pr(x^i)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Roulette-wheel selection chooses each individual with probability equal to its positive fitness divided by total population fitness. Every individual has positive selection probability, and the probabilities sum to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(x^i)=\frac{f^i}{\sum_j f^j}>0,\qquad \sum_i\Pr(x^i)=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bit-Inversion Mutation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For candidates \(x_i\), use \(\overline Y_i=n_i^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{n_i}Y_{ir}\) and estimate its standard error by \(s_i/\sqrt{n_i}\). Allocate additional replications when an estimated difference \(|\overline Y_i-\overline Y_j|\) is small relative to \(\sqrt{s_i^2/n_i+s_j^2/n_j}\), and base elimination or parent selection on a stated confidence, posterior, or indifference-zone rule. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Particle Swarm Optimization Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the extracted minimization algorithm, preserving its position-before-velocity update order, strict incumbent tests, and returned output; it makes no convergence claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a nonempty population of particles $(x_i,v_i,p_i)$, an objective $f$, an iteration count $k_{\max}$, inertia $w$, and coefficients $c_1,c_2$ (with extracted defaults $w=c_1=c_2=1$), initialize $g$ as the current particle position having the smallest evaluated objective value. For $k=1,\ldots,k_{\max}$ and every particle $i$, draw random vectors $r_{1,i},r_{2,i}\in[0,1)^n$, then set
\[
x_i\leftarrow x_i+v_i,
\qquad
v_i\leftarrow wv_i+c_1r_{1,i}\odot(p_i-x_i)+c_2r_{2,i}\odot(g-x_i).
\]
Evaluate $f(x_i)$; replace $g$ by $x_i$ if $f(x_i)$ strictly improves the global incumbent value, and replace $p_i$ by $x_i$ if $f(x_i)<f(p_i)$. After $k_{\max}$ iterations, return the updated population.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the global incumbent from the best current particle. At each iteration, first move each particle by its current velocity, then update its velocity using inertia, attraction to its personal best, and attraction to the global best, with coordinatewise random weights. Evaluate the new position and update global and personal incumbents upon strict improvement. The extracted parameter defaults are w = c1 = c2 = 1, and the procedure returns the updated population.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is evaluable at every visited position and is minimized.}
\text{The particle population is nonempty and each particle has state }(x_i,v_i,p_i).
r_{1,i},r_{2,i}\in[0,1)^n\text{ are freshly sampled random vectors.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns the population obtained after }k_{\max}\text{ particle-swarm iterations.}

children.title: Global-Search Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Practical boundaries caused by inadequate exploration or unreliable noisy comparisons.

children.title: Premature Convergence
children.top_down_role: Loss of exploration before statistically reliable localization.

assumptions_latex: A population method generates finite populations \(P_t\subset\mathcal X\).
Fitness estimates are noisy, and localization is considered reliable only after a specified statistical validation rule is met.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Premature convergence occurs when diversity is lost before the surviving region is statistically validated.

notation.meaning: population diameter under a chosen metric

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure criterion separating diversity loss from statistically supported localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_t=\max_{x,y\in P_t}d(x,y)\) and \(\tau_\delta=\inf\{t:D_t\leq\delta\}\). Let \(V_t\) denote the event that the region containing \(P_t\) has passed the method's prescribed statistical validation against explored alternatives. Premature convergence is the event \(\{\tau_\delta<\infty\}\cap V_{\tau_\delta}^{c}\), together with an update rule that thereafter assigns zero or negligible probability to candidates outside that region. Thus small population diameter alone is not failure; failure is diversity loss before reliable localization, followed by inability to restore meaningful exploration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Premature convergence is diversity collapse before the surviving region has statistically defeated explored alternatives, coupled with negligible ability to explore elsewhere afterward.
knowledge_statements.title: Premature Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the failure-regime leaf, but the event-based definition using a method-specific validation event, diversity threshold, and negligible future exploration is an operational construction rather than a source-backed standard definition. It needs a direct reference or an explicitly sourced diagnostic framework.

children.title: Extreme-Noise Selection
children.top_down_role: Apparent optima created by searching over many noisy estimates.

assumptions_latex: There are \(M\) candidates with identical true objective value \(\mu\).
Their estimates are \(\widehat f_i=\mu+\varepsilon_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent \(N(0,\sigma^2/n)\) variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Searching more candidates can create increasingly optimistic apparent minima even when no candidate is truly better.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian equal-means model illustrating optimizer's curse under minimization.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\widehat f_{(1)}=\min_{1\leq i\leq M}\widehat f_i\). Although every candidate has value \(\mu\), \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_{(1)}]=\mu+(\sigma/\sqrt n)\mathbb E[\min_{1\leq i\leq M}Z_i]<\mu\) for \(M>1\), where the \(Z_i\) are independent standard normal variables. Moreover, as \(M\to\infty\), the leading optimism magnitude is \(\mu-\mathbb E[\widehat f_{(1)}]\sim(\sigma/\sqrt n)\sqrt{2\log M}\). Hence fixed replication permits apparent improvement caused solely by searching over more noisy estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed replication, the best among many equally good noisy candidates looks spuriously better; under Gaussian noise the optimism grows like the square root of log population size.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Noise Selection

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian calculation is mathematically plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the cited general section is not a sufficiently direct locator for the stated extreme-value asymptotic. A source specifically supporting the expectation formula and the leading sqrt(2 log M) behavior is required.

children.title: Search-Distribution Collapse
children.top_down_role: Degeneration of adaptive proposal distributions before adequate exploration.

assumptions_latex: At iteration \(t\), candidates are sampled from a proposal distribution \(Q_t\) on \(\mathcal X\).
A set \(G\subset\mathcal X\) contains points not yet adequately explored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Collapse is a failure whenever proposal mass on a relevant unexplored set vanishes before that set is ruled out.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure condition for adaptive continuous-space proposal distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Search-distribution collapse relative to \(G\) occurs if \(Q_t(G)\to0\) before available evidence statistically excludes \(G\) from containing a competitive solution. For location-scale proposals on \(\mathbb R^d\), a common sufficient diagnostic is \(\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_t)\to0\) while the proposal mean converges outside \(G\); then samples concentrate at a single location and the probability of visiting any separated \(G\) vanishes. Covariance degeneration is not itself erroneous after reliable localization. It is a failure when it precedes adequate exploration and the update mechanism lacks a positive exploration component capable of restoring mass to \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search distribution fails by collapsing when it loses probability mass on a still-plausible unexplored region and cannot restore meaningful exploration there.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-Distribution Collapse

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the definition relative to an arbitrary set G, the statistical-exclusion condition, and the covariance-collapse diagnostic are uncited and proposal-family dependent. A direct source is needed for this named failure regime and its stated sufficient diagnostic.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A first-order response surface represents the local mean simulation response by \(m(x)\approx\beta_0+x^{\mathsf T}\beta\). With rows \((1,x_i^{\mathsf T})\) in \(X\) and observations in \(y\), ordinary least squares chooses \(\widehat\theta\in\arg\min_\theta\|y-X\theta\|_2^2\); if \(X\) has full column rank, \(\widehat\theta=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y\). The fitted value is \(\widehat m(x)=\widehat\beta_0+x^{\mathsf T}\widehat\beta\). For local minimization, \(-\widehat\beta\) is the fitted steepest-descent direction, to be used only within the region where the affine approximation is accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order response surface fits an affine mean model to simulation data; its estimated slope gives a local descent direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order response surface represents the local mean by \(m(x)\approx\beta_0+b^{\mathsf T}x+\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx\), where \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\). Estimate its coefficients by least squares or generalized least squares on the corresponding linear, squared, and cross-product regressors. The fitted gradient is \(\nabla\widehat m(x)=\widehat b+\widehat Hx\). If \(\widehat H\) is nonsingular, the fitted stationary point is \(x_s=-\widehat H^{-1}\widehat b\). It is a strict fitted minimizer when \(\widehat H\succ0\), a strict fitted maximizer when \(\widehat H\prec0\), and a saddle when \(\widehat H\) is indefinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Response-Surface Model and Necessary Design Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic response-surface regression in m inputs and necessary, but not sufficient, design conditions for estimating all coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A second-order response-surface model has the form
\[
y=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_jx_j+\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_{jj}x_j^2+\sum_{1\le j<k\le m}\beta_{jk}x_jx_k+\varepsilon.
\]
The model has \(1+2m+m(m-1)/2\) regression coefficients. Thus, estimating every coefficient by least squares or likelihood-based methods requires at least this many distinct design locations. Estimating pure quadratic terms also requires at least three levels of each corresponding input variable. These counting and level conditions are necessary rather than sufficient for estimability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order response surface contains an intercept, main effects, pure quadratic terms, pairwise interactions, and an error term. It has 1 + 2m + m(m−1)/2 coefficients, so estimating all coefficients requires at least that many distinct design locations. Each input must also have at least three levels for its pure quadratic coefficient to be estimable. These requirements alone do not guarantee full-rank estimation.
assumptions_latex: \text{All displayed regression coefficients are to be estimated by least squares or likelihood-based methods.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{distinct}}\ge 1+2m+\frac{m(m-1)}2,\qquad \#\{\text{levels of }x_j\}\ge 3\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),\quad\text{as necessary conditions for the stated estimability.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ridge Exploration for a Second-Order Response Surface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized exploration of a fitted quadratic response surface in centered coded coordinates, including the singular boundary at the largest eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given
\[
\widehat y(x)=b_0+x^\top b+x^\top Bx,
\]
a centered coded design with center \(x_0=0\), and a bounding box, compute \(\lambda_{\max}(B)\). Choose values of \(\mu\ge\lambda_{\max}(B)\), but evaluate the stationary-point formula only when \(B-\mu I_m\) is invertible:
\[
x(\mu)=-\frac12(B-\mu I_m)^{-1}b,
\qquad R(\mu)=\sqrt{x(\mu)^\top x(\mu)}.
\]
Explore \(x(\mu)\), \(\widehat y(x(\mu))\), and their standard errors near the design boundary while varying \(\mu\). For the regular ridge regime \(\mu>\lambda_{\max}(B)\), increasing \(\mu\) moves the computed point toward the centered origin, while decreasing it moves the point outward toward or beyond the design boundary. Return the explored \((\mu,x,\widehat y)\) tuples and standard errors, optionally mapped from coded to natural units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fitted quadratic response surface in centered coded coordinates, compute the largest eigenvalue of the quadratic matrix. For selected parameter values, solve the parameterized stationary-point equation whenever its matrix is invertible, compute the point's radius, and inspect its prediction and standard error near the design boundary. In the regular regime strictly above the largest eigenvalue, increasing the parameter moves the point toward the center and decreasing it moves the point outward. Return the explored points, predictions, parameters, and standard errors, optionally in natural units.
assumptions_latex: \text{A bounding box for the design region is available.}
B-\mu I_m\text{ is invertible whenever }x(\mu)\text{ is evaluated.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal T=\left\{\bigl(\mu,x(\mu),\widehat y(x(\mu)),\operatorname{SE}(x(\mu))\bigr)\right\},\qquad x(\mu)=-\frac12(B-\mu I_m)^{-1}b.

children.title: Stochastic Kriging
children.top_down_role: Spatial modeling that separates intrinsic simulation noise from response uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic Kriging with Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-augmented stochastic kriging for replicated multivariate simulation observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At design points \(\mathbf x_i\in\mathbb R^d\), stochastic kriging models
\[
y_j(\mathbf x_i)=\mathbf f(\mathbf x_i)^T\boldsymbol\beta+M(\mathbf x_i)+\varepsilon_j(\mathbf x_i),
\]
where \(M\) is a mean-zero stationary random field. Consequently,
\[
\bar y(\mathbf x_i)=\mathbf f(\mathbf x_i)^T\boldsymbol\beta+M(\mathbf x_i)+\bar\varepsilon(\mathbf x_i).
\]
Stochastic kriging with gradients augments this representation by
\[
\bar g^r(\mathbf x_i)=\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf f(\mathbf x_i)}{\partial x_r}\right)^T\boldsymbol\beta+ rac{\partial M(\mathbf x_i)}{\partial x_r}+\bar\delta^r(\mathbf x_i),
\]
for each modeled coordinate \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic kriging represents replicated simulation responses using a parametric trend, a mean-zero stationary response field, and simulation noise. Its gradient-augmented extension also models direct gradient observations as derivatives of the trend and random field plus gradient-estimation noise.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-Extrapolated Stochastic Kriging Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generation of synthetic neighboring response observations from direct stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each design point \(\mathbf x_i\), replication \(j\), and chosen displacement \(\Delta\mathbf x_i\), define
\[
\mathbf x_i^+=\mathbf x_i+\Delta\mathbf x_i,
\qquad
y_j(\mathbf x_i^+)=y_j(\mathbf x_i)+\mathbf g_j(\mathbf x_i)^T\Delta\mathbf x_i.
\]
GESK augments stochastic-kriging data with these linearly extrapolated responses. Multiple displacements may be used; the basic construction uses one common displacement \(\Delta\mathbf x_i=\Delta\mathbf x\) and one additional point per design point. Larger displacements improve neighborhood coverage but can increase linearization bias, producing a bias-variance tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GESK uses gradient estimates at stochastic-kriging design points to generate synthetic responses at nearby points by first-order extrapolation. Larger displacements improve coverage but may increase linearization bias.

children.title: Homoskedastic Stochastic Kriging
children.top_down_role: Spatial simulation modeling with uniform noise structure.

assumptions_latex: Observations satisfy \(y_i=\mu+Z(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), with \(Z\) a zero-mean Gaussian process.
The noises are independent of \(Z\), mutually independent, and have common known or estimated variance \(\tau^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditional Gaussian mean and variance define the homoskedastic stochastic-kriging predictor.

notation.meaning: process covariance matrix at design sites
covariance vector between design sites and x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process prediction with constant independent simulation-noise variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_{ij}=C(x_i,x_j)\), \(k(x)_i=C(x_i,x)\), and \(V=K+\tau^2I\). Conditional on \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^{\mathsf T}\) and known \(\mu\), the latent mean response \(M(x)=\mu+Z(x)\) has predictor \(\widehat M(x)=\mu+k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}(y-\mu\mathbf1)\) and conditional variance \(s^2(x)=C(x,x)-k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}k(x)\). A future noisy observation has predictive variance \(s^2(x)+\tau^2\). The term \(\tau^2I\) distinguishes homoskedastic stochastic kriging from deterministic interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homoskedastic stochastic kriging uses a Gaussian process plus one common simulation-noise variance, yielding a smoothing predictor rather than exact interpolation.
knowledge_statements.title: Homoskedastic Stochastic Kriging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and formulas are appropriate for known-mean homoskedastic stochastic kriging, including the distinction between latent-response and noisy-observation variance, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Heteroskedastic Stochastic Kriging
children.top_down_role: Spatial simulation modeling with input-dependent noise.

assumptions_latex: Observations satisfy \(y_i=\mu+Z(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), with \(Z\) a zero-mean Gaussian process.
The independent noises satisfy \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\tau_i^2\), allowing input-dependent variances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing a common nugget by \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_1^2,\ldots,\tau_n^2)\) yields the heteroskedastic stochastic-kriging predictor.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process prediction with independent, input-dependent simulation-noise variances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_1^2,\ldots,\tau_n^2)\) and \(V=K+D\), where \(K_{ij}=C(x_i,x_j)\). For known \(\mu\), the conditional predictor of the latent mean response is \(\widehat M(x)=\mu+k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}(y-\mu\mathbf1)\), with conditional variance \(s^2(x)=C(x,x)-k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}k(x)\). Thus observations with larger simulation variance receive less effective weight through \(V^{-1}\). If predicting a new simulation output rather than its latent mean, add the new-site noise variance \(\tau^2(x)\) to \(s^2(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heteroskedastic stochastic kriging places input-specific noise variances on the covariance diagonal, reducing the influence of noisier simulation estimates.
knowledge_statements.title: Heteroskedastic Stochastic Kriging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf and the diagonal input-dependent noise formulation is coherent, but the predictor, variance, weighting interpretation, and new-site variance statement require a specific stochastic-kriging source and locator.

children.title: Replication-Aware Stochastic Kriging
children.top_down_role: Metamodel fitting and prediction exploiting replicated evaluations.

assumptions_latex: At distinct design sites \(x_i\), there are \(r_i\geq2\) independent simulation replications with common site mean \(M(x_i)\).
Within-site simulation variance is finite and replications are independent across sites conditional on the latent response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Site averages are kriged with noise covariance \(D_{ii}=\sigma_i^2/r_i\), so replication directly reduces metamodel observation uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic kriging based on replicated site averages and estimated intrinsic variances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For site \(i\), form \(\overline Y_i=r_i^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}Y_{ij}\) and estimate the intrinsic variance by \(S_i^2=(r_i-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}(Y_{ij}-\overline Y_i)^2\). Under independent replications, \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_i\mid M(x_i))=\sigma_i^2/r_i\). Fit stochastic kriging to \(\overline Y=(\overline Y_1,\ldots,\overline Y_n)^{\mathsf T}\) using \(V=K+D\), where \(D_{ii}=\sigma_i^2/r_i\), commonly estimated by \(S_i^2/r_i\). The latent-response predictor is \(\widehat M(x)=\mu+k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}(\overline Y-\mu\mathbf1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replication-aware stochastic kriging fits site averages and divides each site's intrinsic variance by its replication count in the observation-noise covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Replication-Aware Stochastic Kriging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the replication-aware leaf, and the variance-of-the-site-average formula is standard under the stated independence assumptions. However, the complete stochastic-kriging construction and plug-in intrinsic-variance convention have no cited source or locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Replication-aware stochastic-kriging predictor and its limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique-site stochastic-kriging prediction from replicated observations, including computational savings and inferential failure boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $a_i\ge 2$ observations at each distinct site $ ar x_i$, define $ ar y_i=a_i^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{a_i}y_i^{(j)}$, $\widehat\sigma_i^2=(a_i-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{a_i}(y_i^{(j)}- ar y_i)^2$, and $S_n=\operatorname{Diag}(\widehat\sigma_1^2/a_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n^2/a_n)$. With $C_n=[K_	heta( ar x_i, ar x_j)]$ and $k_n(x)=[K_	heta(x, ar x_i)]_{i=1}^n$, the stochastic-kriging BLUP is $\mu_n^{\mathrm{SK}}(x)=
u k_n(x)^	op(
u C_n+S_n)^{-1} ar Y_n$ with prediction variance $\sigma_n^{\mathrm{SK}}(x)^2=
u K_	heta(x,x)-
u^2k_n(x)^	op(
u C_n+S_n)^{-1}k_n(x)$. The matrix-decomposition cost is $\mathcal O(n^3)$ instead of $\mathcal O(N^3)$. However, $( ar Y_n,S_n)$ is not sufficient for full likelihood-based hyperparameter inference; independently estimated site variances do not supply a smooth out-of-sample variance model, and their reliability requires substantial replication, with $a_i\ge 10$ cited as a practical recommendation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic kriging can replace all replicated observations at each input by their mean and estimated mean-noise variance, producing a unique-site BLUP and reducing cubic matrix work from N observations to n unique sites. These summaries are not sufficient for full hyperparameter likelihood inference, do not themselves model smoothly varying variance at new inputs, and yield unreliable local variance estimates when replication is sparse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_n^{\mathrm{SK}}(x),\sigma_n^{\mathrm{SK}}(x)^2)\ \text{gives the unique-site BLUP representation with }\mathcal O(n^3)\text{ decomposition cost, subject to the stated sufficiency, variance-modeling, and sparse-replication limitations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact unique-site reduction for replicated Gaussian-process inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-on-hyperparameters equivalence of full-data and unique-site prediction, likelihood, and derivative calculations under replicated inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $N$ observations occur at $n$ unique inputs with replicate counts $a_i\ge 1$, $A_n=\operatorname{Diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$, unique-site means $\bar Y_n$, covariance matrix $C_n$, and diagonal noise matrix $\Lambda_n$. Under the required covariance-matrix invertibility conditions, the Woodbury identities make the full-$N$ Gaussian-process predictive mean and variance identical to their unique-$n$ counterparts based on $C_n+\Lambda_nA_n^{-1}$. Exact concentrated-likelihood inference additionally uses the weighted full-data sum-of-squares statistic $N^{-1}Y_N^\top\Lambda_N^{-1}Y_N$, which is missing from the replicate summaries used by the approximate stochastic-kriging construction. After $\mathcal O(N)$ aggregation, prediction, concentrated-likelihood evaluation, and closed-form likelihood derivatives require $\mathcal O(n^3)$ matrix work. This algebraic equivalence imposes no minimum replicate count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For replicated inputs, Woodbury reduction makes predictions computed from all N observations exactly equal to calculations using the n unique sites, conditional on the hyperparameters. Exact likelihood inference also needs the full-data weighted sum of squares omitted by the simpler replicate summaries. Aggregation is linear in N and subsequent matrix work is cubic in n, with no minimum replication count required for the identity.
assumptions_latex: N\ \text{observations are grouped among }n\ \text{unique inputs with }a_i\ge 1
C_n+\Lambda_nA_n^{-1}\ \text{and the corresponding full-data covariance matrices are invertible}
\text{Hyperparameters are fixed when asserting predictive equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_N(x),\sigma_N^2(x))=(\mu_n(x),\sigma_n^2(x)),\qquad \text{and exact replicated-data likelihood calculations use }\mathcal O(N)+\mathcal O(n^3)\text{ work together with }N^{-1}Y_N^\top\Lambda_N^{-1}Y_N.

children.title: Local-Polynomial Regression
children.top_down_role: Locally fitted polynomial response approximations.

assumptions_latex: Data are \((X_i,Y_i)\) with \(X_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and a nonnegative kernel assigns local weights around a target \(x\).
The weighted polynomial design matrix has sufficient local rank for the chosen degree \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local-polynomial estimate at \(x\) is the fitted intercept \(\widehat m(x)=\widehat\beta_0(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multivariate local-polynomial regression with kernel weighting and fixed degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix degree \(p\geq0\), target \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), kernel \(K\geq0\), and nonsingular bandwidth matrix \(H\). Define \(w_i(x)=K(H^{-1}(X_i-x))\). A local-polynomial fit chooses coefficients \(\widehat\beta_\alpha(x)\), indexed by multi-indices satisfying \(|\alpha|\leq p\), to minimize \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i(x)\left[Y_i-\sum_{|\alpha|\leq p}\beta_\alpha(X_i-x)^\alpha\right]^2\). The estimated conditional mean at the target is \(\widehat m(x)=\widehat\beta_0(x)\). Degrees \(p=0\) and \(p=1\) give local-constant and local-linear regression, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local-polynomial regression fits a kernel-weighted polynomial around each target point and uses its fitted intercept as the local mean estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Polynomial Regression

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Linear Polynomial Regression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A locally weighted least-squares fit centered at each query or observed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For observations \((x^m,y^m)_{m=1}^n\), kernel weights \(K_h(x^k,x^m)\), and a center \(x^k\), local linear regression chooses \[\theta^{(k)}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta}\sum_{m=1}^nK_h(x^k,x^m)\left(y^m-\sum_{i=1}^I\theta_i x_i^m\right)^2.\] Thus a separate linear model is fitted at each center, with nearby observations receiving greater weight. This can improve local modeling accuracy relative to a response-only kernel average, at the cost of solving weighted regression problems and hence greater computational complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local polynomial regression fits a separate weighted least-squares model around each center. Kernel weights emphasize nearby observations. The richer local model can improve accuracy but is more computationally complex than ordinary kernel averaging.

children.title: Smoothing-Spline Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Penalized spline representations for smooth simulation responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothing-Spline Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalized cubic smoothing spline for a one-dimensional stochastic-simulation response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an integer \(n\ge 2\), distinct design sites \(a\le x_1<\cdots<x_n\le b\), simulation estimates \(y_i\), positive precision weights \(w_i\), and \(\lambda>0\), the smoothing-spline metamodel is the minimizer \(\widehat f_\lambda\in H^2([a,b])\) of
\[\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\bigl(y_i-f(x_i)\bigr)^2+\lambda\int_a^b\bigl(f''(t)\bigr)^2\,dt.\]
The minimizer is the unique natural cubic spline with knots among \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). The parameter \(\lambda\) controls the tradeoff between fidelity to noisy simulation estimates and curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For at least two distinct sampled sites, a smoothing-spline metamodel uniquely balances weighted fit to simulated responses against integrated squared curvature and is a natural cubic spline with knots among those sites.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f_\lambda\) is the unique natural cubic-spline minimizer of the stated penalized criterion.

notation.meaning: Sobolev space of functions with square-integrable weak derivatives through order two.
Precision weight assigned to the estimate at site i.

review_flags: Authoritative support for the penalized natural-cubic-spline characterization is required.

children.title: Adaptive Knot Placement
children.top_down_role: Spline structures whose resolution changes across the decision space.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Knot Placement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential placement of regression-spline knots using residual improvement on a finite candidate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input observations \(\{(x_i,y_i,w_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), spline degree \(p\), a finite candidate set \(G\subset(a,b)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). Initialize the knot set \(K_0=\varnothing\). At iteration \(m\), fit by weighted least squares a degree-\(p\) regression spline \(s_{m,\xi}\) for every \(\xi\in G\setminus K_m\), and choose
\[\xi_m\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\xi\in G\setminus K_m}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\bigl(y_i-s_{m,\xi}(x_i)\bigr)^2.\]
Set \(K_{m+1}=K_m\cup\{\xi_m\}\). Stop when the relative criterion decrease is at most \(\varepsilon\), or a prescribed knot budget is reached, and output the last fitted spline.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Candidate knots are added where they most improve weighted spline fit, stopping when improvement is small or the knot budget is exhausted.
assumptions_latex: \(G\subset(a,b)\) is finite and excludes previously selected knots.
\(w_i>0\), and each candidate spline fit is identifiable.
A maximum number of knots is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a regression-spline metamodel whose knot set was selected sequentially by weighted residual reduction.

notation.meaning: Finite set of admissible knot locations.
Polynomial degree of each spline segment.

review_flags: Adaptive knot placement has multiple standard criteria; no supplied source fixes this residual-reduction version.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but adaptive knot placement admits many criteria. No source supports this particular greedy residual-reduction rule, and the relative-decrease denominator is not defined.

children.title: Regression-Tree Metamodels

knowledge_statements.title: Regression-Tree Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-constant response metamodel on axis-aligned terminal regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be partitioned by a finite binary axis-aligned tree into disjoint terminal regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) whose union is \(D\). A regression-tree metamodel has the representation
\[\widehat f(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\mathbf 1\{x\in R_\ell\},\qquad x\in D.\]
For squared-error fitting to observations \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), each nonempty leaf value is \(c_\ell=|I_\ell|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_\ell}y_i\), where \(I_\ell=\{i:x_i\in R_\ell\}\). Thus predictions are constant within each terminal simulation-input regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regression tree partitions the input domain by binary coordinate splits and predicts the sample-average response within each terminal region.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) form a finite disjoint partition of \(D\).
Every fitted terminal region contains at least one observation.
Squared-error loss is used for leaf fitting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f\) is piecewise constant, with each leaf value equal to its empirical response mean.

notation.meaning: Terminal region or leaf of the tree.
Indices of observations assigned to leaf l.

review_flags: An authoritative locator for regression-tree representation and squared-error leaf estimation is required.

children.title: Recursive Partition Metamodels

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Partition Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy binary partitioning by empirical loss reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input observations \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) on \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), a leaf-model class, admissible coordinate thresholds, and stopping constraints. Initialize the partition as \(\{D\}\). For each current region \(R\), fit its leaf model and compute empirical loss \(L(R)\). Among admissible splits \(R=R^-_{j,t}\mathbin{\dot\cup}R^+_{j,t}\), choose one maximizing
\[\Delta(R,j,t)=L(R)-L(R^-_{j,t})-L(R^+_{j,t}).\]
Apply a split with positive maximal gain, refit the two child models, and repeat. Stop when no admissible positive-gain split remains or a size/depth budget is reached; output the partition and fitted leaf models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive partitioning repeatedly chooses the admissible binary split with greatest empirical-loss reduction, then returns the fitted terminal-region models.
assumptions_latex: The candidate split set is finite at every iteration.
Minimum leaf size or depth constraints make termination finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a finite partition whose terminal regions carry separately fitted response models.

notation.meaning: Minimized empirical loss for the leaf model on region R.
Children produced by splitting coordinate j at threshold t.
Empirical loss reduction from a candidate split.

children.title: Regime-Specific Leaf Models

knowledge_statements.title: Regime-Specific Leaf Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise parametric metamodel allowing distinct response laws across terminal regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) be a finite partition of \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). Assign leaf \(R_\ell\) a feature map \(\phi_\ell:R_\ell\to\mathbb R^{q_\ell}\) and parameter \(\beta_\ell\in\mathbb R^{q_\ell}\). A regime-specific leaf metamodel is
\[\widehat f(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L \phi_\ell(x)^\top\widehat\beta_\ell\mathbf 1\{x\in R_\ell\},\]
where each \(\widehat\beta_\ell\) minimizes the empirical loss using only observations in \(R_\ell\). The dimensions and feature maps may differ between leaves, so local constants, linear surfaces, or other prescribed parametric responses can represent distinct simulator regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each terminal region receives its own fitted parametric response law, allowing different local structures in different simulator regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) form a finite disjoint partition of \(D\).
Each leaf contains enough observations to identify its chosen model.
Each leaf loss has a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f\) equals the independently fitted leaf-specific response model on each region.

notation.meaning: Feature map selected for terminal region l.
Parameter vector for terminal region l.

review_flags: An authoritative locator for heterogeneous parametric leaf models is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bayesian regression-tree likelihood and CGM tree prior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint model specification for independent constant-response leaves and a depth-regularized stochastic tree prior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) partitioned by tree \(\mathcal T\), conditional independence of the leaves gives \(p(y^n\mid\mathcal T,x^n)=\prod_{\eta\in\mathcal L_{\mathcal T}}p(y^\eta\mid x^\eta)\). With \(y_i\mid\mu_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}\sim N(\mu_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\) in leaf \(\eta\) and \(p(\mu_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\propto(\sigma_\eta^2)^{-1}\), integrating out \((\mu_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\) yields the stated closed-form marginal leaf likelihood. Under the CGM process, a leaf at depth \(D_\eta\) splits with probability \(p_{\mathrm{split}}(\eta,\mathcal T)=\alpha(1+D_\eta)^{-\beta}\), where \(0<\alpha<1\) and \(\beta\ge0\), and therefore \(p(\mathcal T)\propto\prod_{\eta\in\mathcal I_{\mathcal T}}p_{\mathrm{split}}(\eta,\mathcal T)\prod_{\eta\in\mathcal L_{\mathcal T}}[1-p_{\mathrm{split}}(\eta,\mathcal T)]\). Under the reference leaf prior, every leaf must contain at least two observations for a proper posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayesian regression tree has a likelihood that factors over independently modeled leaves. Constant Gaussian leaf parameters can be integrated out under the reference prior. The CGM prior penalizes depth by making a node's split probability equal to alpha times one plus its depth raised to minus beta; the tree density multiplies split probabilities over internal nodes and non-split probabilities over leaves. Each leaf needs at least two observations for posterior propriety.
assumptions_latex: \(\{\eta:\eta\in\mathcal L_{\mathcal T}\}\) partitions all observations and leaf models are conditionally independent.
Within each leaf, responses are conditionally independent Gaussian variables with unknown \(\mu_\eta\) and \(\sigma_\eta^2\).
\(0<\alpha<1\), \(\beta\ge0\), and \(D_\eta\) is the depth of node \(\eta\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate linear-regression leaf model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Bayesian treed linear model using analytically marginalized Gaussian linear regressions in terminal regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a leaf \(\eta\), let \(y^\eta\mid\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2,X^\eta\sim N(X^\eta\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2I)\) and take the reference prior \(p(\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\propto\sigma_\eta^{-2}\). When the leaf design supplies an identifiable regression and sufficiently many observations for the marginal integral to be finite, integrating out \((\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\) yields an analytic marginal likelihood determined by the leaf design and residual quantities. Thus the linear leaf model can be used in tree-structure inference without sampling its regression parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayesian treed linear model places a Gaussian linear regression in each leaf and uses a scale-invariant reference prior. With an identifiable leaf design and enough observations, its coefficients and variance integrate out in closed form, producing an analytic leaf marginal likelihood.
assumptions_latex: The leaf design identifies the regression coefficients.
The leaf contains sufficiently many observations for the marginal integral to be finite.

children.top_down_role: Neural approximations of stochastic simulator response.

knowledge_statements.title: Neural Response Surfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feedforward neural approximation of a stochastic simulator's conditional mean response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For simulator input \(x\in D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(Y(x)\) have conditional mean \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x)]\). A feedforward neural response surface with \(H\) hidden units is
\[\widehat f_\theta(x)=\beta_0+\sum_{h=1}^H\beta_h\,\sigma(a_h^\top x+b_h).\]
Given independent simulation outputs \(y_{ir}\) at sites \(x_i\), its fitted parameter \(\widehat\theta\) minimizes a specified regularized empirical loss, for example squared error plus \(\rho\lVert\theta\rVert_2^2\). The resulting deterministic map \(\widehat f_{\widehat\theta}\) approximates the simulator mean and can be optimized over \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neural response surface fits a deterministic feedforward network to noisy simulation outputs as an approximation of the conditional mean response.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and \(\mathbb E[|Y(x)|]<\infty\) for each sampled input.
Simulation outputs are conditionally independent across replications.
The activation and regularized empirical loss are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f_{\widehat\theta}:D\to\mathbb R\) is a fitted deterministic surrogate for \(x\mapsto\mathbb E[Y(x)]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coefficient of Determination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a regression goodness-of-fit statistic applicable to response surfaces, including neural-network response models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For observations $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, predictions \hat y_1,\ldots,\hat y_n$, and $\bar y=\frac1n\sum_{p=1}^n y_p$, define $\mathrm{SST}=\sum_{p=1}^n (y_p-\bar y)^2$ and $\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_{p=1}^n (y_p-\hat y_p)^2$. If $\mathrm{SST}>0$, the coefficient of determination is $r^2=1-\mathrm{SSE}/\mathrm{SST}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For observed responses and their model predictions, the coefficient of determination is one minus the ratio of the residual sum of squares to the total sum of squares about the observed mean. This formula requires nonzero total variation in the observations and may also be used to assess neural-network models.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r^2=1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential D-Optimal Parameter-Estimation Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A batch-sequential procedure that repeatedly maximizes the determinant of accumulated information at the current parameter estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial estimate \widehat\theta_0, allocate n_0 measurements to the initial design, set k=0, n=0, and F_0(\widehat\theta_0,X_0)=0. At stage k, select a batch X=X_{n_k} of n_k inputs maximizing \det\!\left[F_n(\widehat\theta_n,X_n)+F_{n_k}(\widehat\theta_n,X)\right]. Collect the corresponding n_k outputs and update \widehat\theta_n to \widehat\theta_{n+n_k}. Stop if the updated estimate is satisfactory or the measurement budget is exhausted; otherwise set k\leftarrow k+1, n\leftarrow n+n_k, augment X_n by the selected batch, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with an initial parameter estimate and information matrix. At each stage, choose the next input batch to maximize the determinant of the accumulated plus prospective information matrix evaluated at the current estimate. Collect the outputs, update the estimate, and repeat until the estimate is satisfactory or the measurement budget is exhausted.
assumptions_latex: n_k\text{ measurements can be allocated at stage }k.
F_n(\widehat\theta_n,X_n)\text{ and }F_{n_k}(\widehat\theta_n,X)\text{ denote accumulated and prospective information matrices.}
\text{A stopping criterion for estimate adequacy or a finite measurement budget is specified.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_{n_k}\in\arg\max_X\det\!\left[F_n(\widehat\theta_n,X_n)+F_{n_k}(\widehat\theta_n,X)\right],\quad \widehat\theta_n\mapsto\widehat\theta_{n+n_k},\text{ with repetition until adequacy or budget exhaustion.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kiefer–Wolfowitz Equivalence Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For an approximate design in a p-parameter linear model over a compact input domain, D-optimality is equivalent to a uniform sensitivity bound and to G-optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linear model with regression vector h(x), let \mathcal X be compact and let M(\xi_\infty^*) be nonsingular. The following are equivalent: (i) \xi_\infty^* is D-optimal; (ii) h(x)^T M(\xi_\infty^*)^{-1}h(x)\le p for every x\in\mathcal X; and (iii) \xi_\infty^* minimizes \max_{x\in\mathcal X}h(x)^TM(\xi)^{-1}h(x). At every support point \chi_i of \xi_\infty^*, the minimax sensitivity satisfies h_i^TM(\xi_\infty^*)^{-1}h_i=p, where h_i=A(\chi_i).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a p-parameter linear model on a compact input domain, an approximate design is D-optimal exactly when its sensitivity is at most p throughout the domain, and exactly when it minimizes the maximum prediction sensitivity. The sensitivity equals p at every support point of the optimal design.
assumptions_latex: h(x)\text{ is the regression vector of a }p\text{-parameter linear model.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi_\infty^*\text{ is D-optimal}\iff \sup_{x\in\mathcal X}h(x)^TM(\xi_\infty^*)^{-1}h(x)\le p\iff \xi_\infty^*\in\arg\min_\xi\max_{x\in\mathcal X}h(x)^TM(\xi)^{-1}h(x),\quad h_i^TM(\xi_\infty^*)^{-1}h_i=p\text{ at every support point }\chi_i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Response-Surface Optimization Procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sequential local modeling procedure for minimizing the expected experimental response as a function of controllable factor levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a current estimate x^{(0)}. At iteration k: choose several experimental inputs near x^{(k)} using an experimental design; collect responses z; fit a local regression response surface to the resulting (x,z) pairs; estimate a steepest-descent path in factor space; experiment successively along that path until further improvement in z ceases; and set the best tested point as x^{(k+1)}. Repeat until a final factor vector is obtained. A second-order Hessian analysis may then be used to check that the final point is a minimum of E[z].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an initial factor vector, design and run nearby experiments, fit a local response surface, follow its estimated steepest-descent path while the observed response improves, and use the best point as the center of the next cycle. Repeat until a final factor vector is obtained; optional Hessian analysis can check that it is a minimum of the expected response.
assumptions_latex: z\text{ is an observed response, with the objective of minimizing }E[z].
\text{Local experimental responses can be collected and a regression response surface can be fitted.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{(k+1)}\text{ is the best tested point along the locally estimated descent path, and the design-fit-search cycle is repeated until a final factor vector is obtained.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Evaluation of the Morris–Mitchell Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct computation using $L_p$ pairwise distances, including the coincident-point boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given design points $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$, $q>0$, and $p\ge1$, compute $d_{ij}=\|x_i-x_j\|_p$ for every $1\le i<j\le m$ and return
\[
\Phi_{q,p}(X)=\left(\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}d_{ij}^{-q}\right)^{1/q}.
\]
The value is finite when all design points are distinct; if some $d_{ij}=0$, it is $+\infty$ under the extended-real convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute every L-p pairwise distance, sum its negative q-th power, and take the q-th root. The result is finite for distinct design points and infinite under the extended-real convention when two points coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi_{q,p}(X)=\left(\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}\|x_i-x_j\|_p^{-q}\right)^{1/q};\quad \Phi_{q,p}(X)=+\infty\text{ if }x_i=x_j\text{ for some }i<j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise-Distance Comparison of Sampling Plans
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic comparison of sorted $L_p$ pairwise distances, favoring the design with the larger first unequal distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sampling plans $A$ and $B$ having the same number of points, sort their $L_p$ pairwise-distance lists increasingly as $(a_1,\ldots,a_N)$ and $(b_1,\ldots,b_N)$. At the first index $k$ with $a_k\ne b_k$, return $-1$ if $a_k>b_k$ and $1$ if $a_k<b_k$; return $0$ if all entries agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort each plan's pairwise distances from smallest to largest and compare the lists lexicographically. The plan with the larger distance at the first difference is declared more space-filling; identical profiles are equivalent under this criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{compare}(A,B)=\begin{cases}-1,&a_k>b_k\text{ at the first unequal index }k,\\1,&a_k<b_k\text{ at the first unequal index }k,\\0,&a_i=b_i\text{ for all }i.\end{cases}
