knowledge_statements.statement_title: LHS-Based Predictive-Method Bakeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated held-out comparison of applicable predictive methods using Latin-hypercube evaluation sites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) have input dimension \(m\), let \(K\) predictive methods be applicable to \(f\), and choose training size \(n\), validation size \(n'\), and repetitions \(R\). For each \(r=1,\ldots,R\): generate an LHS \(X\) of size \(n+n'\); evaluate \(Y=f(X)\); randomly partition the resulting pairs into training data \(T_n\) and validation data \(V_{n'}\); fit each method \(k=1,\ldots,K\) on \(T_n\); predict on the validation inputs; and compute a held-out metric \(m_r^{(k)}\). Examples are \[m_r^{(k)}=\sqrt{\frac1{n'}\sum_{i=1}^{n'}(y_i^v-\widehat y_i^{(k)})^2}\quad\text{and}\quad m_r^{(k)}=\frac1{n'}\sum_{i=1}^{n'}|y_i^v-\widehat y_i^{(k)}|.\] Return the \(R\times K\) metric matrix, or summaries of its empirical distributions, for method comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each repetition, evaluate the test function at n+n-prime Latin-hypercube sites, split the resulting pairs into training and validation sets, fit all applicable predictive methods, and score their held-out predictions. Return the repetition-by-method score matrix or empirical summaries for comparison.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ candidate fitting or prediction methods are applicable to }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=(m_r^{(k)})\in\mathbb R^{R\times K}\text{, or summaries of its empirical distributions, records the repeated held-out comparison.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy Sequential Space-Filling Subset Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A randomized-initialization, forward-greedy heuristic; no global optimality guarantee is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite set X, an integer \(1\le m\le |X|\), and a set metric d (defaulting to \(d_{\max}\)), initialize \(S=\{x_1\}\) with \(x_1\) sampled from X. For \(i=2,\ldots,m\), choose
\[
x_i\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X\setminus S} d\bigl(X,S\cup\{x\}\bigr)
\]
and replace \(S\leftarrow S\cup\{x_i\}\). Return S.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with one randomly selected point. Until m points have been selected, add an unselected candidate that minimizes the distance objective after its insertion. The procedure returns an m-element subset; the extract gives no global optimality guarantee.
assumptions_latex: d(X,S)\text{ is defined for the candidate set and each nonempty selected subset}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S|=m\quad\text{and each added point minimizes }d(X,S\cup\{x\})\text{ over }x\in X\setminus S\text{ at that iteration.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Space-Filling Subset Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a fixed-cardinality space-filling subset over a finite candidate set and records the exhaustive-search count without asserting a formal complexity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite set of \(d\) design points and let \(1\le m\le d\). A size-\(m\) space-filling sampling plan is any solution of
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{S\subseteq X}\ d_{\max}(X,S)\qquad\text{subject to }|S|=m.
\]
There are \(\binom{d}{m}=\frac{d!}{m!(d-m)!}\) feasible subsets, so exhaustive enumeration tests that many candidates and is described as typically computationally intractable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite candidate set X containing d design points, a size-m space-filling plan minimizes the prescribed d_max metric over all m-element subsets. Exhaustive search tests all d choose m feasible subsets and is typically computationally intractable.
assumptions_latex: d_{\max}(X,S)\text{ is the previously defined set-distance metric}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq X,\ |S|=m}d_{\max}(X,S),\qquad \#\{S\subseteq X:|S|=m\}=\binom{d}{m}.

knowledge_statements.title: Latin Hypercube Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized marginally stratified design on a unit hypercube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\), a randomized Latin hypercube design in \([0,1]^d\) is constructed by drawing, independently for each coordinate \(j\), a uniform random permutation \(\pi_j\) of \(\{1,ldots,n\}\), drawing independent jitters \(u_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) independently of the permutations, and setting
\[x_{ij}=\frac{\pi_j(i)-u_{ij}}{n},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
For every coordinate \(j\) and every stratum \(((k-1)/n,k/n)\), exactly one design point has its \(j\)-th coordinate in that stratum. Coordinatewise transformations extend the design to rectangular domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized Latin hypercube draws random coordinatewise stratum permutations and within-stratum jitters, placing exactly one run in each of n equal strata of every input coordinate.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\pi_j\) is a uniform random permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), independently across coordinates.
The variables \(u_{ij}\) are independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) jitters and are independent of the permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every one-dimensional coordinate projection contains exactly one point in each equal-width stratum.

notation.meaning: Number of design points and marginal strata.
Random stratum permutation for coordinate j.
Random within-stratum jitter for run i and coordinate j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Stratification and Projection Closure of Latin Hypercubes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional stratification and preservation of the Latin-hypercube property under coordinate deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an \(n\)-point Latin hypercube \(X\subset[0,1]^m\), each coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) has exactly one point in every interval \([k/n,(k+1)/n)\), \(k=0,\ldots,n-1\). Consequently, for every nonempty retained coordinate set \(J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), the coordinate projection \(\pi_J(X)\) is an \(n\)-point Latin hypercube in \([0,1]^{|J|}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every coordinate of an n-point Latin hypercube contains exactly one point in each of the n equal unit-interval strata. Dropping any nonempty proper subset of coordinates preserves this condition, so the resulting coordinate projection is also a Latin hypercube.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse-CDF Transformation of a Latin Hypercube
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise quantile transformation of a randomized Latin hypercube to prescribed marginal distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate a randomized Latin hypercube \(U=(u_{ij})\) in \([0,1]^m\). The design retains one point associated with each equal-probability stratum of coordinate \(j\), although atoms of \(F_j\) may map distinct probability strata to equal values.

Each transformed coordinate has the prescribed marginal distribution over the LHS randomization and retains probability-scale stratification; discrete marginals may produce tied transformed values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Latin hypercube sampling on a hyperrectangle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a marginally stratified design with a prescribed number of points in a bounded hyperrectangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given [\ell,u]\subset\mathbb{R}^n and p\in\mathbb{N}, form \Pi\in\{1,\ldots,p\}^{n\times p} so that every row is a random permutation of (1,\ldots,p). Independently choose r_{ij}\in[0,1) and set x_i^j=\ell_i+\frac{\Pi_{ij}-r_{ij}}{p}(u_i-\ell_i) for i=1,\ldots,n and j=1,\ldots,p. Return \{x^1,\ldots,x^p\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a hyperrectangle and a requested positive number of points, randomly permute the stratum labels separately in every coordinate, choose a random within-stratum offset for each coordinate of each point, and scale the resulting coordinates to the hyperrectangle. The returned points form a Latin hypercube design, with one point occupying each coordinate stratum.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each row of }\Pi\text{ is a permutation of }(1,\ldots,p)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x^1,\ldots,x^p\}\subset[\ell,u]\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a Latin hypercube design with exactly one point in each of the }p\text{ strata of every coordinate.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Latin Hypercube Sample Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a randomized Latin hypercube design on the unit hypercube, including the centered deterministic variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m\in\mathbb N\). An \(n\)-run, \(m\)-factor Latin hypercube is an \(n\times m\) matrix \(L=(l_{ij})\) such that every column is a permutation of \(\{-(n-1)/2,-(n-3)/2,\ldots,(n-1)/2\}\). Given independent \(u_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]\), define \[x_{ij}=\frac{l_{ij}+(n-1)/2+u_{ij}}{n},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\quad j=1,\ldots,m.\] Then \(X=(x_{ij})\) is a Latin hypercube sample in \([0,1]^m\). Setting every \(u_{ij}=1/2\) places each coordinate at its stratum midpoint and gives a Latin sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each column of a Latin hypercube permutes the same n equally spaced centered levels. Shifting, normalizing, and adding an independent uniform within-stratum displacement produces a sample in the unit hypercube. Using displacement one-half places every coordinate at its stratum midpoint.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each column of }L\text{ is a permutation of }\{-(n-1)/2,-(n-3)/2,\ldots,(n-1)/2\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{ij}=\frac{l_{ij}+(n-1)/2+u_{ij}}{n}\in[0,1],\quad X\in[0,1]^{n\times m};\qquad u_{ij}=1/2\ \forall i,j\text{ gives the centered Latin sample.}

children.title: Maximin Design
children.top_down_role: Distance-based domain coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximin Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite design maximizing its smallest pairwise separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be compact and contain at least \(n\ge2\) distinct points, and let \(d_D\) be a continuous metric on \(D\). An \(n\)-point maximin design is any set \(X_n^*=\{x_1^*,\ldots,x_n^*\}\subset D\) satisfying
\[X_n^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\substack{X\subset D\\|X|=n}}\delta(X),\qquad \delta(X)=\min_{\substack{x,x'\in X\\x\ne x'}}d_D(x,x').\]
Thus the criterion maximizes the distance between the closest pair of design sites. Under the stated compactness, continuity, and cardinality assumptions, an optimal configuration exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain containing at least n distinct points, a maximin design chooses n sites so that the distance between the closest pair is as large as possible.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is compact and contains at least \(n\) distinct points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_n^*\) exists and maximizes the minimum pairwise design-site distance over all \(n\)-point subsets of \(D\).

notation.meaning: An n-point design in the input domain.
Distance metric used to assess separation.
Minimum pairwise distance of design X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential maximin augmenting design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximin augmentation conditional on a fixed original design; only the new locations are decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the fixed original design be
\[
X_n^{\mathrm{orig}}=\{x_{n'+1},\ldots,x_{n'+n}\}.
\]
An augmenting design $X_{n'}=\{x_1,\ldots,x_{n'}\}$ is sequentially maximin if
\[
X_{n'}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{Y_{n'}}
\min_{\substack{1\le i\le n'\\1\le k\le n'+n,\ k\ne i}}
d(z_i,z_k),
\]
where $z_i=y_i$ for $1\le i\le n'$ and $z_k=x_k$ for $n'<k\le n'+n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a fixed original design of n locations, a sequential maximin, or augmenting, design chooses n-prime new locations to maximize the minimum distance involving a new location and any distinct new or original location. Distances solely between original locations are excluded, because only new locations index the first argument of the minimum.
assumptions_latex: Y_{n'}=\{y_1,\ldots,y_{n'}\}\text{ ranges over admissible augmenting designs}
d\text{ is the selected pairwise separation criterion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_{n'}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{Y_{n'}}\min_{\substack{1\le i\le n'\\1\le k\le n'+n,\ k\ne i}}d(z_i,z_k)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Surrogate-Based Simulation Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic sequential design loop for a deterministic or noisy simulator using a fitted surrogate and an augmentation criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a simulator producing \(y\sim f(x)\), a design domain \(\mathcal X\), sizes \(n_0\leq N\), a flexible surrogate with possibly unknown hyperparameters, and an augmentation criterion \(J\), construct an initial design \(X_{n_0}\), observe its responses, and set \(D_{n_0}=(X_{n_0},Y_{n_0})\). For each \(n=n_0,\ldots,N-1\), fit the surrogate and its hyperparameters using \(D_n\), choose \(x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}J(x\mid D_n)\), observe \(y_{n+1}\sim f(x_{n+1})\), and update \(D_{n+1}=D_n\cup\{(x_{n+1},y_{n+1})\}\). Finally refit the surrogate using \(D_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Create and evaluate a seed design. Repeatedly fit the surrogate and any unknown hyperparameters, optimize the chosen augmentation criterion, evaluate the simulator at the selected input, and append the observation until the final design size is reached. Return the final data and its fitted surrogate.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ provides deterministic or noisy observations }y\sim f(x)\text{ for }x\in\mathcal X
J(\cdot\mid D_n)\text{ is an augmentation criterion that can be optimized over }\mathcal X
\text{The surrogate and any unknown hyperparameters can be fitted from }D_n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_N\text{ and a surrogate fitted using }D_N\text{ are returned after }N-n_0\text{ sequential augmentations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Horizon IMSPE Lookahead over Replication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replication-biased lookahead for selecting the immediate action in heteroskedastic sequential surrogate design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), enumerate \(h+1\) decision paths that introduce at most one new unique site \(\bar x_{n+1}\) and otherwise replicate available unique sites. A new-site step minimizes the continuous IMSPE criterion, whereas a replication step compares discrete candidates using \[I_{n+1}(\bar x_k)=\nu\bigl(1-\operatorname{tr}(B'_kW_n)\bigr),\qquad B'_k=\frac{M_{\cdot,k}M_{k,\cdot}}{a_k(a_k+1)/\lambda_k-M_{k,k}},\quad M=(C_n+A_n^{-1}\Lambda_n)^{-1}.\] Unroll each path to design size \(N+1+h\), compute its terminal IMSPE, and retain a minimizing path. Select \(x_{N+1}\) as a new location if the retained path explores first and as a replicate otherwise. The enumeration uses \(h+1\) continuous searches and \((h+1)(h+2)/2-1\) discrete searches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm compares all allowed timings of at most one new site among future replication actions, scores the resulting designs by terminal IMSPE, and executes the first action of a minimizing path. Horizon zero is ordinary myopic IMSPE search.
assumptions_latex: \text{At most one new unique site is introduced over the lookahead horizon}
a_k(a_k+1)/\lambda_k-M_{k,k}\neq0\text{ for each evaluated replication candidate}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{N+1}=\begin{cases}\bar x_{n+1},&\text{if the retained minimizing path explores first},\\\bar x_k\text{ at an existing site},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.title: Prediction-Directed Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential design minimizing integrated metamodel prediction uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given current simulation data \(\mathcal D_t\), a fitted probabilistic metamodel with updated predictive variance \(s_{t+1}^2(z;x)\) after sampling candidate \(x\in D\), a finite measure \(\mu\) on \(D\), and candidate set \(C_t\), select
\[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C_t}\int_D s_{t+1}^2(z;x)\,\mu(dz).\]
Run the simulator at \(x_{t+1}\), append the response to \(\mathcal D_t\), refit or update the metamodel, and repeat until the simulation budget is exhausted. Output the final metamodel and accumulated design. The criterion targets global predictive precision rather than objective value alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential samples are chosen to minimize the metamodel's anticipated integrated prediction variance over the input domain.
assumptions_latex: \(C_t\subseteq D\) is nonempty and the displayed minimum is attained.
The metamodel supplies finite look-ahead predictive variances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each selected input minimizes the one-step-ahead integrated predictive variance over the current candidate set.

notation.meaning: Simulation data available after t allocations.
Predictive variance at z after a prospective observation at x.
Measure weighting prediction accuracy across the domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrated Mean-Squared Prediction Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-based global predictive-uncertainty criterion for sequential or batch surrogate design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given existing unique sites \(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n\) and a candidate \(x_{n+1}\in\mathcal X\), define \[I_{n+1}(x_{n+1})\equiv\operatorname{IMSPE}(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n,x_{n+1})=\int_{x\in\mathcal X}\breve\sigma_{n+1}^2(x)\,dx.\] IMSPE-based design minimizes this input-space-averaged predictive variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IMSPE is the predictive variance after design augmentation, integrated over the input space; IMSPE design minimizes this quantity.
assumptions_latex: \breve\sigma_{n+1}^2(x)\text{ is the predictive variance after augmenting the design}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal X}I_{n+1}(z)\quad\text{for an IMSPE-minimizing sequential design}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrated Mean-Squared Prediction Error Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prediction-directed Gaussian-process design using normalized, optionally weighted integrated predictive variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Gaussian-process conditional-mean predictor, with model quantities treated as fixed, suppose $\sigma_n^2(x)=\tau^2[1+g-k_n(x)^\top K_n^{-1}k_n(x)]$. Then the conditional mean-squared prediction error satisfies $\operatorname{MSPE}[\widehat y(x)]=\mathbb E[(\widehat y(x)-Y(x))^2\mid D_n]=\sigma_n^2(x)$. Given $w(x)\ge0$ with $\int_{\mathcal X}w(x)\,dx=1$, the IMSPE criterion is $J(X_n)=\int_{\mathcal X}\sigma_n^2(x)\tau^{-2}w(x)\,dx$, and an IMSPE design minimizes $J$. Uniform $w$ assigns equal predictive importance over $\mathcal X$. For rectangular $\mathcal X$ and certain isotropic or separable Gaussian and Matérn kernels, the integral may admit a closed or nearly closed form; otherwise numerical integration may be required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IMSPE design minimizes normalized predictive variance averaged over the input region with a nonnegative unit-mass weight. For the GP conditional-mean predictor, conditional MSPE equals predictive variance. Closed-form integration is available only for suitable domains and covariance kernels.
assumptions_latex: \text{The GP model quantities and hyperparameters are treated as fixed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_n^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{X_n}\int_{\mathcal X}\frac{\sigma_n^2(x)}{\tau^2}w(x)\,dx

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active Learning Cohn Integrated Variance-Reduction Policy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential GP design selecting a new site by its aggregate reduction of predictive uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(D_n=(X_n,Y_n)\), hold the fitted GP hyperparameters \((\widehat\tau_n^2,\widehat\theta_n,\widehat g_n)\) fixed while considering \(X_{n+1}=X_n\cup\{z\}\). Let \(\widetilde\sigma_{n+1}^2(x;z)\) be the predictive variance deduced from the augmented design before observing the response at \(z\), and define \(\Delta\sigma_n^2(z)=\int_{x\in\mathcal X}[\sigma_n^2(x)-\widetilde\sigma_{n+1}^2(x;z)]\,dx\). Then ALC chooses \(x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in\mathcal X}\Delta\sigma_n^2(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal X}\int_{x\in\mathcal X}\widetilde\sigma_{n+1}^2(x;z)\,dx\). The integral may be approximated by a sum over a reference set; for a singleton reference set \(\{x_{\mathrm{ref}}\}\), the stated degenerate choice is \(x_{n+1}=x_{\mathrm{ref}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active learning Cohn holds the current fitted GP hyperparameters fixed and evaluates candidate sites by the aggregate predictive-variance reduction their addition would produce. It maximizes integrated reduction, equivalently minimizing deduced integrated variance. A finite reference-set sum may replace the integral; the singleton case selects its sole reference point.
assumptions_latex: D_n=(X_n,Y_n)\text{ and }\sigma_n^2\text{ is the fitted GP predictive variance}
(\widehat\tau_n^2,\widehat\theta_n,\widehat g_n)\text{ are estimated from }D_n\text{ and held fixed when candidates are evaluated}
\widetilde\sigma_{n+1}^2(x;z)\text{ uses }X_n\cup\{z\}\text{ without requiring the unobserved response at }z
\mathcal X\text{ or a selected reference set supports the integral or its finite-sum approximation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in\mathcal X}\int_{x\in\mathcal X}\left[\sigma_n^2(x)-\widetilde\sigma_{n+1}^2(x;z)\right]dx=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal X}\int_{x\in\mathcal X}\widetilde\sigma_{n+1}^2(x;z)dx.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Reference Approximation of IMSPE
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation of the IMSPE integral by predictive variances evaluated on a finite random, regular, or space-filling reference set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $J(X_n)=\int_{\mathcal X}\sigma_n^2(x)\tau^{-2}w(x)\,dx$, where $w\ge0$ and $\int_{\mathcal X}w(x)\,dx=1$. If the uniform distribution on $\mathcal X$ has density one with respect to the displayed integration measure, as when $|\mathcal X|=1$, then for $x_t\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathcal X)$ one may use $J(X_n)\approx T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T\sigma_n^2(x_t)\tau^{-2}w(x_t)$. If $x_t$ are sampled from the probability measure having density $w$, one may instead use $J(X_n)\approx T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T\sigma_n^2(x_t)\tau^{-2}$. For a uniform law on a domain of volume $|\mathcal X|\ne1$, the first estimator requires the corresponding volume factor. Regular or space-filling reference sets require quadrature interpretation rather than the stated sampling identity. Increasing reference-set resolution trades additional computation for potentially improved integration accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IMSPE can be approximated by averaging normalized predictive variances on a finite reference set. Uniform samples retain the weight explicitly, while samples drawn from the weight-induced distribution use an unweighted average. The displayed uniform-sampling formula assumes a unit-volume or equivalently normalized integration measure; otherwise a volume factor is needed. Grid accuracy is obtained at increased computational cost.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the first displayed form, the uniform law has density }1\text{ relative to }dx
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J(X_n)\approx\begin{cases}\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{\sigma_n^2(x_t)}{\tau^2}w(x_t),&x_t\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathcal X)\text{ under the normalized-measure assumption},\\\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{\sigma_n^2(x_t)}{\tau^2},&x_t\sim\mathcal W.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Directed Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-improvement sequential design for minimizing a stochastic response surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given data \(\mathcal D_t\), suppose the latent mean response at \(x\in D\) has predictive distribution \(F_t(x)\mid\mathcal D_t\sim N(m_t(x),s_t^2(x))\). Let \(f_t^{\min}\) be the best incumbent mean value. Define improvement \(I_t(x)=(f_t^{\min}-F_t(x))_+\), and choose
\[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C_t}\mathbb E[I_t(x)\mid\mathcal D_t].\]
Simulate at \(x_{t+1}\), update \(\mathcal D_t\) and the metamodel, and repeat until the budget is exhausted. Output the sampled decision having the smallest estimated mean response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The next simulation site maximizes expected improvement over the incumbent, concentrating effort where low response values are plausible.
assumptions_latex: The objective is minimization over a nonempty candidate set \(C_t\subseteq D\).
The metamodel supplies finite Gaussian predictive means and variances for the latent mean response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each new site maximizes one-step expected improvement over the incumbent among current candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: New-Location Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget allocation restricted to previously unsampled simulator inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_t=\{x_1,\ldots,x_{k_t}\}\subset D\) be the set of inputs already simulated, let \(C_t\subseteq D\setminus S_t\) be a nonempty candidate set, and let \(A_t:C_t\to\mathbb R\) be a specified acquisition score combining predicted objective value and uncertainty. Select
\[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C_t}A_t(x).\]
Run one or more replications at \(x_{t+1}\), set \(S_{t+1}=S_t\cup\{x_{t+1}\}\), update the metamodel, and repeat until the location or simulation budget is exhausted. Output the expanded sampled set and updated metamodel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation budget is spent at an unsampled input maximizing a chosen acquisition score, thereby expanding the explored set.
assumptions_latex: The acquisition score \(A_t\) is finite and attains a maximum on \(C_t\).
A finite allocation budget is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected \(x_{t+1}\) is new and maximizes the current acquisition score among unsampled candidates.

children.title: Replication Allocation
children.top_down_role: Simulation effort emphasizing local noise estimation and precision.

knowledge_statements.title: Replication Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step allocation among sampled sites to reduce estimation variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At sampled sites \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), let \(n_i\ge1\) be the current replication count and let \(\widehat\sigma_i^2\) estimate the variance of one simulation output. Under independent replications, the estimated variance of the sample mean after one additional replication at site \(i\) is \(\widehat\sigma_i^2/(n_i+1)\). Given nonnegative importance weights \(q_i\), allocate the next replication to
\[i^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le i\le k}q_i\widehat\sigma_i^2\left(\frac1{n_i}-\frac1{n_i+1}\right).\]
Update that site's sample statistics and repeat until the replication budget is exhausted; output the updated sitewise mean and variance estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The next replication goes to the sampled site with the largest weighted reduction in estimated sample-mean variance.
assumptions_latex: Replications are independent within and across sampled sites.
A finite replication budget is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected site maximizes the estimated one-step weighted reduction in sample-mean variance.

notation.meaning: Current number of replications at site i.
Estimated variance of one output at site i.
Importance weight for precision at site i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adapted steepest-descent trial-point rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local first-order response-surface search under homoscedastic uncorrelated simulation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{-0}^{\top})^{\top} be the least-squares coefficients for a first-order response surface with full-column-rank design matrix \mathbf Z. Under white noise, \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\sigma_w^2(\mathbf Z^{\top}\mathbf Z)^{-1}=\sigma_w^2\begin{pmatrix}a&\mathbf b^{\top}\\ \mathbf b&\mathbf C\end{pmatrix}, and hence \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{-0})=\sigma_w^2\mathbf C. For a predictor vector (1,\mathbf x^{\top})^{\top}, if \mathbf C is invertible, predictor variance is minimized at \mathbf x_*=-\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf b. Adapted steepest descent chooses the new simulation point \mathbf d=\mathbf x_*-\lambda\mathbf C^{-1}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{-0}=-\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf b-\lambda\mathbf C^{-1}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{-0}. The noise variance may be estimated by \widehat\sigma_w^2=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{r=1}^{m_i}(w_{i;r}-\widehat y_i)^2}{N-(k+1)}, where N=\sum_i m_i and \widehat y_i=\mathbf z_i^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}. The covariance adjustment gives a scale-independent search direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit a first-order response surface under white simulation noise. Partition the inverse information matrix so that the estimated gradient has covariance σ²C. When C is invertible, the local predictor variance is minimized at −C⁻¹b, and ASD selects the new point −C⁻¹b − λC⁻¹β̂₋₀. The covariance adjustment makes the search direction scale independent. The noise variance can be estimated using residual sum of squares divided by N−k−1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf x_*=-\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf b,\qquad \mathbf d=-\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf b-\lambda\mathbf C^{-1}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{-0},\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{-0})=\sigma_w^2\mathbf C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized response surface methodology for constrained simulation optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm statement; the affine-scaling direction requires positive current slacks and a nonsingular direction matrix, while the source notes that singularity may occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{\mathbf z}\mathbb E[w_0\mid\mathbf z]\) subject to \(\mathbb E[w_{h'}\mid\mathbf z]\ge a_{h'}\), \(h'=1,\ldots,r-1\), and \(\mathbf l\le\mathbf z\le\mathbf u\), GRSM locally fits \(\mathbf y_h=\mathbf Z\beta_h+e_h\) and computes \(\widehat\beta_h=(\mathbf Z^\top\mathbf Z)^{-1}\mathbf Z^\top\mathbf w_h\). The fitted response constraints yield \(\mathbf B\mathbf z-\mathbf s=\mathbf c\), with bound slacks satisfying \(\mathbf z+\mathbf r=\mathbf u\) and \(\mathbf z-\mathbf v=\mathbf l\). When the required inverse exists, GRSM uses \[\mathbf d=-\left(\mathbf B^\top\mathbf S^{-2}\mathbf B+\mathbf R^{-2}+\mathbf V^{-2}\right)^{-1}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0;-0}.\] The extract prescribes \[\lambda=0.8\min_{h'}\frac{c_{h'}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{h';-0}^{\top}\mathbf z_c}{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{h';-0}^{\top}\mathbf d},\] followed by checking the global box constraints, simulating \(\mathbf z_c+\lambda\mathbf d\), testing objective improvement and response feasibility, optionally halving the step repeatedly, and refitting local response surfaces around the best point found. With common random numbers, objective improvement is tested using a paired \(t_{m-1}\) statistic; the multiple response-feasibility tests use Bonferroni-adjusted significance levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GRSM optimizes one expected simulation response subject to lower bounds on other expected responses and box bounds on the inputs. It repeatedly fits local linear response surfaces, computes an affine-scaling direction from estimated gradients and current slacks, takes the source-prescribed conservative step, evaluates improvement and feasibility by simulation, optionally halves the step, and refits around the best point. The direction formula is not defined when its matrix is singular.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf y_h=\mathbf Z\beta_h+e_h\text{ satisfies the local white-noise model for }h=0,\ldots,r-1
\mathbf B^\top\mathbf S^{-2}\mathbf B+\mathbf R^{-2}+\mathbf V^{-2}\text{ is invertible}
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{h';-0}^{\top}\mathbf d\ne0\text{ for every ratio included in the prescribed step-size minimum}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf z_{\mathrm{new}}=\mathbf z_c+\lambda\mathbf d\text{ is simulation-evaluated for objective improvement, }\mathbb E[w_{h'}\mid\mathbf z_{\mathrm{new}}]\ge a_{h'}\text{ for all }h',\text{ and }\mathbf l\le\mathbf z_{\mathrm{new}}\le\mathbf u.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Response Surface Methodology for Simulation Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of classical RSM as a black-box, sequential heuristic rather than a convergence-guaranteed algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Response surface methodology treats a simulation as a black-box input-output map and performs a sequence of local designed experiments. It fits local first-order polynomial metamodels by linear regression to guide the search over input combinations; when the search appears near an optimum, it augments the current model to a second-order polynomial. The procedure is heuristic and, as stated here, carries no convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Response surface methodology treats a simulator as a black box and sequentially runs local designed experiments. It uses linear regression to fit first-order polynomial metamodels that guide the search over inputs, then augments the current model to a second-order polynomial when an optimum appears near. This is a heuristic description, not a convergence guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The simulation model is accessed through observed input-output pairs rather than its internal structure.
Local experiments and polynomial regression models can be constructed from simulation observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{RSM sequentially uses local first-order response surfaces for exploration and a second-order response surface near a putative optimum.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: PROCON Reduced-Gradient Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One iteration for a feasible linear-objective program with a differentiable joint chance constraint, linear equalities, and nonnegativity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G(x)=P(\{\xi\mid Tx\geq\xi\}) and let x=(y,z) be feasible for \min c^{\mathsf T}x subject to G(x)\geq\alpha,\ Dx=d,\ x\geq0. Suppose D=(B,N) has full row rank, B is a basis, c^{\mathsf T}=(f^{\mathsf T},g^{\mathsf T}), and y_j>\varepsilon for every basic component, where \varepsilon>0. For fixed \theta>0, compute (\tau^*,v^*) by maximizing \tau subject to r^{\mathsf T}v\leq-\tau; additionally s^{\mathsf T}v\geq\theta\tau when G(x)\leq\alpha+\varepsilon; v_j\geq0 when z_j\leq\varepsilon; and \|v\|_\infty\leq1, where r^{\mathsf T}=g^{\mathsf T}-f^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}N and s^{\mathsf T}=\nabla_zG(x)^{\mathsf T}-\nabla_yG(x)^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}N. Set u^*=-B^{-1}Nv^*. This linear program has a nonempty bounded feasible set. If \tau^*=0, resolve with \varepsilon=0; a second zero value certifies optimality of x. If 0<\tau^*\leq\varepsilon, repeatedly halve \varepsilon and resolve until \tau^*>\varepsilon. Then accept w^*=(u^*,v^*) as a search direction, use bisection along x+\mu w^*,\ \mu\geq0, to locate the probabilistic-constraint boundary within tolerance, and retain the basis if the next iterate is strictly nondegenerate; otherwise attempt a basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible, strictly nondegenerate point, eliminate the basic direction through u = −B⁻¹Nv and solve a bounded linear program in the nonbasic direction and a progress variable. The program enforces objective descent, probabilistic-feasibility improvement near the chance-constraint boundary, equality feasibility, near-active nonnegativity constraints, and normalization. A zero optimum after resolving at zero tolerance certifies optimality; a small positive optimum triggers tolerance halving; and a sufficiently positive optimum supplies the search direction. A bisection line search locates the chance-constraint boundary, after which the basis is retained or exchanged according to strict nondegeneracy.
assumptions_latex: x=(y,z)\text{ is feasible for }\min c^{\mathsf T}x\text{ s.t. }G(x)\geq\alpha,\ Dx=d,\ x\geq0
G(x)=P(\{\xi\mid Tx\geq\xi\})\text{ is differentiable at the evaluated points}
D=(B,N)\text{ has full row rank and }B\text{ is nonsingular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau^*=0\text{ after resolving with }\varepsilon=0\Rightarrow x\text{ is optimal};\quad \tau^*>\varepsilon\Rightarrow w^*=(-B^{-1}Nv^*,v^*)\text{ is accepted as the search direction.

Globally or multistart optimize \(m_N\) to construct a finite candidate set \(C\subset X\) containing at least one element of \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}m_N(x)\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), collect or augment replicated observations in \(B(x_k,\Delta_k)\cap X\) and fit a local linear or quadratic response surface \(q_k\). Compute \(s_k\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}\{q_k(x_k+s):x_k+s\in X,\ \lVert s\rVert\leq\Delta_k\}\). Using sufficiently replicated estimates \(\widehat f_k\), form \(\rho_k=[\widehat f_k(x_k)-\widehat f_k(x_k+s_k)]/[q_k(x_k)-q_k(x_k+s_k)]\) when the denominator is positive. Accept the step when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\), expand the region when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_2\), and otherwise reject the step and contract the region, where \(0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1\). Stop under a prescribed radius, precision, or budget rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit a local response surface, propose a trust-region step, compare observed and predicted improvement, and accept, reject, expand, or contract accordingly.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_n\subset X\) be the sampled locations and define the random latent incumbent \(f_n^\star=\min_{z\in S_n}f(z)\). For a candidate \(x\), define \(\operatorname{NEI}_n(x)=\mathbb E[(f_n^\star-f(x))_+\mid\mathcal D_n]\), where the expectation is under the joint posterior of latent responses and therefore does not substitute the smallest noisy observation for \(f_n^\star\). Choose a maximizer of \(\operatorname{NEI}_n(x)/c(x)\), simulate at that location, and update the posterior. Replication is permitted by including previously sampled locations in \(X\). Stop when the budget is exhausted or the maximal acquisition value is below a prescribed tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each candidate \(x\in X\), let \(m_{n+1}^{x}\) denote the random posterior mean that would result from one additional noisy observation at \(x\). Define \(\operatorname{KG}_n(x)=\min_{z\in X}m_n(z)-\mathbb E[\min_{z\in X}m_{n+1}^{x}(z)\mid\mathcal D_n]\). Select a location maximizing \(\operatorname{KG}_n(x)/c(x)\), observe the simulator there, and update the posterior. After the sampling budget is exhausted, return \(\widehat x_N\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}m_N(x)\). Thus each sampling decision maximizes the expected one-step reduction in the terminal posterior decision value, rather than immediate observed improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample the alternative giving the largest expected one-step reduction in the minimum posterior mean per cost, then return the final posterior-mean minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(n\), construct the statistical upper score \(U_n(x)=m_n(x)+\beta_n s_n(x)\) and simulate at a maximizer of \(U_n\). The mean term favors locations predicted to have high reward, while the uncertainty term favors locations whose reward remains poorly determined. Incorporate the new noisy observation into the posterior and repeat until the budget or stopping rule is met. For minimizing a cost \(f=-g\), the equivalent rule minimizes the lower score \(L_n(x)=m_n^f(x)-\beta_n s_n^f(x)\). The sequence \((\beta_n)\) must be fixed by the selected confidence or exploration schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For reward maximization, sample where posterior mean plus an uncertainty bonus is largest; for cost minimization, use posterior mean minus that bonus.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For held-out observations \((x_i,y_i)\), define \(e_i=(y_i-m(x_i))/\sqrt{v(x_i)}\). assumptions_latex: A finite validation set \(V\subset X\) contains decision-relevant alternatives.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The surrogate is optimization-adequate on \(V\) only if \(R_V\leq\varepsilon_R\), \(E_{\mathrm{rank}}\leq\varepsilon_{ho}\), and the local-geometry criterion passes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-focused validation on recommendation quality, ranking accuracy, and local geometry near competitive solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in V}m(x)\) and define \(R_V=\widehat f_V(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in V}\widehat f_V(x)\). For declared nonnegative weights \(w_{ij}\), define \(E_{\mathrm{rank}}=\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\mathbf 1\{[m(x_i)-m(x_j)][\widehat f_V(x_i)-\widehat f_V(x_j)]<0\}/\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\). An optimization-aware certificate reports uncertainty for \(R_V\), verifies \(E_{\mathrm{rank}}\leq\varepsilon_{\rho}\), and checks a declared local-geometry statistic, such as directional-slope agreement around \(\widehat x\). It is valid only when the upper confidence bound for \(R_V\) is at most \(\varepsilon_R\) and all declared criteria pass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate a surrogate by bounding recommendation regret, weighted ranking errors among competitive decisions, and disagreement in local geometry near the recommended solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete false optimum created by a surrogate whose minimizer reverses the true objective's minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\) be the true objective on \(X=[0,1]\), and let the fitted surrogate be \(m(x)=x^2\). Then \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}m(x)=\{0\}\), whereas \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}f(x)=\{1\}\). Consequently, optimizing the surrogate recommends \(\widehat x=0\), whose true regret equals \(f(0)-f(1)=1\). Thus numerical accuracy in solving the surrogate optimization problem does not certify quality for the simulator objective; independent simulation at the recommendation or a support-expanding design is required to detect this false optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A surrogate can be optimized exactly yet recommend the worst true decision: the displayed surrogate selects zero while the true objective is minimized at one.
knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate False Optima

children.title: Unsupported Extrapolation
children.top_down_role: Predictions or recommendations outside simulation-supported regions.

assumptions_latex: Simulator data are available only on \(S=[0,1/2]\).
The fitting rule uses only observations from \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Observations confined to \(S\) cannot distinguish whether the minimizer set is \(S\) or the singleton \(\{1\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed objectives agree on sampled support but have different global minimizer sets
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonidentifiability of an optimizer outside sampled support without structural assumptions controlling extrapolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f_0(x)=0\) for \(x\in S\) and \(f_0(x)=x-1/2\) for \(x>1/2\). Define \(f_1(x)=0\) for \(x\in S\) and \(f_1(x)=-2(x-1/2)\) for \(x>1/2\). The two objectives generate identical noiseless responses, and identical noisy-response distributions under a common additive noise law, at every sampled location in \(S\). Nevertheless, \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}f_0(x)=S\), whereas \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}f_1(x)=\{1\}\). Hence observations confined to \(S\) cannot support an optimization claim in \(X\setminus S\) unless additional shape, smoothness, or prior assumptions link sampled and unsampled regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two objectives can agree at every sampled location yet have different global minimizer sets, so extrapolated optimization requires additional structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Extrapolation

children.title: Design-Hull Boundary Risk
children.top_down_role: Reliability loss near or beyond the boundary of sampled designs.

assumptions_latex: The sampled design has convex hull \(H\subsetneq X\).
A surrogate recommendation \(\widehat x\) lies on \(\partial H\).
There exist \(d\in N_H(\widehat x)\setminus\{0\}\) and \(t>0\) such that \(\widehat x+td\in X\setminus H\), with no observations beyond the supporting face in that direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A boundary recommendation alone cannot certify descent beyond \(H\) or local optimality for the true objective on \(X\).

notation.meaning: surrogate recommendation on the hull boundary

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: one-sided design support leaves outward behavior unidentified
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided support at a design-hull face prevents validation of outward behavior and boundary optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\in N_H(\widehat x)\setminus\{0\}\) and suppose \(\widehat x+td\in X\setminus H\) for some \(t>0\). Observations confined to \(H\) provide no comparison with responses beyond the supporting face in direction \(d\). In particular, two response functions may agree at every sampled design point yet be extended outside \(H\) so that one increases and the other decreases along \(\widehat x+sd\) for sufficiently small admissible \(s>0\). Therefore a surrogate minimum on \(\partial H\) is a support warning: its predicted outward gradient and curvature are extrapolations. Certification requires sampling beyond the face, restricting optimization to a supported interior region, or imposing validated structural assumptions on the extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a design-hull boundary, data support only one side of the recommendation; outward gradients and curvature remain extrapolations unless new data or validated structure are supplied.
knowledge_statements.title: Design-Hull Boundary Risk

children.title: Noise-Model Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Failure caused by incorrect replication, dependence, or heteroskedasticity models.

assumptions_latex: The errors \(\varepsilon_r\) are mutually independent, independent of \(Z\), and satisfy \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_r)=\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Treating replications as independent makes the reported variance vanish, although \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_R)\to\tau^2>0\).

notation.meaning: common random effect shared by replications

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: variance decomposition directly establishes the misspecification failure
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete dependence misspecification showing that nominal replication precision can be arbitrarily overconfident.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because the same random effect \(Z\) enters every replication and is independent of the errors, \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_r,Y_s)=\tau^2\) for \(r\neq s\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_R)=\tau^2+\sigma^2/R\). A model that incorrectly treats the \(Y_r\) as independent assigns variance \((\tau^2+\sigma^2)/R\) to their mean. The reported variance converges to \(0\), while the true variance converges to \(\tau^2\). Consequently, increasing the nominal replicate count cannot remove the shared uncertainty, and acquisition scores, confidence intervals, or stopping rules based on the independence model become increasingly overconfident.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared dependence among nominal replications leaves irreducible variance, while an independence model reports variance approaching zero and produces increasingly overconfident optimization decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Model Misspecification

children.title: Irregular-Response Metamodel Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of smooth stationary metamodels on irregular responses.

children.title: Response-Drift Failure
children.top_down_role: Predictive degradation caused by gradual response evolution.

assumptions_latex: For each design point \(x\in\mathcal X\), observations satisfy \(Y_t(x)=m_t(x)+\varepsilon_t(x)\) with \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t(x)\mid x,t]=0\).
The metamodel is fitted as time-homogeneous using observations through time \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistency for the historical average response does not imply consistency for the current response when drift persists.

notation.meaning: Mean simulation response at design x and time t.
Time-homogeneous metamodel fitted through time n.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this formal response-drift failure criterion.
Authoritative source for nonstationary metamodel-assisted simulation optimization is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent temporal drift invalidates a metamodel trained to represent a stationary simulation response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar m_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n m_t(x)\). A response-drift failure occurs when \(\widehat m_n\) consistently estimates \(\bar m_n\), but the optimization target is the current response \(m_n\), and
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|\bar m_n(x)-m_n(x)|>0.
\]
Then even if \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|\widehat m_n(x)-\bar m_n(x)|\to0\) in probability, it need not follow that \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|\widehat m_n(x)-m_n(x)|\to0\). Consequently, a design minimizing \(\widehat m_n\) may remain separated from the minimizers of the current response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary surrogate can learn the historical average accurately yet remain persistently inaccurate for the current objective when the simulator response drifts over time.
knowledge_statements.title: Response-Drift Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematics are plausible, but no cited source supports this particular uniform response-drift criterion or its optimization consequence.

children.title: Change-Point Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Failure to represent abrupt changes between response regimes.

assumptions_latex: The true one-dimensional response has a single jump at \(\tau\): \(m(x)=a\) for \(x<\tau\) and \(m(x)=b\) for \(x\ge\tau\), where \(a\ne b\).
The fitted metamodel places the jump at \(\widehat\tau\ne\tau\) while using the correct regime levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonvanishing change-point location error produces a nonvanishing integrated squared approximation error.

notation.meaning: Change point imposed by the metamodel.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this formal change-point misspecification boundary.
A source on discontinuous or change-point surrogate models is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional single-jump model illustrating irreducible error from a misplaced change point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the fitted response by \(\widetilde m(x)=a\) for \(x<\widehat\tau\) and \(\widetilde m(x)=b\) for \(x\ge\widehat\tau\). On any interval containing both \(\tau\) and \(\widehat\tau\), the two responses disagree exactly between those locations, so
\[
\int |m(x)-\widetilde m(x)|^2\,dx=(b-a)^2|\widehat\tau-\tau|.
\]
Hence, if a sequence of fitted change points satisfies \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}|\widehat\tau_n-\tau|>0\), its integrated squared response error is bounded away from zero. Optimization decisions near the regime boundary can therefore remain incorrect despite accurate estimation of both regime levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Misplacing a response change point creates an error region whose integrated squared bias equals the squared jump size times the location error.
knowledge_statements.title: Change-Point Misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-jump calculation is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the formal misspecification boundary or its optimization interpretation.

children.title: Discontinuity Smoothing Bias
children.top_down_role: Optimization distortion caused by smoothing across response jumps.

assumptions_latex: The response has finite one-sided limits \(m(x_0-)\ne m(x_0+)\) at a discontinuity \(x_0\).
The surrogate locally applies kernel smoothing with \(K_h(u)=h^{-1}K(u/h)\), where \(K\ge0\) and \(\int_{\mathbb R}K(u)\,du=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Kernel smoothing converges to a mixture of the one-sided limits and therefore retains nonzero one-sided bias at a jump.

notation.meaning: Response function with a jump at x_0.
Kernel mass on the positive half-line.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the displayed discontinuity-smoothing limit.
A nonparametric smoothing or surrogate-model source with boundary limits is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel-smoothing limit at an interior jump discontinuity of a one-dimensional simulation response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the population smoother \(m_h(x_0)=\int_{\mathbb R}K(u)m(x_0-hu)\,du\), dominated convergence gives the limiting value
\[
\lim_{h\downarrow0}m_h(x_0)=p_+m(x_0-)+(1-p_+)m(x_0+).
\]
Thus the limit generally equals neither one-sided response. For a symmetric kernel, \(p_+=1/2\), so the limiting value is \(\{m(x_0-)+m(x_0+)\}/2\). Its bias relative to either regime has magnitude \(|m(x_0+)-m(x_0-)|/2\), showing that vanishing bandwidth alone does not remove pointwise bias at the discontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth surrogate averages the two sides of a jump, leaving persistent pointwise bias at the discontinuity even as its bandwidth vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuity Smoothing Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and finite one-sided limits alone do not justify dominated convergence for an arbitrary unbounded-support kernel; additional boundedness or domination assumptions are required.

children.title: Discrete-Event Simulation Optimization Problem
children.top_down_role: Decision problems whose performance is evaluated through event-driven stochastic dynamics.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Alternative Discrete-Event Simulation Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines simulation optimization and its finite-budget allocation formulation for noisily evaluated designs or policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a finite set of designs or policies whose performance is observed through noisy discrete-event simulation. Simulation optimization seeks \(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[F(x,W)]\). If design \(x\) receives simulation run length \(n_x\) under a global budget \(N\), then \(\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}n_x=N\). In a standard frequentist two-stage strategy, an initial sample of size \(n^0\) is collected for every design, and the resulting estimates are used to concentrate the remaining budget on the most promising designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many designs or policies evaluated by noisy discrete-event simulation, simulation optimization maximizes expected performance. A total simulation budget is divided into design-specific run lengths summing to the budget; a standard frequentist two-stage strategy first samples every design and then concentrates the remaining effort on promising designs.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a finite set of designs or policies.
Each \(x\in\mathcal X\) is evaluated noisily through discrete-event simulation.
A global simulation budget \(N\) is available, with run lengths \(n_x\) assigned to designs.
The frequentist two-stage strategy assumes sufficient budget to obtain an initial sample from every alternative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[F(x,W)]\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}n_x=N,\) with initial sampling of every design followed by budget concentration on promising designs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-design simulation optimization and selection objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers simulation-evaluated finite alternatives, including fixed-budget allocation, subset selection, and indifference-zone selection. The malformed coefficient in the extracted indifference-zone sample-size formula is not restated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a finite set of designs whose values are estimated by noisy simulation. Under a total simulation budget \(N\), choose run lengths \(n_x\) satisfying \(\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}n_x=N\). Common objectives are: (i) minimize expected opportunity cost \(\mathbb E[F(x,W)-F(x^*,W)]\), where \(x^*\in\arg\min_x\mathbb E F(x,W)\); (ii) choose a smallest possible subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal X\) with \(\Pr(x^*\in S)\ge 1-\alpha\), where \(1/|\mathcal X|<1-\alpha<1\); or (iii) select, with probability at least \(1-\alpha\), an alternative \(x\) satisfying \(\mu_x\ge\mu_{x^*}-\delta\). With \(n\) equal-variance observations per alternative and known standard deviation \(\sigma\), the stated subset rule retains \(x\) when \(\theta_x^n\ge\max_{x'\ne x}\theta_{x'}^n-h\sigma\sqrt{2/n}\), where \(h\) is the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of the corresponding standardized maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many designs evaluated by noisy simulation, simulation effort may be allocated under a fixed total budget. The objective may be expected opportunity cost, a smallest subset containing the best design with prescribed probability, or selection of a design within an indifference-zone tolerance of the best with prescribed probability. Under equal known observation variance, the subset rule retains designs whose estimated values lie within a quantile-calibrated margin of the largest estimate.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the displayed subset rule, all alternatives have }n\text{ observations with common known standard deviation }\sigma.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}n_x=N,\qquad \Pr(x^*\in S)\ge1-\alpha,\qquad \text{or}\qquad \Pr\!\left(\mu_{\widehat x}\ge\mu_{x^*}-\delta\right)\ge1-\alpha

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Event-parameter optimization selects a feasible parameter minimizing expected simulated performance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An event-parameter optimization problem is
\[
\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}J(\theta),\qquad J(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,\xi)].
\]
The parameter \(\theta\) modifies event dynamics, such as arrival or service rates, event-time distributions, thresholds, or transition probabilities, while the event-system structure and decision rule remain fixed. When constraints are simulated, feasibility is additionally specified by \(G_j(\theta)=\mathbb E[C_j(\theta,\xi)]\le0\) for each \(j\). The simulator supplies noisy observations rather than a closed-form expression for \(J\) or \(G_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose continuous, discrete, or mixed event parameters to minimize expected simulated performance, optionally subject to expected simulation constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Event-Parameter Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An event-policy optimization problem over the policy class \(\Pi\) is
\[
\eta^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta\in H}\mathbb E[C(\pi_\eta,\xi)].
\]
At each decision event, \(\pi_\eta\) maps the available event history or current state to a feasible routing, scheduling, admission, or control action. The system transition law is induced jointly by the event mechanism, the chosen action, and \(\xi\). Optimization is restricted to admissible parameters for which actions satisfy the system constraints and the displayed expectation exists; the simulator estimates the objective by policy replications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select parameters of an admissible event-driven policy to minimize its expected simulated cost over routing, scheduling, admission, or control decisions.

children.top_down_role: Configuration, capacity, and resource decisions in event-driven systems.

assumptions_latex: The feasible design set \(D\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\) encodes configuration, capacity, and resource restrictions.
For every \(d\in D\), the simulated operating measure \(Y(d,\xi)\) is integrable and the deterministic design cost \(c(d)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Event-system design optimization balances deterministic design cost against expected simulated operating performance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed discrete-continuous configuration, capacity, and resource design for event-driven systems.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An event-system design optimization problem has the form
\[
d^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in D}\{c(d)+\mathbb E[Y(d,\xi)]\}.
\]
The design vector \(d\) fixes structural attributes before simulation, including resource counts, capacities, network configuration, or equipment choices. Conditional on \(d\), the discrete-event simulator generates operating outcomes under randomness \(\xi\). Feasibility may also require \(\mathbb E[C_j(d,\xi)]\le b_j\) or sample-path constraints. Unlike event-parameter optimization, changing \(d\) may change the simulated system's structure or available resources, not merely a transition parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose system configuration, capacities, or resources to minimize design cost plus expected operating performance estimated by discrete-event simulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Event-System Design Optimization

children.title: Event Calendar Simulation Model
children.top_down_role: Explicit scheduling and chronological processing of future events.

children.title: Next-Event Representation
children.top_down_role: Simulation advanced by the next scheduled event.

assumptions_latex: At event time \(T_n\), the state \(X_n\) and a finite event calendar \(\mathcal C_n\) are available.
Each calendar entry contains a scheduled time, event type, and event data, and ties are resolved by a fixed rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeatedly removing and executing the earliest scheduled event defines the next-event representation of the simulation path.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the next-event recurrence.
A discrete-event simulation text covering event-calendar representations is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-calendar state recurrence with deterministic tie-breaking among simultaneously scheduled events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The next-event representation advances the simulation by selecting
\[
e_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{e\in\mathcal C_n}t(e),\qquad T_{n+1}=t(e_{n+1}).
\]
After removing \(e_{n+1}\) from the calendar, an event routine updates the state and calendar according to
\[
(X_{n+1},\mathcal C_{n+1})=\Phi(X_n,\mathcal C_n\setminus\{e_{n+1}\},e_{n+1},\xi_{n+1}).
\]
Between \(T_n\) and \(T_{n+1}\), no scheduled event changes the state. Iteration stops at a prescribed terminal event or horizon, and the resulting ordered event times and post-event states represent the simulated sample path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain an event calendar, execute its earliest event, update the state and calendar, and repeat until the stopping condition is reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Next-Event Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The event-calendar recurrence is a suitable next-event representation, but no inspectable citation supports its formalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Future-event-list next-event simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chronological processing algorithm for a discrete-event simulation calendar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain one future-event-list record for each event type whose clock is not halted. Each record contains its event type and scheduled event time and may additionally contain the clock's last reset time and lifetime distribution. Keep the records ordered by scheduled time. Repeatedly: (1) set the simulation time to the scheduled time of the first record; (2) execute that event, update the system state, and cancel, insert, or reschedule records while preserving their ordering; and (3) remove or reschedule the record of the event just executed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store active events in a future event list ordered by scheduled time. Advance the simulation clock to the earliest record, execute its state and scheduling effects while maintaining list order, and then remove or reschedule the event that fired.
assumptions_latex: Each nonhalted event clock has a future-event-list record containing a scheduled event time.
The future event list is maintained in chronological order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration advances to and processes the next scheduled event while preserving the chronologically ordered future event list.

children.title: Process-Interaction Representation
children.top_down_role: Entity- and process-oriented organization of event dynamics.

assumptions_latex: Each simulated entity has a process state consisting of a program location and local attributes.
Process primitives suspend an entity until an event condition, delay expiration, or resource availability is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A process-interaction model represents event dynamics through resumable entity processes whose suspensions induce an event calendar.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the process-interaction formalization.
A discrete-event simulation text comparing process interaction and event scheduling is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entity-oriented representation implemented by resumable processes and scheduled activation events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A process-interaction representation specifies one resumable process \(P_i\) for each entity \(i\). The complete simulation state is \((R,(Z_i)_i,\mathcal C)\), where \(R\) records shared resources and queues. When active, \(P_i\) applies state changes until it executes a suspension primitive such as a delay, wait, seize, or request. A delay of duration \(D_i\ge0\) schedules a resumption at \(T+D_i\); a conditional wait resumes when an event makes its predicate true. Executing resumptions in increasing scheduled-time order yields the same event-time state trajectory as the event calendar generated by these process primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model each entity as a resumable process; delays and resource waits schedule activations whose chronological execution generates the event trajectory.

children.title: Markov Jump-Process Simulation

knowledge_statements.title: Markov Jump-Process Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct event-by-event simulation of a nonexplosive time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(T_0=0\) and \(X_0=i_0\). Given \(X_n=i\), if \(\lambda_i=0\), treat \(i\) as absorbing and schedule no departure. If \(\lambda_i>0\), independently sample a holding time \(H_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i)\) and a destination \(X_{n+1}=j\ne i\) with
\[
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)=\frac{q_{ij}}{\lambda_i}.
\]
Set \(T_{n+1}=T_n+H_n\) and keep the continuous-time state equal to \(i\) on \([T_n,T_{n+1})\). Repeating these steps until the terminal time or event condition generates the nonexplosive Markov jump process with generator \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonabsorbing state, sample an exponential holding time and choose the next state in proportion to its transition rate; a zero-rate state is absorbing.
assumptions_latex: The state space \(S\) is finite or countable, with transition rates \(q_{ij}\ge0\) for \(j\ne i\).
For each \(i\in S\), \(\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}<\infty\), and the generator diagonal is \(q_{ii}=-\lambda_i\).
The resulting minimal jump process is nonexplosive on the simulated time horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exponential holding times and rate-normalized destination probabilities simulate the nonexplosive Markov jump process with generator \(Q\), with zero-rate states treated as absorbing.

notation.meaning: Total departure rate from state i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential Representation and Equicontinuity Criterion for a Markov Semigroup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only the explicit representation and equivalence are retained; referenced properties (2.27)–(2.29) are absent from the supplied item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(\cdot)\) be a continuous Markovian semigroup with intensity matrix \(Q=(q_{ij})\). Equicontinuity is equivalent to \[\inf_i q_{ii}>-\infty.\] Whenever these equivalent conditions hold, \[P(t)=\exp(tQ)\qquad(t\ge0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous Markov transition semigroup is equicontinuous exactly when its diagonal intensities are uniformly bounded below. Under this condition, the semigroup is the exponential of its intensity matrix.

Q\text{ is the intensity matrix of }P(\cdot)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(\cdot)\text{ is equicontinuous}\iff\inf_i q_{ii}>-\infty,\qquad P(t)=e^{tQ}\quad(t\ge0)\text{ under these conditions}

children.title: Semi-Markov Simulation
children.top_down_role: Event simulation with general state sojourn times.

assumptions_latex: The embedded state space \(S\) is finite or countable.
For every current state \(i\), \(Q_{ij}(t)=\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j,H_n\le t\mid X_n=i)\) is a proper semi-Markov kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sampling each next-state and holding-time pair from the semi-Markov kernel generates the associated semi-Markov process.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-by-event simulation from a semi-Markov kernel with generally nonexponential sojourns.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Semi-Markov processes p. 112

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(T_0=0\) and \(X_0=i_0\). At jump \(n\), conditional on \(X_n=i\), sample the pair \((X_{n+1},H_n)\) according to the kernel \(Q_{ij}\), so that
\[
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j,H_n\le t\mid X_n=i)=Q_{ij}(t).
\]
Set \(T_{n+1}=T_n+H_n\) and hold the continuous-time state at \(i\) on \([T_n,T_{n+1})\). Repeat until the stopping rule holds. Unlike a Markov jump process, the conditional distribution of \(H_n\) need not be exponential and may depend on both \(i\) and \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each jump, sample the next state and a generally nonexponential sojourn time from the semi-Markov kernel, then advance the clock.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semi-Markov process representation and stationary performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a semi-Markov process through an embedded Markov chain of sojourn-state pairs and states its stationary performance formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((R,r)\) be a metric space and let \(M(k)=[T(k),Z(k)]\), \(k\ge 1\), be a Markov chain on \(\mathbb{R}_+\times R\), where \(T(k)\) is the sojourn time at state \(Z(k)\), and set \(T(0)=0\). The associated semi-Markov process satisfies \[S(t)=Z(n)\quad\text{if}\quad \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}T(i)\le t<\sum_{i=0}^{n}T(i).\] If \(M\) is ergodic and \([T,Z]\) is distributed according to its stationary distribution, then for a real performance function \(H:R\to\mathbb{R}\), provided the expectations are finite and \(\mathbb{E}[T]>0\), \[\mathbb{E}[H(S(\cdot))]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[T H(Z)]}{\mathbb{E}[T]}.\] In general, this is not equal to \(\mathbb{E}[H(Z)]\); it is a quotient of expectations and is not linear in the stationary law of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semi-Markov process occupies state Z(k) for the generally distributed sojourn time T(k). Under ergodicity, its stationary performance for H is the sojourn-time-weighted expectation of H(Z), divided by the mean sojourn time. This generally differs from the stationary expectation over the embedded states.
assumptions_latex: M(k)=[T(k),Z(k)]\text{ is a Markov chain on }\mathbb{R}_+\times R
M\text{ is ergodic for the stationary-performance formula}
H:R\to\mathbb{R}\text{ has finite required expectations and }\mathbb{E}[T]>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(t)=Z(n)\text{ if }\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}T(i)\le t<\sum_{i=0}^{n}T(i),\qquad \mathbb{E}[H(S(\cdot))]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[T H(Z)]}{\mathbb{E}[T]}.

assumptions_latex: At state \(x\), a finite enabled-event set \(E(x)\) is maintained.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selecting the smallest residual lifetime and updating competing clocks simulates the generalized semi-Markov process.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.3 Simulation of Generalized Semi-Markov processes p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize state \(X_0\), time \(T_0=0\), and one sampled residual lifetime \(r_e\) for every \(e\in E(X_0)\). At step \(n\), choose \(e^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{e\in E(X_n)}r_e\), set \(\delta_n=r_{e^*}\), and update \(T_{n+1}=T_n+\delta_n\) and \(X_{n+1}=\Phi(X_n,e^*,\xi_{n+1})\). Subtract \(\delta_n\) from clocks that remain enabled, discard disabled clocks, and sample lifetimes for newly enabled events. Repeat until the prescribed stopping condition holds. The general lifetime laws permit nonexponential competing clocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain general residual event clocks, execute the earliest expiration, update the state and enabled events, and resample newly enabled clocks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized semi-Markov process
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-oriented definition and augmented Markov representation of a GSMP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Z\) be finite or countably infinite and let \(E_1,\ldots,E_q\) be finitely many event types. A generalized semi-Markov process is a piecewise-constant discrete-event process that has the Markov property after its discrete state is augmented by finitely many clock-time variables. At jump epochs its augmented state can be represented as \(M(n)=[T(n),Z(n),V^{(1)}(n),\ldots,V^{(q)}(n)]\in\mathbb R_+\times\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R_+^q\). If an event of type \(E_i\) occurs, the state changes according to \(N^{(i)}\); event types in the associated canceling set are canceled, those in the scheduling set are reset with delays having distributions \(G^{(j)}\), and all other event clocks remain unchanged. Simultaneous events are handled in increasing event-type order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized semi-Markov process is a piecewise-constant discrete-event process whose state becomes Markov after adding finitely many event-clock times. An event changes the discrete state and may cancel, reset, or leave other clocks unchanged; simultaneous events are processed by event-type order.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal Z\) is finite or countably infinite.
There are finitely many event types with transition maps \(N^{(i)}:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\), disjoint canceling and scheduling sets, and lifetime distributions \(G^{(j)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented sequence \((M(n))_{n\ge1}\) is Markov on \(\mathbb R_+\times\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R_+^q\), although the unaugmented discrete-state process need not be Markov.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual lifetimes and competing-clock hazards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-lifetime and competing-clock identities used in GSMP simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a nonnegative lifetime \(V\) have distribution function \(G\) and integrated hazard \(\Lambda\). For \(s\ge0\) with \(G(s)<1\), the residual lifetime \(V-s\mid V>s\) has distribution function \(G_s(u)=\frac{G(s+u)-G(s)}{1-G(s)}\) and integrated hazard \(\Lambda_s(u)=\Lambda(s+u)-\Lambda(s)\) for \(u\ge0\). If \(V^{(1)},\ldots,V^{(q)}\) are independent nonnegative lifetimes with distribution functions \(G^{(i)}\) and integrated hazards \(\Lambda^{(i)}\), then \(W=\min_iV^{(i)}\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(W\le u)=1-\prod_{i=1}^q(1-G^{(i)}(u))\) and \(\Lambda_W(u)=\sum_{i=1}^q\Lambda^{(i)}(u)\). If hazard functions \(\lambda^{(i)}\) exist, then wherever \(\sum_j\lambda^{(j)}(v)>0\), \(\mathbb P(V^{(i)}=W\mid W=v)=\frac{\lambda^{(i)}(v)}{\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda^{(j)}(v)}\), and \(\mathbb P(V^{(i)}=W)=\int_0^\infty\lambda^{(i)}(u)\exp\{-\sum_{j=1}^q\Lambda^{(j)}(u)\}\,du\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditioning a lifetime on survival through time s subtracts the integrated hazard accumulated through s. For independent competing lifetimes, the minimum has product survival and summed integrated hazard. When hazard functions exist, each clock's instantaneous share of the total hazard determines its probability of being the next clock to ring.
assumptions_latex: The clock-selection identities require the hazard functions \(\lambda^{(i)}\) to exist; the conditional ratio is asserted where \(\sum_j\lambda^{(j)}(v)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Lambda_s(u)=\Lambda(s+u)-\Lambda(s),\qquad \Lambda_{\min_iV^{(i)}}(u)=\sum_{i=1}^q\Lambda^{(i)}(u),\qquad \mathbb P(V^{(i)}=W\mid W=v)=\frac{\lambda^{(i)}(v)}{\sum_j\lambda^{(j)}(v)}.
