children.title: Terminating Event Simulation
children.top_down_role: Event-system replications with natural terminal conditions.

assumptions_latex: For each decision \(x\), the event system has a terminal stopping time \(\tau_x\) satisfying \(\mathbb P(\tau_x<\infty)=1\).
The replication performance \(H_x=h((X_x(t))_{0\le t\le\tau_x})\) is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Independent complete paths through the natural terminal event provide unbiased replication observations of the terminating-system objective.

notation.meaning: Natural terminal stopping time under decision x.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the terminating-replication definition.
A discrete-event output-analysis source distinguishing terminating and steady-state regimes is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon or naturally terminating discrete-event replications with complete-path performance measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A terminating event simulation under decision \(x\) starts from a specified initial distribution and runs until the natural terminal time \(\tau_x\), such as completion of all jobs or occurrence of a designated event. One replication returns
\[
H_x=h((X_x(t))_{0\le t\le\tau_x}),
\]
and the optimization objective is \(J(x)=\mathbb E[H_x]\). With independent simulation inputs, complete replications \(H_x^{(1)},\ldots,H_x^{(n)}\) are identically distributed and their average \(\widehat J_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^nH_x^{(r)}\) is unbiased for \(J(x)\). No artificial warm-up deletion or steady-state horizon is part of this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminating simulation runs each independent replication from its specified initial state to a natural terminal event and evaluates the complete path.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminating Event Simulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and unbiased-replication statement are standard and fit the terminating-run leaf, but no output-analysis source is supplied to support the distinction from steady-state simulation.

children.title: Steady-State Event Simulation
children.top_down_role: Persistent event systems evaluated through long-run behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Steady-State Event Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Long-run performance estimation for a persistent discrete-event system at a fixed design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For design \(x\), let \(Z_x(t)\) be a positive Harris recurrent event-system state process with invariant distribution \(\pi_x\), and let \(r_x\) be integrable under \(\pi_x\). Its steady-state response and time-average estimator are
\[J(x)=\int r_x(z)\,\pi_x(dz),\qquad \widehat J_T(x)=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T r_x(Z_x(t))\,dt.\]
A simulation is steady-state when its target is \(J(x)\), rather than a finite-horizon response. Under the ergodic theorem, \(\widehat J_T(x)\to J(x)\) almost surely as \(T\to\infty\), for every admissible initial distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A steady-state simulation estimates invariant long-run performance by a time average from a persistent recurrent event system.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_x\) is positive Harris recurrent with invariant law \(\pi_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat J_T(x)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}J(x)\) as \(T\to\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Event Regenerative Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ratio estimation from independent regeneration cycles of a recurrent event system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a design \(x\) and regeneration times \(0=T_0<T_1<\cdots\). For cycle \(k\), define its length and accumulated reward by
\[\tau_k=T_k-T_{k-1},\qquad R_k=\int_{T_{k-1}}^{T_k}r_x(Z_x(t))\,dt.\]
If \((R_k,\tau_k)\) are identically distributed independent cycles with \(0<\mathbb E[\tau_1]<\infty\) and \(\mathbb E[|R_1|]<\infty\), then the steady-state response and its regenerative estimator are
\[J(x)=\frac{\mathbb E[R_1]}{\mathbb E[\tau_1]},\qquad \widehat J_n(x)=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^nR_k}{\sum_{k=1}^n\tau_k},\]
and \(\widehat J_n(x)\to J(x)\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Long-run performance equals expected reward per regenerative cycle divided by expected cycle length and is estimated by the corresponding sample ratio.
assumptions_latex: \((R_k,\tau_k)_{k\ge1}\) are identically distributed independent regenerative cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J(x)=\mathbb E[R_1]/\mathbb E[\tau_1]\) and \(\widehat J_n(x)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}J(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Event Infinitesimal Perturbation Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise derivative propagation through differentiable event-state recursions with almost-surely stable event ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(X_0(\theta)\), primitive inputs \((U_k)\), event recursions \(X_{k+1}(\theta)=F_k(X_k(\theta),\theta,U_k)\), and sample cost \(L(\theta)=G(X_0(\theta),\ldots,X_K(\theta),\theta)\), initialize \(D_0=dX_0/d\theta\) and update
\[D_{k+1}=\partial_xF_k(X_k,	heta,U_k)D_k+\partial_\theta F_k(X_k,	heta,U_k).\]
Return
\[\widehat g=\partial_\theta G+\sum_{k=0}^K\partial_{x_k}G\,D_k.\]
If event ties and ordering changes occur with probability zero and differentiation may pass through expectation, then \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=d\mathbb E[L(\theta)]/d\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IPA differentiates each event update along one simulated path and combines the propagated state derivatives into a gradient estimate.
assumptions_latex: The realized event recursion and cost are differentiable in a neighborhood of \(\theta\) almost surely.
Event ties or parameter-induced event-order changes have probability zero.
A dominating integrable derivative permits interchange of derivative and expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E[L(\theta)]\).

notation.meaning: pathwise derivative of the state after event k

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Event Weak Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed-measure differentiation of parameterized event-transition laws without pathwise differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q_\theta(z,\cdot)\) be a parameterized event-transition probability kernel. A weak-derivative representation at \(\theta\) is a scalar \(c_\theta(z)\ge0\) and probability kernels \(Q_\theta^+(z,\cdot)\), \(Q_\theta^-(z,\cdot)\) such that
\[\partial_\theta Q_\theta(z,\cdot)=c_\theta(z)\bigl(Q_\theta^+(z,\cdot)-Q_\theta^-(z,\cdot)\bigr)\]
as finite signed measures. Consequently, for every bounded measurable \(h\),
\[\partial_\theta\int h(y)Q_\theta(z,dy)=c_\theta(z)\left(\mathbb E[h(Y^+)]-\mathbb E[h(Y^-)]\right),\]
where \(Y^+\sim Q_\theta^+(z,\cdot)\) and \(Y^-\sim Q_\theta^-(z,\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transition-law derivative is represented as a scaled difference of two probability laws, enabling derivative estimation from positive and negative event transitions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_\theta(z,\cdot)\) is differentiable as a finite signed measure.

children.title: Discrete-Event Process Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Process-level sensitivity representations for event-system trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Event Process Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak differentiation of the complete event-process law on path space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_\theta\) be the law on a measurable path space \(\mathcal D\) of a discrete-event process over a fixed horizon. A process-derivative representation at \(\theta\) is
\[\dot P_\theta=c_\theta(P_\theta^+-P_\theta^-),\]
where \(\dot P_\theta\) is the signed-measure derivative of \(P_\theta\), \(c_\theta\ge0\), and \(P_\theta^+,P_\theta^-\) are probability laws on \(\mathcal D\). Hence, for every bounded measurable path functional \(H\),
\[\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[H]=c_\theta\left(\mathbb E_{P_\theta^+}[H]-\mathbb E_{P_\theta^-}[H]\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative of an entire event-process law is a scaled difference of two path laws, so path-functional sensitivities become expectation differences.
assumptions_latex: \(P_\theta\) is differentiable as a finite signed measure on \(\mathcal D\).
\(H:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\) is bounded and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[H]=c_\theta(\mathbb E_{P_\theta^+}[H]-\mathbb E_{P_\theta^-}[H])\).

notation.meaning: law of the discrete-event process path
signed-measure derivative of the path law

children.title: Coupled-Path Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity information obtained through coupled event-system sample paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-Path Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity estimation by coupling nearby designs on a shared probability space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(\theta,U)\) and \(L(\theta+h,U_h)\) be event-system outputs coupled on one probability space, and define
\[D_h=\frac{L(\theta+h,U_h)-L(\theta,U)}{h}.\]
If the coupling preserves the intended primitive randomness, \(D_h\to D\) in \(L^1\), and differentiation may pass through expectation, then
\[\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E[L(\theta,U)]=\mathbb E[D].\]
If convergence holds in \(L^2\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(D_h)\to\operatorname{Var}(D)\); effective coupling avoids the variance growth that can occur when the two outputs are generated independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearby event-system designs are simulated on coupled paths; convergence of their difference quotient supplies a valid sensitivity and can control variance.
assumptions_latex: Both outputs are defined on a common probability space with correctly coupled primitive inputs.
Differentiation and expectation are interchangeable at \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E[L(\theta,U)]=\mathbb E[D]\).

children.title: Common-Random-Stream Event Coupling
children.top_down_role: Cross-design event coupling preserving intended random-input alignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Random-Stream Event Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stream-aligned paired simulation for comparing two event-system designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given designs \(x,y\), replication count \(m\), and a semantic stream assignment for primitive input classes, generate for each replication \(i\) one collection \(U_i=(U_{i,s,k})\). Run both event systems using the same \(U_{i,s,k}\) whenever they request the \(k\)-th variate from class \(s\), irrespective of differences in event ordering. Record outputs \(L(x,U_i)\) and \(L(y,U_i)\), and return
\[\widehat\Delta_m=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(L(x,U_i)-L(y,U_i)\bigr).\]
With independent replications and integrable outputs, \(\widehat\Delta_m\) is unbiased for \(\mathbb E[L(x,U)-L(y,U)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two designs use identically indexed random-input streams by input class, producing a paired unbiased estimator of their performance difference.
assumptions_latex: Stream assignment is based on primitive input class and within-class index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat\Delta_m]=\mathbb E[L(x,U)]-\mathbb E[L(y,U)]\).

notation.meaning: k-th random variate from semantic stream s in replication i
paired estimator of the response difference

children.title: Metamodels for Discrete-Event Systems
children.top_down_role: Surrogate representations specialized to event-driven system response.

children.title: Local Discrete-Event Response Surfaces
children.top_down_role: Local approximations supporting directional or region-based search.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Discrete-Event Response Surfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted polynomial approximation of a simulated mean response near a current design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_c\in\mathbb R^d\) be a center, \(u=x-x_c\), and let \((x_i,Y_i,w_i)\) be simulation observations with \(w_i>0\) concentrated near \(x_c\). A local quadratic response surface is
\[m_c(x)=\beta_0+\beta^\top u+\tfrac12u^\top Bu,\]
where \(B=B^\top\) and
\[(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat\beta,\widehat B)\in\arg\min\sum_iw_i\bigl(Y_i-m_c(x_i)\bigr)^2.\]
The fitted surface supplies the local direction \(-\widehat\beta\) or a trial point minimizing \(m_c\) over a prescribed neighborhood of \(x_c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted quadratic model is fitted near the current design and used to select a local search direction or a trial point within the prescribed neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\) lie in a prescribed neighborhood of \(x_c\).
The weighted polynomial design matrix has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_c\) is the weighted least-squares local quadratic approximation used for neighborhood search.

notation.meaning: local fitting weight for observation i

children.title: Global Discrete-Event Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Global approximations spanning broad event-system design spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Discrete-Event Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single fitted predictor covering the full prescribed design domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a prescribed event-system design domain, let \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x)]\), and let
\[\mathcal S=\{(x_i,Y_{ij}):i=1,\ldots,n,\ j=1,\ldots,m_i\}\]
be simulation data with design sites spanning \(D\). Given a model class \(\mathcal M\), a loss \(\ell:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\), a regularizer \(\mathcal R:\mathcal M\to[0,\infty]\), and \(\lambda\ge0\), a global metamodel is a fitted predictor \(\widehat f_D:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[\widehat f_D\in\arg\min_{g\in\mathcal M}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}\ell(Y_{ij},g(x_i))+\lambda\mathcal R(g)\right\}.\]
It induces the surrogate decision
\[\widehat x\in\arg\min_{x\in D}\widehat f_D(x).\]
Unlike a local response surface, its declared prediction and optimization domain is all of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global metamodel fits one possibly regularized predictor to simulation observations across the declared design domain and optimizes that predictor over the entire domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the declared design and prediction domain.
The design sites \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) span the portion of \(D\) where global prediction is required.
The displayed fitting problem has at least one minimizer in \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x\in\arg\min_{x\in D}\widehat f_D(x)\) is the metamodel-based decision over the global domain.

children.title: Heteroskedastic Event-System Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Metamodels representing decision-dependent simulation variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Heteroskedastic Event-System Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-response modeling with simulation noise whose variance depends on the design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For design sites \(x_i\) and replications \(j=1,\ldots,m_i\), a heteroskedastic event-system metamodel uses
\[Y_{ij}=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_{ij},\qquad \mathbb E[\varepsilon_{ij}\mid x_i]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{ij}\mid x_i)=\tau^2(x_i).\]
Thus the replication mean satisfies
\[\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_i\mid x_i)=\frac{\tau^2(x_i)}{m_i}.\]
The fitted model estimates or otherwise represents both the mean surface \(f\) and the nonconstant variance surface \(\tau^2\); prediction uncertainty and replication allocation must use the site-specific noise variance rather than a common nugget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metamodel represents both mean performance and design-dependent simulation variance, accounting for replication-specific precision at each design site.
assumptions_latex: Replications are conditionally independent at each design site.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_i\mid x_i)=\tau^2(x_i)/m_i\), so observation precision is design dependent.

notation.meaning: replication count at design site i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Queueing process and basic FIFO single-server system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines queueing processes and identifies elementary FIFO, M/M/1, and network specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A queueing process is a discrete-event process modeling customers served successively by one or more service units. In a single-server, single-queue FIFO system, customers are served in arrival order, and service of the next customer begins when the preceding service finishes. An $M/M/1$ system has a Poisson arrival stream, exponentially distributed service times, and one server. A queueing network is a graph whose nodes are single-server systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A queueing process is a discrete-event model of customers served by one or more service units. A basic single-server FIFO queue serves customers in arrival order without an intervening delay between consecutive services. M/M/1 queues and networks of single-server queues are standard specializations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The described FIFO, }M/M/1\text{, and network systems are queueing-process specializations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Busy-period size generating-function identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates the busy-period customer-count distribution to positivity probabilities of the associated partial sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $N$ be the busy-period customer count, let $p_n=\mathbb P\{N=n\}$, and define \[\widehat p(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_i u^i.\] For the associated random-walk partial sums $S_n$, \[\log\!\left(\frac{1}{1-\widehat p(u)}\right)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{u^n}{n}\,\mathbb P\{S_n>0\},\] and \[\log\mathbb E[N]=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n\,\mathbb P\{S_n>0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the number N of customers in a busy period, the logarithm of the reciprocal of one minus its probability generating function equals a weighted series of probabilities that the associated random walk is positive. Evaluating the corresponding identity at one gives a series expression for the logarithm of the expected busy-period size.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Little's queueing identities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a contraction factor and distance for the GI/GI/1 Lindley waiting-time process.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: GI/GI/1 Lindley recursion and random-walk representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the finite-horizon representation unconditionally and conditions the stationary representation on existence of a proper stationary waiting time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a $GI/GI/1$ queue, the interarrival times $(\nu_i)$ are i.i.d., the service times $(\xi_i)$ are i.i.d., and there is one server. Let $Z_i=\xi_i-\nu_i$, suppose $(Z_i)$ is i.i.d., set $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i$, and take $W_1=0$. Then \[W_{n+1}=\max\{0,W_n+Z_n\},\qquad W_{n+1}\overset d=\max\{0,S_1,\ldots,S_n\}.\] Consequently, $(W_n)$ is stochastically nondecreasing. If $\sup_{n\ge1}S_n$ is finite almost surely so that a proper stationary waiting-time law exists, then \[W_n\Rightarrow W,\qquad W\overset d=\max\{0,S_1,S_2,\ldots\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A GI/GI/1 queue has iid interarrival times, iid service times, and one server. Its waiting times obey Lindley's recursion, and the waiting time of customer n+1 has the distribution of the running maximum of the associated random walk through time n. A proper stationary running-maximum law follows only when that supremum is finite almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{n+1}=\max\{0,W_n+Z_n\},\quad W_{n+1}\overset d=\max\{0,S_1,\ldots,S_n\};\quad W\overset d=\max\{0,S_1,S_2,\ldots\}\text{ when a proper stationary law exists.}

children.title: Single-Period Staffing

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Period Staffing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer staffing optimization with one fixed capacity level over an operating interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_+^q\) be staffing levels held fixed throughout one operating interval, let \(C(n)\) be staffing cost, and let \(G_r(n,U)\) be simulated service measures under random input \(U\). A constrained single-period staffing model is
\[\min_{n\in\mathcal N} C(n)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \mathbb E[G_r(n,U)]\le b_r,\quad r=1,\ldots,R,\]
where \(\mathcal N\subseteq\mathbb Z_+^q\) contains operationally admissible staffing vectors. Simulation supplies estimators of the expectations because the queueing dynamics need not yield closed-form service measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One integer staffing vector is used throughout the interval and optimized against simulated expected service constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal N\subseteq\mathbb Z_+^q\) is the admissible set of fixed staffing vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n^*\in\arg\min\{C(n):n\in\mathcal N,\ \mathbb E[G_r(n,U)]\le b_r\ \forall r\}\).

notation.meaning: staffing vector fixed over the operating interval

children.title: Time-Varying Staffing

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Varying Staffing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Period-indexed integer staffing schedules for nonstationary arrivals and service demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Partition the planning horizon into periods \(p=1,
\ldots,P\), and let \(n_p\in\mathbb Z_+^q\) be staffing during period \(p\). For admissible schedules \(n=(n_1,\ldots,n_P)\in\mathcal N\), switching costs \(K_p\), and simulated time-dependent service measures \(G_r(n,U)\), a time-varying staffing model is
\[\min_{n\in\mathcal N}\left\{\sum_{p=1}^P C_p(n_p)+\sum_{p=2}^P K_p(n_{p-1},n_p)\right\}\]
subject to
\[\mathbb E[G_r(n,U)]\le b_r,
\qquad r=1,\ldots,R.\]
The simulation propagates congestion across period boundaries, so each constraint may depend on the entire schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A period-indexed integer staff schedule is optimized under nonstationary simulated demand, including service constraints and optional costs for changing staffing levels.
assumptions_latex: Demand and service primitives may vary by period and are represented by \(U\).
\(\mathcal N\) encodes feasible schedules and interperiod staffing rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n^*\) minimizes total staffing and switching cost subject to all simulated expected-service constraints.

notation.meaning: cost of changing staffing between adjacent periods
simulated service measure depending on the full schedule

children.title: Skill-Based Staffing
children.top_down_role: Staffing with heterogeneous skills and routing.

knowledge_statements.title: Skill-Based Staffing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon staffing with heterogeneous server skills and simulation-evaluated service performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let customer classes be \(i\in I\), skill groups be \(k\in K\), and \(A_{ik}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether group \(k\) can serve class \(i\). A skill-based staffing design is represented by
\[\min_{y\in\mathbb Z_+^{K},\,\theta\in\Theta(y)} c^\top y+\mathbb E[L(y,\theta;\xi)]\]
subject to \(g_j(y,\theta)=\mathbb E[G_j(y,\theta;\xi)]\le b_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Here \(y_k\) is the number of group-\(k\) servers, \(\theta\) specifies admissible routing among compatible class-group pairs, and a discrete-event simulation driven by \(\xi\) estimates congestion loss and service constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose integer numbers of differently skilled servers and compatible routing parameters to minimize staffing plus expected congestion cost while satisfying simulation-estimated service requirements.
assumptions_latex: The simulated losses and constraint responses are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y,\theta)\) jointly determines heterogeneous staffing, compatible routing, and simulated service performance.

notation.meaning: number of servers in skill group k

children.title: Queueing Capacity Simulation Model

children.title: Server-Capacity Design
children.top_down_role: Selection of parallel or pooled service capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Server-Capacity Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer selection of pooled parallel-server capacity using simulation-based congestion measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For candidate capacities \(s\in S\subseteq\mathbb Z_+\), let \(C(s)\) be capacity cost and let \(H(s;\xi)\) be an integrable performance response from a finite-horizon or steady-state queue simulation. One server-capacity design formulation is
\[\min_{s\in S} C(s)+\mathbb E[H(s;\xi)].\]
Alternatively, given integrable simulated service measures \(H_j(s;\xi)\), thresholds \(b_j\), and an index set \(J\), a constrained formulation is
\[\min_{s\in S}C(s)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathbb E[H_j(s;\xi)]\le b_j\quad\text{for every }j\in J.\]
The simulation must implement the arrival, service, pooling, abandonment, and queue-discipline assumptions associated with each evaluated capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select an integer number of parallel or pooled servers using either a capacity-plus-congestion objective or capacity-cost minimization subject to simulation-evaluated service constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty finite set of admissible capacities.
Each simulated performance response used in the objective or constraints is integrable.
All compared designs use the same stated queueing conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimizer of the selected formulation is a least-objective admissible server capacity under that formulation's simulated performance criterion and constraints.

notation.meaning: number of parallel or pooled servers
simulated service measure indexed by j
finite index set of service constraints

children.title: Queueing-Network Capacity Design
children.top_down_role: Allocation of capacity across interconnected service stations.

knowledge_statements.title: Queueing-Network Capacity Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer capacity allocation across stations of an interconnected queueing network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be the stations of a queueing network and \(s_v\in S_v\subseteq\mathbb Z_+\) its capacity at station \(v\). With routing and service rules fixed, a simulation-based network design is
\[\min_{s\in\prod_{v\in V}S_v}\sum_{v\in V}c_v(s_v)+\mathbb E[H(s;\xi)]\]
subject, when required, to \(\mathbb E[G_j(s;\xi)]\le b_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). The discrete-event simulator propagates jobs between stations and measures networkwide delay, throughput, loss, or station congestion, thereby retaining interactions that cannot be assessed station by station.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate integer capacity among connected service stations to minimize total capacity and simulated network congestion costs while meeting networkwide requirements.
assumptions_latex: Routing, service, and buffer rules define a well-posed simulation for each feasible \(s\).
All objective and constraint responses are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal vector \(s^*\) allocates capacity jointly across stations according to simulated networkwide performance.

notation.meaning: simulated response for service constraint j

children.title: Capacity-Reliability Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Service reliability and congestion risk in capacity selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Reliability Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-risk frontier for simulation-based queueing capacity selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible capacity design \(s\in S\), let \(C(s)\) be capacity cost and let \(R(s)=\mathbb P\{Z(s;\xi)>z_{\max}\}\) be the probability of violating a congestion threshold. The capacity-reliability tradeoff is represented by the attainable set
\[\mathcal A=\{(C(s),R(s)):s\in S\}\]
and its nondominated frontier. An equivalent reliability-constrained scalarization is
\[\min_{s\in S}C(s)\quad\text{subject to}\quad R(s)\le\varepsilon.\]
Discrete-event replications estimate \(R(s)\); the probability convention, horizon, initial condition, and congestion statistic must remain fixed across designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare capacity designs by cost and simulated probability of unacceptable congestion; efficient designs form the nondominated cost-risk frontier.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty set of feasible capacity designs.
\(Z(s;\xi)\) and the violation threshold \(z_{\max}\) are consistently defined for all \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reliability-constrained solution has minimum capacity cost among designs whose congestion-violation probability does not exceed \(\varepsilon\).

children.title: Queue-Control Parameter Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization of routing, admission, service, and scheduling parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Queue-Control Parameter Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric optimization of queue routing, admission, service, or scheduling rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) parameterize an admissible queue-control policy \(\pi_\theta\), including routing probabilities, admission thresholds, service priorities, or scheduling weights. For simulation input \(\xi\), let \(L(\theta;\xi)\) be the resulting finite-horizon loss or regenerative-cycle cost. Queue-control parameter optimization is
\[\min_{\theta\in\Theta}J(\theta),\qquad J(\theta)=\mathbb E[L(\theta;\xi)],\]
possibly subject to \(\mathbb E[G_j(\theta;\xi)]\le b_j\). Evaluation of every candidate must apply \(\pi_\theta\) causally, using only information available at each decision epoch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize parameters of causal routing, admission, service, or scheduling policies using expected costs and constraints evaluated by queue simulation.
assumptions_latex: The policy \(\pi_\theta\) is nonanticipative for each \(\theta\in\Theta\).
The simulated objective and constraint responses are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any minimizer \(\theta^*\) defines an admissible parameterized queue-control policy with least expected simulated loss among feasible candidates.

notation.meaning: causal policy induced by the parameters

knowledge_statements.title: Inventory Event Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-calendar evaluation of a parameterized inventory replenishment policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a policy parameter \(\theta\), initial inventory position, horizon \(T\), and random stream \(\xi\). Initialize an event calendar with the first demand and any outstanding replenishments. Repeatedly remove the earliest event at time \(t\le T\), update on-hand stock, backorders or lost sales, outstanding orders, and accumulated holding, shortage, and ordering costs; then schedule induced demand or delivery events. At each review epoch apply the policy \(a_t=\pi_\theta(S_{t^-})\). Stop after processing events through \(T\), and output the replication response \(L_T(\theta;\xi)\) and any service statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulate chronologically ordered demand, review, ordering, and delivery events under an inventory policy, returning cost and service responses for optimization.
assumptions_latex: The event-time distributions and tie-breaking rule are specified.
\(\pi_\theta\) maps each pre-event inventory state to an admissible order action.
Only finitely many events occur almost surely before \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(L_T(\theta;\xi)\) is the sample-path performance of policy \(\pi_\theta\) over horizon \(T\).

notation.meaning: inventory state immediately before an event

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Horizon Lost-Sales Inventory Model Assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Application-model conditions for simulating or optimizing a capacitated finite-horizon inventory system with discrete stochastic demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an inventory system over a deterministic known horizon of $T$ stages with known initial inventory $x_1$. Demand in each period is a discrete random variable with known distribution, and unmet demand is lost permanently because backordering is prohibited. An order placed at the beginning of a stage arrives at the end of that stage, when demand is also realized. Inventory is subject to the storage limit $M$, so orders that would cause inventory to exceed $M$ are inadmissible. The unit holding cost $h$, fixed ordering cost $A$, and unit lost-sales cost $p$ are known with certainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model has a known finite horizon and initial inventory, discrete demand with known distribution, no backordering, end-of-stage order arrival and demand realization, a storage capacity, and known holding, ordering, and lost-sales costs.
assumptions_latex: \text{Demand in each period is discrete with known distribution}
\text{Unmet demand is lost permanently and backordering is prohibited}
\text{Orders placed at the start of a stage arrive at its end, when demand is realized}
\text{Orders that would cause inventory to exceed }M\text{ are inadmissible}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These assumptions specify a capacitated finite-horizon lost-sales inventory event model.}

knowledge_statements.title: Fleet Simulation Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simulation-based fleet sizing, assignment, repositioning, and dispatch optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in X\) specify fleet size and composition, and let \(\theta\in\Theta(x)\) parameterize assignment, dispatch, or repositioning rules. For travel requests, service times, disruptions, and travel times represented by \(\xi\), define a discrete-event response \(L_T(x,\theta;\xi)\). Fleet simulation optimization is
\[\min_{x\in X,\,\theta\in\Theta(x)} C(x)+\mathbb E[L_T(x,\theta;\xi)]\]
subject to any simulated service constraints \(\mathbb E[G_j(x,\theta;\xi)]\le b_j\). Vehicle availability, location, load, and trip status are updated at each request, dispatch, departure, arrival, and completion event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose fleet composition and operating-rule parameters by simulating requests, assignments, trips, and vehicle availability, balancing ownership cost with service performance.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty set of admissible fleet designs.
Each operating rule in \(\Theta(x)\) assigns only available compatible vehicles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal pair \((x^*,\theta^*)\) minimizes fleet and expected simulated operating loss while satisfying the stated service constraints.

children.title: Event-Order Instability
children.top_down_role: Abrupt response changes caused by reordered events.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Order Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-path discontinuity caused by a parameter-dependent reversal of competing event times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two pending event times \(\tau_1(\theta)\) and \(\tau_2(\theta)\) depend continuously on a scalar parameter \(\theta\), and suppose \(\tau_1(\theta_0)=\tau_2(\theta_0)\) while their order reverses across \(\theta_0\). If processing the first event changes the feasibility, state transition, or scheduled time of the second, then the simulated response \(L(\theta;\xi)\) need not be continuous at \(\theta_0\). Thus pathwise finite-difference or infinitesimal-perturbation estimates that assume a locally unchanged event sequence can fail at, or across, the event-order boundary \(\tau_1(\theta)=\tau_2(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When parameter changes reverse two interacting events, the simulated state trajectory and response may jump, invalidating derivatives that assume a fixed local event order.
assumptions_latex: The ordering of the two events differs on opposite sides of \(\theta_0\).
The first processed event affects the transition associated with the other.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Continuity or pathwise differentiability of \(L(\theta;\xi)\) at \(\theta_0\) is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: scheduled time of competing event r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and cautious 'need not be continuous' conclusion fit the node, but no citation supports the event-order discontinuity mechanism or the stated limitation of pathwise sensitivity estimators. A specific discrete-event sensitivity source is required.

children.title: Rare-Event Congestion Resolution Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure to resolve infrequent but operationally dominant congestion.

children.title: Rare-Congestion Episodes
children.top_down_role: Infrequent congestion events with large operational impact.

knowledge_statements.title: Rare-Congestion Episodes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-replication resolution boundary for a rare congestion event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the indicator of a congestion episode in one independent replication be Bernoulli with probability \(p\in(0,1)\), and let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). For an integer \(N\geq1\), the episode count \(K\) over \(N\) independent replications satisfies \(K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(N,p)\), and
\[\Pr(K=0)=(1-p)^N.\]
Consequently, the probability of observing at least one episode is at least \(1-\alpha\) if and only if
\[N\geq\frac{\log\alpha}{\log(1-p)},\]
equivalently, if and only if \(N\geq\left\lceil\log(\alpha)/\log(1-p)\right\rceil\). When \(Np\ll1\), \(\Pr(K=0)\approx e^{-Np}\), so ordinary replication is unlikely to resolve congestion behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an event with per-replication probability p, the probability of no observations in N independent replications is (1-p)^N. Detection with probability at least 1-alpha requires N to be at least the ceiling of log(alpha)/log(1-p), and detection is unlikely when Np is small.
assumptions_latex: Each replication has the same congestion-event probability \(p\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(K=0)=(1-p)^N\), and detection probability at least \(1-\alpha\) holds exactly when \(N\geq\left\lceil\log(\alpha)/\log(1-p)\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Probability of a congestion episode in one replication.
Maximum probability of observing no congestion episode.

children.title: Tail-Probability Underresolution
children.top_down_role: Insufficient simulation evidence for low-probability adverse events.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Probability Underresolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-precision boundary for crude Monte Carlo estimation of a rare tail probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I_1,\ldots,I_N\) be independent Bernoulli indicators with \(\Pr(I_i=1)=p\in(0,1)\), where \(N\in\{1,2,\ldots\}\), and define \(\widehat p_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N I_i\). Then
\[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_N)=\frac{p(1-p)}{N},\qquad \frac{\sqrt{\mathbb E[(\widehat p_N-p)^2]}}{p}=\sqrt{\frac{1-p}{Np}}.\]
For any target \(\varepsilon>0\), relative root-mean-square error at most \(\varepsilon\) holds if and only if
\[N\geq\frac{1-p}{p\varepsilon^2}.\]
Thus crude Monte Carlo underresolves the tail when \(Np\) is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Bernoulli tail event of probability p, crude Monte Carlo has relative root-mean-square error sqrt((1-p)/(Np)). Achieving a target epsilon therefore requires N at least (1-p)/(p epsilon squared).
assumptions_latex: \(I_1,\ldots,I_N\) are independent and identically distributed Bernoulli variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{RRMSE}(\widehat p_N)=\sqrt{(1-p)/(Np)}\), so the target \(\operatorname{RRMSE}(\widehat p_N)\leq\varepsilon\) holds exactly when \(N\geq(1-p)/(p\varepsilon^2)\).

notation.meaning: Indicator of the tail event in replication i.
Crude Monte Carlo estimator of the tail probability.

children.title: Extreme-Delay Underestimation
children.top_down_role: Downward distortion of severe waiting-time or delay behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Delay Underestimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point delay distribution exposing missed-tail bias in finite simulation runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(p\in(0,1)\) and \(M>0\), and let a simulated delay satisfy \(D=M\) with probability \(p\) and \(D=0\) otherwise. Although \(\mathbb E[D]=pM\), the sample mean \(\overline D_N\) from \(N\) independent replications equals zero whenever every replication misses the extreme delay. Hence
\[\Pr(\overline D_N=0)=(1-p)^N.\]
On this event, the estimated mean underestimates the true mean by \(pM\). For fixed \(N\), choosing small \(p\) and large \(M\) with \(pM\) fixed makes this failure highly probable while preserving a nonzero mean contribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rare but large delay can contribute materially to the true mean while every finite-run observation remains zero with high probability.
assumptions_latex: \(D_1,\ldots,D_N\) are independent copies of the stated two-point delay.
The estimator is the ordinary sample mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\overline D_N=0)=(1-p)^N\) despite \(\mathbb E[D]=pM>0\).

children.title: Queueing Stability Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Long transients, extreme run lengths, and unreliable steady-state estimates.

children.title: Unstable Queueing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Queueing systems whose workloads fail to remain operationally contained.

knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Queueing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability boundary for a continuous-time single-server Markovian queue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an \(M/M/1\) queue with Poisson arrival rate \(\lambda>0\), exponential service rate \(\mu>0\), and traffic intensity \(\rho=\lambda/\mu\). A stationary probability distribution exists exactly when \(\rho<1\). If \(\rho=1\), the queue-length chain is null recurrent; if \(\rho>1\), it is transient and \(Q(t)/t\to\lambda-\mu\) almost surely. Thus steady-state simulation estimators are not well-defined for \(\rho\geq1\), and increasing warm-up or run length cannot create a stationary regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M/M/1 queue has no stationary probability distribution when arrivals meet or exceed service capacity, invalidating steady-state simulation.
assumptions_latex: Arrivals form a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\).
Service times are independent exponential variables of rate \(\mu\).
The service discipline is non-idling and work conserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stationary distribution exists if and only if \(\rho<1\); no steady-state queue-length target exists for \(\rho\geq1\).

notation.meaning: Number of customers in the system at time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The M/M/1 stability classification and fluid-rate assertion are nontrivial claims requiring an authoritative queueing source with a specific locator.

children.title: Near-Critical Queueing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Queueing systems operating close to their stability boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Critical Queueing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary congestion blow-up as an M/M/1 queue approaches its stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a stationary \(M/M/1\) queue with traffic intensity \(0<\rho<1\), the queue length has distribution
\[\Pr(Q=k)=(1-\rho)\rho^k,\qquad k\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.\]
Consequently,
\[\mathbb E[Q]=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Q)=\frac{\rho}{(1-\rho)^2}.\]
Both moments diverge as \(\rho\uparrow1\). Therefore, even within the stable region, near-critical designs exhibit growing congestion and variability, making fixed-horizon steady-state comparisons increasingly difficult to resolve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queue length and its variance diverge as utilization approaches one from below, producing difficult but formally stable simulation regimes.
assumptions_latex: The queue is an \(M/M/1\) system in stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Q]=\rho/(1-\rho)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Q)=\rho/(1-\rho)^2\), both diverging as \(\rho\uparrow1\).

notation.meaning: Stationary number of customers in the system.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stationary geometric distribution and moment formulas are standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Long-Transient Contamination
children.top_down_role: Bias or variability caused by exceptionally persistent initialization effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Long-Transient Contamination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon bias caused by an initially large queue that cannot drain rapidly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider an \(M/M/1\) queue initialized at \(Q(0)=q_0\), and let \(D(t)\) count potential service completions by time \(t\). Pathwise, arrivals cannot reduce the queue and
\[Q(t)\geq q_0-D(t).\]
Since \(\mathbb E[D(t)]=\mu t\), the finite-horizon time average satisfies
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\frac1T\int_0^T Q(t)\,dt\right]\geq q_0-\frac{\mu T}{2}.\]
Thus, whenever \(q_0-\mu T/2\) substantially exceeds the stationary mean \(\rho/(1-\rho)\), the run remains contaminated by initialization; replication alone does not remove this finite-horizon bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A queue initialized far above stationarity retains a quantifiable finite-horizon bias when the run is too short to drain its initial backlog.
assumptions_latex: The queue has exponential service rate \(\mu\) and starts with \(q_0\) customers.
Potential service completions are counted by a rate-\(\mu\) Poisson process.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[T^{-1}\int_0^T Q(t)\,dt]\geq q_0-\mu T/2\), giving an explicit long-transient contamination boundary.

notation.meaning: Potential service-completion count by time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pathwise and integrated transient bounds are plausible, but the record supplies no source for the potential-completion coupling or the stated contamination boundary.

children.title: Event-Calendar Scalability
children.top_down_role: Computational bottlenecks from large event populations or synchronization.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Calendar Scalability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time and memory cost of a comparison-based future-event calendar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a discrete-event simulation processes \(N\) events while maintaining at most \(M\) pending events in a binary-heap calendar. Each insertion or deletion of the earliest event costs \(O(\log M)\) comparisons, and accessing the earliest event costs \(O(1)\). Hence sequential processing costs \(O(N\log M)\) time and \(O(M)\) memory. If each processed event schedules at most \(b\) new events for a constant \(b\), these bounds remain unchanged up to constants. Large pending-event populations therefore create a logarithmic per-event calendar bottleneck and linear storage demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary-heap event calendar processes N events in O(N log M) time and stores O(M) pending events.
assumptions_latex: The event calendar is implemented as a binary min-heap.
At most \(M\) events are pending at once.
Each processed event schedules at most a constant number of new events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The calendar requires \(O(N\log M)\) processing time and \(O(M)\) memory.

notation.meaning: Maximum number of simultaneously pending events.
Maximum number of events scheduled by one processed event.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary-heap time and memory bounds are standard and the complexity-bound kind fits the container, but the record has no cited source.

children.title: Confidence-Interval Stopping
children.top_down_role: Termination based on uncertainty around performance comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence-Interval Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential termination using simultaneous, optional-stopping-valid confidence bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite set, let \(\widehat x\in X\) be the incumbent, and define \(\Delta_x=f(\widehat x)-f(x)\). Initialize \(n=0\). At each stage, obtain additional paired simulation outputs, increment \(n\), and construct simultaneous upper confidence-sequence bounds \(U_{x,n}\) satisfying
\[\Pr\!\left(\forall n\geq1,\ \forall x\in X:\Delta_x\leq U_{x,n}\right)\geq1-\alpha.\]
Stop at \(\tau=\inf\{n:\max_{x\in X}U_{x,n}\leq\varepsilon\}\) and return \(\widehat x\). On the simultaneous-coverage event, stopping certifies \(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when optional-stopping-valid simultaneous upper bounds show that no competitor can improve the incumbent by more than the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and the objective is minimized.
The bounds are simultaneous over alternatives and all inspected stages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At the stopping time \(\tau\), the returned incumbent is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Upper confidence-sequence bound for the incumbent-versus-alternative difference.

children.title: Fixed-Candidate Gap Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation of a prespecified recommendation.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Candidate Gap Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent simultaneous gap certificate for a recommendation fixed before validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a nonempty finite set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be an objective to be minimized, let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and let \(\bar x\in X\) be fixed independently of the validation data. For each \(x\in X\), set \(\Delta_x=f(\bar x)-f(x)\). Suppose validation produces simultaneous upper bounds \(U_x\) satisfying
\[\Pr\!\left(\forall x\in X:\Delta_x\leq U_x\right)\geq1-\alpha.\]
Define \(G^+=\max\{0,\max_{x\in X}U_x\}\). Since
\[f(\bar x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)=\max_{x\in X}\Delta_x,\]
the pair \((\bar x,G^+)\) certifies with confidence at least \(1-\alpha\) that the fixed recommendation has optimality gap at most \(G^+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a prespecified candidate in a finite minimization problem, simultaneous upper confidence bounds on all candidate-versus-alternative differences yield an upper confidence bound on the candidate's optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty finite set and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is minimized.
The candidate \(\bar x\in X\) is fixed independently of validation observations.
The bounds \(U_x\) have joint coverage at least \(1-\alpha\), where \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(f(\bar x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\leq G^+)\geq1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Upper confidence bound for the candidate-versus-alternative difference.
Certified upper bound on the candidate's optimality gap.
Objective function to be minimized over X.

children.title: Adaptive-Candidate Gap Validation

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Candidate Gap Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-split gap certificate for a candidate selected adaptively from training simulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let training data select a random candidate \(\widehat x\in X\), where \(X\) is finite. Generate independent validation data and, conditional on the training data, construct simultaneous bounds \(U_x\) satisfying
\[\Pr\!\left(\forall x\in X:\ f(\widehat x)-f(x)\leq U_x\mid\text{training data}\right)\geq1-\alpha.\]
Then \(G^+=\max\{0,\max_{x\in X}U_x\}\) obeys
\[\Pr\!\left(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\leq G^+\right)\geq1-\alpha.\]
Independence of validation from selection is the condition that converts fixed-candidate conditional coverage into a valid unconditional adaptive-candidate certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent post-selection validation preserves optimality-gap coverage for an adaptively generated candidate; ordinary bounds from reused selection data need not do so.
assumptions_latex: The candidate is measurable with respect to the training data.
Validation data are independent of training data.
Conditional simultaneous coverage is at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sample-split bound \(G^+\) covers the adaptive candidate's optimality gap with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Conditional validation upper bound against alternative x.

children.title: Variational Optimality Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Variational Optimality Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order variational gap certificate for differentiable convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(f\) be a real-valued convex function on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\) that is differentiable there. For \(x\in X\), define
\[g(x)=\max_{y\in X}\langle\nabla f(x),x-y\rangle.\]
Then
\[0\leq f(x)-\min_{y\in X}f(y)\leq g(x).\]
Moreover, \(g(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) minimizes \(f\) over \(X\). Thus \(g(x)\leq\varepsilon\), for \(\varepsilon\geq0\), certifies that \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For differentiable convex minimization over a compact convex set, the maximum first-order linearization improvement upper-bounds the true optimality gap and vanishes exactly at minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(f\) is real-valued, convex, and differentiable on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq f(x)-\min_{y\in X}f(y)\leq g(x)\), and \(g(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\) minimizes \(f\) over \(X\).

notation.meaning: Gradient of the convex objective at x.

children.title: Sampling-Based Confidence Bounds
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty bounds derived from simulation sampling.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Based Confidence Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Student confidence bound for a simulation-estimated optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N\) be independent normal simulation outputs with unknown mean \(g\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0\), where a candidate's deterministic optimality gap \(G\) satisfies \(G\leq g\). Let \(N\geq2\) be an integer and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). If \(\overline Y_N\) and \(S_N\) are the sample mean and sample standard deviation, then
\[U_{1-\alpha}=\overline Y_N+t_{N-1,1-\alpha}\frac{S_N}{\sqrt N}\]
satisfies \(\Pr(g\leq U_{1-\alpha})=1-\alpha\). Consequently,
\[\Pr(G\leq U_{1-\alpha})\geq1-\alpha,\]
so \(U_{1-\alpha}\) is a valid upper confidence certificate for the candidate's optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent normal simulation outputs, the exact one-sided Student upper confidence bound for their unknown mean also covers any deterministic optimality gap bounded above by that mean.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N\) are independent normal variables with common mean \(g\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0\).
The deterministic optimality gap satisfies \(G\leq g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(G\leq U_{1-\alpha})\geq1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Sample standard deviation of the simulation outputs.
One-minus-alpha quantile of Student's t distribution with N−1 degrees of freedom.

children.title: Hybrid Bound Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate combining a deterministic lower bound with a statistical upper bound for a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the optimal value be \(f^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\), and let \(\widehat x\in X\) be the recommended solution. Suppose \(L\le f^*\) is a deterministic valid lower bound and the simulation-derived random variable \(U\) satisfies \(\mathbb P\{f(\widehat x)\le U\}\ge 1-\alpha\). Then \([L,U]\) is a hybrid bound certificate: with probability at least \(1-\alpha\), \[L\le f^*\le f(\widehat x)\le U,\qquad 0\le f(\widehat x)-f^*\le U-L.\] Thus the certificate verifies an optimality gap of at most \(\varepsilon\) whenever the observed width satisfies \(U-L\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic lower bound and a valid statistical upper bound jointly certify that the recommended solution’s optimality gap does not exceed their difference.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) has simultaneous coverage for the selected recommendation at level \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{0\le f(\widehat x)-f^*\le U-L\}\ge 1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: deterministic lower bound on the optimal value
statistical upper confidence bound on the recommendation's value

children.title: Out-of-Sample Simulation Validation

knowledge_statements.title: Out-of-Sample Simulation Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent fixed-recommendation validation using simulation randomness excluded from optimization and selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a recommendation \(\widehat x\), generate validation outputs \(Y_1(\widehat x),\ldots,Y_m(\widehat x)\) using random streams independent of all optimization data. Compute \(\overline Y_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mY_i(\widehat x)\) and \(S_m^2=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(Y_i(\widehat x)-\overline Y_m)^2\). Under independent normal outputs, or an applicable asymptotic approximation, report \[\overline Y_m\mathbin{\pm}t_{m-1,1-\alpha/2}\frac{S_m}{\sqrt m}.\] Accept the stated validation tolerance \(h>0\) only if the confidence interval lies inside the prespecified acceptable performance region and its half-width is at most \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Re-simulate the frozen recommendation with independent randomness, report a confidence interval, and accept it only under prespecified performance and precision criteria.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge2\) validation replications are independent of the optimization and selection data.
\(Y_i(\widehat x)\) are independent with finite, positive variance.
The acceptance region, \(\alpha\), and \(h\) are fixed before examining validation outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an independent performance estimate and confidence interval for the fixed recommendation \(\widehat x\).

children.title: Simulation-Optimization Complexity

children.title: Simulation-Call Complexity
children.top_down_role: Simulator evaluations required for target decision quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulation-Call Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-call complexity for producing a probably approximately optimal simulation-optimization decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization problem with nonempty decision set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and optimal value \(f^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)>-\infty\). For an algorithm \(A\), accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), and failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), define its simulation-call complexity by \[N_{\mathrm{call}}(A,\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\left\{n\in\mathbb N: A\text{ using at most }n\text{ simulator calls returns }\widehat x^{(n)}\in X\text{ with }\mathbb P\!\left(f(\widehat x^{(n)})-f^*\le\varepsilon\right)\ge1-\delta\right\}.\] A bound \(N_{\mathrm{call}}(A,\varepsilon,delta)=O(g(\varepsilon,\delta,d))\) means that, for the specified problem class and oracle model, a constant independent of \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\), and \(d\) bounds the required number of calls by that multiple of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation-call complexity is the minimum simulator-call budget sufficient for the algorithm to return an epsilon-optimal decision with probability at least one minus delta under a specified problem class and oracle model.
assumptions_latex: Each invocation of the specified simulator counts as one call, regardless of its internal runtime.
The algorithm returns a measurable recommendation, and the problem class and stochastic-oracle information supplied per call are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{call}}(A,\varepsilon,\delta)\) measures the simulator-call budget required for \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Sample Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observation complexity for a prescribed estimation or correct-identification guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) denote scalar observations extracted from simulator calls, and let \(E_n\) be the required statistical success event, such as estimation error at most \(\varepsilon\) or correct selection. The statistical sample complexity is \[N_{\mathrm{stat}}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\left\{n\in\mathbb N:\mathbb P(E_n)\ge1-\delta\right\}.\] In the basic mean-estimation model with independent \(\sigma^2\)-sub-Gaussian observations, the sample mean satisfies the sufficient bound \[n\ge \frac{2\sigma^2}{\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{2}{\delta},\] which ensures \(\mathbb P\{\lvert\overline Z_n-\mathbb EZ_1\rvert\le\varepsilon\}\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample complexity counts observations needed for a specified reliability event; sub-Gaussian mean estimation requires order sigma-squared epsilon-to-minus-two log one-over-delta samples.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{stat}}(\varepsilon,\delta)\le\left\lceil2\sigma^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2/\delta)\right\rceil\) for sub-Gaussian mean estimation.
review_flags: Supplied locators do not specifically support the stated concentration bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sub-Gaussian bound is standard and correctly scoped, but the record supplies no source for either the sample-complexity definition or the stated constant.

children.title: Execution-Time Complexity Family

children.title: Wall-Clock Cost
children.top_down_role: Elapsed-time cost of simulation-optimization execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Wall-Clock Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elapsed-time accounting for simulation, coordination, and finalization in a concurrent run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run beginning at time \(s_0\) and returning its final recommendation at time \(F\), define wall-clock cost as \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=F-s_0\). If simulation jobs \(j=1,\ldots,n\) start at \(s_j\), have realized runtimes \(R_j\), and all completed jobs are required before finalization of duration \(H\), then \[T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\max_{1\le j\le n}(s_j+R_j)-s_0+H.\] This cost includes queuing, synchronization, communication, and idle delays through the realized start and finish times; it is generally not equal to either the number of simulator calls or the sum of their runtimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wall-clock cost is elapsed time from launch to recommendation, including simulation, queuing, communication, synchronization, idle time, and finalization.
assumptions_latex: All required jobs have finite start and completion times.
\(H\ge0\) measures finalization after the last required completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\max_j(s_j+R_j)-s_0+H\).

notation.meaning: realized runtime of simulation job j

children.title: Simulation Runtime Variability
children.top_down_role: Effects of heterogeneous or stochastic replication durations.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulation Runtime Variability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime is modeled as a random computational output distinct from the simulated performance response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x,\xi)\ge0\) be the runtime of one simulation at decision \(x\) under random input \(\xi\). Runtime variability is characterized by its conditional distribution \(F_{R\mid x}\), not solely by \(r(x)=\mathbb E[R(x,\xi)]\). For independent concurrent jobs with runtimes \(R_1,\ldots,R_p\), \[\mathbb E\!\left[\max_{1\le j\le p}R_j\right]\ge\max_{1\le j\le p}\mathbb E[R_j].\] Hence replacing random runtimes by their means can underestimate synchronization time. Quantiles or tail probabilities such as \(\mathbb P\{R(x,\xi)>t\}\) are required when deadline or straggler risk is relevant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random simulation runtimes create stragglers; mean runtime alone can understate synchronization delay, so runtime tails or quantiles may be necessary.
assumptions_latex: Concurrent completion requires all listed jobs to finish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\max_jR_j]\ge\max_j\mathbb E[R_j]\), so mean-runtime substitution can understate expected batch completion time.

notation.meaning: runtime at decision x under simulator randomness

review_flags: Supplied locators do not specifically address stochastic runtime distributions.

children.title: Parallel Makespan Effects
children.top_down_role: Completion-time behavior under concurrent simulation workloads.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Makespan Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic list-scheduling bound exposing workload, worker-count, and longest-job effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(n\in\mathbb N\) nonpreemptive simulation jobs, all available at time zero, with realized processing times \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\ge0\). Schedule them by greedy list scheduling on \(p\in\mathbb N\) identical workers. Let \(W=\sum_{j=1}^n r_j\), \(r_{\max}=\max_{1\le j\le n}r_j\), and let \(C_{\max}\) be the completion time of the last job. Then \[\max\left\{\frac{W}{p},r_{\max}\right\}\le C_{\max}\le\frac{W}{p}+\left(1-\frac1p\right)r_{\max}.\] Thus parallel speedup is limited by both average workload per worker and the longest realized simulation job.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For jobs all available initially, greedy scheduling finishes no earlier than the larger of average workload and the longest job, and no later than the stated workload-plus-longest-job bound.
assumptions_latex: All \(n\) jobs are available at time zero.
Workers are identical and execute at most one nonpreemptive job at a time.
Communication and scheduling overhead are excluded from \(r_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{W/p,r_{\max}\}\le C_{\max}\le W/p+(1-1/p)r_{\max}\).

children.title: Problem-Scale Complexity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Scaling with decision dimension, alternative count, or simulated system size.

children.title: Decision-Dimension Scaling
children.top_down_role: Computational or statistical dependence on continuous or mixed decision dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dimension Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity scaling obtained by varying decision-space dimension while holding other problem parameters explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_d\) be a family of simulation-optimization problems whose decisions lie in subsets \(X_d\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). For a fixed algorithm \(A\), accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and stated regularity parameters \(\theta\), define decision-dimension scaling by the function \[C_d(A;\varepsilon,\delta,\theta)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_d}C(A,P;\varepsilon,\delta),\] where \(C\) is a declared resource such as simulator calls, observations, or elapsed time. A polynomial, exponential, or dimension-free scaling claim refers to the asymptotic growth of \(C_d\) as \(d\to\infty\), with \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\), and \(\theta\) controlled as stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision-dimension scaling tracks worst-case resource growth as the number of decision coordinates increases, with accuracy and regularity parameters explicitly controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(X_d\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) defines the decision dimension consistently across the problem family.
The resource \(C\), success criterion, and controlled parameters \(\theta\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic behavior of \(C_d\) as \(d\to\infty\) is the decision-dimension scaling.

notation.meaning: worst-case resource complexity at dimension d

children.title: Alternative-Count Scaling
children.top_down_role: Dependence on the number of discrete candidate solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative-Count Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity scaling for finite decision sets as the number of alternatives grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_K=\{x_1,\ldots,x_K\}\) be a finite set of simulated alternatives, and let \(\mathcal P_K\) be a specified class of corresponding selection problems. For algorithm \(A\), define \[C_K(A;\varepsilon,\delta,\theta)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_K}C(A,P;\varepsilon,\delta),\] where success means returning \(\widehat x\in X_K\) with \(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in X_K}f(x)\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Alternative-count scaling is the asymptotic growth of \(C_K\) as \(K\to\infty\), with the gap structure, noise parameters, accuracy, and confidence convention recorded in \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternative-count scaling measures resource growth as a finite choice set expands under a fixed approximate-selection guarantee and declared noise or gap conditions.
assumptions_latex: The resource \(C\) and success criterion are fixed across \(K\).
Noise and indifference-zone or gap assumptions are included in \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The growth of \(C_K\) as \(K\to\infty\) is the alternative-count scaling.

notation.meaning: worst-case resource complexity for K alternatives

children.title: Simulated-System-Size Scaling
children.top_down_role: Dependence on the scale of the modeled operational system.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulated-System-Size Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity scaling with the size of the simulated model underlying each objective evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\in\mathbb N\) index simulated-system size, such as the number of agents, network nodes, state variables, or events processed per replication, and let \(\mathcal P_s\) be a specified problem family. For algorithm \(A\), define \[C_s(A;\varepsilon,\delta,\theta)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_s}C(A,P;\varepsilon,\delta).\] Simulated-system-size scaling is the asymptotic growth of \(C_s\) as \(s\to\infty\). The resource \(C\) must be stated: call complexity may remain unchanged while per-call runtime, memory, and consequently wall-clock complexity increase with \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulated-system-size scaling tracks resource growth as the model simulated per evaluation becomes larger, distinguishing call counts from per-call time and memory.
assumptions_latex: The size index \(s\) has one consistent interpretation across \(\mathcal P_s\).
Accuracy, confidence, and controlled structural parameters \(\theta\) are stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The growth of \(C_s\) as \(s\to\infty\) is the simulated-system-size scaling.

notation.meaning: problem family at system size s
worst-case resource complexity at system size s

children.title: Concurrent Simulation-Optimization Architecture
children.top_down_role: Computational organizations for concurrent simulation and asynchronous search.

children.title: Parallel Replication
children.top_down_role: Concurrent simulation runs at a common decision.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Replication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent independent replications at one fixed decision, followed by statistically valid aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a decision \(x\), replication count \(m\), and \(p\) workers, assign replication indices \(1,\ldots,m\) to workers. Generate each output as \(Y_i(x)=G(x,\xi_i)\) using mutually independent random streams \(\xi_i\). Workers return indexed outputs asynchronously or in batches; after all required indices arrive, compute \[\widehat f_m(x)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^mY_i(x),\qquad \widehat v_m(x)=\frac1{m-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(Y_i(x)-\widehat f_m(x)\bigr)^2.\] Stop when the prescribed replication count or a valid sequential precision rule is met, and output the estimate with its uncertainty summary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distribute independent replications of one decision across workers, then aggregate indexed outputs into a performance estimate and uncertainty measure.
assumptions_latex: Random streams \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\) are mutually independent and correctly indexed.
Aggregation waits for every replication required by the stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(\widehat f_m(x)\) and \(\widehat v_m(x)\) from \(m\) independent replications.

children.title: Parallel Candidate Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Concurrent simulation of multiple alternatives or search points.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Candidate Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent evaluation of distinct search points with explicit allocation and aggregation rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given candidates \(x_1,\ldots,x_K\), a total replication budget \(B\in\mathbb N\), and \(p\in\mathbb N\) workers, choose allocations \(m_1,\ldots,m_K\in\mathbb N_0\) satisfying \(\sum_{k=1}^K m_k\le B\). Dispatch tasks \((k,i)\) that generate \(Y_{k,i}=G(x_k,\xi_{k,i})\), using independent streams unless a declared common-random-number design is employed. For every candidate with \(m_k>0\), compute \(\widehat f_k=m_k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m_k}Y_{k,i}\). After the prescribed tasks complete, update the allocation or search state; stop at the budget or a declared statistically valid rule and return the candidate selected by the stated comparison criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate an integer number of simulation replications among several candidates, evaluate them concurrently, aggregate results by candidate, and select or reallocate using a prespecified rule.
assumptions_latex: Every result carries its candidate and replication indices.
Dependence induced by variance-reduction designs is retained in statistical comparisons.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a candidate chosen from concurrently estimated performances under replication budget \(B\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative integer number of replications allocated to candidate k

children.title: Asynchronous Stochastic Approximation
children.top_down_role: Recursive updates using delayed or partially available information.

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous Stochastic Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected coordinate stochastic approximation with bounded information delays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, and initialize \(x_0\in X\). At accepted completion event \(k\), worker \(i_k\) returns \(G_k\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a stochastic gradient estimate computed at \(x_{k-\tau_k}\), and \(D_k\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is a diagonal coordinate-selection matrix. Set \[x_{k+1}=\Pi_X\!\left(x_k-a_kD_kG_k\right).\] Advance the logical counter on accepted completions, rather than synchronized worker rounds. Stop at a prescribed event budget or stopping test and return the latest iterate or a specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each accepted worker completion, the method applies a projected stochastic-gradient update using the delayed iterate and the worker's selected coordinates; the logical counter advances by completions rather than synchronized rounds.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
Relative to a filtration \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\), \(\mathbb{E}[G_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-\tau_k}]=\nabla f(x_{k-\tau_k})\), and the conditional second moments of \(G_k\) are bounded.
\(0\leq\tau_k\leq B\), every coordinate is selected infinitely often, \(a_k>0\), \(\sum_k a_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_k a_k^2<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_X(x_k-a_kD_kG_k)\) defines the asynchronous recursive update.

notation.meaning: age of the iterate used by the completed estimate
Euclidean projection onto the feasible set
information filtration for the stochastic updates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-sure convergence of asynchronous stochastic approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for convergence of the asynchronous recursion to the globally stable equilibrium of its limiting ODE.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the asynchronous stochastic-approximation recursion with drift $F:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}^N$, iterates $X^k$, coordinate step sizes $\alpha^k(l)$, noise $w^k(l)$, and updated coordinate $\Theta^k$. If $F$ is Lipschitz; the noise is conditionally mean zero with $\mathbb{E}[(w^k(l))^2\mid\mathcal F^k]\le z_1+z_2\|X^k\|^2$; $\sum_k\alpha^k(l)=\infty$ and $\sum_k\alpha^k(l)^2<\infty$ for every $l$; $\dot x=F(x)$ has a unique globally asymptotically stable equilibrium $x_*$; $\{X^k\}$ is almost surely bounded; the step sizes satisfy the stated ideal-tapering-size conditions; and coordinate updates satisfy the stated evenly-distributed-updating conditions, then $X^k\to x_*$ almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asynchronous stochastic-approximation sequence converges almost surely to the unique globally asymptotically stable equilibrium of its limiting ODE when the drift is Lipschitz, the noise is a martingale difference with a quadratic growth bound, every coordinate has nonsummable square-summable step sizes, the iterates are almost surely bounded, and the ideal-tapering and evenly-distributed-update conditions hold.
assumptions_latex: \dot x=F(x)\text{ has a unique globally asymptotically stable equilibrium }x_*.

V^k(l)=\sum_{m=1}^k I\{l=\Theta^m\},\qquad \exists\chi>0:\ \liminf_{k\to\infty}\frac{V^k(l)}k\ge\chi\ \text{a.s. for every }l,\text{ together with existence of the stated pairwise EDU accumulated-step ratios over }K^k(z,l).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X^k\xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{\mathrm{a.s.}}x_*.
